exp.17:16:
Here Moses recalls that God answered him: "They have well spoken that which they have spoken." This refers to what the people asked for at Horeb (Mount Sinai): that they not hear the voice of God directly again, because the fire and the greatness of it filled them with fear. God approved that request and decided to speak to them through a prophet.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that God accepted their reverent fear and that he would send them prophets, from among their own brothers, to bring them his word. Many Christians see in this promise an announcement of Christ (as Acts 3:22 does), although it also applies to the prophets who would come afterward.

For today: God understands our fear and our need for him to speak to us with closeness. Listen to his Word with respect and seriousness, and remember that in Jesus God spoke to us clearly and accessibly.
exp.5:12:
This verse says the people must have the Lord as their only God: they are to revere him, serve him, and, when they make a vow, make it in his name. The word "fear" means a deep respect, not a dread that drives people away. "Serve" means living for him in obedience. "Swear by his name" means making a promise before him, in truth, and not before other gods.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them that when they have houses, vineyards, and plenty of food that they did not work for, they must not forget the one who brought them out of Egypt. Comfort can make people forget God and turn to other gods.

For today: when things are going well, pause and thank God for what you have. Let your well-being not draw you away from him, and let your words and promises be honest, as one who knows they stand before him.
exp.31:3:
This verse says that God is the Rock: firm, secure, and unchanging. His work is perfect, that is, complete and without flaw. All his ways are judgment, that is, justice. He is a God in whom one can trust, and there is no wickedness in him; he is just and right.

Moses speaks, near the end of his life, in a song addressed to Israel. He has just invited the people to magnify God. The song then contrasts God's faithfulness with the people's corruption, since they turned away. The fault is not God's but theirs.

For today: when something in your life does not make sense or hurts, you do not have to accuse God of injustice. You can speak to him honestly and rest in the fact that his character is steady and good, even when you do not yet understand everything.
exp.25:3:
This verse describes what the priest did when the Israelite arrived with his first fruits. The priest would take the basket, which is a small basket, and set it down in front of God's altar. The verse quotes an old form of the verb, but in the English verse the same action is expressed as "set it down," so the sentence about the old wording is omitted. In this way, what the people brought passed from their hands to the place where God was worshiped.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He explains how to give thanks to God once they are living there and eating from their harvests. The first fruits were the first things the land produced. Giving them was a way of acknowledging that the land and the harvest came from God, not only from one's own effort.

For today: before you spend what you receive, whether money, time, or talents, give God the first of it with gratitude. Do it as an act of recognition and not out of obligation, remembering that everything good comes from Him.
exp.27:35:
It says that if the people are disobedient, God will allow them to be taken, along with their king, to a nation unknown to them and their ancestors. There they will have to serve false gods made of wood and stone, that is, idols.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings for keeping the covenant and curses for abandoning it. This warning describes the consequences of turning away from the living God. Many understand it to relate to the later exiles of Israel and Judah, though the text itself gives no dates.

For today: whatever we put in place of God, such as money, success, or approval, ends up enslaving us. Today you can ask yourself what holds first place in your heart, and return to trusting God with simplicity.
exp.2:11:
This verse says that Moses gave out the land that Israel won east of the Jordan River. From Aroer, beside the Arnon stream, and half of the hill country of Gilead, with its cities, he gave it to the tribes of Reuben and Gad.

The word "possessed" means that they took possession of that land.

Moses speaks to the people in Moab, near the end of his life, and reminds them of what God did. After defeating powerful kings like Og, the land was divided. Later, the other half of Gilead and Bashan passed to the half-tribe of Manasseh.

For today: God keeps his promises, and it is good to remember with gratitude what he has already given us. When we recognize his past blessings, we trust him more for what is to come.
exp.10:28:
This verse says that when God brings Israel into the promised land, the people are to declare the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal. The word "brought" here means to lead someone into a place, and "put" in the verse means to proclaim or set those words in a visible way.

Moses speaks to the people before they cross the Jordan. He reminds them that obeying God brings blessing, and that turning away from Him to follow other gods brings a curse. These two mountains, facing each other, would serve as a sign to remind them of that choice. Later, in Joshua 8:30-35, the account tells us that this command was carried out.

For today: our daily decisions matter. Before we choose, we can ask ourselves, "Does this bring me closer to God or pull me away from Him?" Remembering His words regularly helps us walk faithfully.
exp.13:13:
This verse continues a list of birds that the Israelites were not to eat. Here the raven is named, and the phrase "after his kind" shows that the prohibition covered all birds of that family, not just one. The names of some birds on the list are hard to identify with certainty, but the raven is fairly clear.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the laws God gave them to live as a people set apart for Him. These rules about clean and unclean animals distinguished them from the neighboring nations. Many scholars also see in them reasons of health or symbolism, although the text emphasizes above all holiness.

For today: God cares for every area of our lives, even the everyday. We can ask ourselves what small habits, such as what we eat or do each day, show that we belong to Him and want to obey Him with gratitude.
exp.27:18:
It says the curse will reach the person in everything they do. The phrase "when you come in" and "when you go out" is an old way of speaking about all of daily life: coming and going, beginning and ending, working and resting. Nothing would be left outside. Being "cursed" means that God withdraws his blessing.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: if they obey, blessing will come; if they abandon it, serious consequences will follow. These words are a serious warning addressed to Israel, not a random threat.

For today: God cares for every part of our lives, not only the religious moments. We can ask ourselves whether we are including him in everyday things, such as work, home and decisions. Christians believe that Christ bore the curse for us (Galatians 3:13), so we can return to God with confidence.
exp.27:51:
It says that an enemy will surround all the cities of Israel with his army and keep them under siege. This will continue until the high, fortified walls in which the people trusted come down. The siege would reach all the land that God had given them.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He is explaining the blessings of keeping the covenant and the serious consequences of abandoning it. This warning describes the horror of an invasion. Many see in it a foreshadowing of the later downfalls of Israel and Judah, though the text itself gives no dates.

It is easy to trust in our own "high walls": money, work, health, or security. But none of these can take the place of God. Today we can ask ourselves what we rest our peace of mind on, and return with humility to trusting Him first.
exp.1:33:
This verse says that Israel conquered all of King Sihon's cities and destroyed them completely, leaving no survivors. The word "destroyed" here comes from the idea of giving something over to the ban, that is, setting it apart for judgment. The "spoils" are the goods taken after the victory.

Moses speaks to the people, reminding them of what God did when they entered the promised land. Sihon attacked Israel first, and the victory is presented as the work of the LORD.

This passage is hard, and interpreters understand it in different ways: as God's judgment on peoples of that time, and always within a unique historical moment for Israel, not as a model for today.

Today we can learn to recognize that God is just and sovereign, and to trust that he judges with perfect justice. That frees us from taking revenge on our own and invites us to seek peace with humility.
exp.2:28:
This verse says that the people of Israel camped in the valley opposite Beth-peor. The word it quotes is an old way of saying "we stopped" or "we camped" in the verse above, so it is a simple note of place that marks where they were when the events before it took place.

Moses is speaking to the people near the end of his life, recalling what happened on the journey. Just before this verse he tells how God did not allow him to cross the Jordan, though he did let him see the promised land from Pisgah and charged him to encourage Joshua. Beth-peor appears later in the book as the place where Moses gives his teaching to the people. We do not know exactly where it was, but it lay in the region east of the Jordan.

For today: God also watches over times of waiting and transition. Even when we cannot see the end of the road, we can encourage and support those who come after us, trusting that God continues his work.
exp.29:6:
It says that when God restores his people, the curses that had fallen on Israel because of their disobedience will turn against the enemies who persecuted them. The word "hate" in the verse refers to those who hate. The phrase "in this context" means "command."

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that if they turn back to God after failing, God will gather them, give them a heart willing to love him, and restore them. Some understand this verse as God's justice toward those who oppressed them; others see it as part of the promise of national restoration.

For today: we can trust that God sees injustice and that justice belongs to him. So instead of taking revenge, we hand our pain over to God and return to him with a sincere heart.
exp.4:30:
God tells Moses to stay here beside Him on the mountain. There He will give him all the commandments, statutes, and judgments (that is, the rules and fair decisions) so that Moses may teach them to the people. The purpose is that they carry them out, that is, that they do them, in the land that God gives them as an inheritance.

God speaks this after the people, frightened by the voice of fire at Sinai, asked that Moses listen on their behalf. God approved that request, and He wanted them to have a heart that respected and obeyed Him. Moses recalls this before preparing the people to enter Canaan.

For today: God does not only want us to hear His Word, but to live it. Choose a biblical command today and look for one concrete action to practice it this week.
exp.27:3:
This verse says that God would bless everything that gave life and provision to the people: their children (the fruit of the body), their beasts of burden and work (the animals used to carry loads and to plow), and their cows and sheep, that is, the livestock that gave them food, clothing and labor. The calves are the young ones born to the herd.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: if they listen to his voice and obey him, blessings would come upon their family, their work and their fields. It was a promise to Israel within that covenant, and not an automatic guarantee for every person today.

For today: recognize that family, work and provision are gifts from God. Thank him today for something concrete in your home or your work, and ask him to help you listen to him and live with gratitude.
exp.3:30:
This verse says that the Lord your God is a merciful God, full of compassion. Because of this, he will not abandon his people, will not destroy them completely, and will not forget the covenant, that is, the solemn promise he made to their ancestors (Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob). He swore it, meaning he gave his firm commitment to keep it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them that if they turn away from God and suffer the consequences, they can still return to seek him with all their heart. This sentence gives them hope: God remains faithful even when they fail.

For today: if you feel far from God or have failed, do not stay hidden. Return to him sincerely, trusting in his mercy. His faithfulness does not depend on your perfection, but on his good character and his promises.
exp.7:8:
It says that in the promised land the people will have bread in plenty and will lack nothing. It speaks of a land rich in minerals: its stones contain iron, and from its hills metal can be dug out, probably copper. "Without scarceness" means without poverty or having to ration food.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, before they enter Canaan. He describes the land to them with gratitude and hope. But he soon warns them not to forget God when they live in abundance.

For today: when you have what you need, do not take it as something you earned on your own. Make a habit of thanking God for your food, your work, and your home, and remember to obey him in the good times too, not only when you need help.
exp.1:10:
This verse says that the Emims, the ancient inhabitants of the land of Moab, were regarded as giants, just like the Anakim. The word "accounted" in the verse means "considered" or "thought of as." In their own language, the Moabites called them Emims, a name that some understand to mean "dreadful" or "frightening," although the exact meaning is uncertain.

Moses reminds the people what God told him as they were on their way to Canaan. God forbade them to fight against Moab, because He had given that land to the descendants of Lot. This aside explains that God had already made room for Moab, even though a great and strong people had once lived there.

For today: God cares for other peoples and has a plan for each one. If He can bring down giants to make room for those He has chosen, we can trust that He also guides our path, without envying what He gives to others.
exp.19:3:
This verse says that God himself goes with his people into battle. He does not leave them alone: he will fight for them against their enemies and save them. The archaic wording of the original rendering is not needed here, since your verse reads plainly as "to fight for you" and "to save you."

The one who speaks is the priest, before Israel enters combat. Moses gives these instructions to the people who are preparing to enter the promised land. The priest reminds them that their confidence is not in the size of the army, but in the presence of God, who had already rescued them from Egypt. Afterward, the officers will give other instructions.

For today: when you face a situation that frightens you, do not face it alone. Before acting, pray and remember that God is with you. That does not remove your responsibility to do your part, but it allows you to do it with peace rather than panic.
exp.28:2:
This verse says that Israel saw with their own eyes the great trials, that is, the hardships and judgments with which God acted in Egypt. They also saw the signs and the great wonders, that is, the miracles. The word "trials" here refers to mighty acts that showed who God is.

Moses speaks to the people in Moab, near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them what God did to Pharaoh in order to encourage them to renew their covenant with Him. But the next verse shows something sad: although they had seen everything, they still had not truly understood. Seeing is not the same as comprehending.

For today: it is not enough to remember what God has done in your life; ask Him to give you understanding and a grateful heart, so that what you have experienced leads you to obey Him and trust Him more.
exp.32:18:
They will call the peoples to the mountain, and there they will offer sacrifices of righteousness, that is, offerings made with uprightness. For this reason, Zebulun and Issachar will enjoy the wealth of the sea and the treasures hidden in the sand of the shore. The words "they shall suck" mean that they will be nourished by, or will benefit from, that abundance.

Moses speaks before he dies and blesses each tribe. Here he addresses Zebulun and Issachar, who lived near the coast and along trade routes. It is not known for certain which mountain is meant; some think of Mount Tabor or of a place of worship. Others see an image of nations drawn toward the God of Israel.

For today: material blessing is not an end in itself. We can recognize what we have as a gift from God and respond with honesty, generosity, and an upright life.
exp.13:25:
This verse says that the Israelite, on reaching the place of worship, could use the money from selling his tithe to buy whatever he wanted: cattle, sheep, wine, or strong drink (a fermented beverage, probably made from fruit). Then he would eat there, before God, and rejoice with his family.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. If the sanctuary was very far away, carrying the tithe in the form of produce was difficult, so they could sell it and carry money instead. The celebration was a feast of gratitude, and right after this the text reminds them to care for the Levite, who had no inheritance of his own.

For today: giving to God is not only an obligation; it can also include gratitude and celebration. Set aside time to thank God with your family, sharing a simple meal, and think of someone in need whom you could invite.
exp.6:8:
This verse says that we should recognize and hold as certain that the Lord is the only true God, a faithful God. He keeps his covenant and shows his mercy (his loyal love) to those who love him and keep his commandments. The phrase "to a thousand generations" means for an extremely long time; many understand it as a way of expressing that his faithfulness never runs out.

Moses is speaking to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God did not choose them because they were great, but out of love and because of the promise made to their ancestors. For this reason he calls them to trust in him and to obey him.

For today: when you feel small or insecure, remember that God does not love you for your achievements, but because of his faithfulness. Respond to that love with simple obedience each day, trusting that he keeps what he promises.
exp.22:12:
This verse says that every soldier was to carry, along with his weapons, a small stake or spade. When he went out to relieve himself outside the camp, he was to dig a hole and then cover his waste with earth. "Camp" is the word for the camp, and the waste is what is buried.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. These instructions were for when the army camped in time of war. The reason the text gives is that God walks in the midst of the camp, so the place had to be kept clean and respectful. In addition, this practice helped protect the health of the group, although the text emphasizes the spiritual reason.

For today: God is concerned with everyday life, even with the small and unpleasant things. We can honor him by caring for the order and cleanliness of our home, our work, and our church, and by faithfully doing what no one sees.
exp.5:24:
It says we will be considered righteous when we carefully put into practice all of God's commandments, just as he gave them. Doing so means carrying them out faithfully. Here, being righteous means being in right standing with God and living in the way that pleases him.

Moses is speaking to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God brought them out of Egypt and gave them his laws so that they would live well and with reverence toward him. This obedience grew out of a relationship with the God who had already rescued them. Some understand righteousness here to mean living faithfully within the covenant.

Today we might ask ourselves: what do I know God is asking of me that I have not yet done? Choose one concrete thing this week and obey it with gratitude, not out of fear, but because God has already been faithful to you.
exp.2:20:
Here Moses tells how he gave a command to Joshua. He reminded him that his own eyes had seen what God did to two kings, Og and Sihon, whom Israel defeated. Moses tells him that God will do the same to all the kingdoms through which Joshua will pass.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He already knows he will not cross the Jordan, and Joshua will be the new leader. For that reason he prepares him, recalling past victories to strengthen his trust in God for what lies ahead.

For today: when you face a great challenge, remember how God helped you before. Recalling his faithfulness in the past can give you courage and calm for the future, knowing that he remains the same.
exp.30:13:
God tells Moses that the time of his death is drawing near. He instructs him to call Joshua, his successor, and to present themselves together at the tabernacle of the congregation, the tent where God met with his people. There God would give them their instructions. Moses and Joshua obey and wait together.

The Lord speaks to Moses near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. Israel is about to enter the promised land, and Moses will not go in with them. For this reason God prepares the transfer of leadership. Right away God appears in the cloud and tells Moses that the people, in time, will turn away from him. So Joshua receives his charge knowing the task will be hard.

For today: God makes sure his work continues when leaders change. If you serve in your church or family, prepare and encourage others, and wait on God before taking important steps.
exp.14:18:
It says that every firstborn male that is born from your cattle and your sheep belongs to God and must be set apart for Him. Therefore, that animal must not be used for work, nor may its wool be cut. "Set apart" means dedicating something to God, and cutting wool is shearing it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. Shortly before, he had commanded them to free their Hebrew servants and treat them generously. Now he reminds them that the firstborn of their herds also belongs to God. It then explains that they were to eat it before Him, in the place He would choose, together with their family, and that it had to be an animal without defect.

For today: we can give God the first and the best, not the leftovers. For example, setting apart with gratitude the first part of the day to pray, or a portion of our income to help others, recognizing that everything comes from Him.
exp.8:3:
This verse says that Israel should not think, once the Lord their God has driven those nations out before them, "The Lord brought me in to possess this land because of my righteousness." The phrase "speak not thou in thine heart" means "do not think or tell yourself inwardly." "Wickedness" is evil or rebellion against God. According to the text, God drives out these nations because of their wickedness, not because of Israel's goodness.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. They will see strong enemies, and defeating them could fill them with pride. That is why Moses reminds them that the victory comes from God, from his promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and not from their own merits. He even tells them they are a stubborn people.

For today: when you receive blessings or achievements, give thanks instead of boasting. Everything good comes from God's grace, not from our deserving it.
exp.32:28:
It says Israel is a very happy or blessed people, because no one is like them: the Lord saved them. God himself is their shield, that is, the one who protects and helps them, and also their sword, the one who gives them strength and glory. The word "blessed" means very richly blessed. "Excellency" refers to his greatness. "Tread" means to walk on or trample, and "high places" can mean the strong or elevated places of the enemy, such as their defenses.

Moses speaks just before he dies. He is blessing the tribes of Israel and closes with this song of praise. He wants the people to remember that their victory and their future depend on God, not on their own strength. Some scholars understand the "treading on high places" as a military victory, and others as a picture of complete security.

For today: when you feel weak or threatened, remember that God cares for you and sustains you. Rest in his help, and give thanks for his salvation instead of trusting only in your own strength.
exp.28:9:
It says that the whole people of Israel were gathered that day before God. Moses names the leaders: the chiefs of the tribes, the elders (experienced men who guided the people), the officers (those in charge of carrying out the orders), and all the men. "Before the Lord" means in his presence, as one who gives an account.

Moses speaks near the end of his life, on the plains of Moab. A new generation is about to enter the promised land. He reminds them of what God has done and calls them to renew the covenant, that is, the commitment of faithfulness between God and his people. The verses that follow add the children, the women, and the foreigners.

For today: faith is not only for the leaders. Every person, whatever their place, stands before God and is called to obey him. Today you might ask yourself: what concrete step of obedience can I take?
exp.21:1:
If you find a lost animal and its owner does not live nearby or you do not know who he is, do not leave it abandoned. You should take it to your own house, care for it, and keep it until its owner comes looking for it. Then you give it back. The word "pick up" here means that you take the animal under your care.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them how to live as God's people. Here, "brother" refers to a fellow Israelite and neighbor. The law shows that loving others is lived out in concrete actions, even when no one sees us or forces us to act.

For today: if you find something that is not yours, make a sincere effort to return it. Ask, let people know, or look for the owner. In this way you honor God with your honesty and your care for others.
exp.11:3:
It says that the people of Israel were not to worship the LORD by copying the customs of the neighboring nations. The words "Ye shall not do so" refer to what comes before: altars on high places, green trees, images, and sacred groves.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He orders them to destroy the places of pagan worship, and then tells them to worship God in the place He would choose. He wanted to protect them from mixing true faith with false practices. Scholars debate how this was applied over time, but the central idea is clear.

For today: God deserves to be worshiped as He asks, not as it seems right to us or as fashion dictates. Let us examine whether anything in our faith has been mixed with customs that do not honor God, and return to His Word.
exp.0:8:
Here Moses reminds the people what he told them at Mount Horeb: "I am not able to bear you myself alone." He means that he by himself could not carry the responsibility of guiding, caring for, and settling the problems of a nation so large. The word "I spake unto you" means "I said to you," and "bear you" means carry you, uphold you.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, before Israel enters the promised land. He goes over the history of the journey. Just before this, God had commanded them to advance and take possession of the land. And just after, Moses gives thanks that God had multiplied them like the stars of heaven, as he had promised Abraham. The burden was great precisely because God had kept his promise.

For today: recognize that we do not have to carry everything alone. Asking for help, sharing responsibilities, and working as a team is not weakness, but wisdom.
exp.21:13:
This verse describes a man who, after marrying, stops loving his wife. Then he accuses her of wrongdoing, begins speaking badly of her in public, and says she was not a virgin when they married. The phrase "spread a bad reputation" means spreading rumors that damage her good name. Saying he came in to her means that he had sexual relations with her.

Moses is giving laws to Israel before they enter the promised land. This law seeks to restrain false accusations and to protect the young woman. Parents could present evidence before the elders, at the city gate, where cases were judged. Some of that evidence has been understood in different ways.

For today: let us be careful with our words. Speaking badly of someone to justify ourselves or to harm them is unjust. Let us seek the truth and defend those who are accused without reason.
exp.11:24:
This verse repeats the prohibition against eating blood. "Thou shalt not eat it" refers to the blood of the animals. Moses adds a promise: if the people obey, it will go well with them and with their children, because they do what is right (what is correct) in the sight of God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. In that time, blood was connected with life, and that is why God asked for respect toward it. It was to be poured out on the ground, and the blood of the sacrifices was offered upon the altar. Some think that the aim was also to set Israel apart from the practices of other peoples, although the text mainly underlines the holiness of life.

Today we can learn that obedience to God affects not only us but also our family. Doing what is right, even in small things, leaves a good mark on those who come after us.
exp.0:29:
This verse says that God himself goes ahead of his people and that he will fight for them. He will do it just as he did in Egypt, when everyone saw it with their own eyes.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel almost forty years after the events. He reminds them of the moment when the spies returned afraid, talking about strong cities and giants. Moses wanted them to trust in God, not in their own strength. Yet, as the verses that follow say, they did not believe.

For today: when you face something that seems too big, remember how God has helped you before. That memory can strengthen your trust and help you take the next step, knowing that you are not alone.
exp.15:13:
This verse commands rejoicing during the feasts, and that joy must include the whole household and the whole community. Holy festivals are the sacred feasts; the men and women who served in the house, whether as hired workers or as slaves, are included in the celebration; the towns or cities where people lived are the places where this community gathered. The Levite, the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow were people without land of their own or without anyone to support them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they were slaves in Egypt, and for that reason they must treat the most vulnerable with kindness. Here the text refers to the Feast of Tabernacles, which was celebrated after the harvest as thanksgiving to God for his blessing.

For today: when God blesses you, do not celebrate alone. Think of someone who is alone or in need, such as a neighbor, a migrant, or a widow, and invite them to your table. True gratitude becomes generosity.
exp.9:3:
This verse says that God wrote again on the new stone tablets the Ten Commandments, just as he had on the first ones. The Ten Commandments are also called the ten words. "The day of the assembly" refers to the day when the people were gathered at the foot of Mount Sinai. And at the end, Moses says that the Lord gave them to him.

Here Moses speaks, reminding the people of what happened after they sinned with the golden calf and he broke the first tablets. God, in his mercy, gave them a second chance and renewed his covenant. The tablets were kept in the ark.

For today: God knows how to forgive and to start over with us. If we have failed, we do not have to remain in guilt. We can come to him with humility, and he offers us again his guidance and his friendship.
exp.8:13:
God says to Moses, "Let me alone," that is, "do not stop me." He says he wants to destroy the people and blot out their name from under heaven, meaning from the earth, so that no one will remember them. Then he promises to make Moses into a nation greater and mightier than they are.

Moses is telling the people what happened at Mount Sinai. While he was receiving the tablets of the law, the people made a golden calf. God calls them a stiff-necked people, stubborn. Moses recalls this so that they will not consider themselves good on their own account. Some see in the "let me alone" an invitation for Moses to intercede, and that is what he did.

For today: when you see the wrong of others, pray for them before you condemn them. And remember that God treats us with mercy, not according to what we deserve.
exp.10:25:
It says that God, through Moses, sets two paths before the people: the blessing and the curse. The word "Behold" in the verse, used to draw attention, is what the verse addresses. It is not a hidden threat, but a clear choice placed in full view of everyone.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just reminded them of the victories God will give them. Now he prepares them to live there, showing them that enjoying that land would depend on hearing and following the Lord's commands, as the verses that follow explain.

For today: God invites us to choose, and our daily decisions lead us in one direction. Today you can pick one concrete decision, such as speaking the truth or forgiving, and ask God for help to obey him in that, trusting that his way is good.
exp.21:2:
This verse says that the same rule given for the lost ox and sheep also applies to the donkey, to clothing, and to anything else that your brother loses and you find. The phrase about not being able to pull away means that you cannot pretend you did not see it or look the other way. You must help return it.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel, near the time they will enter the promised land, and explaining how to live as God's people. Here "brother" refers to a fellow Israelite. The law protects the property of one's neighbor and shapes a community where no one ignores another's need. The instructions that follow, about the fallen donkey, belong to the same line of thought.

For today: if you find something that is not yours, such as a wallet, a cell phone, or a set of keys, make a real effort to return it. Loving your neighbor includes caring for what belongs to them, even when no one is watching.
exp.31:41:
God says, in very strong images, that his arrows will be drunk with blood and his sword will devour flesh. The "arrows" here are simply the arrows of war. The verse speaks of the dead and of captives, and the phrase "from the heads" is hard: some understand it as enemy leaders, others in a different way. The word "vengeance" here means just punishment.

God speaks within the Song of Moses, just before Israel entered the promised land. It is poetic language of war. It shows that God defends his people and that he does not leave evil without an answer.

For today: when someone hurts you, do not take payment into your own hands. Leave justice to God, as Romans 12:19 says, and ask him for strength to forgive, to do good, and to trust that he judges with perfect justice.
exp.21:22:
It says that if a young virgin who is already pledged to be married to a man is found in the city by another man, and he has relations with her, the case that follows in the next verses applies. A "damsel" is a young woman, and "betrothed" means formally engaged, something more serious than dating today. "Lie with her" means to have sexual relations.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and explains God's laws for their life as a nation. An engagement was taken as an almost marriage covenant. This case concerns what happens inside the city, where she could call for help; the case of the field is distinguished afterward. The details of how this law was applied are interpreted in various ways.

For today: God values faithfulness and protects commitments. Today we can keep our promises and always respect people, without taking advantage of anyone.
exp.23:5:
This verse forbids a creditor from taking the lower or the upper millstone as a pledge from his debtor. The millstone was the stone used to grind grain into flour for bread. A pledge is an object left as security for a loan. And the millstone, whether the lower or the upper one, was essential, because without it the family could not prepare its food. That is why the verse says that taking it would be taking a man's life as a pledge.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel and passes on God's laws before they enter the promised land. The verses nearby aim to protect people: the wife, the newlywed, the brother who could be kidnapped. God wants a society where no one uses their advantage to harm another.

For today: if you lend money or collect a debt, do not demand what the other person needs to survive and work. Seek to be fair without taking away anyone's livelihood or dignity.
exp.10:6:
This verse says that the people are not hearing old stories, but that their own eyes saw the great works God did. The verse of the name of God and the verb in the older wording has been removed, since those words do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what God did in the wilderness, including when the earth swallowed Dathan and Abiram because of their rebellion. That generation were direct witnesses, and Moses uses this to call them to obey God's commandments.

For today: remember what God has done in your life, whether as help, protection, or correction. Write it down if you can. Remembering his faithfulness in the past strengthens trust and encourages us to obey him today, even when the future seems uncertain.
exp.27:22:
This verse uses a very strong image: the sky would be like bronze, which does not let rain through, and the ground would be hard as iron, which does not allow anything to grow.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: if they obey, there will be blessing; if they turn away from Him, consequences will come. This passage is part of the warnings, or curses, of the covenant. These were words for Israel within that specific agreement.

For today: we should not read every hardship as punishment from God, since the Bible does not teach that. But this text invites us to examine with humility whether we are listening to God, and to return to Him when we feel that the sky is "shut."
exp.24:17:
It says that Amalek came out to meet Israel on the way and attacked from behind the weakest, the stragglers at the back of the group, when the people were exhausted. The sentence about the rear guard being broken into means he destroyed or scattered those at the end of the line. Those who were weak or worn out are the ones meant. And the phrase about not fearing God means he showed no respect for God or for God's justice.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He asks them to remember this abuse, which happened after leaving Egypt (Exodus 17). He teaches them that God cares for the vulnerable and that cruelty against them is serious in God's sight.

Today we can care for those who are at the back: people who are tired, elderly, sick, or discouraged. One practical step is to call or visit someone this week who is going through a hard time, and never to take advantage of another person's weakness.
exp.9:2:
Moses tells that he made an ark of shittim wood, which is acacia wood. He also hewed two tables of stone, like the first ones, and went up the mount having the two tables in his hand, just as God had asked him to do.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of his life, and he reminds them of their history. The first tables were broken when the people sinned with the golden calf. Even so, God gave a new opportunity and wrote his words again. Moses obeyed step by step.

God knows how to restore what was broken. If you have failed, do not stay in guilt: return to God, and obey what he shows you today, even if it is a small step. His mercy opens a new beginning.
exp.19:13:
It says that in a war against a distant city that rejected peace and attacked, the men would be killed, but the women, the children, the animals, and all the goods of the city would remain as plunder for Israel. "Plunder" refers to the things taken from a defeated enemy. "Inheritance" is the land received as a possession.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. These rules of war belong to the old covenant with Israel, in a world where wars were brutal. Notice that peace was offered first, and that the nearby cities, within the promised land, were treated differently and more severely. Interpreters debate how to understand these commands, and it is honest to admit that they are difficult.

For today: Jesus calls us to seek peace and to love even our enemies. Before fighting or disputing, offer peace first, as this text shows it was to be done.
exp.11:20:
This verse says that if the place of worship that God chooses is very far away, the Israelite may kill animals from his cattle and sheep in his own town and eat them there, as much as he desires. "Within your gates" means inside your city or village. Here "your soul" means your appetite or your desire.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. Until now they were to bring their offerings and sacrifices to the place chosen by God. Moses makes clear that eating meat at home, in everyday life, would be permitted and would not be a sacrifice. God did not want to make life impossible for them because of distance. But he still required that they respect the blood.

For today: we can receive our daily food with gratitude as a gift from God, without unnecessary guilt. At the same time, we can eat with thankfulness and moderation, remembering that everything comes from his hand.
exp.28:24:
This verse is the answer to a question. The nations ask why God left the land of Israel as a desert of sulfur and salt. The answer is clear: the people abandoned the covenant, that is, the solemn promise the Lord made with their fathers when he brought them out of Egypt.

Moses speaks to the people on the plains of Moab, before they enter the promised land. He warns them what would happen if they left God. He wants them to understand that the punishment would not be random, but the consequence of abandoning the one who rescued them and gave them his promise.

For today: remember what God has done for you and do not let it be forgotten. Spend a few minutes this week thanking him for a specific help he gave you, and let that memory keep you faithful to him in your daily decisions.
exp.3:43:
This verse says that what follows is the law that Moses set before the people of Israel. The word "set before" means that he presented it or laid it out clearly so that everyone could hear it.

Moses is speaking to the people on the plains of Moab, before they enter the promised land. He has just finished speaking about the cities of refuge, where a person who had killed unintentionally could flee. Now he begins a new part of his message, in which he repeats and explains God's commandments to a generation that did not see their parents leave Egypt, but who were to live out that faithfulness.

For today: God does not hide his will, but presents it clearly. We can read his Word with confidence, knowing that it is made to be understood and lived, not merely admired. Choose a teaching from the Bible today and ask yourself how to put it into practice.
exp.18:9:
This verse says that the cities of refuge exist so that innocent blood is not shed in the land that God gives Israel as an inheritance. "Inheritance" means property received as a family gift. The phrase "blood be upon thee" means that if an innocent person was killed by mistake or injustice, the guilt would fall on the people.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. God commands them to set apart cities where a person who killed without intent could flee, so that he would not be put to death in revenge without a trial. But the following text makes clear that a murderer acting out of hatred would not be protected there.

For today: value life and justice. Avoid judging or taking revenge in haste, seek the truth before acting, and protect the person who could be treated unjustly.
exp.3:13:
Moses reminds them that, besides giving them the Ten Commandments, God also charged him to teach them the statutes and judgments, that is, the laws and rules for everyday life. These instructions were meant to be put into practice, in the land they were about to conquer and possess.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel on the plains of Moab, before entering the promised land. He reminds them of what happened at Horeb, where they heard the voice of God out of the fire but saw no form. For this reason, obedience had to be based on his word, not on images.

For today: God gives us his Word not only to know it, but to live it. Choose today one biblical teaching you already know and look for one concrete action to put it into practice this week.
exp.29:2:
This verse promises that God will bring back his people who were held captive.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that if they turn away from God, consequences will follow, but that if they acknowledge their wrong and return to him with all their heart, God will restore them. His promise rests on his mercy, not only on what they deserve.

For today: if you feel far from God because of your mistakes, do not think there is no way back. Return to him sincerely, and trust that his mercy remains open to receive you.
exp.27:52:
This verse says that during a terrible siege, people would reach such extreme hunger that they would eat their own children. The phrase in the verse, "the fruit of thine own body," means the children. A siege is the enemy's blockade of a city, and the verse's "straitness" refers to a very great anguish.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets out blessings if they obey God and curses if they abandon him. This is a very harsh warning about the consequences of breaking the covenant. The Bible records that something similar happened later, for example in Samaria (2 Kings 6:28-29) and in Jerusalem (Lamentations 4:10).

For today: let us take God's warnings seriously, not out of fear of punishment, but because he loves us and wants to care for us. Today we can examine our hearts, return to God with humility, and trust that Christ bore the curse for us (Galatians 3:13).
exp.5:11:
This verse is a warning.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He tells them they will receive cities, houses, cisterns, vineyards, and olive groves that they did not work for. Moses fears that, once they are comfortable and satisfied, they will forget who gave them everything and turn to other gods, as the next verse says.

For today: when things are going well for you, it is not easy to remember God. You can pause each day, perhaps at mealtime, to thank him for something specific you received that you did not achieve on your own. Gratitude helps keep the heart close to God.
exp.32:4:
It says that God was king in Jeshurun, a poetic name for Israel that means something like "the upright one." "Was" is written as "was" at that time. This happened when the heads of the people and the tribes of Israel gathered together. The text does not say who the king is, but almost everyone understands it to refer to Jehovah. Some think it could refer to Moses.

Moses speaks just before he dies, blessing the tribes. Earlier he recalled how God gave the Law at Sinai. Here he shows that Israel, gathered under the Law, acknowledged God as its true ruler. Then he begins to bless each tribe, starting with Reuben and Judah.

For today: putting God as king over our life is not just an idea, it is a daily decision. We can gather with other believers and ask ourselves: in what area do I need to let God rule?
exp.26:5:
It says the altar for the Lord was to be made of whole stones, that is, complete, just as they were found, without being dressed or cut. On that altar the people would offer a burnt offering, that is, a sacrifice that was burned up entirely in honor of God. "The Lord" is the name of God, and "offer" means to present.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before his death. He tells them what they must do when they cross the Jordan and enter the promised land: build an altar on Mount Ebal and write the law. It was a way of renewing their commitment to God. Scholars explain in various ways why iron was not used; one common idea is that it emphasized that worship did not depend on human ingenuity.

For today: come near to God with sincerity and simplicity, without ornaments or pretense. He looks for a devoted heart, not a perfect image.
exp.22:7:
It says that the children of the Edomites and of the Egyptians, starting from the third generation, could enter the "congregation of the Lord," that is, the assembly of God's people. The Edomite is the descendant of Edom, and the word "a" is the preposition "to." What that entry exactly meant (worship, rights, or citizenship) is debated among scholars.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. Shortly before, God forbids admitting Ammonites and Moabites. Here, by contrast, he asks for a more open attitude toward Edom, because Edom was related to Israel (descended from Esau), and toward Egypt, where Israel had lived as a foreigner. The shared history is remembered.

For today: God invites us not to be carried away by old resentments. We can remember how we have been treated and offer others, even those who hurt us or are different from us, a patient and fair welcome.
exp.1:27:
He says that Israel asks permission to cross Sihon's territory without stopping to settle or taking anything for free. They offer to pay for whatever food and water they need, and they promise to go only on foot, that is, without causing harm or leaving the road.

Moses speaks, reminding the people of what happened when they sent messengers to Sihon, king of Heshbon. Israel was on its way to the promised land and sought a peaceful passage. Moses recalls that Sihon refused, and the text says that God hardened his spirit. Some understand that God confirmed a stubbornness the king already had.

For today: when we need something from others, let us ask with respect, offering to pay what is fair and without taking advantage. Seeking peace and acting with honesty is a way of honoring God, even when others do not respond well.
exp.32:20:
This verse says that the tribe of Gad chose for itself the first land conquered, east of the Jordan. There it was given a portion reserved by the lawgiver, that is, Moses. Even so, Gad did not settle back at ease: it marched at the head of the people to help conquer Canaan. In doing so it fulfilled the justice God required and what it had agreed with Israel.

Moses speaks before his death, blessing each tribe. Gad had asked to stay on the other side of the Jordan (Numbers 32), and Moses agreed on the condition that its warriors would fight alongside their brothers. Here he acknowledges that they kept that promise.

For today: Keeping what we promised, even after we have received our own share, honors God. We can ask ourselves whom we should help before we rest.
exp.21:18:
It says that if a husband falsely accuses his wife of not having been a virgin and her parents prove the opposite, the man receives a punishment. He must pay one hundred pieces of silver (coins by weight) to her father. Next, he must keep her as his wife, and he may never divorce her.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law protected the woman and her family from false accusations that damaged her honor and her future. It obliged the husband to answer for his words. The text that follows deals with the opposite case, which is harsh, and it has been interpreted in several ways.

For today: our words can wound or protect others. Before accusing someone, let us seek the truth and take responsibility for what we say.
exp.23:1:
This verse says that when a woman has already left her husband's house with a certificate of divorce, she is free to go and marry another man. The word "departed" means she has already been sent away, and "may" shows that she had permission to do so.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel and gives a rule about divorce. He does not say that God approved of it as an ideal; the law regulated a practice that already existed. Its effect was to protect the woman, since the certificate proved she was free and could rebuild her life. Jesus commented on this passage in Matthew 19:8, and explained that Moses permitted it because of the hardness of the people's hearts.

Today it reminds us that God cares for the vulnerable when relationships break down. We can treat those who have gone through a separation with respect and justice, without judging them or leaving them without support.
exp.3:8:
This verse says that the people must watch over themselves and guard their soul with great care, so that they do not forget what their own eyes have seen. Those things must not leave their heart all the days of their life. In addition, they must tell them to their children and their grandchildren.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just reminded them that God is near to them and that his law is just. What they saw includes what happened at Horeb, when God spoke to them from the mountain. Moses knows that forgetting God is a real danger.

For today: set aside a moment each week to tell your children, nephews, nieces, or friends how God has helped you. In this way your faith does not stay in memory alone, but passes on to others.
exp.27:47:
It says that if Israel turns away from God, they will have to serve enemies whom God himself will send against them. They will live with hunger, thirst, lack of clothing, and want of all things. The "yoke of iron" is an image of harsh oppression, like the heavy wooden frame that was placed on oxen, but here it would be made of iron. "Until he have destroyed thee" shows that the harshness would reach very far.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He is renewing the covenant with God. Before this passage he listed blessings for obedience; here he warns about the consequences of rejecting God. The reason is clear: they did not serve him with joy when they had abundance. It is a warning to that people under that covenant.

When we have everything, it is easy to forget God. Today we can ask ourselves whether we give thanks to him and serve him with joy in abundance, not only when we need help.
exp.20:16:
This verse says that a father must recognize as firstborn the son who was born first, even when his mother is the wife he loves least. That son receives a double share, meaning twice the inheritance that the others receive. The word "hated" here means less loved, not necessarily hated. The phrase "the beginning of his strength" refers to the fact that he was the father's first son.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and he passes on God's law to them. This rule protected the firstborn son from injustice or family favoritism, in a situation of polygamy, which the law regulates without approving it as an ideal.

For today: God calls us to treat everyone fairly, without letting our preferences or emotions decide what each person is due, especially within the family.
exp.19:16:
It says that Israel was to completely destroy six peoples who lived in the promised land: the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. "Thou shalt utterly destroy them" means "without fail, completely." It is a command that, according to the text, God had already given.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, instructing the new generation before they enter Canaan. The command is limited to those peoples, and the text gives the reason: so that they would not teach Israel their idolatrous practices. It is a very difficult passage, and scholars interpret it in different ways, for example as divine judgment or as the typical language of warfare of the time.

For today: God takes very seriously everything that draws us away from him. We can ask ourselves what influences today pull us toward sin, and turn away from them with determination, without harming anyone.
exp.27:65:
Your life will seem to hang by a thread before you, as if it could fall at any moment. You will be afraid day and night, and you will have no assurance that you will go on living.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains the blessings of obeying God and the consequences of turning away from him. This passage describes the wearing toll of living far from God, scattered among the nations, as a result of breaking the covenant.

For today: when fear and uncertainty take away your peace, do not carry them alone. Pray, rest in the faithfulness of God, and seek to live close to him, because in Christ there is a peace that the world cannot give.
exp.0:27:
This verse says that the people of Israel lost their courage before the promised land. "They have discouraged our heart" means that they took away their courage. The spies reported that the people were stronger and taller, that the cities had enormous walls (the phrase about walls reaching up is an exaggeration meant to say the cities were very high), and that they saw the sons of the giants, descendants of men of great stature.

Moses speaks at the end of the wilderness journey and recalls what the people said forty years earlier. The Israelites rebelled, complained, and even doubted God's love. Moses reminds them that God had already fought for them in Egypt, and that they should trust him.

Today, when a problem seems enormous, let us not allow fear and the comments of others to take away our faith. Let us remember how God has helped us before, and ask him for courage to take the next step.
exp.22:17:
This verse forbids bringing to the temple money earned in a shameful way to fulfill a promise to God. The "wages of a prostitute" is the payment received for prostitution. The "price of a dog" is a difficult expression: many believe it refers to the payment of a man who prostituted himself in pagan worship, although some scholars understand it in another way. A "vow" is a solemn promise made to God. "Abomination" means something that God detests.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. In these chapters he gives them laws to live as a people set apart from the pagan practices of their neighbors, where prostitution was mixed with worship. God wanted pure worship.

For today: God is not pleased with offerings that come from injustice or deceit. What we give to God should be the fruit of honest work, offered with a sincere heart.
exp.33:11:
This verse closes the book of Deuteronomy and the Law of Moses. It says that Moses was remembered for his "mighty hand," that is, for acts done with great power. It also speaks of "the great terror," which refers to the impressive and fearsome deeds that caused amazement. All of this took place "in the sight of all Israel," that is, before the eyes of the whole people.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book, not Moses, since the account already describes his death. Tradition attributes it to Joshua or another later writer, though this is not known for certain. The purpose is to sum up who Moses was: a unique servant, whom God dealt with face to face, and through whom He delivered Israel with the signs in Egypt and in the wilderness.

For today: God does great works, but He does them through people who obey Him. Moses is remembered for his power, but that power came from God. We can serve with humility, trusting that God works through us and giving Him the glory.
exp.10:0:
This verse calls the people to love the LORD their God and to keep his charge, his statutes, his judgments, and his commandments at all times. "Charge" is what God asks them to guard; "statutes" are his set rules; "judgments" are his just decisions; and "commandments" are his orders. "At all times" means this is not something for a single moment, but for the whole of life.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they themselves saw the mighty works of God in Egypt. For this reason, their obedience should spring from what they have seen and from their relationship with God, not from rules alone.

For today: love for God is shown in daily obedience. Remember how God has cared for you, and choose today one concrete, small, and faithful action that pleases him.
exp.22:10:
It says that when evening came, the man who had become unclean had to wash himself with water. And when the sun had already gone down, he could return to the camp. "When evening cometh on" means when the day is already coming to an end. "When the sun is down" is the time of sunset.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them rules for the military camp. God was present among them, so the camp had to be kept clean and orderly. The uncleanness in this law was ceremonial, not a sin. It was a way of teaching respect for the holiness of God.

For today: God cares about the details of our daily lives. We can care for our hearts and our habits, knowing that He is near, and return to Him with confidence whenever we need to be renewed.
exp.11:17:
This verse says that the people were to eat their tithes, firstfruits, vows, and offerings in the place God would choose, not in their own towns. There the whole family, the servants, and the Levite would eat together. "Towns" means cities or villages, and "Levite" refers to a member of the tribe of Levi, who served in worship and had no land of his own. All of this was to be done with joy before God, from the fruit of their labor.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter Canaan. He teaches them that worship must center on the place God chooses, not on just any location. He also reminds them to care for the Levite, who depended on the generosity of the people.

For today: give with gratitude and do it in community. Enjoy with others what God has given you, and do not forget to support those who serve others or are in need.
exp.21:20:
If it was proven that a young bride had had relations before marriage and had hidden it, the men of her city would bring her out to the door of her father's house and stone her. She was charged with "vileness" (something shameful) and with "fornication" (having relations outside of marriage). The phrase "thou shalt put evil away from among you" means cleansing from the community what was harming it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. These are civil laws for a nation under covenant with God, where faithfulness and purity in the family protected the community. The case assumes a judgment based on evidence, and the verse before it punishes a husband who made a false accusation. Christians often understand that these penalties belonged to Israel as a nation.

Today we can learn that God values truth, faithfulness, and justice. We should avoid false accusations and always seek the forgiveness and purity that Christ offers.
exp.11:21:
It says that the meat of animals that Israel killed to eat at home could be eaten just like the meat of the roebuck and the hart, game animals that were not offered on the altar. The roebuck is a small kind of deer. The one who was ceremonially impure and the one who was not both could eat of that meat.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He explains that, when the place of worship is far away, they may eat meat in their towns and not only at the sanctuary. This was a practical allowance, on the condition that they not eat the blood.

For today: God cares for everyday life, such as food and the table. We can enjoy his gifts with gratitude and, at the same time, respect the limits he sets, without separating daily life from reverence toward him.
exp.11:13:
This verse says that God himself would choose a place, within one of the tribes of Israel, where the people were to offer their burnt offerings to him. A burnt offering was a sacrifice that was burned completely on the altar. There they were also to do all that God commanded them regarding their worship.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He warns them not to worship God in just any place, as the surrounding nations did with their false gods. God wanted an orderly and obedient worship, not one invented by each person. The text does not give the details of which place this would be here.

For today: worshiping God is not doing whatever seems right to us, but drawing near to him as he has made himself known. Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith rests on what God says or only on our own preferences.
exp.27:56:
This verse describes something very painful. It speaks of a woman so refined that, in the midst of famine, she will not even share with her newborn daughter what she brings forth. The newborn child is the one "that comes out from between her feet," and the phrase about eating them "in secret" describes doing so privately, because of a lack of everything. The siege is the encirclement of the cities, when the enemy surrounds them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them the blessings for obeying God and, in very harsh words, the consequences of abandoning his covenant. It is a warning about the horror of war and hunger, not a command from God.

For today: obedience to God is the path of life. We can take his warnings seriously, seek his guidance every day, and remember that his correction aims to bring us back to him.
exp.10:19:
It says that Israel was to write God's words on the doorposts of their houses and on the gates, that is, on the entrances and the frames of the doors. The gates are the doors or entryways of the house and of the city. The idea is that, as they came and went, they would always see God's word.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He asks them to remember and obey the law, and to teach it to their children. Some understand this in a literal way, as many Jews do today with the mezuzah; others see it as a vivid way of saying that God should be present in everything.

Today we can put a verse where we can see it at home, at the entrance, or on our phone, and decide to read it together as a family. In this way the Word becomes part of daily life, not only of Sunday.
exp.17:9:
This verse forbids the people of Israel from practicing pagan customs. It speaks of making children pass through the fire, which probably refers to sacrificing them or offering them to false gods (some scholars debate whether it always meant death or sometimes a rite of dedication). It also forbids trying to learn the future, interpreting omens, casting lots for hidden purposes, and practicing sorcery.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He warns them not to imitate the practices of the nations living there, because those nations sought guidance and power apart from God. He wanted Israel to trust in Him alone.

Today we can ask ourselves where we look for security about the future. Instead of horoscopes, mediums, or other occult practices, we can pray, read the Bible, and seek wise counsel, trusting that God guides our steps.
exp.30:21:
This verse says that Moses wrote down a song that same day and taught it to the people of Israel. The old wording is easy to follow: the phrase meaning "he taught it to them" is simply the way the verse says he passed the song on to the people. The song is the one found in Deuteronomy 32.

Moses speaks this after God had told him that the people, once they were settled and well fed in the promised land, would turn away from Him and follow other gods. God wanted this song to serve as a witness, easy to remember, so that in times of distress the people would return to Him.

For today: what we sing and repeat stays in the heart. We can learn verses or hymns that remind us who God is, so that in difficult moments, or even in times of comfort, we do not forget Him.
exp.19:8:
This verse says that when the officers have finished speaking to the people, the captains of the army will take charge and lead the troops. The words "have made an end of speaking" mean that the officers had finished talking, and "to lead the people" means that the military commanders would be put in charge of the soldiers.

Moses is giving Israel instructions before they enter the promised land. The officers would first speak to the men and let go home those who had unfinished business, such as a new house, a vineyard, or a promise of marriage, as well as those who were afraid. This looked after families and kept fear from spreading to the rest. After that, the captains organized the army.

For today: before a difficult task, it is wise to stop and examine the heart and one's priorities. God cares about people, not only about results, and He invites us to move forward with order, honesty, and trust in Him.
exp.10:13:
It says that God himself will send the rain to the land of Israel in its proper time. "The first rain" is the rain of autumn, which softened the ground for sowing. "The latter rain" is the rain of spring, which helped the harvest ripen. This way there would be grain (wheat and barley), wine, and oil (from olives).

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God cares for that land all year long. The promise depends on obeying him and loving him with all your heart. In contrast with Egypt, here they would not depend on watering the land by their own means, but on the rain that God gives.

For today: you can work hard and at the same time recognize that everything you have comes from the hand of God. Before planning your day, give thanks for what you have already received and trust that he cares for you, while you obey him with love.
exp.32:16:
He says that Joseph is like a young bull, strong and full of dignity, like the firstborn bull of the herd. His horns are "like the horns of unicorns," and the word used there probably refers to a wild ox or large buffalo, a very powerful animal. With that strength he will push the peoples to the ends of the earth. Ephraim and Manasseh, the two sons of Joseph, are his "ten thousands" and his "thousands," that is, great multitudes.

Moses speaks. Before he dies, he blesses each tribe of Israel. Here he blesses Joseph, represented by Ephraim and Manasseh, promising them strength and victory when they enter the promised land. It is poetic language, not a literal description.

For today: our strength does not come from ourselves, but from the grace of God, as the verse before it says. Trust that He gives you courage to face your challenges, and use it with humility.
exp.26:18:
It says that God condemns the one who twists or manipulates justice against three vulnerable people: the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow. "Twisting the judgment" means misusing the law or authority to take away what is rightfully theirs. "Cursed" means that person falls under God's judgment. And all the people respond "Amen," that is, "so be it," accepting this warning.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. At Shechem, according to the passage, the people were to repeat these curses as part of renewing their covenant with God. These three groups had no strong family or land to protect them, and God cares for them in a special way.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I treat fairly those who have less power than I do? It may be an immigrant, a child without support, or a widow. Defending them, rather than taking advantage of them, is obeying God.
exp.31:20:
This verse says that Israel made God angry by worshiping what is not God, that is, idols, empty things. "I will move them to jealousy" means to provoke jealousy, and "provoke them to anger" means to stir up wrath. God answers that He too will provoke Israel with a people that is not a people, a nation of no importance, and with a foolish nation, people without understanding.

God speaks within the Song of Moses, which warns Israel before it enters the promised land. God sees the unfaithfulness of His people and announces the consequences. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 10:19, and some connect it to the opening of the gospel to other nations, although it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: examine what things are taking the place of God in your heart, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Return to Him sincerely, for God desires to be loved with the whole heart.
exp.3:1:
This verse says that the people must not add anything to what God commands, nor take anything away from it. The purpose is that they can obey God's commandments just as he gave them, without changing them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel just before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that obeying God will give them life and allow them to possess the land. Next he recalls what happened at Baal-peor, where those who followed other gods died, while those who stayed faithful to God remained alive.

For today: we can read the Bible with humility, without twisting it to say what suits us or ignoring what makes us uncomfortable. Before deciding what to think, ask yourself: "What does God's Word actually say?" And then ask him for help to obey it.
exp.4:22:
It says that after the people heard the voice of God coming out of the darkness and saw Mount Sinai wrapped in flames, the leaders came near to Moses. They were the heads of the tribes and the older men with authority over the people. Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, before they enter the Promised Land. He reminds them of what happened at Sinai, when God gave the Ten Commandments. The leaders came near with fear, because God's presence was so overwhelming that they felt they could not bear it. Moses recalls this so that they do not forget the seriousness of God's Word.

For today: when we feel fear or reverence before God, the best thing is to draw near to Him and not pull away. We can listen to His Word with humility, and leaders can also guide the people to do so with reverence.
exp.3:38:
It says that today we should learn and fix in our hearts one truth: the Lord is the only God, both in heaven and on earth, and there is no other. "Know therefore this day, and consider it in thine heart" is an old-fashioned way of saying to bring something to mind and think it over until you take it very seriously. The name "Jehovah" is the name of God.

Moses speaks near the end of his life, addressing the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them how God brought them out of Egypt with great power, out of love for their ancestors. For this reason he calls them to acknowledge that only God deserves their loyalty, and then to obey him.

For today: when you feel fear or pressure, remember in prayer what God has done for you. Repeating that he rules over all helps you trust him and live in obedience, not just believe it in your mind.
exp.31:50:
God tells Moses why he will not enter the Promised Land. The verse of the old wording is removed here since the verse above is the King James text. God says that Moses and Aaron did not honor him as holy before the people, at the waters of Meribah, at Kadesh, in the wilderness of Zin.

God speaks shortly before Moses' death. He commands Moses to climb Mount Nebo to see the promised land. The episode is recorded in Numbers 20, when the people complained for lack of water and Moses struck the rock instead of speaking to it, as he had been instructed. Interpreters point to different details of his failure, such as anger, disobedience, or taking credit for the miracle.

For today: those who serve God are responsible for honoring him through their attitude and obedience, even under pressure. God forgives, but some consequences remain. With humility, let us ask him for help to reflect his character.
exp.21:14:
It says that when a husband accuses his wife of not having been a virgin, her parents must present the proof before the elders of the city, who would gather at the gate. The words "young woman" and "maiden," which appear in the older wording, are old terms for a young woman, so I've rendered that phrase here as the "damsel" of the verse above. The "tokens of virginity" seem to be a cloth or sheet, as verse 17 suggests, though some scholars debate exactly what it was.

Moses speaks to Israel, giving laws for life in community. The city gate was the place where legal cases were settled. This law protected the young woman and her family from a false accusation and from a damaged reputation invented by a husband who no longer wanted her.

For today: God cares about truth and about the honor of people. We should not spread accusations without proof or harm the reputation of others. Let us always seek justice and defend those who are slandered.
exp.32:7:
God gave the tribe of Levi the Thummim and the Urim, objects that the priests used to seek God's will. The verse speaks of a "good man," a faithful man, whom God tested at Massah and with whom he contended at the waters of Meribah. Here "tested" means "tried." "Contend" means to argue or dispute.

Moses speaks just before his death and blesses each tribe. To Levi he recalls their priestly service. Scholars do not agree on who the "good man" is: it could be Moses, Aaron, or the whole tribe.
