The episodes at Massah and Meribah show moments of testing in the wilderness, and Levi appears as a tribe that was tried and found faithful.

For today: God uses trials to reveal and strengthen our faithfulness. When you go through a difficult season, ask him to help you respond with trust and obedience, not with complaint.
exp.20:8:
This verse says that the people of Israel would remove from among them the guilt for an unjust death. They would accomplish this by doing what God considers right. "Guilt for innocent blood" refers to the responsibility for having killed someone who was not guilty. What is "right in the sight of the Lord" means what God sees as just.

Moses speaks to the people in the book of Deuteronomy. Before this verse, a case is described in which a dead body is found and it is not known who the killer was. The elders of the nearest city would perform a ritual, declare their innocence, and ask God to forgive the whole people. In this way the land would not be stained by that injustice.

For today: God takes injustice seriously, even when we do not know the guilty person. We can do what is right by being honest, defending the vulnerable, and not looking the other way when others are harmed.
exp.30:6:
Moses calls Joshua in front of all the people and tells him: "Be strong and of a good courage." He assures him that he will lead Israel to the land God promised to their fathers, and that he will cause them to inherit it.

Moses is 120 years old and will not enter the promised land. He is saying goodbye and hands the leadership to Joshua in public, so that the people will respect him and follow him. His encouragement does not rest on Joshua's abilities, but on God's promise, who goes with them.

When God gives you a task that feels too big for you, do not wait until you feel capable. Remember what He has promised, take the next step with courage, and encourage also those who are beside you.
exp.33:2:
This verse continues the list of what God showed Moses from the mountain. Here "the south" is mentioned, which is the Negev, the dry region to the south. Also appearing is "the plain," that is, the flat lowland, and "the plain of the valley of Jericho," the fertile valley next to that city, called "the city of palm trees." The survey ends at Zoar, a place south of the Dead Sea whose exact location is not entirely certain.

The narrator of the book tells of Moses' final moments. God allows him to see from Nebo the whole promised land, although he will not be able to enter it. Who wrote this chapter is debated; many think another person added it after Moses' death.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even though we do not always see it fulfilled in our own lives. We can trust his promises and serve him faithfully, knowing that others will receive the fruit of what we sow.
exp.7:1:
God tells his people to remember the whole journey of forty years through the desert. There the Lord led them, humbled them (the word "humble" here means making them go through need and lowliness) and tested them, to show what was in their hearts: whether they would keep his commandments or not.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, just before they enter the promised land. He asks them to look back so they understand that the desert was not a meaningless punishment, but a time of teaching. God cared for them, but he also shaped them.

For today: think of a difficult season you have lived through. Ask yourself what it revealed about your heart and how God took care of you in that time. Remembering that can help you trust him more and obey him with humility.
exp.16:5:
This verse says that no one could be sentenced to death on the word of just one person. Two or three witnesses who agreed were required. The word "mouth" in the verse means testimony or statement, and the phrase about the guilty person who deserved that penalty refers to the one who deserved that punishment.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them laws to live justly. Before any serious punishment, such as in cases of idolatry, a thorough investigation was required. The witnesses were even expected to act first, which made them think very seriously about the truth of their words.

Today we can learn not to judge or repeat accusations based on a single rumor or a single version of events. Before forming an opinion about someone, let us look for facts, listen to more people, and be fair, remembering that the truth matters greatly to God.
exp.7:2:
It says that God allowed Israel to go through need and hunger in the desert, and then fed them with manna, a food that no one knew. "Humbled" means to bring low or put through hardship. "Fed" is the word for nourished. The purpose was to teach them that life does not depend on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.

Moses speaks to the people at the end of the forty years in the desert, before they enter the promised land. He asks them to remember the path they have traveled. The trials were not senseless punishment: God wanted to show what was in his heart and whether they would truly obey him.

For today: even though we work and need material things, we also need to nourish the soul. We can set aside a moment each day to read the Bible and trust God, especially when we go through scarcity or uncertainty.
exp.31:11:
This verse says that the Lord alone was the one who guided his people, Israel. The phrase "guided him" means that he led him and took him along the way. The verse's line that there was no strange god with him means that no foreign god accompanied him or helped him. God had no partners in caring for his people.

Moses speaks in the song he left to Israel before he died. He recalls how God found them in the wilderness and cared for them the way an eagle watches over its young. He does this to show that Israel has no reason to go after other gods, because the Lord alone sustained them. The song also warns what would happen if they forgot him.

For today: remember the times God sustained you in difficult seasons. Thank him and trust in him, instead of looking for security in other things.
exp.10:22:
It says that God himself will drive out from before the people all those nations that lived in Canaan. Although those peoples were greater and stronger, Israel would take possession of their land. "Drive out" means to expel, and "possess" means that they will receive that land as an inheritance.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the promise depends on obeying God and loving him, as the verses before it say. He wants them to trust in God's help and not in their own strength. Scholars discuss how the conquest should be understood, but the text stresses that God is the one who acts.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, do not rely only on your own strength. Love God, obey him step by step, and trust that he sustains you.
exp.29:16:
This verse describes the opposite of what God asked for. It speaks of a heart that turns away, that stops listening, and that lets itself be "drawn away," that is, dragged along or seduced, until it bows down to "foreign gods," meaning strange gods, and serves them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in Moab, just before they enter the promised land. He repeats the covenant with God and sets two paths before them: life and blessing if they love and obey the Lord, or death and loss if they abandon him. He wants them to choose well.

For today: the problem begins in the heart, before the actions. Today "foreign gods" can be anything that takes the place of God, such as money, success, or comfort. Ask yourself honestly what is holding your attention, and give God first place again.
exp.13:7:
It says that pork could not be eaten among the people of Israel. It has a hoof that is split in two, but it does not chew the cud, meaning it does not bring back up food it has already swallowed to chew again. For that reason it was "unclean," which means not fit for use by God's people. Its dead body was also not to be touched.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the laws God gave them to live as a people set apart, holy to Him (Deuteronomy 14:2). Scholars explain the exact reason for these rules in different ways: some see a symbol of holiness, others reasons of health or of setting themselves apart from other nations. The Bible does not fully explain it.

For today: Christians are not under these dietary rules (Mark 7:19; Acts 10), but we can still ask ourselves how to live set apart for God in our everyday decisions.
exp.5:2:
This verse says that Israel should listen carefully and also obey what God commands. If they do, it will go well with them and the people will increase, just as God promised. Practicing, or doing what one hears, is what the verse is calling for, and the image of a land flowing with milk and honey stands for a very fertile and abundant land. The "fathers" refers to the ancestors, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they enter the promised land. He repeats God's law to them so that they will teach it to their children and grandchildren. Right after this comes the well-known call, "Hear, O Israel," which urges loving God with one's whole being. Obedience springs from that love and from trust in God's promises.

For today: it is not enough to just listen to the Bible; decide today on one concrete action to put into practice what God has shown you, and do it with gratitude, not out of mere obligation.
exp.0:7:
Here is what it says: God invites the people to look at the land He has already given them and to go in and take possession of it. That land is the one He promised with an oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to their descendants. "Descendants" means offspring. "Take possession" means to take hold of what is given. "Swore" means that He promised solemnly.

Context: Moses speaks to the people of Israel, near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them of what God said at Horeb (Sinai), when He commanded them to leave that mountain and move forward. Moses wants the new generation to remember that the promise comes from God and that He is faithful.

For today: God keeps what He promises, but He often asks us to take steps of faith. Think of something God has shown you to do, and take one concrete step today, trusting His faithfulness more than your own strength.
exp.3:23:
He says that God is like a consuming fire, and that he is "jealous." "Consuming" means that he destroys whatever opposes him. "Jealous" does not speak of petty envy, but of an exclusive love: God does not share the loyalty of his people with idols.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He will not cross the Jordan, so he gives them a final warning: do not forget the covenant, and do not make images to worship them. He reminds them that God is holy and that his people, by being unfaithful, would face serious consequences.

For today: examine what things compete with God in your heart, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Take God seriously, but without servile fear, for his zeal springs from a love that wants what is best for you.
exp.27:5:
This verse says that God will bless his people in everything they do: "entering" and "leaving" mean arriving and departing, that is, the comings and goings of each day, such as work, travel, and life at home. It is understood as a blessing that covers the whole of life.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: if they listen to his voice and obey, blessings will come. It is part of a list that includes fields, family, livestock, and harvests. Later he also warns of consequences if they turn away.

Today we can begin the day by entrusting to God our going out and our coming back with a simple prayer. It is not a guarantee that everything will be easy, but it is a reminder that his care accompanies us when we live trusting in him and seeking to obey him.
exp.0:28:
Moses reminds the people of what he told them when they were about to enter the promised land. He asked them not to be afraid of the inhabitants of Canaan. "Dread" means feeling a sudden fear, and "be afraid" reinforces the same idea: not letting panic take control.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, and he reviews their history. Forty years earlier, at Kadesh-barnea, the Israelites heard that the peoples were great and strong, and they grumbled against God in their tents. Moses reminded them that God was going before them and had already cared for them before.

When fear makes us doubt God, it is good to remember how he has helped us before. Looking back with gratitude gives us strength to take the next step with confidence, instead of complaining or freezing up.
exp.28:3:
This verse says that, although the people saw many miracles, God had not yet given them a heart that understood, eyes that truly saw, or ears that really listened.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel on the plains of Moab, at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them of what God did in Egypt and along the way, in order to call them to be faithful to the covenant. Interpreters explain this phrase in different ways: as a complaint about their hardness, or as a reminder that deep understanding is a gift from God.

For today: it is not enough to see good things from God; we need to ask him humbly to open our hearts so that we may understand and obey what he has already shown us.
exp.24:2:
If a court sentenced someone to be beaten, the punishment had a limit: forty strokes, never more. The verse notes that the verse's wording means the judge would have the guilty person struck. The phrase about the person being treated as worthless means being humiliated and degraded. The reason is that the guilty person was still "your brother," that is, a member of the people.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. In this part of the law he explains how the judges were to act. The punishment was to fit the offense and be carried out in an orderly way, before the judge. Even a person who did wrong kept his dignity. Some think that later thirty-nine strokes were used so as not to go over the limit, but that is a later tradition.

For today: even when we must correct or set limits, let us do it without humiliating or exaggerating. Every person still has value before God.
exp.10:11:
It says the promised land is a place that God himself cares for. "Cares for" means that he looks after it and attends to it. His eyes are always upon that land, throughout the whole year, from beginning to end.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter Canaan. He explains that this land is different from Egypt, where they watered the crops through their own effort, and the method described there likely refers to some manual system of irrigation, though its exact form is debated. In Canaan they would depend on the rain, that is, on God's provision. For that reason he asks them to obey him and to love him.

Today we can remember that we do not live alone or depend only on our own effort. God cares for us every day. We can work diligently and, at the same time, trust him and give thanks for every provision, because his gaze is upon us.
exp.13:10:
This verse says that the people of Israel could eat any bird that was "clean," that is, the kind God allowed as food. The word "clean" does not speak of dirt, but of what was acceptable under the law. Then the text lists the birds that could not be eaten, such as the eagle and the vulture.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the laws God gave them to live as a set-apart people. These rules about food distinguished them from the neighboring nations. Scholars explain the exact reason for each rule in various ways, and the Bible does not always spell it out.

For today: God cares for every area of our lives, even the everyday, such as food. We can ask ourselves whether, in our daily decisions, we seek to please Him and to live with gratitude and self-control.
exp.13:11:
It says that the people of Israel were not to eat certain birds of prey. Here the eagle, the ossifrage, and the ospray are named. The ossifrage is a bird of prey similar to a hawk, and the ospray is a small hawk. The exact Hebrew names are hard to identify, so some of these birds may vary from one translation to another.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the laws God gave them to live as a set-apart people. These rules about food distinguished them from other nations. Many think the birds listed were those that hunt or feed on dead flesh, although the Bible does not give a detailed reason here.

For today: Christians are not under these food rules (Mark 7:19; Acts 10), but we can learn to live with intention, letting God guide our daily decisions and set us apart by our love and obedience.
exp.7:9:
This verse says that the people will eat until they are satisfied, and that then they will give thanks to the Lord their God for the good land he has given them. Quedarás lleno, sin hambre, is the meaning of the phrase about being full; in the translation, "when thou hast eaten and art full" conveys that same sense of having enough to eat and no longer being hungry. Blessing the Lord here means giving thanks and praising God.

Moses speaks to Israel at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, just before they enter the promised land. He describes a land of plenty and teaches them to respond with gratitude. The verses that follow warn that abundance can lead them to forget God.

For today: before or after eating, pause and truly thank God. May comfort not lead you to forget that every good thing comes from him.
exp.27:53:
It says that even the gentlest and most refined man, used to a comfortable life, will become hard toward his own brother, his wife, and the children who remain to him. The words used for him describe someone raised in great comfort. His eye will be evil means he will look at others with selfishness and refuse to share, even with those closest to him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them the blessings for obeying God and the curses for abandoning his covenant. This passage describes the horror of an enemy siege, with extreme hunger, as the consequence of turning away from God.

For today: scarcity and fear can harden even the kindest people. We can ask God to guard our hearts and practice generosity now, so that anxiety does not make us selfish toward our family.
exp.25:6:
This verse says that the people of Israel asked Jehovah, the God of their ancestors, for help. God heard their voice and looked upon their suffering. The phrase "affliction" means pain and distress; the word "labour" refers to the hard burden of slavery; "oppression" is the mistreatment of someone who has power over others.

Each Israelite speaks this when presenting to God the firstfruits of his harvest in the promised land. Moses teaches them to remember their history: they came from a wandering father (many understand this to be Jacob) and were slaves in Egypt. In this way they acknowledged that the land was a gift from God, not their own achievement.

For today: when you are going through a difficult time, cry out to God with confidence, because He sees and hears. And when He helps you, do not forget it; bring Him your gratitude and tell others what He has done for you.
exp.31:0:
Moses calls on the heavens and the earth to listen to what he is about to say. "The words of my mouth" refers to the words he speaks. It is like opening a solemn speech, asking all of creation to pay attention.

This verse begins the Song of Moses, which he speaks at the end of his life, before Israel enters the promised land. Moses wants the people to remember God's faithfulness and not turn away from Him. Calling the heavens and the earth as witnesses was a way of giving weight to the message. The verses that follow compare his words to rain and dew that bring life.

For today: come to God's Word with attention and reverence, like someone receiving rain on dry ground. Before reading the Bible, pause and ask God for a heart willing to listen.
exp.8:25:
Moses recounts that he prayed to God and asked him not to destroy Israel. He calls them "thy people" and "thine inheritance," that is, his most cherished possession. To be "redeemed" means to be rescued by paying a price or through an act of deliverance. The "mighty hand" speaks of God's power in bringing them out of Egypt.

Moses speaks to the people, reminding them of their rebellion in the wilderness, especially when they made the golden calf. He tells how he interceded for them for forty days. He does not defend the people's sin; he appeals to what God had already done for them and to his promises.

For today: when you see wrongs in others, or in yourself, do not stop at reproach. Pray for them with humility and with confidence in God's mercy and promises, remembering that his work of rescue remains the foundation of our hope.
exp.11:26:
This verse says that the Israelite was to bring his burnt offerings, that is, offerings burned completely for God, to the altar of the Lord. The blood of the sacrifices was poured out on the altar, and the person could eat the meat of the other offerings. "Jehovah" is the name of God.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions so that worship would be orderly and obedient, in the place that God would choose. Shortly before, eating blood is forbidden, and they are promised that things will go well for them if they do what is right before God.

For today: God cares about how we approach him, not only about what we do. We can ask ourselves whether we worship him with obedience and reverence, and not out of habit. Today, Christians see in Christ the complete sacrifice, and we respond with gratitude and a life given over to him.
exp.24:10:
It says that if two men fight and the wife of one wants to defend her husband, but grabs the other man by his private parts (in an older way of speaking, these are called the "shame"), she would be committing a serious offense. The law that follows orders that her hand be cut off, without mercy.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, going over laws for their life together. The case protects the dignity of the body and the ability to have children, which was very valuable in that culture. The punishment is very harsh, and it is not clear how it was carried out; some scholars believe it was a symbolic or different kind of penalty, and this is debated.

For today: even with good intentions, such as defending someone we love, we cannot justify actions that harm or humiliate others. Let us look for ways to help that always respect the dignity of people.
exp.4:3:
It says that God spoke directly with the people of Israel on Mount Horeb, also called Sinai. "Face to face" is a way of saying it was a close and direct communication. The words "out of the midst of the fire" show that God revealed himself with an overwhelming presence, surrounded by fire. "Lord" is the name of God.

Moses is speaking near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds the Israelites of God's covenant before they enter the promised land. He speaks to them as if they had all been there, because the covenant remains in force for every generation. The verses that follow clarify that Moses acted as a go-between because the people were afraid of the fire. Some understand "face to face" as an expression of closeness, not of seeing God's face.

God is not distant; he wants to have a relationship with you. Today you can speak to him in prayer and read his Word knowing that he listens. Do it with respect and confidence, and do not let your faith become merely an inherited custom.
exp.1:35:
From Aroer, which lies on the edge of the river Arnon, and from the city that is by the river, all the way to Gilead, there was not one city too strong for us. The Lord our God handed all of them over to us.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them how they advanced against King Sihon, and he stresses that the victory was not their achievement but God's. He also points out that God set limits: Israel was not to touch the land of the Ammonites. This is a very harsh passage about war, and scholars interpret it in different ways; the central point here is that God directs history and marks out boundaries.

For today: when you accomplish something, recognize that God was behind it and do not take all the credit for yourself. And accept with humility the limits He sets.
exp.3:21:
Moses says that he is going to die in the land east of the Jordan and will not cross the river. Instead, the people will cross it and take possession of that good land. To "possess" means to receive it as an inheritance, and "cross" means to go over the river.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. Shortly before, he explained that God had refused to let him enter the land, and he connects this to the people's situation. In this way he reminds them that the promise still stands, even though their leader will not see it fulfilled. Right after, he warns them not to forget the covenant or make idols.

For today: Moses did not become bitter over what he did not receive, but encouraged others to move forward. We can serve God with generosity, preparing and blessing those who will follow, even when we do not see all the fruits ourselves.
exp.17:13:
This verse says that the nations Israel was going to displace in the promised land listened to observers of times (people who predicted the future from signs) and to diviners (those who practiced magic and enchantments). But God did not allow Israel to take that path. The words "but as for thee" mark that Israel's situation was different.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He has just forbidden practices such as divination and consulting the dead, and he explains that these customs were part of why God judged those nations. Instead, God promised to send a prophet to guide his people with his word.

For today: when you feel anxiety about the future, avoid seeking answers in horoscopes or occult practices. Turn to God in prayer and to his Word, where he makes himself known and guides with confidence.
exp.6:23:
It says that God would give the Israelites victory over the kings of the nations of Canaan. "Shall deliver them into your hand" means that God would give them the triumph. "Destroy their name" means that their memory and their power would disappear. "No one shall stand before you" promises that no enemy would stop them while God was at work.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the victory would come from God, not from their own strength. This is the language of conquest typical of that moment and of that covenant with Israel. Moreover, the following verse shows the central concern: that the people not fall into the idolatry of those nations.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, trust that God sustains you, but obey Him faithfully. His help is not an excuse for complacency, but a reason to remove from our lives whatever draws us away from Him.
exp.31:16:
They sacrificed to demons, not to God, and the verse says Israel offered sacrifices to false spiritual powers rather than to God. The Hebrew word for these beings (shedim) appears only a few times and is usually understood as spirits or demons behind the idols. They were gods that had only recently arrived from neighboring peoples, gods that neither the people nor their ancestors had known or honored.

Moses speaks in his final song, shortly before he dies. He wants to warn the people that when they prosper and grow comfortable, they will forget God, their Rock and Creator, and will seek out other gods. God grieves and is angered by that unfaithfulness.

Today, when things are going well for us, it is easy to put our trust in new things: money, success, or passing trends. We can stop and ask ourselves: to what am I giving my time and my trust? Thanking God each day helps us remember who sustains us.
exp.30:17:
God says that when the people turn to other gods, he will hide his face from them. The quoted words in the source are not in the King James wording, so I will leave them out. The phrase about the people's wrongdoing is simply "for all the evils which they shall have wrought," and the sense is that they have done these things and turned away.

God speaks with Moses shortly before Moses dies. He tells him that Israel, once settled in the promised land, will forget the covenant and worship idols. For this reason he commands Moses to write a song that will serve as a witness. God does not speak of punishment with pleasure; he warns honestly. Interpreters understand this hiding of the face as the consequences of turning away from him, not as a permanent abandonment.

For today: examine which things take God's place in your heart, such as money, success, or comfort. Return to him sincerely, for he always invites repentance.
exp.21:17:
It says that when a husband falsely accuses his wife of not having been a virgin, the leaders of the people, called the elders, must take him and discipline him. The word "discipline" here means that they would impose a penalty or correction on him. The verses that follow make clear that he would also have to pay a fine of one hundred pieces of silver.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law protected a young woman and her family from a false accusation that could ruin her name and her future. The parents would present the evidence before the elders, who acted as judges at the city gates.

For today: God takes seriously words that damage the reputation of others. Before accusing someone, or repeating a rumor, let us ask ourselves whether it is true and whether we are saying it out of a love for justice or out of resentment.
exp.20:17:
This verse describes a son who is "stubborn and rebellious": someone set against all authority, who resists being guided. It is not a passing mistake. His parents have already spoken to him and corrected him, and still he does not obey.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and explains how to live as a just community. This case comes after a law about inheritance, which protected the rights of the firstborn. The verses that follow show that parents did not decide alone: they brought the case before the elders. This limited the father's power. Scholars debate how this law was applied in practice.

For today: correction in the family requires patience, consistency, and also the support of a wise community. If you care for children or young people, seek help rather than acting in anger.
exp.10:27:
The passage says there will be a curse if the people do not listen to God's commandments and turn aside from the way Moses commands them. That turning aside consists of following other gods, that is, strange gods, which they had never known.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He sets before them two ways: to obey God and receive a blessing, or to abandon him and suffer the consequences. He reminds them of what God had already done for them, so that they will follow him with confidence.

For today: let us ask what things compete with God in our hearts. We can begin the day by listening to his Word and deciding to follow him, trusting that his way is the best.
exp.2:24:
Moses asks God to let him cross the Jordan River to see the good land on the other side. The phrase "I pray thee" in the verse is simply a polite way of saying "I beg you," so that sentence has been rewritten to match the wording of the verse your reader sees. The phrase "that goodly mountain" probably refers to the mountainous region of that land, and "Lebanon" is the mountain area to the north, famous for its cedars.

Moses speaks after leading the people of Israel through the desert for many years. They had already defeated some kings, and he longed to enter the promised land. However, God told him he would not cross over, and allowed him only to look at it from Mount Pisgah. The text connects this with what had happened earlier between Moses and the people.

For today: we can bring our desires before God with sincerity, as Moses did. If the answer is no, let us trust that God remains good and wise, and give thanks for what he does allow us to see and live.
exp.23:4:
He says a newly married man should not go out to war or be given other public duties or burdens. He had one free year at home to bring joy to his wife. "Cheer up" here means giving her joy, company, and security. The phrase about being given other duties means that no other tasks would be assigned to him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and repeats God's laws for life in community. This command protects the beginning of marriage. It belongs among laws that care for people, especially the most vulnerable, such as the wife and the poor. Some think it also aimed to keep a young woman from being left a widow without children, though the text does not say so.

For today: give your marriage real priority, especially at the beginning. Devote time, attention, and affection to your spouse, and do not let work take over everything.
exp.27:1:
This verse promises that God's blessings will come upon his people and "overtake" them, as if they were chasing and catching up with them along the way. The condition is to listen closely to the voice of the Lord, which in biblical language means to listen and obey.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, just before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: if they obey him, they will live under his care. These blessings were given to Israel as a nation, within that specific covenant.

For today: God does not ask for obedience in order to control us, but to guide us toward a good life. Today you can choose one concrete action that God asks of you, such as forgiving or being honest, and do it with trust in his care, without using obedience as a formula to get things.
exp.16:15:
It says that the king of Israel was not to gather many horses for himself, nor send the people back to Egypt to get them. The Lord had already told them not to go back that way.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions for the day they might ask for a king. In that time, horses were military strength, and Egypt was famous for them. Many understand that God wanted the king to trust in Him and not in his armed power. It also reminded them that Egypt had been the place of their slavery. The instructions that follow speak of not multiplying wives or riches.

For today: let us ask ourselves in what things we trust more than God, such as money, connections, or security. We may use them with gratitude, but without putting them in His place.
exp.5:3:
Here the verse says that Israel must listen closely: the Lord, whom the people call "our God," is "one." The name of God is rendered in the traditional form. The phrase "the Lord is one" can be understood as meaning that the Lord is unique, or that only the Lord is our God. Scholars debate which nuance weighs more, and both fit with the rest of the Bible. "Hear" here means to listen and obey.

Moses speaks near the end of his life to a new generation ready to enter the promised land. He reminds them that God gave them his commandments so that they would respect him, so that things would go well for them, and so that they would pass them on to their children. This verse is the center of that message, and what follows is to love him with all one's being.

For today: before rushing off with your own concerns, take a few minutes to listen to God in his Word. Ask him to be first in your heart, without dividing your loyalty among many things.
exp.27:66:
It says the person will live with such distress that they will never be at rest. In the morning they will wish it were evening, and in the evening they will wish it were morning, seeking to escape the fear. "Would God it were" means "I wish it were." "Terrified" means filled with dread. Also, the fear comes from what their eyes will see.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them the blessings of obeying God and the consequences of abandoning his covenant. This passage describes the last part of those warnings: exile, insecurity and slavery. It is a serious warning, not a hopeless threat, since other passages speak of restoration.

For today: when fear does not let you rest, do not keep it to yourself. Pray honestly, seek God, and also seek help from trusted people. His peace sustains the anxious heart.
exp.25:5:
This verse tells that the Egyptians mistreated the people of Israel. "Mistreated" and "afflicted" speak of abuse and suffering. "Hard bondage" means forced, heavy labor, like that of a slave.

The one speaking is the Israelite who brings the first part of his harvest to the sanctuary. The priest receives the basket, and the person recites this brief history of the people. Moses gives these instructions before they enter the promised land. Remembering the past pain, and also how God rescued them, gave meaning to their offering of gratitude.

For today: when you thank God, remember also the difficult times from which He sustained or delivered you. Seeing your whole story, with its struggles and its help, makes your gratitude more honest and more deep.
exp.4:18:
This verse forbids taking what belongs to another person without their permission. The word "steal" here refers to taking something that is not yours, keeping for yourself what belongs to someone else. It is one of the Ten Commandments.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the law that God gave on Mount Sinai. This commandment protects each person's property and labor, and helps the community live with trust and justice. Some scholars think it also included the kidnapping of people, but this is understood in different ways.

Today we can apply it by being honest in small things: not copying another person's work, not using pirated software, paying fairly those who work for us, and returning what was lent to us. Honesty shows that we trust that God provides.
exp.10:5:
It says that God also acted against Dathan and Abiram, sons of Eliab, of the tribe of Reuben. The earth opened and swallowed them, along with their households, their tents, and everything they had, in the midst of all Israel. The word "substance" refers to their goods or property; "after them" points to everything that followed them.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what they themselves saw: the rescue at the sea and the judgment on the rebels. This event is told in Numbers 16, when Dathan and Abiram rose up against the leadership that God had put in place. Moses wants that memory to lead them to obey.

For today: remembering what God has done helps us take it seriously and walk in humility. When I feel pride or the urge to rebel, I can stop, ask forgiveness, and trust again in his guidance.
exp.13:0:
It says the Israelites are children of God, and for that reason they must not cut their bodies or shave the front of their heads as a sign of mourning for the dead. (The phrase here meaning shaving the hair from the forehead is rendered in the verse above as "make any baldness between your eyes.") "Cutting" means making gashes in the skin.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they belong to God and must be different. Many neighboring peoples had mourning rites involving wounds; some scholars link these to pagan religious practices, though the exact details are not fully known. The next verse gives the reason: they are a holy people, chosen by God.

For today: we can truly grieve those we lose, since mourning is human. But we do it as children of God, with hope, without despairing or harming ourselves, trusting that our Father cares for us.
exp.6:14:
This verse promises that God would take sickness away from his people. It also says that the terrible plagues of Egypt, which the Israelites knew well, would not fall on them. Those plagues would instead fall on those who hate them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the blessings of the covenant if they obey God and remain faithful to him, without following the gods of other peoples. This is a promise given to that nation in that covenant. Christians interpret it in different ways regarding how it applies today.

For today: we can trust that God cares for us and sustains us, even though he does not always keep us free from every illness. His faithfulness invites us to obey him with gratitude and to rest in his protection.
exp.21:11:
This verse says that the people of Israel were to put tassels or fringes on the four corners of the cloak they wrapped themselves in. "Corners" means the corners or edges, and fringes are hanging threads.

Moses speaks to God's people before they enter the promised land, giving them instructions for living as a set-apart people. The verse sits among laws about keeping different things separate and about everyday life. Numbers 15:37-41 explains the purpose: the tassels helped people remember the Lord's commandments. Other details about how they were used are interpreted in different ways.

For today: God is interested in the ordinary and wants us to remember him in simple things. We can choose a small habit, such as praying as we get dressed or reading a verse as we leave the house, that reminds us to obey him throughout the day.
exp.12:1:
This verse speaks of a prophet or dreamer who announces a sign or wonder, and that sign really does come to pass. Yet he uses that fulfilled event to invite the people to follow other gods, meaning strange gods that Israel had not known, and to serve them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them that a miracle is not enough to prove that someone speaks on God's behalf. According to the text, God allows that test to see whether they love him with all their heart and all their soul.

Today, let us not measure truth only by how impressive or successful someone appears. Let us compare every message with what God has already revealed in his Word, and let us remain faithful to Jehovah.
exp.0:33:
It says that God heard what the people of Israel had said, became angry, and confirmed it with an oath, that is, a solemn promise. "Was wroth" means "was angry." "The voice of your words" means "what you said."

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them of what happened at Kadesh-barnea: after the report of the spies, the people doubted and complained, even though God had guided them with fire and cloud. Because of that lack of trust, that generation did not enter the promised land. Only Caleb, who followed God faithfully, would receive that promise.

God hears our words, including words of complaint and distrust. Today we can be careful about what we say in difficult times and, instead of grumbling, remember how God has guided us before and trust Him.
exp.14:8:
It says we must take care not to have a wicked thought in our heart. Someone might think: "The seventh year, when debts are canceled, is almost here, so it's better not to lend anything." "Evil eye" means looking at the needy with selfishness or contempt. "Poor man" refers to a person who is poor. If the poor person cries out to God, the selfishness will be counted as sin.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains the law of the year of release, when debts between Israelite brothers were forgiven. God wanted to prevent anyone from using that law as an excuse not to help.

Today, we can examine our motives when we give or help. If someone is in need, let us not look for excuses to refuse. Let us ask God for a generous heart and help in concrete ways, according to what we are able to do.
exp.3:14:
It says that the people must take great care of their inner life and their faithfulness to God. The reason is that when the Lord spoke to them from the fire on Mount Horeb, they heard his voice but saw no form or shape at all. "Take heed to yourselves" means to be very careful with yourselves. "Likeness" means a visible form or image.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant and the Ten Commandments. Since God showed no image, they must not make idols to represent him. It is a warning against idolatry, which comes up in the verses that follow.

Today we too can invent an idea of God that suits us. To take care of your soul, know God by what he has said in his Word, not by what you imagine or what is convenient for you. Read the Bible with humility and let it correct your ideas about him.
exp.3:20:
Moses says that God was angry with him "for your sakes." (The source phrase is rendered here as the reader's own wording: the anger was because of what happened with the people.) God swore that Moses would not cross the Jordan River or enter the good land that God would give Israel as an inheritance, that is, as a possession received as a gift.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He warns them against idolatry and reminds them that God brought them out of Egypt. His own prohibition from entering the land serves as a serious example. According to Numbers 20, Moses did not honor God as holy at Meribah. Here, however, he connects his own situation with the situation of the people.

For today: God is good, but he is also holy and serious. Obeying him matters, and his promises stand firm even when we face consequences. We can learn to take his word with respect and trust.
exp.18:4:
This verse gives an example of accidental death. Two men go together into the forest to cut wood. One swings the axe, the head comes loose from the handle and kills his companion. The one who caused the death without meaning to may flee to one of the cities of refuge and save his life. Those cities are the ones God commanded to be set apart.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. God orders the creation of cities of refuge to distinguish between murder and accident. In this way, a relative moved by anger could not kill an innocent person, and justice was protected in the land.

For today: before judging someone, try to understand their intentions and the circumstances. God is concerned with the heart, not only with the result. This invites us to be fair, to show mercy, and not to act driven by anger.
exp.21:28:
It says that if a man takes a young virgin who was not engaged, and lies with her, and they are discovered, he must pay her father fifty pieces of silver. Also, she will be his wife, and he may never divorce her. "Lie with her" is an old way of speaking about sexual relations. "Humbled her" means that he dishonored her or left her in a situation of shame and disadvantage.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, giving them laws for their life together as a community. In that society, a woman without a husband was very vulnerable. This law obligated the man to answer financially and to take on his responsibility for life. Scholars debate whether the woman could refuse the marriage; the text does not make this clear.

For today: God expects that no one uses another person and then walks away. Every act has consequences, and we must honestly take responsibility for the harm we cause.
exp.11:2:
It says that Israel was to tear down the altars of the peoples of Canaan, break their pillars or sacred images, and burn their wooden poles, which were posts or trees dedicated to the goddess Asherah. It also says they were to cut down the carved images of their gods and wipe out their names from that place.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them the laws for living there. He wants to protect them from idolatry, which could turn them away from God. The verses that follow say that they would worship God in a different way, in the place He chose.

For today: Jesus does not ask us to destroy other people's places of worship, but to guard our hearts. We can ask ourselves what thing has taken the place of God in our lives, such as money, fame, or pride. With God's help, we need to remove that place and put Him back first.
exp.22:22:
This verse commands that the promises we make to God be kept. The word translated as "keep" in the original text means to fulfill faithfully. "That which is gone out of thy lips" refers to the words you have spoken, and "freewill" means that you made the promise willingly, without anyone forcing you to.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He repeats God's law to them. Vows were voluntary promises made to God, such as an offering or a commitment. No one was required to make them, but whoever did make one had to keep it without delay, because God takes seriously the word that has been given.

For today: think before you promise something to God or to others. If you have already promised, keep your word. And if you cannot do it, it is better not to promise carelessly, but to speak with sincerity.
exp.30:10:
This verse commands that when all Israel gathers before God in the place he chooses, this law be read aloud so that everyone can hear it. The word "come" in the verse is the form of the word for "gather" or "arrive," and "before the Lord" means coming together to worship him. The phrase "in their hearing" means they were to hear it directly.

Moses speaks shortly before he dies. He has already written the law and handed it to the priests and the elders. He orders that every seven years, during the Feast of Tabernacles, it be read before the whole people: men, women, children, and foreigners. He wanted the people not to forget the covenant when they entered the promised land, and for the new generations to also learn to fear God.

For today: God's Word is not only for specialists. Find a regular time to read and listen to it, at church or at home with family, and include the children so that they also come to know it.
exp.16:2:
This verse describes the sin of an Israelite who turned away from the true God to serve other gods. He bowed down before them, including the sun, the moon, or any of the host of heaven, that is, the stars. "Strange gods" means gods belonging to others, foreign gods. God makes it clear that this is something he had not commanded.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God had rescued them and made a covenant with them. Worshiping other gods was breaking that covenant, like a betrayal. That is why, in this law for Israel, the punishment was very severe and required a careful investigation before any action was taken.

Today we do not worship the stars, but we can give other things the place that belongs to God: money, fame, work, or pleasure. Ask yourself honestly what occupies your heart, and give God first place.
exp.2:2:
It says that God gave Israel victory over Og, king of Bashan, and over all his army and his people. Israel defeated them until no survivor was left. The word for "smote" means they struck them down or defeated them in battle, and the phrase "delivered into our hands" means that God gave them the triumph.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them how God helped them before they entered the promised land. Og came out to fight against them, but God had already promised the victory, just as with King Sihon. This war is hard to read; the text presents it as a judgment and a unique action in Israel's history, not as a model for today.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, remember how God has helped you before. That remembrance strengthens confidence to keep going, without fear and with obedience.
exp.32:24:
This verse is part of the blessing on the tribe of Asher. "Shoes" refers to the bars or bolts of the gates, according to some translators, or to footwear; the word in the original is rare and is understood in several ways. "Iron and brass" speak of firmness and protection. The second part promises that Asher's strength will reach him each day, according to what he needs.

Moses speaks just before he dies. He blesses the twelve tribes of Israel, one by one. To Asher he speaks of abundance, with oil and good relations with his brothers. Then comes this promise of protection and strength. Afterward Moses reminds them that the true source of everything is God, who is a refuge and sustains with everlasting arms.

For today: God does not promise that there will be no hard days, but strength enough for each one. Today you can face your tasks and trials trusting that He sustains you, without being anxious about tomorrow.
exp.2:14:
This verse says: "And I gave Gilead unto Machir." The word "gave" in the verse is the one the verse discusses, and it means "handed over" or "assigned."

Machir was a descendant of Manasseh, and Gilead was a region east of the Jordan River.

Here Moses speaks, reminding the people of Israel how the conquered lands were divided before they entered Canaan. God had given them victory over the kings of that area, and Moses assigned part of the territory to the half-tribe of Manasseh, in particular to the family of Machir. Some details of how that region was divided are explained more fully in other passages, such as Numbers 32.

For today: God takes care that each person and each family has a place and a responsibility. We can give thanks for what He has entrusted to us and manage it faithfully, without comparing ourselves to others.
exp.16:11:
This verse says that whoever acts presumptuously, refusing to obey the priest who serves before God or the judge, must die. The phrase "do presumptuously" means acting with arrogance and deliberate rebellion. "Put away the evil from Israel" means that this wickedness had to be removed from the people so that it would not spread.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. In difficult cases they were to go to the place God would choose and accept the decision of the priest and the judge. The penalty was severe because Israel was a nation under its covenant with God, and open defiance of that justice threatened the unity of the people. This law was meant for that time and that nation.

Today we can learn to live with humility: to listen to wise counsel, to respect fair authorities, and not to harden our hearts when someone corrects us.
exp.1:16:
This verse is short: Moses tells that God spoke to him, and what follows is what God said to him. "Jehovah" is the name of God, and "spoke unto me, saying" introduces a command or instruction.

Moses is reminding the new generation of Israel of the years in the wilderness. The whole generation of fighting men who had rebelled had already died, just as God had said. Now, as that time of waiting comes to an end, God gives the first instruction: to pass through the region of Moab and not to trouble the Ammonites, descendants of Lot, because God had given them that land.

For today: God has his time and his tasks for each stage. After waiting, he speaks again and guides. We can learn to listen to his voice and to respect the limits he sets, without wanting to keep what does not belong to us.
exp.11:16:
It says that the Israelite could not eat in his own town the things dedicated to God: the tithe of the grain, of the wine and of the oil, the firstborn of his herds and flocks, what was promised in vows, and the freewill offerings. "Towns" are the cities or villages. "Firstlings" are the first young of the animals. "Elevated offerings" were those presented by lifting them up before God.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He teaches them that they could eat ordinary meat in any place, but what was set apart had to be brought to the place God would choose. There they would eat it as a family, with joy, together with the Levite. In this way, the worship and those who served in it were cared for.

For today: what we give to God is not a formality, but an act of gratitude. We can set aside the first of our resources and time for God, and share it joyfully, remembering also to support those who serve in the church.
exp.29:15:
This verse says that God, through Moses, commands his people to love him, to live as he teaches, and to obey everything he has commanded. "Statutes" are his rules and "judgments" are his just decisions. If they do this, they will have life, they will increase in number, and God will bless them in the land they are about to receive.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before his death, when they are about to cross the Jordan. He reminds them that God's word is not distant or impossible: it is near, in their mouth and in their heart. He sets before them two ways, life and death, so that they may choose with responsibility.

For today: love for God is lived out in daily decisions. Today you can choose a concrete action, such as praying before deciding something or being honest in a difficult situation, and do it out of love for God.
exp.13:22:
This verse says that the people were to eat, in the presence of God, a tenth of their harvest (grain, wine, and oil) and the firstborn of their animals. They would do this in the place that God chose to set his name there. "Firstlings" are the firstborn young of the animals; the "herds" are the larger livestock and the "flocks" the smaller. The purpose was to learn to fear the Lord their God always, that is, to respect him and to live in reverence toward him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they are a holy people, set apart for God. This tithe was brought to the place of worship and shared with joy, like a festival before the Lord.

For today: make your gratitude to God something concrete and constant. Giving generously, and gathering with others to celebrate his blessings, helps you remember that everything you have comes from him.
exp.22:18:
It says that an Israelite was not to charge another Israelite any "interest" on what he lent. That is, no extra gain on the loan. This applied to money, food, or anything else that was commonly lent at a profit.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and reminds them of God's laws. Loans in that time were usually meant to help a brother in need, not to make a business deal. That is why God asked for compassion and not for taking advantage of the poor. The next verse permits charging interest to a foreigner, and promises blessing to whoever obeys.

For today: when someone in your family, church, or close circle goes through a hard time, help them generously and without seeking to profit from it. Lend with their good in mind, not your own gain.
exp.14:5:
He says that when God blesses Israel as he promised, they will have such abundance that they will be able to lend to many nations and will not need to borrow. The phrase about ruling over them means you will have dominance or influence over those nations, and the phrase about them not ruling over you means that no one will dominate you.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the blessing depends on faithfully obeying God. The passage speaks of the year of debt release and of caring for the poor, so that there would be no beggars among them.

For today: God's blessing is not only meant to be enjoyed, but also shared. We can live wisely in handling money, avoiding debts that enslave us, and be generous toward those who are in need. It is a promise given to Israel, so it should not be read as an automatic guarantee of wealth.
exp.22:14:
It says that if a servant escapes from his master and comes to you seeking refuge, you must not return him. "Deliver" means to give back or to put into another's hands. "Servant" is a slave or a bound worker, and "master" is his owner. "Escaped" means that he fled.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and passes on the laws of God. Many interpreters believe this refers to a servant who flees from a cruel master, perhaps from another nation. Others think the text is broader. The following verse lets him live freely among them, without anyone oppressing him.

For today: God cares for those who flee oppression. We can be people who offer refuge, protection and fair treatment to those who suffer abuse, without taking advantage of their weakness.
exp.31:33:
God asks whether he has not stored up, as something sealed among his treasures, what is coming upon the wicked. "Sealed" means closed and secured, so that nothing is lost or changed. The idea is that judgment has not been forgotten; it is kept for its proper time.

These words are part of the Song of Moses, where God speaks about the rebellion of Israel and of hostile nations. The verses before describe their wickedness as bitter grapes and poison. Many understand that this refers to Israel's enemies, though some think it also reaches the unfaithful people. The verses that follow say that vengeance belongs to God.

For today: when you see injustice, do not grow bitter or take revenge on your own. Trust that God sees everything, keeps it in mind, and will act with justice in his time.
exp.0:23:
They say that the twelve chosen men set out, went up into the mountain country, and came as far as the valley of Eshcol. There they searched out the land. Here "searched out" means to explore and to observe carefully.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, and reminds them of what happened at Kadesh-barnea. It was the people who asked that scouts be sent, and Moses agreed. The twelve returned saying the land was good, but the people did not want to go up and rebelled against God.

For today: seeing the good that God has prepared is not enough; trust in Him and taking the step is needed. When God shows you an open door, ask Him for courage to obey instead of remaining paralyzed by fear.
exp.1:32:
It says that God handed King Sihon over into the hands of Israel, and that the Israelites defeated him together with his sons and all his people. The phrase "delivered him before us" means that God gave them the victory. The word "smote" means that they defeated him in battle.

The one speaking is Moses, who is reminding the new generation of Israel, before they enter the promised land, of what happened when Sihon came out to fight against them at Jahaz. Moses wants them to remember that the victory came from God. These accounts of war are difficult, and they are read within the ancient history of Israel and its entry into Canaan.

For today: when you face something great, remember the times God has sustained you. Give thanks, trust in Him, and move forward with humility, without boasting in your own strength.
exp.9:4:
Moses tells how he came down from Mount Sinai with the two new stone tablets and placed them in the chest he had made. The "tablets" were the two stones with the Ten Commandments. Moses adds that they are still there, just as the Lord commanded him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of his life and reminds them of their history. Earlier, the people had sinned with the golden calf, and Moses broke the first tablets. God, in his mercy, wrote new ones. Moses wants them to remember that grace and to be faithful.

God gives us his word to keep carefully and to obey. We can give it a central place in daily life: reading it, remembering it, and trusting it, grateful that God gives us new opportunities.
exp.30:25:
Moses commands the Levites to take the book of the law and put it beside the ark of the covenant. There it must remain as a witness against the people. The words "Take" and "put it" are used in the same sense as "take" and "put" in the verse above, and "remain there as a witness" means that it will serve as proof of what God said.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, just after finishing writing down the law. He knows the people have been stubborn, and so he says they will rebel even more after he dies. The book was not placed inside the ark but beside it, and scholars understand this as a place of safekeeping and constant reminder.

God speaks to us clearly so that we cannot say we did not know. Today we can read his Word with humility, letting it correct us in time and guide us back to him.
exp.9:18:
It says that the people must love the stranger, that is, the person who lives among them but comes from another land. The reason is that they themselves were strangers in Egypt.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just told them that God is just, defends the orphan and the widow, and loves the stranger by giving him food and clothing. If God cares in this way, his people should imitate him. Besides, they remembered what it was to live without a home of their own and without rights.

Today we can notice some immigrant, new neighbor, or person who feels out of place in our church or workplace. We can greet them, help them with something concrete, and treat them with respect, remembering how much God helped us.
exp.13:23:
This verse deals with a practical problem. If the place God chose for worship was very far away, and the road was so long that a person could not carry the tithe (the tenth part of the harvest and of the animals), the person was not left without options. The phrase "carry it" refers to carrying the tithe along that road, as the verse itself says. The phrase "when the Lord thy God hath blessed thee" shows that the problem arises because God had given a good harvest.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions for their life there. The tithe was to be eaten with joy before God, so that they would learn to revere and honor him. The law took into account the distance and the real difficulty people faced.

For today: God is concerned with our practical limitations, but he wants us to honor him with gratitude. When he blesses us, let us use what we have with joy, generosity, and thankfulness, without making excuses.
exp.26:6:
It says that, after offering the burnt offering, Israel was to present peace offerings, eat right there with their families, and rejoice before God. The peace offerings are sacrifices of fellowship or thanksgiving, of which the people could eat.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He tells them that, on crossing the Jordan, they are to build an altar on Mount Ebal, using uncut stones, and write down the law. That moment would be a renewal of the covenant: God was making them his people, and their response included dedication, gratitude, and celebration.

For today: life with God is not only duty, it is also joy. Make your gratitude something concrete: share a meal with your family or your church, thank God out loud for what he has done, and rejoice freely in his presence.
exp.33:10:
This verse continues the previous sentence: no other prophet arose like Moses, in the signs and wonders that God sent him to perform in Egypt. Those works were directed at Pharaoh, his servants (his officials and attendants), and all his land.

These words close the book of Deuteronomy. They were probably added after the death of Moses, and it is not known with certainty who wrote them. The text sums up the greatness of Moses, recalling the plagues and Israel's deliverance from Egypt, which showed the power of God.

Today we can remember that God is the one who acts and sustains his servants. Moses was great because God was with him. If God has given you a task, trust in his power more than in your own strength, and give him the glory.
exp.10:15:
Take heed to yourselves, so that your heart is not deceived. It means we must watch ourselves so that our heart is not led astray, not fooled, and not filled with pride and foolishness. When that happens, a person turns away from God, serves other gods, and bows down before them to worship them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. Just before this, he reminds them that God will give them rain and an abundant harvest. Then he warns them that if they worship other gods, the rain will stop. In that time, the harvest depended greatly on rain, and the neighboring peoples worshiped gods connected with it.

When everything is going well, it is easy to trust in what we receive and forget the One who gives it. Today we can guard our hearts by thanking God every day and asking ourselves what things are taking his place in our trust.
exp.4:9:
This verse says that God shows loyal and kind love to thousands of people, that is, to many generations, who love him and obey his commandments. Here "mercy" means loyal, kind love. "Thousands" means a great number. Some understand it to refer to thousands of generations, and others simply to a very large number of people.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, who are about to enter the promised land. He repeats the Ten Commandments to them. Just before, God speaks of his zeal against idolatry and of the consequences of sin. This verse shows the contrast: God's kindness outweighs his judgment, and his love reaches much farther.

For today: loving God and obeying him is not a cold burden. It is a response to someone who loved us first. Today you can choose one concrete act of obedience, and trust that God is faithful and kind.
exp.12:15:
If a city of Israel gave itself entirely to worshiping other gods, all its spoil was gathered into the middle of the street and burned together with the city, as a whole offering to the Lord. "Spoil" is what is taken from a conquered city. It would be left as "a heap," that is, ruins, and it was never to be rebuilt.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He warns them against idolatry, which could corrupt the whole nation. The law requires careful investigation before any action is taken. The "devoted" things were set apart for God and could not be used for personal gain. It is a hard text, tied to the unique situation of Israel as a nation under that covenant. Christians do not take it as a model for punishing others.

For today: God deserves total loyalty. Ask yourself what thing competes with God in your heart, and remove its place there with determination, not with violence toward anyone.
exp.3:45:
This verse tells where the people of Israel were when Moses explained the law to them. They were on the east side of the Jordan River, in a valley facing Beth-peor, in the land that once belonged to Sihon, king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon. Moses and the Israelites defeated him after they had come out of Egypt. The word "smote" here means that they won the battle against him.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who presents the place where Moses spoke. Israel was about to enter the promised land. Moses was reminding them of the law and showing them how God had already given them victories along the way.

For today: when you doubt the future, remember how God has helped you in the past. That grateful memory can give you courage to obey Him and trust Him with what is ahead.
exp.19:10:
It says that if a distant city accepted the offer of peace and opened its gates, all its people would become "tributaries," that is, they would pay taxes or provide labor, and they would "serve you," meaning they would work for Israel.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. These rules refer to cities outside Canaan; for the cities of Canaan a different and harsher rule applied (vv. 16-18). First they were to offer peace, which limited violence. Today people debate how to understand these ancient laws of war, but it is clear that peace came first.

For today: when a conflict arises, before raising your voice or looking for a fight, offer a way toward peace. Speak first, listen, and work for reconciliation, as Romans 12:18 teaches.
exp.7:17:
This verse says that we should always remember the Lord, because it is God who gives us the strength or ability to acquire wealth. He does this so that his covenant is fulfilled, that is, the solemn promise he swore to Israel's ancestors. The verse's phrasing, as it is this day, is seen in the words "as it is this day" in the King James Version, which points to the present time.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them how God cared for them in the desert with the manna. He fears that, once they prosper, they will think everything came from their own effort and forget God.

For today: when something goes well for you at work or in your finances, thank God and recognize that he gave you health, opportunities, and abilities. Also, use what you have with generosity and humility, without boasting.
exp.13:5:
This verse gives a general rule: Israel could eat any animal that had a split hoof and that also chewed the cud, that is, that brings back up and chews again the food it has already swallowed. The word "claws" here means the parts of the hoof, the divided sections. The animals in the list before this verse meet that rule.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the laws God gave them so that they would live as a people set apart for Him. The verses that follow give examples of animals that were considered unclean. Scholars explain the purpose of these rules in several ways: identity, obedience, or symbolism of purity. The Bible does not give all the reasons.

For today: although Christians are not under these dietary rules, we can learn to obey God in everyday life, even in small things, remembering that our whole life belongs to Him.
exp.3:22:
It says the people must take great care not to forget the covenant God made with them. "Take heed" means "be careful." A carved image is a figure cut or shaped from material, and a likeness is a representation of something. "Forbidden" means "prohibited." Thus, God forbids them to make figures to worship them, whatever they may be.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He himself will not cross the Jordan, and so he warns them with urgency. He wants them, once he is no longer with them, to remember what God commanded them. He is also speaking with their children and grandchildren in mind.

For today: we can ask ourselves what things have taken the place of God in our hearts. To avoid forgetting him, it helps to read his Word every day and to remember with gratitude what he has done for us.
exp.31:40:
God says that if he sharpens his glittering sword and takes judgment in his hand, he will repay his enemies and give their due to those who hate him. The words "vengeance" and "payment" in the source are not part of the English verse, so they are simply rendered by the verse's own wording: "render vengeance" and "reward." The phrase about taking hold firmly is translated directly from the verse's "mine hand take hold on judgment."

It is part of the Song of Moses. God speaks to the people of Israel, who often abandoned him for other gods. He reminds them that he alone is God, that he gives life and takes life, and that in the end he will defend his people and bring justice against evil and oppression.

For today: we do not have to take revenge on our own. We can hand over to God our wounds and injustices, trust that he is just, and ask him for strength to forgive and to do good, as the New Testament teaches in Romans 12:19-21.
exp.27:32:
It says that another nation, one unknown to Israel, would eat what the land produces and everything that cost labor to obtain. "Broken" means shattered, crushed inside and out. "Oppressed" means treated harshly and unjustly. And this would be the case all the time, without rest or relief.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings if they obey God, and curses, or serious consequences, if they abandon him. This verse is part of a serious warning about losing the fruits of their work under the rule of enemies.

For today: God warns us out of love because he wants to see us well. Today you can examine whether there is something in your life where you have stopped listening to him, and return to him with humility, trusting that his forgiveness and his guidance are still available.
exp.31:21:
It says that God's anger is like a fire that is kindled and reaches to the lowest depths. "The lowest hell" in the verse is rendered here as the place of the dead, and that fire consumes the earth, its harvests, and even the foundations of the mountains. It is a poetic image that shows how serious God's judgment is.

God speaks in the Song of Moses, shortly before Moses died. God warns that Israel, after receiving so many blessings, would turn to idols. For that reason he announces harsh consequences, but the song also speaks of his compassion, for in the end he has pity on his people.

For today: let us not take faithfulness to God lightly. If anything takes the place that belongs only to him, it is wise to return to him soon, for he is just, but also merciful.
exp.23:8:
It says that the people must remember what God did to Miriam, the sister of Moses, during the journey after they came out of Egypt. "The Lord" is the name of God, and "Miriam" is the same name as "Mary" in other translations. The text does not repeat the story here, but it refers to Numbers 12, when Miriam spoke against Moses and was struck with leprosy for a time.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just given instructions about leprosy and about obeying the priests. This example shows that no one is above God's correction, not even a person very close to the leader. It is a warning to take sickness and obedience seriously.

For today: learn from the mistakes you already know. If God has corrected you, or you have seen how he corrects others, do not harden your heart. Guard your words, especially about those who lead you, and respond with humility.
exp.3:31:
Moses invites the people to investigate all of human history, from the day God created man and from one end of heaven to the other, to see whether anything as great as what Israel experienced has ever happened. The words "created," "end," and "anything like this great thing" are the ones the verse uses, so no further explanation of them is needed here.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God spoke to them from the fire on the mountain and brought them out of Egypt with great power.
