He wants their faith to rest on what God truly did, so that they will remain faithful to Him and not turn away after other gods.

For today: when you doubt or feel far from God, remember what He has done, both in the Bible and in your own life. Remembering His faithfulness strengthens trust and encourages us to obey Him with gratitude.
exp.8:28:
This verse says that the people of Israel belong to God. An "inheritance" means something very precious that a person owns and cares for, like something passed down to them. God brought them out of Egypt by his "mighty power" and his "outstretched arm," which are ways of speaking of his power to rescue.

The one speaking is Moses. He tells how he prayed to God after the people made the golden calf. Instead of defending the people on the basis of their merits, Moses appeals to God's character, to his promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to his reputation among the nations.

For today: when you fail, do not trust in your good behavior, but in the fact that God loves you and rescued you. That assurance is not an excuse to sin, but a reason to return to him with humility and to pray for others as well.
exp.24:13:
This verse says that in your house you must not keep two different measures: one large and one small. The measure for grain and dry goods was a standard unit. Having two meant you could cheat: using the large one to buy and the small one to sell.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and he gives them laws for living justly. The verse before this one also forbids having false weights in your bag. Then it says that God regards fraud as detestable. Merchants of that time depended on weights and measures, and it was easy to take advantage of others.

For today: be honest in what you give and in what you charge. Whether in your work, your business, or your dealings, do not use two measures. Treat others as you would want to be treated.
exp.21:0:
This verse says that if you see your brother's ox or sheep has gone astray, you must not pretend you didn't see it and simply walk away. The phrase about turning away from them means setting yourself apart from them, washing your hands of them. And the phrase about bringing them back means that without fail you must return them to him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and explains how to live as God's community. Animals were the livelihood of a family, so losing them was a serious blow. The law asks people to care for their neighbor's property, even if he lives far away or you don't know him.

For today: if you find something that isn't yours, such as a wallet, a phone, or money, make an effort to find its owner and return it. Loving your neighbor includes caring for what is his, even when no one sees you or requires it of you.
exp.16:7:
This verse says that when a case is too hard to settle in a city's courts, it must not be left without justice. It speaks of three kinds of cases: deaths, disputes between people, and wounds or assaults. The person was to go to the place that God would choose.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions for living with justice. Earlier, he spoke of requiring enough witnesses, and afterward it says that the Levitical priests and the judge would give the final decision.

For today: when something is too complicated or unjust to resolve on your own, do not be carried along by pride or by haste. Seek wise and trustworthy counsel, and accept the guidance you are given.
exp.8:21:
This verse names three places in the wilderness where the people of Israel provoked the Lord to anger. Taberah, Massah and Kibroth-hattaavah are the names of those places. Taberah is related to a word meaning burning, and Massah is related to a word meaning testing. Kibroth-hattaavah is related to a word meaning graves of those who craved food. The word "ye provoked" in the verse means "you made the Lord angry."

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they do not deserve the land because they are good, but that God gives it because of his faithfulness. In those places, according to the accounts in Exodus and Numbers, the people complained, put God to the test, and craved food. Moses lists these failures so that they will not feel proud.

For today: remembering our past mistakes helps us to be humble and thankful. Everything we have comes from the grace of God, not from our merits. When we complain, we can stop and give thanks.
exp.10:30:
It says that the people of Israel are about to cross the Jordan River to enter the land that God is giving them. It assures them that they will possess it and dwell in it. "Possess" means to take as one's own; "dwell" means that they will live there.

Moses speaks to the people at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, shortly before his death. He reminds them of God's promise and asks them that, upon entering, they proclaim the blessing and the curse on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal. Then he asks them to obey all of God's commandments.

For today: God keeps what he promises, but he invites us to respond with obedience. If you are facing a new step, trust in his faithfulness and walk day by day according to his Word.
exp.32:15:
It says that Moses asks that the land of Joseph be filled with good things, and that the favor of God, the one who appeared to him in the burning bush, rest upon Joseph. The phrase "the top of the head" refers to the crown of the head. The phrase "him that was separated from his brethren" can mean the one set apart from them, or the prince among them. The thought is of Joseph, sold by his brothers and later honored.

Moses speaks shortly before he dies. He is blessing the tribes of Israel, one by one. Here he blesses Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph. He mentions the bush because it was there that God called him and promised to be with his people (Exodus 3).

For today: even if you have been rejected or left alone, God does not forget you. His grace can cover you and give you a place. Trust that the God who drew near to Moses is also near to you.
exp.18:16:
It says that when two people have a dispute, and one accuses the other with a witness suspected of lying, both must present themselves "before the Lord." That means going to the place where God was sought, before the priests and judges who were serving at that time. The people in dispute are the ones who are opposed to each other in the case.

Moses speaks to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He gives them rules so that justice would be serious and fair. Requiring two or three witnesses protected the innocent, and bringing the case before judges and priests reminded them that God sees everything.

For today: if you are in a conflict, do not speak on the basis of rumors or hasty accusations. Seek the truth, go to wise people, and speak as if God were listening, because he is.
exp.2:22:
This verse says that Moses began to pray to God at that moment. The verse for "I prayed to the LORD" is simply that Moses prayed to the Lord. It is only the introduction to a prayer that continues in the verses that follow.

The speaker is Moses, as he reviews the history of Israel before the people, now close to the promised land. He had just encouraged Joshua not to be afraid, because God fights for his people. Then Moses asks God to let him cross the Jordan and see the good land. Later God answers him that he will not cross over (Deuteronomy 3:26-27). The reason is explained in other passages of the book.

For today: when you have a deep desire, bring it to God with sincerity and humility. And if the answer is not the one you hoped for, keep trusting that he is good and faithful.
exp.27:16:
It says that if the people turn away from God, even the most everyday part of their food would suffer. The "basket" was the container where bread or the harvest was kept. The "leftovers" translates a word that others understand as the kneading trough, where dough was prepared. In other words, what is stored and what is prepared to eat would fall under a curse, that is, without blessing or benefit.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: obeying him would bring blessing, and rejecting him would bring painful consequences. These are warnings about a specific covenant with Israel, given to call them to faithfulness.

For today: don't take for granted what you have on your table. Thank God for your food each day, and seek to live with honesty and trust in him, without assuming that every suffering is a punishment.
exp.32:0:
This verse presents the last words of Moses to Israel. It says that Moses, called "man of God," blessed the children of Israel shortly before his death. "Blessing" means words of favor and care from God. "Man of God" was a title for someone who spoke on behalf of the Lord. The phrase "before his death" indicates that these are his final words.

Moses had led Israel out of Egypt through the wilderness for forty years. Now the people were about to enter the promised land, and he would not go in with them. Like a father saying farewell, he blesses each tribe. This chapter resembles the blessing Jacob gave his sons in Genesis 49. Here the narrator introduces the speech, and then Moses begins to speak.

Even at the end of his life, Moses thought of the good of others. We can make the most of our opportunities to bless those we love: speaking words of encouragement to them, praying for them, and reminding them of God's faithfulness, without waiting until the last moment.
exp.30:14:
This verse tells us that God made his presence known in the tabernacle, which was the tent where the people of Israel worshiped him. He did this through a pillar of cloud, which was a visible sign of his presence. The cloud stopped at the entrance of the tent.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Moses was already very old, and God had told him that his death was near. So Moses and Joshua went to the tabernacle, where God was going to entrust Joshua with the task of leading the people. Right away, God also warns Moses that the people would turn away from him.

For today: God continues to guide his people even when the leaders change. We can trust that he is present and seek his direction with humility and prayer.
exp.16:8:
This verse says that when a case was too difficult to settle, the person was to go to the Levite priests and to the judge who was serving in those days. There he would inquire, and they would explain to him what the correct decision was. The sentence that refers to the "á" and the "a" is not needed for your reader, so it has been removed, and the phrase "sentencia del juicio" is covered by the words "the sentence of judgment" in the verse above, which means the decision or ruling of the case.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions so that there will be justice in the cities. When the local judges could not decide, there was a central place, the one God would choose, where the difficult cases were resolved on the basis of God's law.

For today: you do not have to settle the complicated matters alone. When you are unsure between what is right and what is wrong, seek wise, humble counsel grounded in God's Word, and then be willing to obey what you learn.
exp.11:29:
It says that when Israel enters the land and God has destroyed the nations who lived there, they must take care not to fall into the trap of imitating them. "Be snared by following them" means being caught by following them. "Do not inquire about their gods" means: do not even be curious about how they worshiped, in order to copy it.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land, in his farewell. He warns them that the danger would not only be war, but the temptation to mix their faith with the customs of the neighboring peoples. The verses that follow explain that those practices included terrible things, such as sacrificing children.

Today we too can fall into copying what most people do, even when it does not please God. Before following a trend or custom, ask yourself: "Does this honor God according to his Word?" Let that Word be your guide, not the crowd.
exp.0:12:
Moses asks the people to choose from among their tribes men who are wise, discerning, and well known. He will appoint them as leaders. Those who are "discerning" are the ones who reason with good judgment, and those who are "well known" are people with experience who are respected for their good character. "Leaders" means heads or authorities.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, recalling what happened earlier. He felt he could not carry the problems, burdens, and disputes of such a large nation alone. So he proposed sharing the leadership, and the people took part by choosing the individuals, something the verses that follow confirm.

For today: no leader should have to carry everything alone. In the family, the church, or the workplace, it is wise to share responsibilities with people who are wise and of good character, and also to encourage others to serve. In this way the work is cared for, and so are those who carry it.
exp.13:9:
Says that, among the water animals, the people could eat only those that had fins and scales, that is, common fish. Everything else, such as shellfish or eels, was to be avoided. "Unclean" means ceremonially impure, not fit for the people of God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the laws God gave them to live as a set-apart people. These food rules taught them to distinguish the clean from the unclean. Scholars explain the exact reasons in several ways: hygiene, symbolism, or setting themselves apart from other nations. The text emphasizes that they are God's holy people.

Today Christians do not follow these food rules, because Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). But we can learn to live with intention: asking whether our daily habits show that we belong to God.
exp.27:61:
This verse says that the people of Israel, who had grown as numerous as the stars of heaven, would be reduced to very few in number. The reason is plain: they did not obey God. "Few in number" means small in count, and "hearken to the voice of the Lord" means listening to God and heeding what he says.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He sets before them the blessings of obedience and the consequences of rejecting the covenant. This warning follows a long list of curses. It recalls the promise made to Abraham of a numerous descendants, which here would be affected by disobedience.

For today: God gives us blessings and hopes that we will listen to him with a sincere heart. We can ask ourselves which area of our life needs more attention to his voice, and take one concrete step of obedience today, trusting in his goodness.
exp.4:11:
God commands that the Sabbath day be set apart as a special day. The word for "keep" in the source means to look after it and take it seriously. The word for "sanctify" means to treat it as something separated and dedicated to God, different from the other days. The verse then adds "as the Lord thy God hath commanded thee," meaning this had already been taught to them before.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He repeats the Ten Commandments to them. This commandment included sons, servants, animals, and foreigners, so that all could rest. In this version of Deuteronomy, moreover, the rest is linked to the remembrance that God freed them from slavery.

Today we can set apart a weekly time to rest, pray, and be with God and family, without living as slaves to work. We can also look after the rest of those who work alongside us.
exp.7:4:
It says that Israel must acknowledge, that is, reflect on and accept in their hearts, that God corrects them the way a father corrects his son. The verse notes that the wording of the verse, in older language, carries the sense of correcting, disciplining and teaching, not of venting anger.

Moses speaks to the people at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, just before they enter the promised land. He asks them to look back: the hunger, the manna and God's care all had a purpose. God was shaping them so that they would learn to depend on Him and to obey Him.

For today: when you go through a difficult season, do not immediately conclude that God has abandoned you. Ask Him sincerely what He wants to teach you, and trust that His correction comes from a Father's love. Seek His guidance in His Word.
exp.14:10:
He says there will always be people in need in the land, and that is why God commands an open-handed generosity. The needy are those who are poor or in want. "Open your hand" means giving willingly, without clinging to what you have. The command includes your brother, the poor person, and the person in need who lives near you.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. Shortly before, he warned them not to refuse to lend simply because the seventh year was approaching, when debts were canceled. God wanted a generous heart, not a calculating one. This verse probably does not say that poverty is unavoidable, but that it is a constant reality that calls for a response.

For today: think of a person in need close to you, such as a neighbor, a relative, or someone in your church. Ask God how you can help them, and do it this week with joy and without excuses.
exp.6:13:
It says that God would bless Israel more than all the other peoples. No one in the nation, neither man nor woman, would be barren, that is, unable to have children. The same would hold for their animals, which would reproduce well. The word "beasts" refers to livestock or domestic animals.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God will bless them if they obey him and keep his covenant. This promise was given to a specific nation, under the covenant of Moses. For that reason it is not a guarantee that every believer will have children or prosperity.

For today: learn to see life and what you have as a gift from God, and respond with obedience and gratitude. If you are going through a painful situation, such as not being able to have children, remember that God loves you and is with you just the same.
exp.19:7:
This verse says that the officers would speak again to the people before the battle. They would ask who is afraid and weak in spirit. That person could go home. The reason was so that his fear would not spread to his companions. "Fearful" means afraid, "tender of heart" means fragile in courage, and "fainthearted" means that he should not weaken or discourage others.

Moses is giving Israel instructions about war. The officers, who were responsible for passing orders on to the people, would speak before the captains took command. Earlier, they had already allowed anyone with unfinished business to return home. Here the unity of the army is being protected. Some think that the teaching also was that victory depended on God, not on the number of soldiers.

For today: be honest about your fears and ask God for help. Also watch your words, so that instead of spreading discouragement, you encourage those who stand beside you.
exp.31:23:
It says that God will send very harsh calamities on his people: hunger that weakens them, burning fever, a bitter plague, attacks from wild animals, and bites from poisonous snakes. The words "burnt with hunger" mean they will be worn away and destroyed little by little, and "devoured with burning heat" means they will be consumed by the sickness.

It is part of the Song of Moses. God speaks through Moses and announces what would happen if Israel turned away from him to follow other gods. These are warnings about the consequences of breaking the covenant. The verses that follow show that God also limits the punishment and does not destroy them completely.

For today: God warns us out of love, because he does not want to see us suffer. Let us listen to his correction in time, return to him when we stray, and trust in his mercy, which always offers a way back.
exp.25:4:
This verse says that the Israelite, when presenting the firstfruits of his harvest, was to remember his humble origins. The phrase "A Syrian ready to perish" refers to Jacob, who is called an Aramean, from Aram, or Syria. The word rendered "ready to perish" can mean wandering, frail, or close to dying of hunger; translators understand it in several ways. He went down into Egypt with a few men, and there God made him a nation, great, mighty, and numerous.

Moses instructs the people before they enter the promised land. When they bring their basket of firstfruits to the priest, they are to recite this confession. It was not only an offering: it was telling the story of God's faithfulness, from a frail old man to a free people with their own land.

Before boasting of what you have, remember where God brought you from. Gratitude is born when you recognize that what you enjoy today was a gift, not merely the fruit of your own effort. Today, tell someone how God has sustained you.
exp.4:10:
It says we should not use God's name in an empty, false, or disrespectful way. "Taking in vain" can include swearing falsely, using his name carelessly, or calling on him to deceive. "Will not hold him guiltless" means that God will not overlook this offense.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, who are about to enter the promised land. He repeats to them the Ten Commandments, given earlier on Mount Sinai. This is the third commandment. The name of the Lord represents who God is, and for that reason it should be treated with reverence and truthfulness.

For today: take care with your words about God. Avoid saying "I swear to God" over small things, or using his name in jokes or in anger. Also strive to make your life consistent with what you say you believe, so that his name is honored.
exp.6:2:
This verse says that the Israelites were not to marry their children into the families of the seven nations who lived in Canaan. It explains that to make marriages means to join families by marriage. Neither were the daughters of Israel to marry their sons, nor were their sons to take the daughters of those nations.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God would bring them in to possess it. The following verse gives the reason: such marriages could turn the hearts of their children toward other gods. The emphasis is spiritual, not a question of race.

For today: take care with your closest relationships, because they shape your faith. Before you commit to someone or to an important project, ask yourself whether it draws you closer to God or pulls you away. And seek wise counsel and prayer.
exp.32:13:
Here Moses continues blessing the tribe of Joseph. He asks that its land receive the best of the sun and the moon: fruits ripened by the sun and the produce that each month brings. The word "precious" means valuable and excellent. "The precious things put forth by the moon" refers to what the months produce, that is, the harvests of each season.

Moses speaks shortly before he dies. He is taking leave of Israel with blessings for each tribe. For Joseph he wishes a fertile land, and all of it is understood as a gift from God, not as the result of one's own merit.

For today: learn to see everyday things, such as food, the weather, and the work that bears fruit, as gifts from God. Give thanks before you eat, and share generously what you have received.
exp.16:3:
It says that if someone reports to the people a case of idolatry, action should not be taken right away. First one must listen carefully and inquire thoroughly, that is, investigate in depth. Only if it is confirmed that it is true and certain that this abomination (something God detests) was committed in Israel does one move to the next step.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the covenant with God demanded total loyalty, and that worshiping the sun, the moon, or the stars was breaking that covenant. Even so, he requires a fair investigation and, as the text goes on, more than one witness.

For today: before accusing someone or repeating a rumor, let us find out the facts carefully. Truth and justice matter just as much as faithfulness to God.
exp.28:10:
This verse continues the list of those who were present before God: the little ones, the wives, and the foreigners who lived among the people. It even mentions those who did the simplest tasks, such as cutting firewood and carrying water. The phrase about those who lived within the camp means that they lived inside the encampment.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel on the plains of Moab, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God. What matters is that no one is left out: everyone, from the leaders to the most humble, is invited to enter into God's promise.

For today: God does not show partiality in his calling. We can ask ourselves whether in our church or family there is someone we treat as if they mattered less. Today you can reach out to that person, include them, and let them know they are also welcome before God.
exp.6:12:
God promises that he will love his people, bless them, and make them grow. That blessing would reach their children, their harvests, and their animals. The children are the fruit of the womb; the new juice of the grape is the wine; the young of your cattle are the calves. All of this would happen in the land that God promised with an oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God made a covenant with them and calls them to obey his commandments. The blessing is tied to that covenant relationship with God. It was given to Israel in their particular situation, so it should not be read as an automatic promise of wealth for everyone.

For today: God is faithful and generous, and every good thing we have comes from him. Today you can thank him for everyday things, such as your family, your food, and your work, and respond to him with trusting obedience.
exp.12:6:
This verse continues a sentence that begins in the previous verse. It describes the gods that someone may try to persuade you to serve: the gods of the peoples who live near you or far from you, from one end of the earth to the other. The word "end" in that phrase is the one the verse itself uses, so the idea is that it does not matter where such false worship comes from, whether near or far; it is still a path that turns people away from God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them that the temptation can come even from the people they love most, and that God, who rescued them from Egypt, deserves their complete loyalty. The severe penalty that follows reflects the law of Israel at that time, when the nation was a covenant with God.

For today: not everything that draws us away from God looks like a threat. It can come from people close to us or from popular ideas. Examine with humility which influences shape your faith, and stay firm in God with love and respect toward others.
exp.33:5:
God himself buried Moses in a valley in the land of Moab, opposite Beth-peor. The verb in this verse means "he buried him." The verse adds that until the day this was written, no one knew the exact place of his grave.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who closes the account of Moses. God had just shown Moses the promised land from the mountain, but did not allow him to enter it. Who wrote this ending is not known for certain; some think it was Joshua or someone else, and the Bible does not make it clear. It is also not known why God kept the grave hidden. Some believe it was to keep the people from turning it into an object of worship.

For today: God cares for his servants to the very end, and the glory belongs to him, not to people. We can serve faithfully without needing recognition, trusting that God takes care of us always.
exp.30:28:
Moses says that he knows that, after he dies, the people will utterly corrupt themselves and leave the way God taught them. The phrase "utterly corrupt yourselves" means that they will become morally perverted. "In the latter days" means future times, not necessarily the end of the world. "The work of your hands" refers to their actions, and probably also to the idols they would make.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, alongside Israel, before they enter the promised land. That is why he gathers the elders and officers, and calls heaven and earth as witnesses. Then he teaches them a song so that they will remember this warning. He does not speak with contempt, but with sorrow and honesty.

For today: it is not enough to rely on good leaders or an inherited faith. It is wise to cultivate our own relationship with God, to read his Word faithfully, and to surround ourselves with people who help us stay firm.
exp.6:3:
It says that marrying people from those nations would put the faith of the children of Israel at risk. The one who "will turn away" is the pagan son-in-law or daughter-in-law, who could lead the son away from following God. "Other gods" are the gods of other peoples. "Suddenly" means soon, and "anger" is the wrath of God in response to unfaithfulness.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He reminds them that God chose them as his own people, and he forbids alliances and marriages with the Canaanite nations, because their idolatry could corrupt Israel's faith. Some scholars see the command to destroy them as a particular judgment of that time, and it is a topic that is interpreted in several ways.

Today we can guard the influences that most shape our heart and the heart of our family. Choose friendships, relationships, and habits that draw you closer to God, and not ones that little by little pull you away from Him.
exp.26:2:
This verse says that, on crossing the Jordan and entering the promised land, the people were to write all the words of the law on the stones. "Thou shalt plaster them with plaster" means covering them with a white coat, like a layer of plaster. "A land that floweth with milk and honey" describes a good and abundant land. "The Lord" is the name of God.

Moses, together with the elders of Israel, speaks to a people about to enter Canaan. He already knows he will not cross with them. He wants Israel to remember that the land is a gift from God and that living in it means obeying his word. Scholars debate exactly how the law was written on the stones, and the text does not make this clear.

For today: before beginning a new stage, put God's Word in a visible place. You could note a verse in your home or in your planner, so that it guides your decisions.
exp.30:3:
This verse says that the Lord will do to the peoples of Canaan what he did to Sihon and Og, kings of the Amorites. The verse of an old spelling is removed here, since the reader sees only the King James wording. And "destroyed" means that God defeated them completely, along with their land, and gave it to Israel.

Moses is speaking. He is 120 years old and already knows that he will not cross the Jordan. He says farewell to the people and reminds them that God will guide them, and that Joshua will be the new leader. Moses points to a recent victory, one they saw with their own eyes, to strengthen their trust before they enter the promised land.

For today: when you face something that frightens you, remember how God has helped you before. What you have lived through with him yesterday can give you courage to trust him tomorrow.
exp.0:30:
This verse says that God cared for his people in the wilderness the way a father carries and bears his small son. The people saw that God went with them through the whole journey, until they came to where they were.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, close to entering the promised land. He reminds them of what God did so that they would trust him. But the context that follows shows that, despite all this care, the people did not believe. God was caring for them, and they still doubted.

For today: when you go through a difficult time, remember how God has sustained you before. Write down some of the times he cared for you, and let that memory strengthen your trust for the road ahead.
exp.32:6:
Here Moses blesses the tribe of Judah shortly before he dies. He asks God to hear the voice of Judah and bring him back to his people, that is, to be with the other tribes. He also asks that his hands be sufficient for him, meaning that he would have strength to fight, and that God himself would be his help against his enemies.

Moses speaks to all Israel in his final words, blessing tribe by tribe. Some understand that Judah was separated or in danger, and so needed unity and protection. The text does not explain this with certainty. Later, from Judah would come King David.

For today: even when you do your part with your own strength, recognize that you need God and your community. Ask him for help in your struggles, and do not isolate yourself from your church or your family.
exp.11:8:
This verse says that the people of Israel had not yet entered the promised land, which here is called "rest" and "inheritance." The word "inheritance" means a property that is received as a gift and passed on to the children. "Even until now" means "still up to this very moment."

Moses speaks to the Israelites before they cross the Jordan, at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He explains how they must worship God once they live in the land. In the wilderness each person did "whatever seemed right to them," but there they would have a place of worship that God would choose. Moses reminds them that the best was still to come.

For today: sometimes we live in a season of waiting, not yet seeing what God has promised. While you are on the way, do not simply do "whatever seems right to you." Follow God with order and gratitude, trusting that he keeps what he promises.
exp.18:13:
This verse forbids moving the boundary markers, that is, the stones or marks that separated one piece of land from another. Shifting a boundary stone to take a piece of someone else's land is what this law is about. The earlier generations who set those marks are the ones who placed them in the family's share, and that share of land is what each family received as an inheritance.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the land of Canaan. In that time land was the livelihood of each family and a gift from God. Changing a boundary was a quiet theft that harmed the most vulnerable. It appears among laws about justice, such as murder and witnesses, because God wants a people where no one is robbed.

For today: be honest in small things. Do not take advantage in measures, accounts, contracts or land, even when no one sees you. Respecting what belongs to another honors God.
exp.5:15:
This verse says the people must not "test" God, that is, put him to the proof with distrust, demanding signs or doubting his care. "Massah" is the place where Israel did that. The word "tempt" here does not mean enticing someone toward evil, but trying God to see whether he is truly with them.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what happened at Massah (Exodus 17), when they were thirsty and asked whether God was among them or not. Moses wants them to learn from that mistake and remain faithful to him.

For today: trust God without demanding proof every time we go through a need. We can ask him sincerely, even with tears, but without threatening him or doubting his love. Remembering how he has cared for us before helps us wait with peace.
exp.1:9:
This verse is an explanatory note placed in parentheses. It says that before the Moabites lived in that land, the Emims dwelt there. They were a great people, numerous and tall, like the Anakims. The name "Emims" probably means "the terrible ones" or "the ones who cause dread," though its exact meaning is not entirely certain.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel and recalls their journey through the wilderness. God had commanded them not to fight against Moab, because He had given that land to the descendants of Lot. Moses adds this detail to show that God had already done the same with other peoples, removing some and giving the land to others according to His plan.

For today: God governs history, even when something seems huge or intimidating. We can trust that He carries out His plans and respect what He has given to others, without envy or violence.
exp.18:19:
This verse says that when a false witness receives the punishment he deserves, the others will hear of it and feel respect and fear. In this way no one will again commit such evil among the people. The word "temerán" here means that they will take justice seriously, and the sentence about "Á" and "a" is removed since the reader does not see that wording.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. God gives laws to protect the innocent in trials. If a witness lied to harm someone, he received the same penalty he had wished on his brother. The punishment aimed at justice and also at preventing wrongdoing. This is a law for the judges in Israel.

For today: our words carry weight. Telling the truth, especially when another person's good name is at stake, is a way of loving our neighbor. Before speaking about someone, ask yourself whether what you are saying is true and just.
exp.16:1:
This verse begins a law about a serious case. It says that if, in any town that God gives to Israel, a man or a woman is found doing what is evil in the sight of God, breaking his covenant, action must be taken. The word "transgressing" means breaking faith or stepping over the line. A covenant is the solemn commitment between God and his people. The offense is made clear in the next verse: worshiping other gods.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that being God's people requires total faithfulness. Just before this, he spoke of offering God sacrifices without defect, and now he moves to something even more serious: loyalty of the heart.

For today: God cares about our loyalty more than about outward religious appearances. It is worth asking ourselves what things occupy God's place in our hearts, and returning to him with sincerity.
exp.4:28:
God expresses a deep longing: "O that there were such an heart" means "I wish it were so" or "if only." He desires that the people have a heart that holds him in reverent awe ("fear") and that they keep all his commandments always. God wants things to go well for them and for their children forever.

Moses recalls what happened at Mount Sinai (Horeb). The people were afraid to hear God's voice directly and asked that Moses speak for them, promising to obey. God says that what they said was good, but he makes clear that what matters is not only the words, but a heart that truly follows him.

Obeying God is not just keeping rules on the outside. God looks for our heart, and his desire is our good and the good of our family. Today you can pray to him, "Lord, give me a heart that honors you," and take one concrete step of obedience at home this week.
exp.18:6:
Moses reminds the people of a command from God: they were to set apart three cities within the land they would receive. The expression "thou shalt separate" means that they were to choose them and dedicate them to a special purpose. These were cities of refuge, where a person who had killed someone without intending it could flee, as in the example of the axe head that flies off the handle.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and repeats what God had commanded him. The purpose was to protect life in two ways: to prevent an innocent person from being killed out of revenge, and to keep innocent blood from defiling the land. God cares for justice and also for mercy.

For today: God calls us not to act in anger or revenge, but to make room for truth and compassion. We can be a place of refuge for others, listening before we judge and seeking justice with humility.
exp.29:17:
Here Moses says with great seriousness: "I warn you today that you will surely perish." To declare solemnly means to make a formal statement of warning, and the phrase about perishing means that they would be destroyed. If they turn away from God, they will not live long in the land they are about to receive after crossing the Jordan.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of his life, just before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God and sets before them two paths: obey and receive blessing, or serve other gods and suffer the consequences. It is a call to decide.

For today: God invites us to choose life by trusting in Him. Today you can make a concrete decision, such as praying before acting or giving up something that pulls you away from God, remembering that He Himself is your life.
exp.17:14:
Moses tells the people that God will raise up for them a prophet from among themselves, one of their fellow Israelites, like Moses. The word "hearken" means listen and obey. "Lord" is the name of God.

Moses speaks near the end of his life, before Israel enters the promised land. The neighboring peoples sought guidance from diviners and sorcerers, but God promises to speak to them through prophets. This answers the fear the people felt at Horeb, when they did not want to hear God's voice directly. Some see here a promise of a line of prophets; the New Testament (Acts 3:22) applies it to Jesus.

For today: before seeking direction from horoscopes or popular opinions, take time to listen to God in His Word and in Christ, and put into practice what He tells you.
exp.8:8:
Moses reminds the people that he went up Mount Sinai (Horeb) to receive the stone tablets, which represented God's covenant with Israel. There he stayed forty days and forty nights without eating or drinking. The name of God is LORD, and a covenant is a solemn commitment.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, shortly before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of their history so that they will not think they are righteous in themselves. While he was with God receiving the covenant, the people soon rebelled by making the golden calf. The text does not explain how he was able to sustain himself this way; it presents that time as the work of God.

Today we can remember that God is faithful even when we fail. Before judging others or boasting of our achievements, it is good to recognize with humility how much we need His grace and to return to Him sincerely.
exp.20:18:
The verse says that the parents of the rebellious son were to bring him before the elders of the city. The elders were the leaders who judged cases. The gate of the city was the public place where legal matters were handled.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law was not about a mischievous child, but about a son who, even after being corrected, remained in total rebellion. The parents could not decide alone: the case was public and required a judgment. Scholars debate how many times it was actually applied in practice, and we do not know for certain.

For today: when a problem in the family overwhelms us, we do not carry it alone or hide it. Seeking the counsel of wise and mature leaders, with humility and patience, is always a good path.
exp.18:3:
This verse explains who may flee to a city of refuge and save his life: the person who killed another person without intending to, by mistake or accident. The source's phrase meaning "by mistake" is rendered in the verse as "ignorantly." The phrase describing an old way of saying there had been no hatred or quarrel between them before is conveyed here by the verse's words "whom he hated not in time past." The word for "neighbour" here refers to the other Israelite.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. God commands that three cities of refuge be set apart, with well-prepared roads, so that an angry relative of the dead person would not kill, without justice, someone who was not guilty of murder. In this way life was protected and a distinction was made between accident and crime.

For today: before judging someone, try to understand his intentions and the facts. God cares for justice and also for mercy; we can avoid impulsive revenge and look for ways to protect the innocent.
exp.22:6:
It says that Israel was not to despise or hate the Edomites, because they were their relatives, descended from Esau, the brother of Jacob. Nor was Israel to loathe the Egyptians, because Israel had lived as a foreigner in their land. This verse says that "to loathe" means to look upon with disgust, rejection, or hatred.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land, giving them rules for living as God's people. Just before this, Ammonites and Moabites are mentioned, who were barred from entering the assembly. Here a different treatment is shown for Edom and Egypt, appealing to kinship and to memory. The Egyptians had oppressed Israel, but they had also taken them in during times of famine. Interpreters explain this in several ways.

For today: even when someone has hurt us, remembering our own history of need helps us treat others with respect and humanity.
exp.28:27:
God uprooted his people from their land, the way a tree is pulled up by its roots. He did it in anger, in intense fury and great wrath, and sent them into another land. The words "as it is this day" indicate that, for the one telling it, that situation is already visible.

Moses speaks to Israel in Moab, when he renews the covenant before they enter the promised land. He describes what future generations would say if the people turned away from God to serve other gods. It is a serious warning about the consequences of breaking the covenant, not a prediction that God would abandon them without any remedy.

Today we can take faithfulness to God seriously. Ask yourself what things occupy the place that only God deserves, and return to Him sincerely, trusting in His mercy.
exp.28:11:
This verse says that the whole people are gathered to enter into God's covenant. A covenant is a solemn agreement between God and his people. The oath is that promise made with seriousness and confirmed. God makes this covenant with them, and "this day" stresses that it is a present and real moment.

Moses speaks to Israel on the plains of Moab, before they enter the promised land. He gathers everyone: leaders, men, children, women, and foreigners. His purpose is to renew the covenant with the new generation, so that they themselves choose to follow God and do not simply rely on the faith of their parents.

For today: faith is not inherited automatically; each person is invited to respond to God personally. You can pray a simple prayer today, renewing your commitment to trust Him and obey Him, regardless of your age or your story.
exp.12:0:
This verse speaks of someone who may arise among the people and claim to be a prophet, or to receive messages from God through dreams. That person announces a sign or a wonder, that is, something amazing or out of the ordinary. The source's comment on the wording of the verse is removed here, since the reader's verse uses "arise" and "dreamer of dreams," which already convey the meaning.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them that a miracle is not enough to prove that someone speaks on behalf of God. According to the verses that follow, if that prophet invites them to follow other gods, they must not listen to him. God allows that test to see whether they love him with all their heart.

Today we can learn to measure every spiritual message by what God has already revealed in his Word. Even if something seems impressive, if it draws us away from God, it does not come from him.
exp.20:20:
The verse says that the men of the city would stone the rebellious son until he died. In this way the evil would be taken away from the midst of the community, that is, the wickedness would be removed from among the people. All Israel would hear of it and would fear, that is, have a serious respect for the law and for the authority of parents.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. This law refers to a stubborn son, meaning one who is obstinate and rebellious beyond remedy, who refuses all correction. It was not a matter of a mischievous child: the parents themselves brought him before the elders, and scholars debate how often it was applied. The Bible does not record a single case.

Today we do not apply this penalty, since Jesus calls us to grace and forgiveness. But the teaching remains: the family needs respect and loving correction, and we must take persistent rebellion seriously, seeking help and praying for restoration.
exp.3:16:
This verse is part of a list of things God forbids being made into an idol. Here it mentions the animals that walk on the earth and the birds that fly through the air. The word "likeness" means an image or representation. The phrase continues from the previous verse: do not make any image to worship it.

Moses speaks to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that at Horeb they heard God's voice in the middle of the fire, but they did not see any form. Therefore they were not to invent a shape for God or worship creation.

For today: it is easy to turn good things in life, such as money, success, or fame, into "gods." Today we can ask ourselves what has taken God's place in our hearts, and return to worshiping only the one who created us.
exp.24:16:
It says that the people of Israel were to remember what Amalek did to them as they walked toward freedom, when they came out of Egypt. "Remember" is a command not to forget that injustice.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. Just before this, he speaks about using honest weights and measures. Then he recalls Amalek, who attacked from behind those who were weak and tired, without fearing God (Exodus 17). Some see a contrast: justice against the abuse of the strong over the weak.

For today: let us remember that God cares about the vulnerable. Let us be honest in our daily lives and take care of those who are tired and lagging behind us, rather than taking advantage of their weakness.
exp.25:0:
This verse says that a time will come when the people of Israel will enter the land that God gives them as an inheritance. There they will take it as their own and live in it. The word "inheritance" means something received as a gift, not earned by one's own merit. The phrase "possessest it" means taking possession of it, and "dwellest therein" means living there.

Moses is speaking to the people, near the end of his life, before they enter Canaan. This verse is the introduction to a ceremony: bringing the firstfruits, the first produce of the harvest, to God in gratitude. In this way they would acknowledge that the land was a gift from Him.

For today: before enjoying what you have, whether your work, your home, or your livelihood, pause to thank God. Give Him the first and the best, remembering that everything comes from His hand.
exp.10:20:
This verse says that God wants the Israelites and their children to live many years in the land he promised to their ancestors. "That your days may be multiplied" means that they would have a long life. "As the days of heaven upon the earth" is a way of saying "for a long time," for as long as the heavens stay over the earth.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He asks them to teach God's commands to their children at all times: at home, on the road, when they lie down, and when they rise. The promise of a long life is tied to obeying and passing on their faith from one generation to the next.

For today: let us make faith a part of daily life. Let us speak about God naturally at home, at the table, or on the road, so that our children come to know him through our example and our words.
exp.0:16:
It says that Israel's judges had to judge with complete impartiality. "Not showing favoritism to persons" means not favoring someone because of their importance, their wealth, or their position. The small and the great were to be heard alike. They were not to be afraid of anyone, because the judgment belongs to God, that is, the one who judges stands in God's place. If a case was too hard for them, they were to bring it to Moses so that he could hear it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them how, in the wilderness, he appointed wise leaders and judges to help him govern. He gave these instructions so that justice would be even for everyone, including the foreigner.

For today: when you have to decide or give your opinion about someone, whether at work, in the family, or in the church, try to hear everyone with the same respect. Do not let yourself be swayed by pressure or by likes and dislikes, and ask for help when the matter is beyond you.
exp.5:6:
This verse says that parents should teach their children the words of God, teaching them with constancy. It is not a one-day lesson: it speaks of talking about them at home, on the way, when lying down, and when rising up. The word "teach" here means to teach with insistence, again and again. The word "unto" is an old way of writing "to".

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that loving God with all the heart (verse 5) must pass from one generation to the next. These "words" are the commandments of God that Moses has given them.

For today: faith is best passed on in everyday life. Take simple moments, such as breakfast, a trip, or bedtime, to talk with your children about God, pray together, and tell them how God has helped you.
exp.15:0:
This verse commands the people of Israel to "observe" the month of Abib, that is, to keep it in mind and honor it. In that month they were to keep the passover to the Lord their God. Abib means "ripening ears of grain," and it was the spring month when the barley ripens. Later it came to be called Nisan. The phrase "by night" recalls that God brought them out of Egypt in the depths of darkness.

Moses speaks to the people in Deuteronomy, shortly before they enter the promised land. He repeats the law so they will not forget what God has done. The passover was an annual festival of remembrance and thankfulness for their deliverance from slavery.

For today: make a habit of remembering how God has helped you. Once a month, write down something God has done for you and give him thanks. A grateful heart trusts God more easily.
exp.18:15:
This verse begins a law about what to do when someone rises up as a false witness to accuse another person of a wrong. The word "wrong" here refers to a deviation or serious offense, such as disobeying what God commanded. The verse does not finish the idea; the answer comes in the verses that follow.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just explained that one witness alone is not enough to condemn someone. Now he teaches how to protect the innocent from lying accusations, bringing the case before the priests and judges, before the LORD.

For today: before repeating an accusation against someone, make sure it is true. If you are not sure, it is better to stay silent, because a lie told against another person can do them great harm.
exp.1:30:
God told Moses that he had already begun to place Sihon, king of the Amorites, and his land at Israel's disposal. Now it was their turn to take the step: to begin to possess. The reference to "possess" should instead be understood in terms of the verse above, where the Lord says "begin to possess."

Moses is speaking to the people, near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them of what happened before entering the promised land. Sihon refused to let them pass, and the text says that the Lord hardened his spirit. This has been understood in several ways, but here God is shown at work within that king's decisions.

For today: God sometimes has already begun to act, but he waits for us to take the first step of faith. Trust his promise and act in obedience, without simply waiting around.
exp.15:3:
The passage says that during the seven days of the Passover feast no leaven was to be seen in any house or anywhere in Israel's territory. It also says that the meat sacrificed on the evening of the first day was to be eaten that same night, and not kept until morning.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them how they left Egypt in haste, and that is why they ate bread without leaven, called "bread of affliction." These rules helped Israel not to forget what God did in freeing them. Some see in leaven an image of sin, but in this passage the main thing is memory and obedience.

For today: take a moment to remember with gratitude how God has helped you, and obey Him without putting off until tomorrow what He asks of you today.
exp.31:22:
God says he will bring disasters upon his people. "Heap" means to gather or pile up, and "arrows" are the shafts that the verse calls "mine arrows." The arrows represent the punishments God will send, one after another, until they are spent, as the next verse describes with famine, plague, and war.

This is part of the Song of Moses, where God speaks. Israel had abandoned him for idols, which were "not God," and God answers with grief and judgment. The context shows this is not a whim of anger but the consequence of breaking the covenant. Scholars understand the language of arrows and fire as poetic images of judgment.

Today we can take seriously that turning away from God to trust in empty things, such as money, success, or image, brings painful consequences. But the song does not end in judgment; further on it speaks of compassion. Examine where you have placed your trust, and return to God with humility.
exp.2:17:
Moses recalls what he commanded the tribes of Reuben and Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, when he gave them their land east of the Jordan. God had given them that land, but they were to cross over ready for battle at the front of their Israelite brothers, all the men fit for war. The word "possess" means taking the land as their own. Being "armed" means being ready to fight.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life, before they enter Canaan. He reviews what has already happened. Those tribes already had their inheritance, but the other tribes still had to conquer theirs. So Moses asks them for help and unity: they could not rest while their brothers were still fighting.

For today: if God has given you rest or blessing, do not simply stay comfortable. Ask yourself whom you can accompany, help, or support in their struggle, whether in your family, your church, or your community.
exp.3:39:
Moses asks the people to keep God's statutes and commandments. "Statutes" are the laws and rules that God establishes. If they obey, things will go well for them and for their children, and they will live a long time in the land God gives them. The phrase "for ever" most likely speaks of a continuing permanence, tied to faithfully following God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God brought them out of Egypt and will give them the land, and that Jehovah alone is God. For this reason, obedience arises from recognizing Him and trusting in Him.

Today we can obey God not out of fear, but out of trust in his goodness. Choose a teaching from the Bible that you already know and put it into practice this week in your home. Your example also leaves a mark on your children and on those around you.
exp.2:4:
It says that the sixty cities of Bashan were well defended: they had high walls, gates, and bars (the wooden or metal bolts that secured the gates). Besides these, there were many other towns without walls, that is, smaller and open ones.

Moses speaks near the end of his life, recalling for the new generation of Israelites the victories won before entering Canaan. He stresses that Bashan seemed impossible to defeat, yet God gave the victory. These accounts of conquest are hard to read, and scholars interpret them in different ways.

For today: when you face something that seems impossible, remember how God has helped you before. That grateful memory strengthens confidence for the challenges that come.
exp.23:18:
It says that if, when you harvest the grain, a sheaf (a bundle of ears tied together) is left behind in the field, you must not go back for it. It must be left for the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow. The verse says "the grain" is the ripe crop, and the phrase "that the Lord thy God may bless thee" means that God will bless all the work of your hands. The promise is that God will bless all the work of your hands.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they were slaves in Egypt and that God rescued them. For that reason they must treat with compassion those who had no land and no protection. The verses that follow apply the same principle to the olive trees and the vineyard.

For today: practice generosity without making it burdensome. You can deliberately set aside a part of your income, your time, or your food to help someone in need, without seeking recognition. Remember that everything you have comes from the grace of God.
exp.21:29:
This verse forbids a man from marrying his father's wife, or having sexual relations with her. The phrase "discover his father's skirt" is an old expression that refers to marital intimacy. Here it refers to dishonoring the father by taking his wife. It is understood to speak of the stepmother, that is, the father's wife who is not the man's own mother.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and reminds them of God's laws for their life in the family. This rule protected the honor of the household and prevented rivalries and abuses within the family. In the Bible, the Scripture also repeats it in Leviticus 18:8.

For today: let us care for respect within the family. God desires homes where there is trust and protection, not abuse or betrayal. We can ask ourselves whether our relationships honor those who live with us.
exp.0:18:
It says that the people left Horeb, which is Mount Sinai, and traveled through a very great and dreadful wilderness, the one they themselves saw. They followed the way toward the mountain country of the Amorites, just as God commanded, and they arrived at Kadesh-barnea, a place on the border of the promised land. "Dreadful" here means that it caused fear or awe.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them of their history so that they will obey God. After speaking about the judges, he goes over the journey. Kadesh-barnea was the point where God invited them to enter the land.

For today: God guides us even along difficult paths, and remembering how He sustained us before strengthens our trust for the next step. If today you are going through a "wilderness," obey what God shows you, one step at a time, remembering that He has already brought you this far.
exp.18:8:
It says that if the people keep all the commandments that Moses gives them that day, loving God and walking always in his ways, they must add three more cities of refuge to the three already set apart. The verse of the old wording is removed, since the reader's verse uses "keep" and "do them," which are the words this comment would have needed to explain.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. The cities of refuge protected those who killed someone without meaning to, so that they would not be put to death in revenge. God promises to enlarge the territory, and then more cities would be needed. The text joins obedience with justice and with care for innocent life.

For today: loving God should show in how we protect and treat others. We can seek justice and mercy, and not let anger or revenge take control of us.
exp.4:2:
This verse says that God made his covenant not only with the ancestors of Israel, but with the people who were there listening to Moses. The name of God and the word for a serious commitment between God and his people, both found in the original wording, are not in the verse your reader sees, so they are simply left out here.

Moses speaks to all of Israel, near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, before entering the promised land. Almost all the adults who had been at Horeb (Mount Sinai) had already died. Those listening were their children, or were very young at that time. Moses reminds them that the covenant is also for them and that they must take it as their own. Some understand "our fathers" to mean the patriarchs; others understand it to mean the previous generation.

For today: it is not enough to inherit the faith of one's family. Each person must respond personally to God, listen to his Word, and obey it today, as something living and present.
exp.2:0:
This verse says that the Israelites turned around and went up the road toward Bashan, a region north of the Jordan, and there Og, king of Bashan, attacked them. He came out with all his army to fight against them, near a city called Edrei. The phrase "came out against us" is older wording that means "came out to meet us."

Moses is speaking to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them of what they have already lived through, before entering the promised land. He tells them this battle was not chance: God gave them the victory, as before with King Sihon. Moses wants them to remember and to trust God.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, remember how God has helped you before. That memory strengthens trust to keep moving forward.
exp.30:24:
This verse says that Moses gave an order to the Levites, who were in charge of carrying the ark of the covenant of the Lord. It is an introductory phrase: what Moses will say comes in the next verse. The word "commanded" means ordered, and the ark of the covenant was the sacred chest that reminded the people of God's agreement with his people.

Moses had already finished writing the law in a book and had encouraged Joshua, who would replace him. Now, before he dies, he speaks to the Levites so that they will keep that book beside the ark. There it would serve as a witness, because Moses knew that the people tended to rebel.

For today: God left us his Word to remind us of the way when we forget it. Set aside a fixed time each day to read the Bible, and let it speak to you, even when it corrects you.
exp.0:43:
This verse says that the Amorites, who lived in that mountain region, came out against the Israelites like a swarm of bees. They pursued them, defeated them, and chased them as far as a place called Hormah. The word "Amorites" in the verse is the name of a people who lived in Canaan. "Seir" refers to the mountainous area of Edom.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the desert, and reminds them of what happened at Kadesh. God had told them not to go up to fight because he would not go with them, but they disobeyed out of pride. Their defeat was the result of acting without God.

For today: it is not enough to have good goals or a lot of courage; we need to listen to God and obey him. Before making an important decision, it is wise to pray, seek guidance from the Bible, and act with humility, not stubbornness.
exp.21:15:
Here the young woman's father speaks before the elders of the city. He says he gave his daughter to this man as his wife, and that now the man hates her, meaning he no longer wants her.

The setting is a public hearing at the city gate, where legal matters were settled. A husband had falsely accused his wife of not being a virgin in order to get rid of her. Her parents defend their daughter by presenting the evidence. The law protected the woman, who was vulnerable, and punished the man who slandered her. The details of the proof (the cloth) are understood in different ways among scholars.

For today: God takes truth and the good name of people seriously. Today we can guard our words, not make up accusations or damage anyone's reputation, and defend with courage someone who is treated unjustly.
exp.29:4:
It says that God will bring his people back to the land that their ancestors had received as an inheritance. There they will take possession of it, God will do them good, and he will make them grow in number more than their fathers.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that, if they turn away from God and suffer exile, they can still return to him. The promise shows that God's mercy is greater than the people's failure. Then the text adds that God will change their hearts so that they love him.

For today: if you feel that you have drifted away, or that your situation can no longer be repaired, remember that God knows how to restore. Come to him with sincerity, trusting in his mercy, and let him be the one who heals your heart.
exp.31:10:
God cares for his people the way an eagle cares for its young. The phrase "stirreth up her nest" means that she shakes the nest to encourage the chicks to come out. "Fluttereth" means that she flies gently over them. Then she spreads her wings, takes them, and carries them on her feathers, to hold them up when they are still not able to fly well.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, in the song he teaches to Israel. He reminds them how God found them in the wilderness, guided them, and protected them. He wants them not to forget his faithfulness or to go after other gods.

For today: sometimes God shakes our "nest" with changes or uncomfortable trials. Even when they hurt, you can trust that he does not let you go. When you feel insecure, remember how he has sustained you before, and take a step of faith today.
exp.9:0:
God tells Moses to cut two new stone tablets, like the first ones, and to come up the mountain. He also commands him to make an ark of wood. "Hew" means "cut" or "prepare," and "come up unto me" means "come up to where I am."

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel, reminding them of what happened on Mount Sinai. The first tablets had been broken when the people made the golden calf. Even so, God decides to renew his covenant. The ark would serve to keep the new tablets. According to the next verse, the wood was acacia (Sittim).

God knows how to give new opportunities. When we fail, he does not abandon us, but invites us to return to him with humility. If today you feel you have ruined things, come to God with sincerity and let him restore what was broken.
exp.11:12:
It says that the people of Israel had to take care not to offer their burnt offerings, that is, offerings burned completely for God, in any place that occurred to them. The verse's wording "take heed to thyself" is rendered here simply as "be careful."

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The peoples of Canaan worshiped their gods in any place, and God wanted Israel to worship him in the way he indicated, in the place he would choose. In this way the unity of the people and the purity of their worship were protected.

For today: worshiping God is not doing whatever seems best to us, but drawing near to him as he teaches us in his Word. Ask yourself whether your way of following him comes from what he says or only from your customs and preferences.
exp.9:17:
This verse says that God defends those who have no one to defend them: the orphan and the widow. He also loves the foreigner, that is, the person who lives in a land that is not his own, and he gives him bread and clothing, which means what is basic for living. "He executes justice" means that he acts on their behalf.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He asks them for an obedient heart and reminds them that God does not show favoritism toward anyone and cannot be bought. Since God is like this, his people should imitate him, and the next verse reminds them that they too were foreigners in Egypt.

For today: notice someone vulnerable near you, such as an immigrant, a widow, or a child without support, and help them with something concrete: food, clothing, company, or your voice to defend them.
exp.21:4:
It says that a woman should not wear "men's clothing," that is, clothing or items that belong to a man, nor should a man wear women's clothing. "Abomination" means something God rejects strongly. The Hebrew word translated as "clothing" can also include weapons or tools.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and gives them instructions for living as God's people. Neighboring texts speak of caring for what belongs to others and of respecting life. The exact reason is not known with certainty; some think it was meant to avoid pagan religious practices, others to protect order and identity within society.

For today: fashions change according to culture, so rather than focusing only on clothing, we can ask ourselves whether we live with honesty and respect for how God created us, without disguising who we are or mocking others.
exp.15:17:
This verse commands Israel to appoint judges and officers in all the cities that God would give them, distributed among their tribes. The "officers" mentioned here refer to overseers or assistants who helped carry out the judges' decisions. Their task was to judge the people with righteous judgment, that is, with uprightness and impartiality.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He has just spoken about the yearly feasts, when everyone presented themselves before God. Now he turns to daily life: worshiping God and practicing justice go together. The verses that follow call for not bending justice and not accepting bribes.

For today: if you have any responsibility over others, in your home, your work, or your church, make decisions with honesty. Do not favor anyone out of sympathy, self-interest, or pressure, and treat everyone with fairness.
exp.11:4:
It says that God himself would choose a place, out of all the tribes of Israel, to put his name there and to dwell in a special way. The people were to seek that place and go there. "Habitation" means the place where God dwells, and "put his name there" speaks of his presence and authority.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He orders them to destroy the pagan altars of Canaan and tells them not to worship God the way those nations worshiped their gods. Worship was to be done as God directed, not as each person wished. The text does not say here what that place would be.

For today: worshiping God is not a matter of following what seems best to us, but of drawing near to him as he has made himself known. We can ask ourselves whether our life of prayer and faith is guided by his Word and not only by customs or personal tastes.
exp.0:45:
This verse says that the people of Israel stayed in Kadesh for a long time. The word "abode" means "stayed" or "remained." The final phrase, "according unto the days that ye abode there," is hard. It probably means that it was a long stay, just as the time they spent in other places was long. No one knows exactly how many years it was.

Moses speaks to the new generation before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what happened when they did not trust God at Kadesh, tried to conquer on their own, and were defeated. After they wept, God did not change the situation, and they had to remain there for a long time.

Today we learn that disobeying God can bring consequences that last. But we can also listen to his voice in time and obey him with humility, instead of grieving when it is already too late.
exp.28:5:
For forty years in the desert the people had no bread, wine, or strong drink, as they would have had in a normal life with crops and vineyards. The "strong drink" was a strong fermented beverage, different from wine. God sustained them in another way, with manna and water, so that they would know that he is the Lord, their God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel on the plains of Moab, close to entering the promised land. He reminds them of what God did: he cared for them, gave them clothing that did not wear out, and victories over Sihon and Og. He wants them not to forget and to be faithful to the covenant.

For today: when you go through times of scarcity or change, do not look only at what is missing. Look at how God has sustained you until now. Write down three ways he has cared for you, and give him thanks; this strengthens your trust in him.
exp.20:5:
It says that the leaders of the town nearest to where a murdered man was found had to wash their hands over a heifer whose neck had been cut in a valley. A "heifer" is a young cow, and "beheaded" means its neck was cut.

Moses gives this law to Israel before they enter the promised land. When a dead body was found and the person responsible was not known, the community had to acknowledge that the blood that had been shed had weight before God. Washing the hands was a public act: they declared that they were not guilty and asked God to forgive his people.

For today: God takes injustice seriously, even when no one has resolved it. We can be sensitive to the pain of others, ask for justice, and live with honesty, without washing our hands when we are able to help.
exp.29:19:
This verse sums up what God asks: to love the LORD, to listen to his voice, and to cleave to him, that is, to be joined to him and to stay close to him. The reason is that God himself is the life of his people and the one who gives them length of days. In this way they could live in the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of his life, before they enter Canaan. He has set before them two paths: life and blessing, or death and curse. He pleads with them to choose life, and here he explains that choosing life means loving and obeying God, who keeps his promises.

For today: a full life is not found in having more things, but in staying close to God. You can set aside a few minutes each day to read the Bible, listen to God in prayer, and obey what you understand, trusting that he is your life.
exp.19:6:
It says that a man who has already become engaged to a woman, but has not yet married her, may return to his home and not go to war. The word "betrothed" means engaged, and the phrase "taken her" means marrying her and bringing her into his home. The reason is that he might die in the battle and another man would marry her.

These words are instructions from Moses to the people of Israel before they entered the promised land. The officers were to repeat them before each battle.
