Together with the new house and the vineyard, the text shows that God cared that no one would lose what was just beginning to live. Some scholars think it also protected the morale of the army.

For today: God values the important moments of life, such as an engagement or a home that is just beginning. We can care for those stages and support those who are going through them, without demanding more from them than they can give.
exp.16:18:
This verse says that the king of Israel was to keep his own copy of the law with him and read it every day of his life. The purpose was that he would learn to fear the Lord, that is, to respect him and honor him with reverence, and that he would keep his words and commands. The word "this" in the verse refers to the law itself, and "to do them" means to obey them in practice.

Moses is speaking to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions in case they ever asked for a king. That king was not to fill himself with many wives, silver, and gold, but was to submit to the Word of God, like any other Israelite. In this way he would not consider himself superior to his brothers.

For today: no one is so important or so mature that they can stop reading the Bible. Setting aside a moment each day to read it with humility helps us live out what we learn.
exp.3:40:
Moses set apart three cities on the east side of the Jordan River, "toward the sunrising," that is, toward the east. The word "severed" in the verse means that he chose them and designated them for a special purpose. The verses that follow explain that they were cities of refuge.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. After asking them for obedience to God, he recalls this fact: a safe place had already been provided for the one who caused a death without intending to. In this way justice and mercy walked together. They were for cases of accidental death, not of planned wickedness.

For today: God cares for both justice and compassion. We can imitate him by being people who help others find protection and a new opportunity, without ignoring the truth or responsibility.
exp.17:3:
It says the people were to give the priest the first and best of their harvests: of the grain, of the new wine, of the oil, and also the first wool they sheared from their sheep. The "firstfruit" words mean the first fruits or first products of each season. The phrase "shalt thou give him" refers to the Levitical priest.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. The Levites would not receive a territory of their own, so God arranged for them to live from the people's offerings. It was a way of supporting those who served in worship, and at the same time a reminder that everything they had came from God.

For today: before you spend or share what you have received, ask yourself how you can honor God first, with generosity toward your church and toward those who serve, trusting that he provides.
exp.17:15:
This verse recalls what the people asked of God at Mount Horeb (another name for Sinai). That day, when they gathered, they were afraid and said: "Let us not hear the voice of God again or see this great fire any more, or we will die." The phrase "according to all that thou desiredst" means "in line with everything you asked for."

Moses speaks near the end of his life to the new people who are about to enter the promised land. He reminds them that God accepted their request and promised to raise up a prophet like Moses who would speak in his name. In this way they would not need to seek out fortune-tellers or sorcerers like the neighboring nations. Christians see in this a sign that points to Jesus, though others also understand it as a line of prophets.

Today, instead of looking for answers in horoscopes or superstitions, we can listen to God in his Word, with respect and trust.
exp.3:6:
The verse says that no other nation is as great as Israel, because their God is so near to them whenever they call on him. The Hebrew-era phrasing about gods being present and reachable is not needed here; the verse speaks of God being nearby to his people whenever they call on him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that keeping God's law will show them to be wise before the other nations. Their greatness would not come from their own strength, but from God himself being near them and guiding them with justice.

For today: God is still near to those who seek him. Today you can speak to him with confidence, without intermediaries or complicated rituals. Try this this week: set aside a few minutes each day to pray and to read his Word, remembering that he listens to you.
exp.7:5:
This verse calls the people to obey God's commandments, to live according to his ways, and to hold him in reverence. Where the verse says "keep," it means to follow through and take care of what God has commanded. The phrase about walking in his ways means living each day as God teaches. The idea of fearing him speaks of deep respect and awe toward God, not of a fear that pushes him away.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, just before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God cared for them, corrected them as a father corrects his child, and sustained them. For this reason he encourages them to respond with obedience and respect.

Today we can remember how God has cared for us and corrected us in the past. That memory helps us obey him in the small matters of each day, with gratitude and not out of mere obligation. You might choose one decision for today and ask yourself how it would please God.
exp.2:26:
God tells Moses to climb to the top of Mount Pisgah and look in every direction: west, north, south, and east. He will be able to see the land with his own eyes, but he will not cross the Jordan River.

Here the LORD speaks to Moses. Moses had pleaded to enter the promised land, but God said no. Moses mentions that God was angry with him because of the people, meaning what had happened with them. Even so, God gives him a farewell: to see the land and to prepare Joshua, who will lead the people.

For today: sometimes God does not grant what we ask, but he gives us another task and his company. We can accept his limits with humility and devote ourselves to encouraging and preparing those who will carry on what we have begun.
exp.27:21:
It says that God would punish the people with serious diseases. The word "consumption" refers to an illness that wastes away the body; the text also mentions fever, inflammation and a scorching heat. It names "sword," which means war or violence, and sudden calamities. "Blasting and mildew" refers to a fungus that ruins crops. All of this would pursue them until it brought them to ruin.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings if they obey and curses if they turn away from God. These words are part of the covenant with Israel, and they warn of the consequences of leaving Him. To see each suffering as a direct punishment in every concrete case would go beyond the text.

For today: do not use this passage to judge someone who is suffering. Use it as a call to take God seriously, to return to Him when you have drifted away, and to trust in His mercy, which reaches us in Christ.
exp.31:18:
Deuteronomy 32:19 says that the Lord saw what his people had done, and he abhorred them. Here "abhorred" means that he regarded them with deep disgust: his own sons and daughters had rejected him.

Moses is speaking in the Song of Deuteronomy 32, shortly before his death. He reminds the Israelites how God cared for them, and how they forgot him and went after other gods. God's anger here is a response to betrayal, like that of a father hurt by children who turn away from him.

For today: God is not indifferent to our rejection, because he loves us as a Father. Today we can ask ourselves what things we have put in his place, and return to him with gratitude, remembering all that he has given us.
exp.27:2:
It says that God's blessing would reach all the people, both in the city and in the field. That is, in the work of trade and in the work of the land, in public life and in everyday life. "Blessed" means favored and cared for by God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: if they listened to his voice and obeyed, they would receive his favor. These blessings were tied to the life of Israel as a nation under that covenant, and so Christians read them carefully, without taking them as automatic promises.

Today we can learn that God wants to be Lord of every area of our lives. Ask yourself in which place, whether work, home, or school, you need to listen to him and obey him more.
exp.5:0:
This verse introduces what follows in the book: the commandments, laws, and just decisions that God commanded Moses to teach the people. The words "statutes" and "judgments" refer to established rules and to fair decisions, and the purpose was that they would keep them, that is, put them into practice, in the land they were about to enter and possess.

Moses is the one speaking. Israel is on the plains of Moab, about to cross the Jordan, after years in the wilderness. Moses reminds them of God's law so that a new generation would live by it in the promised land. This is the beginning of a major section of teaching in the book.

For today: God's word is not given to us only to know, but to live. Choose one biblical teaching you already know today and decide how you will put it into practice this week, at home or at work.
exp.9:14:
It says that, although the whole world belongs to God, he set his affection on the ancestors of Israel (Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob) and loved them. Afterward he chose their descendants, that is, the people who were listening to Moses, above all the other peoples. "Descendants" here means the offspring who come after, and the phrase "set his affection on them" means that he placed his love upon them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God owns the heavens and the earth, so his choosing of them was not because of anything they had earned, but out of love. For that reason he asks them to obey with a willing heart, not a hard one.

For today: if God has reached you with his love, it was not because you deserved it. Let that gratitude lead you to obey him with sincerity and humility, not out of mere obligation or pride.
exp.32:17:
Moses blesses two tribes of Israel. To Zebulun he says to rejoice "in thy going out", that is, when he goes out to his labors and journeys. To Issachar he says to rejoice "in thy tents", that is, in his life at home. The two tribes are mentioned together, as sisters.

Moses speaks shortly before his death, and blesses each tribe. Some understand that Zebulun went out to trade or to sail, and that Issachar stayed in the field and the home. The text does not explain this, so that is an interpretation. What we do see is that God gives different tasks to each tribe.

For today: God calls us in different ways, and all of them have value. You can rejoice in your work outside the home as well as in your life at home, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.23:3:
A man who sent his wife away cannot take her back as his wife if she has since married another. "Defiled" means stained or made unclean. "Sent away" refers to a divorce. Scholars explain in several ways what exactly that stain consists of, and the text does not spell it out.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land and reminds them of God's law. This rule was meant to restrain divorces made lightly and to keep a woman from being treated as an object that is discarded and reclaimed at will. Jesus later explained that Moses allowed divorce because of the hardness of the people's hearts.

Today we can take our commitments seriously and treat people with respect, never as things to be used and then thrown away. Before we promise something, let us think carefully about what we say.
exp.17:0:
This verse says that the priests, the Levites, that is, the whole tribe of Levi, would not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes of Israel. Instead, they would live from what the people brought to God: the offerings made by fire, which were the offerings burned on the altar, and the Lord's inheritance, that is, the portion that belonged to Him.

Moses is speaking to the people before they enter the promised land. He explains how they are to care for the Levites, who served in worship and taught the law. Since they would have no land to farm, God himself would be their inheritance, and the people would support them.

For today: we can support with generosity and gratitude those who serve God and his people, and remember that having God is the most secure inheritance.
exp.14:6:
It says that when someone from your own people is in need within your city or your land, you must not harden your heart or close your hand. The word "poor" in the verse is the one that means needy, and "brother" refers to a fellow Israelite. Closing your hand means refusing to help.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains how to live there with justice. Just before this verse, he mentions the year of release, when debts were forgiven. God wants his people to care for the poor and not be selfish.

For today: when you meet someone in need, do not stop at good intentions alone. Ask God what you can give them, whether help, time, or money, and do it generously and without resentment.
exp.28:22:
It says the land would be like a burned-out desert: full of brimstone and salt, where nothing can be sown, nothing bears fruit, and not even a blade of grass grows. It would be like Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboim, cities that God overthrew, that is, utterly destroyed and tore down, in his anger.

Moses speaks almost at the end of his life, renewing the covenant with the people before they enter the promised land. He warns them what the land would look like if they abandoned God and worshiped idols. Those who came later, even foreigners, would ask what happened, and the answer would be: they forsook the covenant of the Lord.

For today: God is serious when he warns us, but he does so so that we will be faithful to him. Today you can examine whether anything is taking God's place in your heart, and return to him sincerely. His mercy is always near to whoever repents.
exp.27:37:
It says the people will sow much seed in the field, but will harvest very little, because the locust will devour the crops. The verse of the word "gather" here means taking in what has grown, or harvesting. The locust was a plague of insects that stripped the sown fields bare.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings if they obey God and curses if they turn away from Him. This verse is part of the warnings. His words remind them that life in the field depended entirely on God, and that turning away from Him would bring loss and sorrow.

Today we can remember that our effort, however great, does not guarantee everything by itself. Work with diligence, but trust in God and do not place your security in your own strength or your possessions. Give thanks for what you receive and seek to obey Him with humility.
exp.21:16:
Here a trial at the city gate is described. The husband accuses his wife of not having been a virgin. The father responds by presenting the signs of her virginity, which was a sheet or cloth, and they spread it out before the elders. To bring false charges against someone means to accuse or discredit them. A young woman is a girl. But means "but."

Moses gives this law to the people of Israel. Its purpose was to protect the woman from a false accusation and to punish the husband who slandered her. The elders judged at the city gate. Scholars do not fully agree on exactly what the cloth proved, but the central point is clear: the accusation had to be proven, and the one who slandered her paid the penalty.

For today: do not repeat or believe serious accusations without evidence. If someone is slandered, defend them with truth and justice. God cares for the honor of people.
exp.20:3:
It says that the elders of the city nearest to a dead body found in the field must bring a young heifer to a rough valley, where the ground has never been plowed or sown. There, they shall strike off the heifer's neck, that is, kill it by breaking its neck. "Heifer" is a young cow, and "rough" means rocky or with a stream of water, depending on how it is translated.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. If someone was found murdered and no one knew who did it, the land was burdened with guilt for the blood that had been shed. This ritual showed that the community took human life seriously and did not want to be indifferent. Scholars explain the uncultivated valley in several ways, and the Bible does not detail it.

For today: let us not ignore injustice by saying "it's not my concern." We can pray, speak out, and help those who suffer near us.
exp.1:5:
This verse says Israel was to buy with money the food and water it needed from the descendants of Esau. Food is what is meant by the word that the verse calls "meat." They were not to take it by force or take advantage of them, but to pay a fair price.

Moses recalls what God commanded them while the people were going around the region of Seir, near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. The Edomites were distant relatives, descendants of Esau, the brother of Jacob. God had given them that land, so Israel was not to take it from them or stir up conflict. Although the Edomites were afraid, Israel was to treat them with respect and honesty.

For today: We can trust that God takes care of us without having to take advantage of anyone. Deal honestly with those who have something you need, pay what is fair, and respect what belongs to others.
exp.12:13:
It says that if someone hears a rumor that people in a town are being led to worship other gods, they should not act on impulse. They must "inquire, make search, and ask diligently," that is, investigate carefully and ask many questions. Only if it turns out to be true and well established, that the thing is certain, is it an "abomination," something God detests.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. At that time God was their King, and idolatry amounted to betrayal of the covenant. The verses that follow give a very severe punishment, which is understood within that particular covenant with Israel. But this verse first asks that the facts be looked into with justice.

For today: before accusing someone or repeating a rumor, especially in matters of faith or about people, investigate patiently and seek the truth.
exp.10:10:
This verse says that the land the Israelites were going to enter has hills and valleys, and that it drinks rain water from the sky. The low, fertile fields are not named here, so nothing needs to be explained about them. The word "go to possess" is simply the verse's own wording, so no separate explanation is needed.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He explains that it will not be like Egypt, where they watered their crops with their own effort. There they would depend on the rain, that is, on God's provision. For this reason he asks them to obey and love the Lord.

For today: we often want to control everything, like someone who waters with their own foot. This text invites us to work with responsibility, but also to trust that God sustains our lives. Today you can offer a simple prayer of thanks for what does not depend on you.
exp.21:21:
This verse says that if a man was found lying with a married woman, both the man and the woman were to die. The phrase about the wrongdoing being found out describes being caught in the act, and "lying with" means having sexual relations. The phrase about putting away evil from Israel speaks of cleansing the people from a serious wrong.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and he reminds them of the laws of their covenant with God. In that time marriage was a sacred covenant, and the whole community cared for its holiness. The law treats both the man and the woman equally, without favoring either one. Christians understand that Christ fulfilled the law and that today it is not applied in this way.

For today: this text reminds us that faithfulness in marriage is something very serious to God. Take care with your promises, avoid situations that tempt you, and if you have failed, seek God's forgiveness and reconciliation.
exp.20:1:
This verse says that if a man is found slain in the field and no one knows who struck him, the elders and judges of the people must go out to the place. There they shall measure the distance from the body to the cities around it. The verse of the verse's "measure" is that it means working out which city is nearest.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law was meant so that an unsolved death would not be ignored. Measuring the distance decided which city was responsible for carrying out the ritual that follows, to remove the guilt of blood from the land. The text does not say here why measuring was necessary, but the next passage makes it clear.

For today: God takes human life and justice seriously. We can take responsibility for what happens near us, by helping those who suffer and not looking away.
exp.27:63:
It says that if the people of Israel turn away from God, He will allow them to be scattered among all the nations, from one end of the earth to the other. There, in exile, they would end up worshiping false gods that neither they nor their ancestors knew, that is, idols of wood and stone. Scatter means to disperse or spread apart. Strangers means foreigners or people from other nations.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the Promised Land. He sets before them the blessings for obedience and the consequences for disobedience, as part of the covenant with God. It is a serious warning, given so that they will choose faithfulness. Later, Israel's history shows periods of exile, and scholars discuss how these relate to this passage.

For today: when we move away from God, something else takes His place. Ask yourself which things, such as money or success, receive your trust, and return to God with sincerity, for He welcomes those who come back.
exp.11:5:
This verse lists what the people were to bring to the place of worship that God would choose: burnt offerings (offerings burned entirely), sacrifices, tithes (a tenth of what they earned), the heave offering (a portion presented to God), fulfilled vows, freewill offerings, and the firstborn males of their animals.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He tells them not to worship as the peoples of Canaan did, in any place they chose. God would choose one place for his name, and there they were to bring everything. This protected the purity of their worship and kept them united as a people.

For today: giving to God should be a deliberate and orderly act, not left to chance. We can ask ourselves whether we offer the best of our time, money, and affection with gratitude, or only what we have left over.
exp.22:23:
If someone passes through another person's vineyard, the verse says they may eat as many grapes as they want until they are full. But they may not carry any grapes away in a container. The verse's comment about the word "vessel" and the phrase "fill his desire" is removed here because the reader's verse already states this plainly.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law protected the poor and travelers, who could satisfy their hunger, and at the same time it looked after the owner, so that no one would take advantage of his generosity. It comes alongside commands about keeping promises and about honesty.

For today: we can be generous with those in need, and at the same time be honest people who do not take advantage of what others share. Receiving with gratitude, without exploiting others, is one way of loving our neighbor.
exp.5:5:
This verse says that the words God commands should be "upon your heart." In biblical language, the heart is the center of a person: their thoughts, their will, and their affections. It is not only a matter of knowing the words, but of carrying them inside, very close, and letting them guide one's life.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just reminded them that God is one and that they must love him with all their being. Now he shows them how that love is lived out: by keeping his word in the innermost place, and then teaching it to their children.

For today: choose a verse this week, read it each morning, and repeat it through the day. In this way, little by little, that word stops being only on the page and begins to shape your way of thinking and acting.
exp.32:2:
It says that God loved the peoples, and that all his holy ones are in his hand. Those holy ones drew near to his feet, as one sits down to listen to a teacher, and received his words. "Sayings" means words or teachings. "Drew near" means that they came closer. The phrase "the peoples" can be understood as the tribes of Israel, though some interpret it more broadly, as the nations.

Here Moses speaks, at the end of his life, blessing the tribes of Israel. He has just recalled how God revealed himself at Sinai with his law. This verse shows God's care for his people, who received his word.

For today: God holds us in his hand, and our natural response is to draw near to him and listen. We can set aside a moment each day to read his Word carefully and seek to obey it, trusting that his love cares for us.
exp.11:25:
This verse says that the gifts a person had set apart for God, and the promises he had made, were not to be left at home or taken to just any place. They had to be taken and brought to the place God would choose. The word meaning "but" is left out here because the verse itself uses "only" to introduce the point. "Set apart" means dedicated to God, and "vows" are promises made to Him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that once they settled there, worship was to take place in the place God designated, and not in just any place. Earlier, the text speaks of not eating the blood, because the life was in it. All of this aimed at order, reverence, and obedience.

For today: if you have promised something to God, such as serving, giving, or changing a habit, do not put it off for later. Keep what you have promised sincerely and in an orderly way, with a grateful heart.
exp.32:1:
It says that God revealed himself to his people like a light that rises with the dawn. First he "came" from Sinai, then he shone from Seir and from mount Paran, places near the desert where Israel traveled. To "shine forth" means to give light, and to "shine" means to glow strongly. The "saints" here are often understood as angels or heavenly beings who accompany him. "From his right hand" means from his right side, and a "fiery law" recalls the fire of Sinai.

Moses is speaking shortly before he dies. He is blessing the tribes of Israel and begins by recalling how God made himself known to them and gave them his law. Some scholars debate exactly how to understand the phrase "ten thousands of saints" and "fiery law," but the general sense is the greatness of God in giving his law.

Today we can remember that God's Word is not simply advice, but a gift that comes from a holy and near God. Before asking him for something, you can begin by reading his Word with respect and gratitude.
exp.29:13:
This verse says that the word of God is not far away or hard to reach. It is very near: in your mouth, because it is known and repeated, and in your heart, because it is kept within you. It also has a clear purpose: "para que la cumplas," that is, so that you put it into practice.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God's commands are neither a distant nor an impossible secret. God has already given them and explained them. For that reason they have no excuse for saying they cannot obey. Right after this, he sets life and death before them so that they may choose.

For today: do not wait until you feel ready or until you find something extraordinary to obey God. Choose a truth you already know from the Bible, repeat it aloud during the day, and look for one concrete action to live it out today.
exp.15:15:
This verse commands that all the males of Israel appear before God three times a year, at the place He would choose. The feasts were the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Tabernacles. "Shall appear" means "shall present themselves," and "empty" means without bringing an offering.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that these feasts are for rejoicing and for giving thanks to God for His blessing. For this reason he includes servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows. The place of gathering would be one only, and the next verse says that each person would bring according to what God had given him.

For today: set aside regular times to meet with God and with His people, and come with gratitude. Give generously according to what you have received, and make sure that those in greatest need also have a place in the joy.
exp.13:26:
This verse says that the Israelite must not forget or leave without help the Levite who lived in his town. "Forsake" means to abandon or neglect. The reason is that the Levite did not receive a piece of land of his own, as the other tribes did, to support himself.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He teaches them to bring their tithe to the place of worship and to celebrate with joy before God. In the middle of that feast, he reminds them of the Levites, who served God and depended on the people's generosity. Then he also mentions the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow.

For today: when you enjoy what God has given you, think about who needs support, such as a pastor, a missionary, or a neighbor in need, and share generously.
exp.27:67:
It says that God would bring the people back to Egypt on ships, by a route they had been told they would never travel again. There they would try to sell themselves as male and female slaves to their enemies, but no one would buy them. The word "return" here means going back. It is an image of total humiliation: not even as slaves would they have any value.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This closes a long list of the blessings and curses of the covenant. It is the final warning about what would happen if they abandoned God: they would lose their freedom and return to the place of their former slavery. Some scholars see figurative language here, and others see a prediction of actual exiles.

For today: turning away from God leads us back into bondage that He has already rescued us from. Today you can guard your relationship with Him, thanking Him for his deliverance and obeying Him every day.
exp.1:36:
This verse says that the Israelites did not go near the land of the Ammonites, nor to the area beside the Jabbok stream, nor to the cities in the hill country. Nor did they enter any place that God had forbidden them. The verse of the word "á" and of "arroyo" has been left out, since those words do not appear in the verse you are reading.

Moses is the one speaking. Near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, he reminds the Israelites how they fared when they defeated King Sihon. He explains that even in the midst of victory, they stopped where God had set a limit. God had already said earlier that they were not to trouble the Ammonites (Deuteronomy 2:19).

For today: success does not give us permission to go beyond what God has allowed us. If things have gone well for us, we can humbly ask where God is asking us to stop, and obey with gratitude.
exp.0:13:
This verse says that the people agreed with Moses' proposal. They answered, "The thing which thou hast spoken is good for us to do." That is, they thought it was a good idea to choose leaders who would help govern and solve the people's problems.

Here Moses is speaking, reminding Israel of what happened years earlier, near Mount Sinai (Horeb). He felt weighed down by having to carry so many conflicts and responsibilities alone. So he asked them to choose wise, understanding, and experienced men, and the people accepted. Afterward Moses appointed them as heads and judges.

For today: no one is made to carry everything alone. Asking for help and sharing responsibilities is not weakness but wisdom. And when someone gives us good advice, we can listen with humility and put it into practice, in the family, the church, or at work.
exp.11:10:
He says that when Israel lives in the promised land, they must bring their offerings to one single place, the one God chooses so that his name dwells there. There they will bring the burnt offerings (offerings completely burned), the sacrifices, the tithes (the tenth part), the heave offerings (those lifted up before God) and the best of what they have promised in their vows.

Moses speaks to the people before they cross the Jordan. He explains how to worship God in the new land. The Canaanites worshiped wherever they wanted, but God wanted Israel to worship him with order, unity and obedience, according to his word and not according to their own ideas.

For today: God deserves the best of us, not what is left over. We can ask ourselves whether we seek him with sincerity and obedience, and whether we give him our time, affection and resources with joy and commitment.
exp.13:20:
It says that the Israelites were not to eat any animal that had died on its own. They could give it to the foreigner living in their towns, or sell it to a foreigner. The reason is that Israel was a holy people, set apart for God. Finally, it forbids boiling a young goat in its mother's milk.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land, reminding them how to live as God's people, even in what they ate. Scholars do not fully agree on why he forbids the young goat in its mother's milk; some think it relates to religious customs of other peoples, but this is not certain.

For today: our holiness shows in small, everyday things. Ask yourself which daily habit you can give to God, so that your way of living shows that you belong to him.
exp.20:6:
The verse says that the elders of the city will declare aloud: "Our hands have not shed this blood, neither have our eyes seen it." The word "protest" here means to declare or answer solemnly, not to complain. They speak of their innocence in an unsolved murder case.

Moses gives this instruction to the people before they enter the promised land. If someone was found dead in the field and it was not known who had killed him, the nearest city carried out a ceremony with a heifer and the priests who were present. Washing their hands showed that they were not guilty, and they asked God not to hold that blood against his people. Every human life mattered greatly to God.

For today: let us take seriously the injustice around us. Even if we are not directly guilty, we can pray, speak, and help so that truth and justice are cared for.
exp.26:15:
It says that God takes very seriously anyone who treats their father or mother with contempt. To "dishonor" someone here means treating them as if they were worth little: mocking them, ignoring them, or being disrespectful toward them. "Cursed" means that the person falls under God's judgment and outside his blessing. And the people respond with "Amen," which means "so be it": they acknowledge that this warning is just.

Moses gave these instructions before Israel entered the promised land. The Levites would read aloud a series of curses, and all the people would respond. It was a public way of renewing the covenant with God. Here sins are mentioned that are sometimes committed in secret, such as hidden idolatry, along with wrongs within the home.

For today: honor your parents with respectful words, with your time, and with concrete help. If they are elderly, call them, visit them, and listen to them with patience, even when things are not easy.
exp.0:25:
This verse says that the people of Israel did not want to enter the land that God had promised them. The word "Notwithstanding" in the verse above means "nevertheless" or "even so," and it marks the contrast with what God had offered. The phrase "rebelled against the commandment of the Lord your God" means that they opposed the word or command of God. It was not a lack of information, but a decision not to obey.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them of what happened at Kadesh-barnea. The spies had seen that the land was good, but fear grew when they heard about large peoples and walled cities. Instead of trusting God, they grumbled and doubted his love.

For today: we often know that God calls us to something good, but fear holds us back. Before deciding, let us remember what God has already done for us and trust his word, even when the path seems difficult.
exp.4:13:
It says that the seventh day is a day of rest dedicated to the Lord, Jehovah. No one was to work: not the head of the household, nor his sons, nor his servants, nor the working animals, nor the foreigner who lived in the town. The word for those who worked for the family is replaced here with the verse's own wording: "manservant" and "maidservant" are the people who worked for the household, and "stranger that is within thy gates" is the foreign resident living among you. The reason: that those who serve you may rest just as you do.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land, and repeats the Ten Commandments to them. Here the rest is not only for the head of the household, but for everyone. Afterward he reminds them that Israel was a slave in Egypt and that God set them free.

For today: set aside a regular time to rest and give thanks to God. And notice those who depend on you or work with you, so that you also give them space for rest and fair treatment.
exp.22:20:
If someone makes a solemn promise to God, they should not delay in keeping it. Fulfilling what was promised means carrying it out. God will require it, and to put it off or fail to keep it would be sin.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He repeats God's law for their life together in community. Vows were voluntary offerings or commitments made to God. No one was required to make them, but once spoken, they had to be kept seriously, as the following verses show.

For today: think before you promise something to God or to others. If you have already promised something, such as serving, helping, or giving, keep it without leaving it for later. And if you cannot keep it, pray and seek counsel with humility.
exp.17:12:
It says that God's people must be "perfect" before Him. The Hebrew word behind "perfect" speaks of being whole, without duplicity, complete in loyalty. It does not mean having no faults, but belonging to God wholeheartedly, without mixing in other sources of guidance.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just warned them against magic, divination, and contact with the dead, practices of the peoples of Canaan. God promises them something better: a prophet who would speak to them on His behalf. Many Christians see in that promise an announcement of Jesus.

For today: when you seek direction, do not divide your loyalty between God and other voices such as horoscopes or superstitions. Pray, read the Bible, and seek counsel from mature believers. Trust God with a whole heart.
exp.6:20:
This verse says that the people of Israel should not lose heart or give up before their enemies. The reason is that God himself is present among them. The word "afraid" in the verse, which refers to being overcome by fear, is what the verse describes as losing strength or courage out of fear. "Terrible" does not mean evil, but that God inspires respect and awe because of his power.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them how God brought them out of Egypt with signs and wonders. If God did that once, he can do it again against the nations that now frighten them. The hornets can be understood literally or as a picture of God's judgment; scholars interpret this in different ways.

When you face something that frightens you, remember what God has already done in your life. His presence with you is greater than your fear. You can pray calmly and take the next step trusting in him.
exp.12:3:
This verse brings together six actions of the faithful people: walking after the Lord, fearing him, keeping his commandments, obeying his voice, serving him, and cleaving to him, which means joining yourself to him and holding on to him with loyalty. "Fear" here speaks of deep respect and reverence, not of terror.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them that a prophet with miraculous signs might invite them to follow other gods. Moses explains that God allows that test to show whether they love him with all their heart. The answer is not to be swayed by miracles, but to remain faithful to what God has already said.

Today, before following a teaching or a leader, let us compare what they say with the Word of God. A message is not true simply because it is impressive. Set aside time each day to listen to God in his Word and to obey him.
exp.30:11:
Deuteronomy 31:12 says that Moses commands the whole people to be gathered together: men, women, children, and also the foreigners who lived within their towns. The purpose is that they hear the law and learn it, that they stand in awe of God and honor him, and that they make every effort to obey everything he has said. To carry out the law means to put it into practice.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, when Israel is about to cross the Jordan without him. He orders that every seven years, in the year when debts were released, and during the Feast of Booths, the law be read aloud. In this way the new generations, who had not lived through all that came before, would also come to know God.

Today, faith is learned in community and is not only for a few. We can set aside a regular time to read the Bible together as a family or in church, including the children and those who come from outside, and ask God for help to live out what we hear.
exp.6:4:
It says Israel was to destroy the places of worship of the nations of Canaan. The "altars" were where they offered sacrifices to their gods. The "statues" were sacred stone pillars. The "groves" were probably wooden poles or trees dedicated to the goddess Asherah (some translators understand it this way). The "carved images" were carved idols.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He warns them not to mix with those nations, because their worship could draw them away from God. Destroying these symbols was a way of protecting their faithfulness, since God had chosen them as a holy people.

Today it is not about destroying other people's things, but about examining our own hearts. We can ask ourselves: what in my life is pulling me away from God? Firmly removing what competes with him, such as a habit, a relationship or a distraction, protects our faith.
exp.7:18:
This verse says that if Israel forgets the Lord their God, follows other gods, serves them, and bows down to worship them, God warns them with complete seriousness that they will perish. The verse says "I testify against you this day," which means Moses is solemnly declaring this warning as a witness would. Bowing down to worship means bending low in devotion. "Other gods" refers to the gods of other peoples.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He has just told them that there they will have abundance, and he warns them of the danger of thinking that their wealth is only the fruit of their own effort. He reminds them that God is the one who gives the strength to prosper. Forgetting him would lead to idolatry and to the same consequences suffered by the peoples of Canaan.

For today: when things are going well, it is easy to trust only in oneself. Set aside a moment each day to thank God for what you have, and put God first before money, work, or success.
exp.10:14:
God promises that if his people obey him, there will also be grass in the fields for the animals, and the people will have enough food.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the rain and the harvests depended on God, and that their well-being was tied to loving and serving him wholeheartedly. Then he warns them not to turn aside to other gods.

For today: we can see that everything we have, food, work, and health, comes from the hand of God. Today you can thank him before you eat and trust that he cares for you, remembering that God seeks our heart first, not just rewards.
exp.11:18:
This verse says that the people of Israel were always to care for the Levites and not leave them without help as long as they lived in the land. To forsake someone means to leave them alone, without help or support. A Levite is a member of the tribe of Levi, set apart to serve in the worship of God.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The Levites did not receive a portion of land like the other tribes, so they depended on the tithes and offerings. That is why Moses reminds them to include the Levites in the feasts and meals before God, with joy and generosity.

Today we can think of those who devote themselves to serving in the church or teaching the Word. A practical way to do this is to support them with regular offerings, prayer, and encouragement, so that they lack nothing they need and can serve with joy.
exp.19:5:
This verse says that a man who has planted a vineyard and has not yet eaten its fruit may go back to his house and not go to war. The reason is that if he died in battle, another man would enjoy what he had worked for.

The officers of the people speak to the Israelites before the battle, following the instructions that Moses gave them. First they are reminded that God fights for them. In the text, the vineyard is the second of several exceptions, together with the new house, the engagement to be married, and fear. Scholars explain the exact purpose in different ways, but a concern for people can be seen.

For today: God values our everyday life, our work, and our families. We can serve Him without neglecting what He has entrusted to us, and we should treat others with compassion.
exp.14:20:
It says that if the firstborn male of the cattle or the sheep had a defect, such as being blind, lame, or having any other serious fault, it was not to be sacrificed to God. The word "blemish" in the verse above means a defect or stain, and "fault" means an imperfection, so the verse covers any kind of flaw.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the firstborn belonged to God and that they were to bring them before Him every year. God asked for the best, not for what was left over. An animal with a defect could be eaten at home, but it was not offered on the altar.

For today: let us give God the first and best of our time, care, and resources, not just what we have left over. Giving with sincerity and effort shows that we truly value Him.
exp.32:25:
This verse says that no god compares to the God of Israel. "Jeshurun" is a poetic name for Israel, which probably means "the upright one" or "the beloved." The image of God "riding upon the heavens" pictures him coming across the sky and the clouds, showing his power and majesty, and doing so to help his people.

Moses is speaking. He is about to die and, before Israel enters the promised land, he blesses each tribe. With verse 26 he finishes the blessings tribe by tribe and begins a song of praise to God. He reminds them that their strength and their victory do not come from themselves but from God, who protects them and will give them rest in the land.

When you feel small before a problem, remember that God is above all things and comes to your aid. You can pray with confidence, saying to him: "Lord, you are greater than this."
exp.14:12:
The verse says that when the servant is sent out free from you, you shall not let him go away empty-handed. This verse says that when a Hebrew servant finishes his six years of service and is set free, his master must not let him leave with nothing. The word "send out" means to let go or grant freedom. "Empty" means without anything, without provisions.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. A poor Hebrew could sell himself to serve another person in order to pay his debts. God commands that in the seventh year he be released and receive generous help to start over. The verses that follow remind Israel that they too were slaves in Egypt and God rescued them.

For today: if God has given you blessing, think about whom you can help get back on their feet, such as an employee, a relative or a neighbor. Give generously and without resentment, remembering how much you yourself have received.
exp.30:5:
It says that the people should be strong and brave, and not be afraid of their enemies, because God himself goes with them. "Be strong" means make yourselves strong; "take courage" means take heart. "Forsake" means to leave behind, to leave alone.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before he dies. They are about to enter the promised land, but he will not cross over with them. He reminds them how God helped them against the kings Sihon and Og, so that they trust he will also help them in what is coming. Then he says the same thing to Joshua, the new leader.

For today: when you face something that frightens you, do not rely only on your own strength. Remember how God has helped you before, and take the next step with the certainty that you are not alone.
exp.1:2:
God tells Moses that the people have already gone around this mountain enough, that is, the mountain region of Seir. He orders them to change direction and head north. The verse of the wording is set aside here, since the verse your reader sees already says "turn you northward" and needs no gloss.

Moses is reminding the new generation of Israel of their journey through the desert, after years of wandering caused by the unbelief of the previous generation. God speaks and marks the end of that stage. Right away he tells them how to pass through the territory of Edom, the descendants of Esau, without fighting them, because that land was an inheritance God had given them.

For today: sometimes we go around in circles for years in the same situation, without moving forward. Ask God for clarity, and when He shows you that the time has come, be bold enough to obey and take the next step.
exp.17:7:
It says that a Levite who comes to serve at the sanctuary will receive a portion equal to that of the other Levites who are already there. The word "portion" refers to the share of food and provision that was due to them for their service. The phrase "beside that which cometh of the sale of his patrimony" can be understood in two ways: either that he also received whatever he might have from his family or from selling his property, or that he received his share without anything being deducted because he had other income. Scholars do not fully agree.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The Levites had no territory of their own and lived from the offerings. Here the Levite who comes from another town is protected so that he is not treated as less.

For today: treat with equality and generosity those who serve in your church, regardless of where they come from or how long they have been there. Support with what you can those who dedicate themselves to the work of God.
exp.18:5:
This verse explains why God commanded that cities of refuge be set apart. If someone killed another person without meaning to, they could flee to one of them. This kept the victim's relative, burning with anger, from chasing the killer down and catching him if the road was long. Killing him would have been unjust, because there had been no hatred beforehand.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them this law to protect the innocent and to keep more unjust blood from being spilled. It distinguishes between an accident and a deliberate murder.

For today: when something angers us, it is wise to pause and look at the facts before reacting. Anger can blind us and lead us to do harm. Let us seek justice with calm, and care for the one who acted without evil intent.
exp.29:9:
It says that the blessings promised come when the people listen to God and obey what is written in his law. But it is not enough to keep rules: one must also turn back to God with all your heart and with all your soul, that is, with sincerity and wholeheartedly. The word "hearken" means "listen to," and "turn" means "return" or "come back."

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He explains that, even if they fail and suffer the consequences, if they return to God with sincerity, he will receive them again with compassion. The following verse clarifies that this command is neither impossible nor far away.

For today: if you have drifted away from God, you do not need a special feat to come back. Begin with a sincere prayer, and ask him for help to listen to him and obey him in one concrete thing this week.
exp.3:44:
This verse gives a summary of what Moses is about to teach. It names three kinds of instruction: the "testimonies" (what God has spoken as a sign of his covenant), the "statutes" (the lasting ordinances), and the "judgments" (the fair decisions for living together in community). The word "announced" means he made them known, he made them clear. This happened after the people had come out of Egypt.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel on the plains of Moab, before they enter the promised land. He has just named the cities of refuge, and now he introduces the law that follows. He reminds them that this teaching is not new: it comes from God and from the journey they have already made since Egypt.

For today: God does not guide us blindly; he speaks to us clearly. We can read his Word not as a burden, but as a guide that helps us live with wisdom, justice, and gratitude for what he has already done.
exp.31:12:
He says that God made his people ride on the high places of the earth, that is, on high and safe ground. There they ate what the fields produced. He also made them draw honey out of the rock and oil out of the hard stone. These are images of abundance that comes from places where no one would expect it. The verse of the word itself is left out here because it refers to a term that does not appear in the verse above.

Moses speaks near the end of his life, in the song he teaches to Israel. He recalls how God guided and cared for them, like an eagle with its young. He does this to show that when they later forgot God, their failure was ingratitude.

For today: God often gives good things even in difficult times. It is wise to thank him regularly, because the verse that follows shows that comfort can lead us to forget the Giver.
exp.24:4:
This verse says that if two brothers live together (in the same land or family) and one dies without leaving a son, his widow must not marry someone from outside the family. His brother-in-law must marry her and fulfill toward her the duty of a close relative. This is called levirate marriage.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law protected the widow, who could be left without support, and cared for the name and inheritance of the family. The verses that follow explain that the first son would carry on the name of the dead man.

For today: God cares for those who are vulnerable. We can ask ourselves who near us needs help, such as a widow or a family in need, and help them with responsibility and respect.
exp.26:12:
This verse says that six tribes of Israel would stand on Mount Ebal to speak the curses: Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, and Naphtali. Speaking the curse means declaring aloud the consequences of disobeying God. The other half of the tribes would stand on Mount Gerizim to bless.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He commands that, when they cross the Jordan, they hold a solemn ceremony between two mountains. The Levites would read out the curses, and all the people would respond with "Amen." In this way it was remembered that obedience brought blessing and disobedience brought consequences. It is not known with certainty why the tribes were divided in this way.

For today: it is not enough to hear the Word of God; we must respond to it. Saying "Amen" is a commitment. Today you can ask yourself in what area you need to obey God more sincerely, even in what no one sees.
exp.23:11:
It says that if the person who borrowed is poor and has left a pledge as security, you must not keep that item overnight. A "pledge" is something a person hands over as assurance that they will repay their debt. The phrase "thou shalt not sleep with his pledge" means not spending the night with it in your possession, since the following verse makes clear that it was the cloak the poor man used to keep warm.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land, and repeats God's laws to them. This rule protected the most vulnerable. Lending was permitted, but one could not take advantage of another's need or force your way into the debtor's house.

Today we can learn to help without taking advantage. If we lend something or demand payment, we should take care that the person does not lose what is basic to living with dignity. God calls for mercy and justice in how we treat those who have less.
exp.20:4:
This verse says that the priests, who were descendants of Levi, were to come forward at this time. God had chosen them to serve him and to bless in his name. In addition, whatever they decided would settle any dispute and any case of violence or injury.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He is explaining what to do when a dead body was found and it was not known who had killed the person. The priests were present as representatives of God, so that the process would be serious and fair, and the community would be cleared of guilt.

For today: God takes justice and human life seriously. We can learn not to ignore the injustices around us, to seek the truth with humility, and to ask for God's guidance when we face conflicts.
exp.6:22:
This verse says that God himself will hand over the enemy nations before Israel and throw them into great confusion and defeat, until they are overcome. The phrase about breaking them with great destruction means that God will defeat them completely, and the word about being destroyed speaks of the total collapse of their power.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He asks them not to be afraid, because God goes with them. This language of war belongs to that specific historical moment and to Israel's mission as a nation. Christians read it carefully and do not apply it to peoples of today.

Today we can take from this the confidence that God does not leave us alone before what seems impossible. When you face a big problem, such as a fear or a bad habit, remember that God works in his own time and often little by little. Ask him for help and keep going forward in faith.
exp.26:10:
This verse is an introductory sentence. It says that Moses gave the people a command that same day. The word "charged" means that he gave an instruction with authority. The colon at the end signals that what they were to do comes right after.

Moses speaks to Israel shortly before his death, when the people are about to cross the Jordan and enter the promised land. He had already reminded them to obey God. Now he gives them a specific instruction: a ceremony on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, where the tribes would speak blessings and curses. In this way the people would remember that their life in the land depended on their faithfulness to the covenant with God.

God speaks to us with clarity, and sometimes he asks for concrete actions, not just good intentions. Today you can choose one simple step of obedience, such as praying daily or forgiving someone, and put it into practice without waiting.
exp.31:15:
This verse says that the people of Israel provoked God to jealousy by worshiping foreign gods, that is, gods of other nations. The sentence about the word "provoked" can be rewritten: the verb here means they stirred God to anger. The "abominations" are practices that are detestable to God, above all idolatry and the things that went along with it.

Moses speaks in the song he leaves them at the end of his life, before Israel enters the promised land. He reminds them how God cared for them and made them prosper. But, once they felt satisfied, the people, here called by a poetic name for Israel, forgot God. God's jealousy is not a whim, but the pain of a faithful God when his people abandon him.

For today: when everything is going well for us, it is easy to put God in second place. Ask yourself which things occupy the place that belongs to Him alone, and thank Him today for what He has given you.
exp.5:1:
This verse says that God wants his people to fear him, meaning to respect him and hold him in reverence, and to obey all his commands. This is meant to be passed down from generation to generation: you, your son, and your grandson. The word "statutes" refers to rules or laws, and the word "prolonged" means lengthened. God promises a long life to those who obey him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel just before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what God commanded, so that they will keep it once they are there. Shortly after comes the well-known "Hear, O Israel: the Lord is one."

For today: if you are a father, mother, or grandparent, do not keep your faith only for Sunday. Live it at home through your example, and talk about God naturally, so that the younger ones also learn to respect and love him.
exp.26:17:
It says that God regards it as a very grave thing to deceive or lead astray a blind person so that they go wrong on the road. "Cursed" means that the one who does it falls under God's judgment. The verse of the wording "to make to err" would be rewritten here as: to make someone go astray, lead them into error. And the people answer "Amen," which means: "So be it, we agree."

Moses speaks with the elders of Israel before they enter the promised land. He orders them to proclaim a series of curses from Mount Ebal, and the people accept them with their "Amen." Many of them deal with sins committed in secret, such as taking advantage of someone weak. This one protects the most vulnerable, just as those that speak of the orphan, the widow, and the foreigner do.

Today we can care for those who depend on our honesty: giving clear directions, reporting with truth, and not taking advantage of someone who knows less or cannot see the deception.
exp.14:15:
This verse speaks of a Hebrew servant who has completed his six years of service and could go free. But if he says, "I will not go away from you," because he loves his master and his household, and things go well for him with them, he has the option of staying.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they were slaves in Egypt and that God rescued them. For that reason they must treat with generosity the servant who goes free. If he decides to stay out of love, he does so by his own choice, not out of obligation.

For today: treat with kindness and fairness those who work with you or depend on you. Let your treatment be so good that whoever is at your side feels valued, and not trapped.
exp.11:23:
This verse says that the people were not to eat the blood of the animals. When they killed an animal for food, they had to let the blood run out onto the ground, like pouring out water. "Shalt pour out" means to spill or let the liquid fall. "Shalt eat" means to eat.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that they could eat meat in their own towns, without bringing the animal to the sanctuary. But the blood remained special, because it represented life, and God had set it apart for sacrifice. For that reason, blood was not treated as ordinary food.

For today: life is a gift from God and deserves respect. We can practice this by caring for people and creation, and by thanking God for every food we receive.
exp.31:19:
He says that God, grieved by his people's abandonment, decides to withdraw his visible care from them: "I will hide my face." He wants to see what their end will be, that is, how things will finally turn out for them. He calls them "a very froward generation," crooked and rebellious people, and "children in whom is no faith," who are neither faithful nor reliable.

God himself speaks here, within the Song of Moses. Moses teaches it to Israel before he dies, so that they will remember what happens when they forget God, the Rock who formed them, and go after idols. God does not act on a whim; he responds to repeated betrayal.

For today: let us not take God's presence for granted. If we notice that we have grown cold, let us return to him soon and sincerely. The Bible also shows that God welcomes whoever repents and comes back.
exp.23:0:
Here is what the verse says about Deuteronomy 24:1. It describes a man who takes a wife, and then she finds no favor in his eyes because he has found some uncleanness in her. In that case he is to write her a bill of divorcement, giving her a formal written document of divorce. He places it in her hand and sends her out of his house.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law does not command or approve divorce; it regulates it, to bring order and to protect the woman with a written document. What exactly the uncleanness was has been interpreted in various ways, and it is not known for certain. Jesus explained that Moses permitted this because of the hardness of the people's hearts (Matthew 19:8).

Today, this reminds us that marriage is serious, and that vulnerable people deserve respect and protection. Let us seek help, dialogue, and counsel before breaking a covenant.
exp.15:12:
This verse commands the people of Israel to celebrate the Feast of Booths for seven days. They were to do so after gathering in the grain from the threshing floor, the wheat and barley, and the wine and oil from the winepress, where the grapes were trodden.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the yearly feasts. This was a feast of thanksgiving for the harvest, and everyone was invited: family, servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans and widows. They were also to remember that they had once been slaves in Egypt. Other passages of the Bible say that living in booths reminded them of the journey through the desert.

For today: when God gives you something good, such as a job, a harvest or unexpected help, take some time to thank him. And share your joy with those who have less.
exp.29:5:
It says that God himself will circumcise the heart of the people and of their descendants. To circumcise the heart means to remove the hardness that keeps a person from loving God. The phrase "for the purpose of" points to the result: loving God with all one's heart and soul, and living.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, near the entrance to the promised land. Earlier he had said that, if they turned away and later returned to God, he would gather them from among the nations. Here he promises something deeper: that God himself would change their inner life. Many Christians see in this a foretaste of the new covenant, although there is debate about how it is fulfilled.

Today you can ask God each day to soften your heart. The love of God does not arise from your effort alone; he gives it and makes it grow. Pray simply: "Lord, give me a heart that loves you."
exp.12:16:
It says that when an Israelite city was condemned for leading the people to worship other gods, no one was to keep anything from what was "devoted" to destruction, that is, what was set apart for destruction for God. If they obeyed, God would turn away the heat of his anger, would show them kindness and compassion, and would make them grow in number, as he had promised to their ancestors.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He is warning against idolatry, which put the covenant with God in danger. This command applied to one very specific legal case in ancient Israel; it is not a general instruction for today.

For today: God expects complete obedience, without holding on to "a little bit" of whatever pulls us away from him. We can ask ourselves what we are keeping that competes with our loyalty to God, and sincerely hand it over to him.
exp.6:24:
This verse says that Israel was to burn the carved images of the gods of Canaan. They were not to desire the gold or silver that covered them, nor keep it for themselves. The reason is that they could be snared by it, because God regards such things as an abomination, something He utterly detests.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God Himself would defeat the nations who lived there. But he warns them that the danger was not only war, but that idolatry would draw them in and turn them away from God. For that reason they had to separate themselves completely from those objects.

Today we may not have wooden idols, but we do have things that can take the place of God, such as money, success, or certain habits. Ask God to show you what has hold of you, and stop keeping it just in case. Turning away from it is an act of love toward Him.
exp.12:8:
It says that if someone tried to draw an Israelite away to worship other gods, that person should not be covered up or spared out of pity. The witness had to strike the first blow, and then the whole people would follow.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. God had rescued them from Egypt and made a covenant with them. At that time, idolatry was seen as treason against the King, and it could destroy the entire nation. This is a civil law for ancient Israel, not a command for the church today.

Today we do not use violence, but we can take seriously our loyalty to God. If anything or anyone pulls us away from Christ, we should not excuse it out of affection or comfort. With humility and love, let us put God first.
exp.1:13:
This verse says that from the time Israel left Kadesh-barnea until they crossed the brook Zered, thirty-eight years passed. During that time all the generation of the fighting men, meaning the adults fit for battle, died out. This happened just as the Lord had sworn it would. The phrase "until all... were wasted out" means that they kept dying until none of them were left.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, and he reminds them of their history. At Kadesh, the earlier generation did not trust God and refused to enter the land (Numbers 14). Because of this, God swore that they would not see it. Moses tells them this so that the new generation will learn and obey.

For today: God's words are serious and faithful, both in his promises and in his warnings. Today you can trust him and obey him without delay, knowing that he does what he says.
exp.4:15:
It says that we should honor our father and our mother, just as God had already commanded before. To honor means to give them respect and value, not merely to obey. The promise is to live many years and to have things go well for us in the land God was giving to his people. "Á" is the old form of "a", and "te vaya bien" means that you may have a good life.

Moses speaks to Israel, about to enter the promised land, and reminds them of the Ten Commandments given on Mount Sinai. This is the first commandment about relationships between people, and it comes right after the day of rest. The promise was addressed to the nation in its land, and it can be understood as an invitation to live in order and stability.

Today, honoring your parents can mean calling them, listening to them with patience, and caring for them as they grow old, even when you do not always agree with them.
exp.32:5:
He says that Reuben should live and not die, and that his men should not be few but should grow to a good number. The phrase about his men being numerous means that his people should be counted in great numbers and not be reduced. Some translators understand the verse to mean that his men should not be few, and the wording allows for both readings.

Moses speaks before he dies. He is blessing the tribes of Israel one by one. Reuben was the oldest son of Jacob, but he had lost his place of privilege because of a serious sin (Genesis 35:22; 49:4). This blessing seems to be a prayer for mercy, so that the tribe would not be wiped out.

For today: God knows how to give new chances to those who have failed. We can pray for people who carry mistakes from the past, asking that God sustain and restore them, and treat them with that same mercy.
exp.13:12:
This verse follows a list of birds that the people of Israel were not to eat. It mentions the glede, the kite, and the vulture, "after his kind," that is, together with all the birds of a similar kind. "Glede" is an old word; it is not known with certainty which bird it refers to, and other translations use "kite" or "bird of prey." Almost all of these are birds of prey that feed on flesh.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they are a people set apart for God, and for that reason he gives them rules about what they could eat. The Bible does not explain every reason; some think it relates to holiness and obedience.

For today: God calls us to live differently, even in ordinary things. We can ask ourselves whether, in our daily decisions, such as what we look at, say, and do, we seek to please Him with an obedient and grateful heart.
exp.2:18:
This verse says that the wives, the little ones, and the livestock of the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh would stay in the cities that Moses had already given them east of the Jordan. "Only" marks the exception: the men of war would cross over. "Livestock" refers to the herds and flocks, and "I know that you have much livestock" shows that Moses was well aware of their situation.

Moses speaks to the people as he recalls what they have lived through in the wilderness. He reminds them of what he commanded these tribes: to help their brothers conquer the land on the other side of the Jordan before returning to their homes. Their families would be protected while they carried out that commitment.

For today: God blesses when a person cares for their own, but He also expects us to help others. Let us not rest thinking only of ourselves; let us look for ways to support those who are still fighting, without neglecting our family.
exp.31:45:
Moses tells the Israelites to set their hearts, that is, all their attention and their will, on the words he is solemnly giving them today. Here "solemnly" carries the sense of declaring or warning with seriousness. They are to teach these words to their children and take care to put them into practice.

Moses has just recited the song of Deuteronomy 32 before the whole people, together with Joshua. He is about to die, and the Israelites are about to cross the Jordan into the promised land. He wants them not to forget God's law or set it aside once he is no longer with them.

For today: God invites us to take his Word seriously, not only to hear it. We can choose a passage of the Bible this week, think about it calmly, put it into practice in something specific, and share it with our children, family members, or younger friends.
exp.17:6:
It says that a Levite who comes from another town to the place of worship may serve in the name of the Lord his God, just like his fellow Levites who are already there.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The Levites did not receive land of their own, so they lived scattered among the towns and depended on the offerings. Here, any Levite who sincerely wants to serve in the sanctuary is protected: he will have a place and a share just like the others.

For today: God values those who serve with a willing heart, no matter where they come from. In the church, let us welcome with joy anyone who desires to serve, and make room for them without comparing or excluding.
exp.8:19:
It says that the Lord was very angry with Aaron, so much that he wanted to destroy him, and that Moses also prayed for him. "Being very angry" means feeling a very strong wrath, and "destroy him" means to end his life.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the sin of the golden calf, when Aaron took part in making the idol (Exodus 32). Moses wants them to remember that they were saved by God's mercy and not by their own merits. This verse shows that even the high priest needed forgiveness.

For today: praying for others, even for leaders who have failed, is an act of love. All of us need God's mercy, and we can ask for it for those around us too, without feeling superior.
exp.4:21:
This verse says that God spoke the Ten Commandments to all the people from the mountain, in the midst of the fire, the cloud and the darkness, with a loud voice. "And he added no more" means that God did not add other words at that time. Then he wrote those words on two tables of stone and gave them to Moses. "Assembly" is the gathering of the people; "darkness" speaks of a thick cloud.

The one speaking is Moses. He is reminding the new generation of Israel, before they enter the promised land, what happened at Mount Sinai (also called Horeb). He wants them to remember that the law was not a human idea, but the direct word of God, given with solemnity and in writing.

For today: God wanted his word to be clear and firm. We can take the Bible seriously and with reverence, setting aside a fixed time each day to read it and ask ourselves: "What is God asking of me today?"
exp.11:22:
He says the people had to make a firm effort not to eat blood. The reason he gives is that blood represents life, and the life was not to be eaten together with the flesh of the animal. "Soul" here means life, and "make a firm effort" means that you stay determined.
