Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that, if they lived far from the place of worship, they could kill animals to eat in their homes. But he reminds them that the blood was poured out on the ground, not eaten. This showed that life belongs to God. Christians understand that later this points to the blood of Christ, though interpreters differ on how to apply this dietary rule today.

For today: value life as a gift from God. When you eat, give thanks and remember that everything that sustains your life comes from Him.
exp.0:41:
God tells Moses to warn the people: do not go up to fight, because He is not with them. If they go, they will be defeated by their enemies. The words "you" and "lest ye be smitten" in the source are dropped here, since the verse itself already says "lest ye be smitten before your enemies."

Moses is reminding the new generation of what happened in the desert. Because of their unbelief, the earlier generation had been condemned not to enter the land. Later they said, "We have sinned; now we will surely go up." But changing their minds was not the same as obeying. God had already told them not to go, and they went anyway. As the following text says, they lost the battle.

Today, obedience cannot be put off until it is convenient. Admitting a mistake in words is not enough if we keep acting on our own. Before we throw ourselves into a project, it is wise to pray, seek God's guidance in His Word, and ask ourselves: am I going with Him, or only with my own desires?
exp.29:18:
Moses says that heaven and earth are called as witnesses that God has given the people two paths: life with blessing, or death with cursing. He asks them to choose life, so that they and their children may live.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, shortly before Israel crosses the Jordan and enters the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God. If they turn toward other gods, they will lose the land; if they love God and obey him, they will live there. The following text says that God himself is their life.

For today: choosing life is a daily decision, not only an idea. Today you can choose to listen to God, pray, and obey him in something concrete, knowing that your decisions also affect your family.
exp.23:9:
It says that if you lend something to another person, you may not enter their house to choose and take what they will give you as security.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land, and reminds them of God's laws for living together in community. This rule protected the dignity and privacy of the person in financial trouble. The lender had to wait outside, and the debtor chose what to hand over.

For today: when someone owes you something or needs help, treat them with respect. Do not use your position to pressure them or to intrude on their privacy. Ask for what is fair, but always protect the dignity of the other person.
exp.27:10:
It says that God will give His people abundance: children, livestock, and harvests. The quoted phrase about having more than enough is rewritten here: it means to have more than enough. "The fruit of your body" refers to children; the young of the livestock are the offspring of the animals; and the harvests are the fruit of the ground. Everything would happen in the land that God promised, with an oath, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter Canaan. He presents the blessings of the covenant with God, which depended on obeying Him and walking in His ways. It was a promise to the nation of Israel within that covenant, not a guarantee for each individual person.

For today: God is a generous Father, and we can thank Him for what we have as a gift from Him. Moreover, obeying Him helps us live with trust and gratitude, without measuring blessing only by money.
exp.26:9:
This verse asks the people to truly listen to God and do what he commands. The word translated here as "obey" means to obey, not merely to hear with the ears. The word "statutes" refers to the rules and regulations God gave to Israel. The word "this day" stresses that the decision is for that very moment.

Moses, together with the Levitical priests, speaks to all Israel. They are about to enter the promised land and have just heard that they are God's people. Before crossing the Jordan, they are reminded that being his people means living according to his law, written clearly on stones. Afterward will come a ceremony of blessings and curses.

For today: it is not enough to know the Bible or to agree with it. Choose one specific teaching you already know and decide to live it out this week, asking God for the strength to do so.
exp.27:20:
This verse says that if the people turn away from God, a deadly sickness will come upon them that will "cling" to them, meaning it will reach them and will not let them go. "Plague" means death in large numbers, like an epidemic. "Destroy" here means to bring them to an end, until they are removed from the land they were about to possess.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of their covenant with God: obedience would bring blessing, and abandoning him would bring serious consequences. These warnings show how seriously God took the faithfulness of his people.

For today: let us not take God's blessings for granted. We can humbly examine whether anything is pulling us away from him, and return to him promptly, trusting in his forgiveness and his mercy.
exp.19:15:
Here the word "but" means the same as "however", and "inheritance" is the word for what is handed down as property. Moses commands that in the cities of Canaan, the land God was giving to Israel, no living person was to be left alive.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The text gives the reason: to keep Israel from learning the idolatrous practices of those peoples and sinning against God. It is a very harsh command, limited to that moment and to those peoples. Scholars understand it in different ways: as divine judgment, or as the exaggerated war language of that time, since those peoples remained there afterward. It is a difficult passage, and we should not soften it.

Today it does not justify any violence. Christ teaches us to love our enemies. It does invite us to be serious about whatever pulls us away from God, and to cut firmly from influences that harm our faith.
exp.16:9:
It says that when a case is very hard to decide, the Israelite must go to the place the Lord chooses, listen to the decision given by the priests and the judge, and carefully carry it out. The decision or verdict is what the verse calls the sentence. The people who serve there as authority are the ones who inform the person. Carefully doing what is written means paying close attention to obeying everything that is told.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions for living with order and justice. When local judges could not settle a complicated case, there was a higher court. In this way endless conflicts were avoided and justice was protected in the community.

For today: when you face a disagreement you cannot resolve, seek wise and trustworthy counsel, such as a pastor, a mentor, or a mediator. Then humble yourself to accept with respect what they advise, always comparing it with the Bible.
exp.0:26:
This verse says that the people of Israel complained quietly, inside their tents. "Murmured" means to protest in secret, without facing the matter openly. They said that God hated them and had brought them out of Egypt to hand them over to the Amorites, a people who lived in Canaan, in order to destroy them.

Moses is speaking about forty years later, reminding the new generation of what happened at Kadesh-barnea. The spies had brought back good news about the land, but the people became afraid and did not want to go in. Moses shows them that their problem was not only fear of their enemies, but that they doubted God's love.

For today: when we are afraid, we should not draw conclusions about God from our fear. Instead, let us remember what He has already done for us, and bring our doubts to Him in prayer, not in hidden complaints.
exp.14:9:
It says we should give generously to the needy, without fail and without bitterness. "Without fail" means "without doubt, for certain." An "evil heart" is a stingy or resentful heart, one that gives with reluctance. "All that you put your hand to" means all that you undertake or work at. God promises to bless the one who gives with a good attitude.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. Near the seventh year, debts were forgiven, and someone might refuse to lend so as not to lose his money. Moses forbids this and reminds them that God sees the heart of the one who gives.

For today: when you help someone, do it willingly, without complaints or calculations. Before giving, check your attitude and ask God for a generous and joyful heart. God not only looks at the help, he also looks at how we give it.
exp.27:59:
It says that if the people disobey, God will allow the same diseases and calamities they saw in Egypt, the ones that used to frighten them, to come back upon them. The phrase about them staying with them means they will remain with them, like something that cannot be easily removed. The word for "this" in the original wording is an old form of "this."

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This chapter presents blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience to the covenant. The plagues of Egypt had fallen on the Egyptians, and here God warns that if Israel turns against Him, they would lose that protection. The warning seeks to lead them to take their faithfulness seriously.

For today: God warns us out of love so that we do not turn away from Him. Today you can ask Him to help you obey Him from the heart, trusting that His way cares for your life.
exp.32:21:
He says the tribe of Dan is like a lion's cub, young and strong, that leaps from Bashan. Bashan was a fertile region northeast of the Jordan, known for its mountains and forests. The word "leap" suggests a quick and brave movement.

Moses speaks just before he dies, blessing each tribe of Israel. Dan was a small tribe. Later, many of its people settled in the north, near Bashan, although it is not known for certain why Moses mentions that place. Some think the image refers to its impetus or its conquest of territory, but there are several interpretations.

For today: God can give strength and courage even to those who seem small or young. If you feel unable, remember that God equips you for what He asks of you. Trust in Him and take the first step with courage.
exp.4:5:
This verse says that God presents himself by his name, Jehovah, and reminds the people that he is the one who brought his people out of Egypt. The phrase "from the house of bondage" refers to a place of slavery, where the Israelites lived under forced labor. God begins the Ten Commandments by recalling what he has already done for them.

Here God speaks through Moses, who repeats the law to a new generation of Israelites before they enter the Promised Land. Moses reminds them that God spoke to them from the mountain, out of the fire, and that he himself served as the messenger. Before giving the commandments, God shows them who he is: their deliverer.

For today: before asking us for obedience, God reminds us of his love and his help. We can obey him with gratitude and not out of fear, remembering the times he has rescued and sustained us.
exp.0:17:
Moses reminds the people that, at that time, he gave them clear instructions about how they were to live and organize themselves. The phrase "all the things which ye should do" means everything that was their responsibility to carry out. It is a summary of the commands he had already given them.

Moses is speaking to the new generation of Israel, close to entering the promised land. He reviews the history of the wilderness. Just before this verse he recalls that he appointed judges to decide cases fairly, without favoritism. Here he closes that topic: they were not left without guidance, but he explained to them how to act.

God gives us direction for living well, and that direction includes treating everyone with justice. Today we can apply this by listening to both sides before judging a conflict in the family, at work, or in the church, and not favoring anyone out of sympathy or position.
exp.14:7:
This verse says that when a poor brother is in need, you should help him generously. "Open your hand wide" means giving gladly and without stinginess. "Sufficient for his need" means enough, and "in that which he wanteth" means what he truly needs. "Needy" means someone in want.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them laws to live as God's community. Shortly before this, he commanded that debts be forgiven every seventh year. Here he warns that no one should refuse to help on the grounds that the year of release is near and they would not get their money back.

For today: when you meet someone in difficulty, do not look for excuses not to help. Ask yourself what they truly need and give gladly what you can, whether money, food or time, trusting that God cares for you.
exp.27:19:
This verse says that if the people abandon God, cursing, confusion, and failure will come upon them in everything they set out to do.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: obeying him would bring blessing, and turning away from him would bring serious consequences. These words are a solemn warning, given so that the people will choose the path of life.

Today we can remember that turning away from God is never a small matter. Instead of living in fear, we can honestly examine our hearts, return to him quickly when we go astray, and trust that his grace receives us when we repent.
exp.33:0:
Moses goes up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top called Pisgah, opposite Jericho. There God shows him the promised land, from Gilead in the east to Dan in the north. The sentence about the wording is replaced: the verse says "the top of Pisgah, that is over against Jericho," where "over against" means "opposite" Jericho.

This is the beginning of the last chapter of Deuteronomy. Moses had already finished his speeches to the people. God had told him that he would see the land, but that he would not enter it. The text does not explain every detail here, but the scene is the close of his life and of his leadership.

We can trust that God keeps his promises, even when we do not see them fulfilled in our own time. Moses served faithfully and accepted with humility what God decided. Today we can do the same: serve well, leave the future in God's hands, and rejoice in what others will enjoy after us.
exp.8:4:
This verse says that Israel does not enter the promised land because they are righteous or have a good heart. God drives out the peoples who lived there because of their wickedness, and also to fulfill the promise he made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The phrase "drive out" means to force out.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they enter Canaan. He wants to keep them from becoming proud when they have victories. Right away he reminds them of their stubbornness and their rebellions in the wilderness. The land is a gift, not a reward. Some scholars note that the judgment on those peoples is also a warning for Israel.

Today we can remember that everything good we receive comes from God's grace and faithfulness, not from our merits. That leads us to gratitude and humility, and to treating others without feeling superior.
exp.29:1:
It says that, after having turned away from God, the people return to Him and obey Him again. "Turn back" means to come back, to change direction toward God. "Obey his voice" means to listen to what He commands and do it. This is to be done together with the children, and "with all thine heart, and with all thy soul," that is, with sincerity and complete devotion, not just on the outside.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has set before them the blessing and the curse of the covenant. He warns them that they could be scattered because of their disobedience, but he gives them hope: if they return to God, He will restore them, as the following verses say.

For today: if you feel that you have drifted away from God, you can always come back. A perfect life is not required, but a sincere heart is. Start today with an honest prayer and one concrete step of obedience, and invite your family to walk with you.
exp.21:10:
This verse forbids wearing a garment made from a mixture of wool and linen woven together.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, reminding them of God's laws. This command appears alongside others about not mixing seeds or different kinds of animals. Many believe it taught Israel to live separate and orderly as God's people. Others think it guarded against pagan customs. The Bible does not explain this clearly, so it cannot be stated with certainty.

For today: although Christians are not under this law about clothing, we can learn to ask ourselves whether in our lives we are mixing faith in God with things that weaken it, and to seek a whole heart, devoted to Him.
exp.20:10:
This verse continues the previous sentence: when Israel wins a war and takes prisoners, and a man sees among them a beautiful woman, desires her, and wants to marry her. "Desire" here means wanting or being drawn to someone. The verse only describes the situation; what must be done comes afterward.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. This law regulates a situation of war in a very harsh ancient world. It sets limits: the woman must be brought into the home, have a month of mourning for her family, and only after that may she be married. Some readers see here a protection for her; others point out that even so it reflects a culture very different from our own.

For today: even when desire is strong, God calls us to restraint, to respect the dignity of the other person, and not to treat her as an object. Before acting, one must give time and think with justice and compassion.
exp.0:0:
This verse opens the book of Deuteronomy. It says that what follows are the words Moses spoke to all Israel, on the east side of the Jordan River, in the wilderness. The place names in the verse (Paran, Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Dizahab) are geographical references, and for several of them no one knows for certain where they were.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, before they enter the promised land. The new generation needed to remember what God had done and commanded. That is why Moses reviews the history and the law of the covenant.

For today: God wants us to remember his work and his Word, especially before taking an important step. Before beginning something new, take a moment to review how God has guided you and what he has taught you.
exp.6:15:
God commands Israel to destroy the peoples of Canaan whom he will hand over to them. "Consume" means to destroy completely. The phrase about the eye showing no pity means they must not show them compassion. He also orders them not to serve their gods, because this would be a snare, that is, a trap that would make them fall.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God fights for them, and the following verse tells them not to be afraid. His greatest concern is idolatry. Scholars debate how literal or total this command was, but the text stresses the danger of turning away from God.

Today this is not a call to violence. It invites us to be firm with whatever pulls us away from God, whether habits, ambitions, or influences, and to trust that he gives us strength.
exp.10:3:
This verse recalls what God did to the army of Egypt: its soldiers, horses, and chariots. When they came pursuing Israel, God made the waters of the Red Sea (here called the sea of reeds) overflow them, and destroyed them. The phrase "unto this day" shows that this display of God's power was still being remembered. The sea's waters flowed over them and covered them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel just before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what they themselves saw, so that they will obey God with reverence and trust. Those events were a real proof of his faithfulness and his power.

For today: when you face a great fear or difficulty, remember the times God has cared for you and carried you through. Recalling his past faithfulness strengthens faith and encourages us to obey him today.
exp.2:8:
This verse is a short parenthetical note. It says that Mount Hermon had different names depending on the people: the Sidonians (people of Sidon, on the coast of present-day Lebanon) called it Sirion, and the Amorites called it Shenir.

The speaker is Moses, who reminds the people of Israel what happened when they took the lands east of the Jordan. He has just said that the territory reached as far as Mount Hermon, and since that mountain was known by several names, he adds this detail so that the listeners would understand clearly where the conquered land ended.

For today: the Bible takes care with details and clarity. We can learn to explain things patiently, using words the other person understands, and to remember that God works in real places, with real names and real dates.
exp.10:21:
This verse says that if you carefully obey all the commandments that Moses gives you, doing them out of love for God, following his ways and staying close to him, blessings will come. The word "cleave" in the verse means to draw near to someone, to stay joined closely to them. "Keep" here means to obey. Love and obedience are joined together.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God freed them and asks them for faithfulness. After the verse, he promises that God will help them take possession of the land, even though the peoples living there were stronger than they were.

Today we can learn that obeying God is not only following rules, but a way of loving him and staying close to him. A practical idea: each morning, read a passage of the Bible and ask God for help to live it out that day.
exp.27:44:
This verse says that all the curses announced earlier would fall upon the people of Israel as if they were chasing them and catching up with them, until they were destroyed. The reason is clear: they did not listen to the voice of the Lord nor keep his commandments and statutes (his laws and rules). "Destroyed" means they would be ruined. "Hearkened" means paying close attention and obeying.

Moses speaks to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He presents them with two paths: blessing if they obey, or curse if they turn away. These words are part of the covenant, a serious warning, given so that they would think carefully and choose obedience.

For today: God speaks to us frankly because he wants our good. We can ask ourselves what instruction of his Word we have been ignoring, and today take a concrete step to obey it, trusting in his mercy that accompanies us.
exp.6:9:
This verse says that God does not leave without a response those who hate him. "He repays them to their face" means that he answers them directly and surely. "Destroying them" speaks of a severe judgment. "He will not delay" means that he will not keep them waiting endlessly: God does not stay inactive, nor does he overlook persistent rejection of him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just reminded them that God is faithful and keeps his covenant with those who love him. This verse shows the other side: God is just. Interpreters debate the timing and the form of this repayment, but all agree that God takes wickedness and rebellion seriously.

For today: you can trust that God is faithful and also just. You do not have to take revenge on someone who has wronged you; hand that person over to God. And examine your heart so that you live close to him in love and obedience.
exp.7:14:
This verse reminds us that God led Israel through a vast and terrifying desert, full of fiery serpents, whose bite was very painful, as if it burned, and scorpions. There was no water, but God brought water out of a rock so hard that it was like flint.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the Promised Land. He warns them that, when they have houses, livestock, and wealth, they must not become proud or forget God. He reminds them that it was He who cared for them when they had nothing.

For today: when things are going well for you, stop and remember the times God sustained you in hard seasons. Give Him thanks with humility, and do not think that you achieved everything by your own strength alone.
exp.31:42:
It says the nations should rejoice along with God's people. The word "praise" here invites celebration. God will defend the blood of his servants, that is, he will not leave unanswered the wrongs done to those who were mistreated. The phrases "he will avenge" and "will render vengeance" mean that God will bring justice against his enemies. The phrase "will be merciful to his land" means that he will cleanse or restore the land and the people.

This is the end of the Song of Moses. Moses recites it before Israel shortly before he dies, to remind them that God is faithful, that they tend to turn away from him, and that even so God will do justice and show mercy. Some older translations of the verse differ, so scholars read it in several ways.

For today: when you are treated unjustly, do not carry the burden of revenge. Leave the matter in God's hands, for he judges with perfect justice, and ask him to help you forgive and to do good.
exp.29:7:
This verse says that the people of Israel will return to God, listen to his voice, and obey all his commandments.

Moses is speaking to the people before they enter the promised land. He has warned them that disobedience would bring punishment and exile, but here he promises restoration. What stands out is that God himself circumcises their hearts (v. 6), that is, he transforms them so that they can love him. Obedience appears as the fruit of God's work in them.

For today: if you have drifted away from God, returning is possible. Ask him to change your heart, and take one concrete step of obedience today, trusting that he sustains you.
exp.30:0:
Deuteronomy 31:1 says that Moses went and spoke these words to all Israel. The verse notes that the wording used in this verse is an old form; today we would simply say the word as it appears in the verse. It is a simple sentence that opens Moses' final address, which continues in the verses that follow.

The speaker is Moses, the leader who brought Israel out of Egypt. He is at the end of his life, and the people are about to enter the promised land. He will not go in with them, so he says farewell and prepares everyone for the change, announcing that Joshua will lead them. Some scholars point out that the Hebrew text differs a little in this verse, but the general sense is clear: Moses is addressing the whole people.

For today: when a season of life changes, we can follow Moses' example. He spoke plainly, encouraged the people, and reminded them that God was going ahead of them. Our leaders change, but God remains faithful.
exp.19:11:
If a enemy city refuses the offer of peace and decides to fight, the Israelites could surround it and lay siege to it. The verse's wording is "will make war against thee, then thou shalt besiege it," so the sentence explaining the meaning of certain words is removed, and the quoted phrases are rendered in plain English.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan, giving them rules for war. The first step was to offer peace. This passage refers to distant cities; for the peoples of Canaan, the same chapter gives other instructions, which are more severe. These are difficult texts, and readers have understood them in different ways, but here it is clear that peace came first.

For today: when facing a conflict, look first for the path of peace. Offer dialogue, forgiveness, or an honest conversation before hardening your position or responding in anger.
exp.6:0:
He says that when God brings Israel into the promised land, he himself will drive out many nations from there. Seven are named: the Hittites, Girgashites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. They were nations more numerous and mightier than Israel. The phrase "cast out before thee" means that God would drive them out, and "to possess it" means to take it as an inheritance.

Moses speaks to the people on the plains of Moab, just before they enter Canaan. He reminds them that the victory will come from God and not from their own strength. The verses that follow speak of destroying those peoples and avoiding alliances with them, since the danger was that Israel would turn away from God. Scholars debate how to understand that command of destruction, and it is best read in its particular historical context, not as a general command for today.

Today, when you face something that seems bigger than you, remember that God can work where your strength falls short. Trust in him, and keep faithfully doing what is your part.
exp.16:6:
It says that when someone was condemned to death for idolatry, the witnesses who accused them had to throw the first stone, and then all the people. In this way Israel would remove the evil from the midst of the community. The phrase "remove the evil" in the verse above is the one this comment refers to, and it means to take away or put out of the way.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. This command deals with idolatry, which broke the covenant with God. Two or three witnesses were required, and they had to act first, so that no one would accuse lightly: whoever made a false accusation would bear the responsibility. Today many Christians understand this law as part of the old covenant with Israel, not as a current civil rule.

For today: before accusing someone, think about the weight of your words. Speak with truth, with evidence, and with humility, knowing that God asks for justice and care for your neighbor.
exp.0:20:
It says that God has already placed the promised land in front of the people. Moses tells them to go up and take it, just as God had said to their ancestors.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, and he reminds them of what happened at Kadesh-barnea. There God showed them that the land was ready. However, as the text goes on, the people proposed sending spies first. Moses agreed to the idea, although later that decision led the people to doubt and not obey.

For today: when God has already given you a promise or a clear direction, you do not need to wait until you feel completely sure of everything. Take the step with confidence, relying on what He has said, and ask Him to replace your fear with courage.
exp.0:5:
Moses recalls what God told the people at Mount Horeb, another name for Sinai. God says to them: "You have dwelt long enough in this mount," meaning that they had stayed there long enough. It was time to leave that place and move forward.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, on the plains of Moab, before they enter the promised land. He retells the story so they will remember what God did. They had spent about a year at Horeb, where they received the law. Now God was calling them to move on and take possession of the land he had promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

God gives times of rest and learning, but he does not want us to stay there forever. If he shows you that it is time to take a step of faith, do not settle down out of fear or habit. Pray, trust his promise, and move forward.
exp.2:16:
This verse completes the description of the territory east of the Jordan that Moses gave to Reuben and Gad. It includes the plain (the flat land), the Jordan River as the boundary, and the strip running from the Sea of Chinnereth (the Sea of Galilee) to the Sea of the Arabah, which is the Salt Sea (the Dead Sea). On the east it reached the slopes of Mount Pisgah.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, near the end of his life, and reminds them how God gave them victory over the kings of that region. He repeats the boundaries in detail so that they would know that this land was a gift from God and that each tribe had its assigned place.

For today: God cares for the details of our lives. Just as He set clear boundaries for each tribe, He also gives us what we need for each stage. We can give thanks for what we have received, instead of living with our eyes on what others have.
exp.22:9:
It says that if a man in the army became unclean because of something that happened to him during the night, such as an involuntary emission, he had to leave the camp and not come back in right away. The phrase about what happens "by night" means something that occurs without intent while a man is asleep, and the word about being unclean means that he was ritually impure.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them rules for when they go out to war, and he places them alongside the command to keep themselves from "any wicked thing." God was present in the middle of the camp, so it had to be kept as a place set apart for Him. This impurity was ceremonial, not a sin.

For today: God cares about order and reverence, even in small things. We can ask ourselves which things, though not serious sins, we should set apart so that we can draw near to Him with a clean and attentive heart.
exp.28:8:
Moses tells the Israelites to keep the words of the covenant carefully, that is, the agreement God made with them. "Keep" means to obey and to guard, and "do them" means to put them into practice. "Prosper" here means that things go well for them in life, in whatever they undertake.

Moses speaks to the people on the plains of Moab, at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them how God gave them victory over the kings Sihon and Og, and so calls them to renew their commitment to God before entering the promised land. The whole community was present, including children and foreigners.

For today: God's blessing is tied to a life of practical obedience. Today you can choose a teaching from the Bible that you already know and put it into practice this week, trusting that God cares for your path. This does not guarantee material success, but it does mean a life firmly rooted in Him.
exp.20:7:
This verse is a prayer. It asks God to forgive Israel, the people He rescued. It also asks that God not hold against them the death of an innocent person. At the end, it promises that the guilt of that blood will be forgiven.

Moses is giving instructions for a special case: someone is found dead in the countryside and no one knows who killed him. The elders of the nearest town would carry out a ritual with a young cow and declare that they were innocent. Then they would pray in this way. This shows that God takes human life seriously, even when no guilty person is known.

For today: let us not be indifferent to injustice. Even if we have not done the harm, we can pray, seek the truth, and work to protect life. And we can rest in the fact that God forgives.
exp.3:19:
God chose Israel and rescued them from Egypt, which the verse describes as a place of very harsh suffering and slavery, a kind of furnace. The word "but" introduces the contrast with what the people were before. The phrase about belonging to God means a people who belong to him in a special way, like a precious inheritance. The phrase "as ye are this day" points out that they were already like this at that very moment.

Moses speaks near the end of his life to the new generation of Israelites before they enter the promised land. He warns them not to make idols or to worship the sun, the moon, or the stars. He reminds them that, unlike the other nations, they were rescued and chosen by God.

For today: before we seek security or worth in created things, let us remember that God has rescued us and calls us his own. That grateful remembrance helps us to be faithful and not to depend on other things.
exp.3:26:
This verse says that if the people of Israel turn away from God, the Lord will scatter them among other nations. Few of them will be left there, because their number will shrink. The word "scatter" means to spread out or sow across many places, and "nations" here refers to other peoples.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He warns them that if, after many years, they become corrupt and make idols, they will face the consequences. But the warning does not end there: the verses that follow promise that if they seek God with all their heart from exile, they will find him. It is a serious warning, but one with hope.

For today: let us not take lightly the small things that take God's place in our hearts. And if you feel far from him, remember that you can always return to seek him sincerely.
exp.27:48:
It says that God would allow a distant nation, from the far ends of the earth, to attack Israel. Its speed is compared to the flight of an eagle. In addition, they spoke a language the Israelites would not understand. The phrase "end of the earth" means the far edge or a very remote place.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He presents the blessings for obedience and the consequences for disobedience. This warning comes after saying that they would not serve God with joy, despite having everything. Many see an echo of later invasions, such as those of Assyria or Babylon, though no single one can be pinpointed.

For today: let us not take God's blessings for granted. When everything is going well, it is easy to forget him. Let us take a moment each day to thank him sincerely and to serve him with joy.
exp.20:11:
The verse says that the soldier was to bring the captive woman to his house, and that she would shave her head and trim her nails. The word "shave" here means to scrape off or shave the hair from the head. The Bible does not explain the meaning of these gestures: some see them as a sign of mourning, others as a rite of separation from her former life, and others as a way of leaving behind her status as a captive. There is no single certain interpretation.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law regulates a situation of war, which was common in that time, and sets limits to protect the woman: it gives her a month to mourn her family, forbids selling her, and protects her from abuse. It does not approve of war or violence, but rather restrains what would otherwise be cruel treatment.

Today we can learn that God cares about protecting the most vulnerable. If we have power over someone, we should use it with respect, patience, and compassion.
exp.16:14:
It says that, if Israel comes to want a king, God himself must be the one who chooses who it will be. That king had to be one of the Israelites, "one from among thy brethren," and not a foreigner.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He warns them ahead of time that one day they will want a king like the nations around them. He does not forbid it, but he sets limits: the king would not be the highest authority, but someone under God's direction and a part of the people. The verses that follow ask him for humility, without piling up horses, wives, or riches.

Today we can pray for those who govern us and remember that leadership is a service, not a privilege. Before choosing a leader, it is worth asking ourselves whether he or she is close to the people, has integrity, and respects God and the people.
exp.33:9:
This verse says that, after Moses, there never arose in Israel another prophet like him. The Lord knew him face to face, that is, spoke with him in a very close and direct way. The word "prophet" refers to someone who speaks on behalf of God.

The narrator, who is not named in the text, closes the book of Deuteronomy and the whole Law of Moses. Israel has just mourned his death, and Joshua is now the new leader. The verse does not diminish Joshua's worth; it shows that Moses held a unique place because of his close dealings with God and the signs he performed in Egypt. Some scholars believe these lines were added later, but the text does not make this clear.

God desires a close relationship with us. We can speak to him with confidence in prayer and read his Word to know him better. We can also thank those who have guided us in the faith.
exp.20:14:
This verse describes a specific case: a man has two wives, one he loves more and the other he holds in less favor, meaning he cares for her less or treats her with less affection. Both bear him children, and the firstborn son is the child of the wife he cares for less.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. The Bible does not approve of having several wives here; it simply regulates a situation that already existed and protects the most vulnerable. The law prevents a father's affection from taking away the firstborn son's rights of inheritance.

For today: justice must not depend on our likes and dislikes. In the family, at work, or in the church, God calls us to treat everyone fairly, even those we like less.
exp.27:43:
The foreigner who lives among the people will have more money and power than they do. He will lend, and they will have to borrow. To be "head" means to be on top, with authority; to be the "tail" means to fall behind, to end up in a position of dependence instead.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings if they obey God and curses if they abandon him. This verse is a warning within the covenant: disobedience would bring loss, debt, and dependence on others.

For today: this text should not be read as a condemnation of the poor or those in debt, since poverty has many causes. It does invite us to live with wisdom and to trust God, taking care with our decisions about money and asking him for his guidance every day.
exp.13:16:
This verse continues a list of birds that the Israelites were not to eat.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they are a holy people, set apart for God. These food laws helped them live differently from the neighboring nations and remember that they belonged to the Lord.

Christians are not under these food rules (Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15). But we can still learn that God cares about our whole life, even the everyday things. Today you might ask yourself: what habit of my daily life can I offer to God to show that I belong to him?
exp.8:23:
It says that the people of Israel have been rebellious against God the whole time Moses has known them. "Rebellious" refers to those who resist obeying. The phrase about having been against the Lord means "they have been against the Lord." The name of God in the Old Testament is the name the text uses for him in that period.

Moses speaks near the end of his life, before the people enter the promised land. He reminds them of their failures: they complained in the wilderness and did not believe God at Kadesh-barnea. He does this so that they will not think they deserve the land for being good. Right after, he tells how he prayed for them, asking that God not destroy them, because they were his people.

For today: let us be humble and honest about our failures. Everything good we receive comes from God's grace, not from our merits. And like Moses, we can pray with love for those who have failed.
exp.22:2:
It says that no Ammonite or Moabite could be admitted into "the congregation of the Lord," that is, the assembly of the people of Israel gathered for worship and community life. "Even to their tenth generation" indicates a very long time, and "for ever" reinforces that idea. Some believe the tenth generation is an expression of prolonged exclusion, not an exact count.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. The following verses give the reason: Ammon and Moab did not help Israel with bread and water, and Moab hired Balaam to curse them. Even so, God turned the curse into a blessing. Scholars debate whether this refers to full participation in worship or in civic life. Later, Ruth, a Moabite, was welcomed and became an ancestor of David.

Today we can remember that God sees how we treat his people. We also learn to trust that, when someone tries to harm us, God can turn it into a blessing.
exp.3:29:
This verse says that when the people are in distress and all the difficult things foretold come upon them, they will have an open door: to turn back to the Lord, their God, and listen to his voice. The phrase "in tribulation" refers to a time of hardship, and "in the latter days" means the future time when all of this takes place. The sentence is left unfinished and is completed in the next verse.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them that if they turn away from God and worship idols, consequences and exile will come. But he also gives them hope: God is merciful and does not forget his covenant with them.

For today: if you are going through a difficult time, or if you have drifted away from God, do not think it is too late. Return to him sincerely, pray, and listen to his word. He welcomes whoever comes back wholeheartedly.
exp.3:46:
This verse says that the people of Israel took possession of the land of King Sihon and the land of Og, king of Bashan. They were two kings of the Amorites who lived east of the Jordan River. The phrase "toward the sunrising" in the verse simply means to the east, the direction where the sun rises.

Moses is speaking to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the victories God gave them after they left Egypt. With this he introduces the teaching of the law: God had already been faithful, so now they were to obey him.

For today: when you are unsure of what lies ahead, remember how God has helped you in the past. That grateful memory strengthens trust and encourages us to follow him in obedience.
exp.17:21:
It says that if someone speaks as a prophet in the name of the Lord, and what he announces does not happen or come to pass, then that word did not come from the Lord. The word "presumptuously" means proud or arrogant: the prophet spoke on his own account, pretending to have authority. For that reason the people were not to be afraid of him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He had promised them that God would raise up true prophets, and now he gives them a test to tell them apart from false ones, who could mislead them or lead them toward other gods. Some scholars point out that this verse is a test, and that it should be read together with the verse before it and with Deuteronomy 13, where it also matters that the message be faithful to God.

Today, let us not accept without examination everything someone says "in the name of God." Let us compare their words with the Bible, observe their fruit, and not live in fear before voices that speak with great confidence.
exp.27:42:
It says that the foreigner who lives among the people will keep growing in power and wealth, while the Israelites will keep sinking lower and lower. It is a picture of reversal: the outsiders up top, the insiders down below. "Very high" and "very low" show a strong and gradual change.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. In Deuteronomy 28 he sets out blessings for obeying God and curses for disobeying him. This verse is part of the warnings: if the people abandon the covenant, they will lose their stability and their place. These words were addressed to Israel under that particular covenant.

Today we can learn that ignoring God's voice leaves us without the foundation that holds our lives up. A practical application: before making important decisions, set aside time for the Bible and prayer, and ask yourself whether you are listening to God or only to your own desires.
exp.17:19:
It says that a prophet who dares to speak in God's name something God did not command him to say, or who speaks in the name of other gods, must die. "But" means "but." "Presume" means that he dares with arrogance. "Other" means strangers, those who are not the true God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. God had promised to send them faithful prophets, and so he warns firmly against false ones. At that time, speaking in God's name was something very serious, because the life and faithfulness of the people depended on it. This penalty corresponds to the law of Israel at that time.

Today it reminds us that speaking on behalf of God is a great responsibility. Before saying "God told me," it is good to check whether it agrees with the Bible. And when we listen to others, we can test what they teach with humility and with the Word.
exp.1:14:
It says that God himself acted against that generation of Israel until all the fighting men died in the wilderness. "The hand of the Lord" is a way of speaking of his power in action. The quoted phrases in the source that refer to the verse's wording are rendered here in plain terms: "until they were consumed" means that not one of them was left, and "from among the host" refers to the camp of the people.

Moses speaks, reminding the people of their history before they enter the promised land. That generation refused to trust God at Kadesh-barnea (Numbers 14), and God swore that they would not enter. They spent thirty-eight more years on the journey, until they crossed the brook Zered. Moses wants the new generation to learn from that.

For today: disobedience and unbelief have serious consequences, yet God is faithful to his word and carries on with his plan. Today we can ask ourselves in what area it is hard for us to trust God, and decide to obey him with humility and confidence, without putting it off.
exp.23:16:
This verse commands that justice not be denied to the most vulnerable. The "stranger" is the foreigner who lives among the people, without family or land of his own. "Pervert the judgment" means to judge unjustly or to take advantage of someone. "Take as a pledge" means to keep an item as security for a debt; here it is forbidden to do so with a widow's clothing, which was perhaps something she needed to cover herself.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and passes on God's laws to them. He reminds them that they were slaves in Egypt and that God rescued them. For this reason they must treat with compassion those who today have no one to defend them.

For today: if you have any power, whether as a leader, a neighbor, or a lender, use it with justice and tenderness. Think about who near you has the least voice, and make sure you treat them fairly, without taking advantage of their need.
exp.31:34:
It says that only God has the right to punish wrongdoing and give what is justly owed. The word "vengeance" here means corrective justice, not resentment. The phrase about their foot sliding means that they will stumble and fall. The day of their calamity is near, and the punishment waiting for them is coming quickly.

It is part of the Song of Moses, which God gave to remind Israel of his faithfulness. It speaks of the enemy nations who oppress his people, whose wickedness is already stored up to be judged. The verses that follow show that God also judges his own people, but then has compassion on them. Some believe the passage also speaks of correction for Israel; the text allows for that reading.

When someone wrongs you, do not take payment into your own hands. Hand the hurt over to God, who is just, and ask for strength to forgive and to do good. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 12:19 for that same purpose.
exp.19:19:
It says that, if Israel besieged a city, they could cut down the trees that did not bear fruit for eating. With that wood they would build siege works against the enemy city, until they defeated it.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them rules for war. Shortly before, he had commanded them not to cut down fruit trees, because they were a source of food. Here he clarifies that they could use the other trees. The law sets limits even in war, and it cares for what serves to sustain life.

For today: even when we have to use resources or make difficult decisions, we can do so with care and without waste. Before destroying something, let us ask whether it can give life or food to others. God calls us to be responsible and just with what He has entrusted to us.
exp.8:16:
Moses tells how he took the two tablets of the law, threw them down from his hands, and broke them before the eyes of the people. The verbs he uses mean that he threw them and that he broke them.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, before they enter the promised land, and reminds them of their sin with the golden calf. When he came down from Mount Sinai he saw that the people had already broken their covenant with God. His action showed, with grief, that the agreement had been violated. Some also understand that it expressed his holy anger.

Today we can learn to take sin seriously, without excusing it or minimizing it. But, as Moses did afterward, we can also come to God with humility, ask him for forgiveness, and trust in his mercy.
exp.31:2:
This verse says that Moses is going to proclaim the name of the Lord, that is, to speak about who God is and what he is like. Then it invites everyone to acknowledge his greatness. Here "I will publish" means to announce or proclaim. The phrase "ascribe ye greatness" means: recognize and declare that God is great.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, near the entrance to the promised land. This song was given so that Israel would remember it. Before pointing out the people's failures, he begins by praising God. The verses that follow show him as a faithful and just Rock.

For today: before asking God for something or talking about your problems, begin by giving him thanks and remembering what he is like. This helps you see everything with more confidence and humility.
exp.30:16:
God warns that if the people abandon him to follow other gods, his anger will be kindled against them. "Hide my face" means withdrawing his favor and protection. "They shall be devoured" speaks of being consumed by troubles. Then many evils and troubles will come upon them, and the people themselves will acknowledge: "Is it not because our God is no longer among us that these evils have come upon us?"

The one speaking is God, addressing Moses in the tabernacle, shortly before Moses' death. God already knows that Israel, once in the promised land, will turn toward idolatry and break the covenant. For this reason he commands that a song be written to serve as a witness and reminder for the people.

For today: when hard times come, it is wise to examine with humility whether we have drifted away from God. And although the text is serious, it serves as a call to return to him, who always invites people to repentance.
exp.29:11:
This verse says that God's command is not in heaven, meaning it is not out of anyone's reach. No one has to wonder who will go up to get it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that if they turn back to God with all their heart, they should not think that his law is too hard or far away. God has already given it to them in writing, and it is within reach.

The apostle Paul quotes this passage in Romans 10:6-8, applying it to faith in Christ.

Today, you do not need to wait for an extraordinary experience to know God's will. His Word is within your reach. Read a passage every day, and put into practice today one thing you clearly understand.
exp.32:12:
He says that Moses asks God to bless the land of Joseph, that is, the territory of his descendants. He speaks of the "precious things of heaven," that is, the good things that come from above, such as the rain and the dew. He also mentions "the deep that coucheth beneath," which refers to the underground waters that rise from the earth and make it fertile.

Moses is near the end of his life and blesses the tribes of Israel before they enter the promised land. Here he addresses Joseph, represented by Ephraim and Manasseh. His blessing shows that the fertility of the land depends on God. Some scholars see in these words an echo of the blessing Jacob gave to Joseph in Genesis 49.

Today we can remember that everything that sustains our life, such as food, water, and weather, is a gift from God. Before you worry about what is missing, give thanks today for a simple provision you already have.
exp.7:0:
Moses tells the people that they must take care to obey all the commandments he gives them today. The reason is that in this way they will be able to live, grow in number, go into the land, and possess it. It is the land that God promised with an oath to their fathers, that is, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, just before they enter Canaan. He reminds them that obedience and God's promise go together. The verses that follow invite them to remember how God guided them, tested them, and sustained them with manna.

For today: God gives us his words so that we may live well, not to burden us. Today you can choose one specific command from the Bible that you already know and put it into practice this week, trusting that God is faithful to his promises.
exp.19:14:
This verse says that the rules of war in the verses before this one applied to the cities that were far away, that is, those outside the land God was giving to Israel. The phrase "these nations" refers to the peoples of Canaan. The old words in the text are adapted here: where it uses an archaic form for "to," it is simply the word "to"; and the old word for "despojo," meaning what is taken in war, is explained as the plunder seized in battle.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He distinguishes two cases: distant cities, which first had to be offered terms of peace (verses 10-11), and the Canaanite cities, treated as a special judgment. It is a difficult text. Some read it as a limited and unique historical command; others note the exaggerated language typical of ancient warfare. Scholars discuss how it should be understood.

Today it does not authorize us to use violence in God's name. It invites us to approach these passages with humility, reading them in the light of Christ, and to seek peace and justice with those with whom we have differences.
exp.24:6:
This verse speaks of a man who refuses to marry his brother's widow. In that case, she was to go up to the city gate, where the elders gathered, and bring her complaint. Raising up a name for the dead brother meant giving continuity to his name through a son. The duty of family meant carrying out the obligation owed to a brother's household.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law, known as levirate marriage, protected childless widows and kept a family's inheritance and name from disappearing. The city gate was the place where legal matters were settled.

For today: God cares for the vulnerable, such as widows. We can fulfill our family responsibilities and generously help those who have been left alone or need support.
exp.3:2:
It says the Israelites saw with their own eyes what God did because of what happened at Baal-peor. All who went after that false god were destroyed from among the people.

Moses speaks near the end of the journey through the wilderness, before the people enter the promised land. He reminds them of an event they lived through (it is told in Numbers 25), when many joined in the worship of Baal-peor. He does this so that they will obey God and not repeat that mistake. According to the next verse, those who stayed faithful to God remained alive.

For today: faithfulness to God protects life. Today we can ask ourselves what things compete for our hearts, and with God's help, turn away from them and stay close to Him.
exp.12:11:
This verse begins a new situation: God warns that Israel could hear a rumor about one of the cities that He gave them to live in. The phrase "Cuando oyeres," which means "if you come to hear," is not quoted in the reader's verse, so it is left out here.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. Shortly before, he dealt with the case of a person who led others to worship idols. Now he speaks of a similar problem, but one that affects an entire city. His purpose is to protect the people's faithfulness toward God, who brought them out of Egypt. Notice that he does not command action based on a simple rumor; he calls for careful investigation.

Today this teaches us not to believe or repeat everything we hear. Before judging, it is wise to investigate honestly and seek the truth, always taking care to remain faithful to God.
exp.19:12:
The verse says that when God gave a city into Israel's hands after a siege, the soldiers were to put to death every male in that city. "With the edge of the sword" means with the sword, leaving no survivors among the men. The phrase about God giving it into their hand means that God would grant them the victory.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land, giving rules of war. First, peace had to be offered; only if the city refused and fought was this applied. It refers to distant cities, not to the nations of Canaan, which had even harsher rules. It is a difficult text, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: this passage reminds us that God offers peace first. Before pursuing a dispute or conflict, seek reconciliation as the first option, as Jesus taught (Matthew 5:9).
exp.27:33:
It says that the people, seeing with their own eyes the tragedies that will come upon them, will be so distressed that they will lose their reason.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. In this chapter he sets out the blessings for obeying God and the curses for abandoning his covenant. This verse is part of a serious warning: disobedience brings painful consequences, such as invasion, oppression, and the loss of what is loved.

For today: when suffering overwhelms us, we should not carry it alone. We can bring our pain to God in prayer and seek the support of trusted brothers and sisters, and professional help too if needed. Moreover, this text invites us to take seriously the way of God, who seeks our good.
exp.15:4:
This verse says that the people of Israel could not sacrifice the Passover lamb in any of their towns, even though God himself was giving them those towns. The word "sacrifice" here means to offer and kill the animal for the feast. The sentence continues in the next verse: they were to do it only in the place that God would choose.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the departure from Egypt and teaches them to celebrate the Passover in an orderly way. By centering the feast in one place, the whole nation gathered to remember what God had done. Scholars agree that this place later became Jerusalem, although the text here does not name it.

For today: let us worship God as he asks, not only as is convenient for us. Setting a fixed place to remember his work, together with other believers, strengthens our faith.
exp.6:18:
This verse reminds the people of Israel what God had already done for them in Egypt. The "temptations" are the plagues and hardships they saw with their own eyes. The "mighty hand and stretched-out arm" speaks of God's power in rescuing them. And it says that God will do the same for any people they come to fear.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. They saw the nations of Canaan as more numerous and stronger. Moses encourages them to look back: if God defeated Pharaoh, he can also go with them now.

When you feel fear before a great problem, remember the times God sustained you. Write those moments down and go over them again. Recalling his past faithfulness strengthens confidence to face what lies ahead.
exp.15:18:
It says that those who judge must not twist justice, nor show favoritism toward someone because of who they are, nor accept gifts in exchange for special treatment. "Showing partiality" means treating some people better than others because of their position or their friendship. A "bribe" is money or gifts given to sway a decision. The verse warns that a bribe blinds even the wise and corrupts the words of the righteous.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just commanded that judges and officials be appointed in every city. Because God is just, he wanted his people to reflect that character in their courts. The following verse stresses this: "Justice, justice shalt thou follow."

For today: be honest in your decisions, whether at work, in your family, or in your church. Do not let yourself be swayed by favors, sympathies, or self-interest. Before deciding something that affects others, ask yourself: "Am I being fair, or is something that benefits me influencing me?"
exp.8:20:
Moses tells how he took the golden calf, which he calls "your sin," and destroyed it completely. He burned it, ground it up until it was as small as dust, and threw that dust into the stream that came down from the mountain. Where the verse defines "ground it very small" and "stamped it," the reader's verse already shows these words: "stamped it, and ground it very small, even until it was as small as dust." So no further definition is needed here.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of their rebellion at Sinai, when they made the calf while he was on the mountain (Exodus 32). He wants them to understand that they do not deserve the land because they are good, but because of God's mercy. Destroying the idol showed that it had no power.

For today: it is not enough to regret what draws us away from God; we must remove it at its root. Ask God to show you what has taken his place in your heart, and with his help, rid yourself of it, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.10:8:
This verse says that if the people obey God's commands, they will live many years in the land God promised. The phrase "that ye may prolong your days" means living a long time there. The word "sware" means that God made a solemn promise. "Seed" means descendants, that is, children and grandchildren. "A land that floweth with milk and honey" is a way of saying the land is fertile and good.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of his life, before they enter Canaan. He reminds them of what God has done for them and encourages them to obey, so that they will be strong and not lose the blessing promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

For today: God keeps his promises, and obedience grows out of remembering his faithfulness. Think today about something God has done for you, and respond with one concrete step of trust and obedience.
exp.1:3:
It says that God orders Moses to warn the people of Israel: when they pass through the territory of their relatives, the descendants of Esau who live in Seir, those people will be afraid of them, but the Israelites must be very careful not to provoke them. The word "coast" means the border or territory. The phrase "take ye good heed unto yourselves" means: be very careful.

Moses recalls how God spoke after years of wandering in the wilderness. It was time to move forward toward the north. Edom, the land of Esau, belonged to the brother of Jacob (Israel), and God had given them that territory as an inheritance. For that reason Israel was not to take it from them or fight with them.

For today: even when we have strength or advantage, God calls us to respect what he has given to others. We can act with humility, avoid unnecessary conflicts, and treat others justly, even those who fear us or think differently from us.
exp.22:4:
God says he would not listen to Balaam, the man who was hired to curse Israel. Instead of letting that curse fall on the people, God turned it into a blessing. The reason the text gives is simple: God loved his people. The word "listen" here means "to pay attention to" or "to answer."

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that Moab and Ammon did not help them on the way, and that the king of Moab paid Balaam to curse them. Moses wants Israel to remember how God cared for them, even when they did not know what was being planned against them.

For today: when you feel that someone wishes you harm or that circumstances are against you, remember that God's love sustains you. Trust that he can work for good, and respond with gratitude rather than resentment.
exp.1:34:
The verse says that the Israelites, after defeating King Sihon, kept only the livestock and the goods taken from the conquered cities. "Cattle" means farm animals, and "spoil" refers to the riches taken from the defeated. Everything else was destroyed.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, reminding the new generation how God gave them victory over Sihon, king of Heshbon. This account is harsh. Scholars understand it in several ways, and the text says that God himself handed over those lands and that he respected the boundaries he had set, such as those of Ammon.

Today we can learn that victories come from God, and that he also sets limits. Before we profit from an achievement, let us ask ourselves humbly: am I within what God permits me?
exp.15:16:
Every person was to bring their offering according to what God had given them. Not everyone gave the same amount; each one gave in proportion to what they had received. The phrase "from their own hand" means what a person could offer with their own hands, and "blessing" refers to what God had given them, such as the harvest and their work.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains the three festivals of the year: the feast of unleavened bread, the feast of weeks, and the feast of booths. These were times of joy and thankfulness. For that reason, no one was to appear before God "empty-handed," but with a grateful offering.

For today: give with gratitude and in keeping with what God has given you, without comparing yourself to others. What matters is not the amount, but a joyful heart that recognizes that everything comes from God.
exp.23:13:
It says we must not mistreat, deceive, or exploit a worker who lives on his daily wage and is poor. A "wrong" means unfair treatment or harm. A day laborer is someone who works for pay each day, and a person in need is someone who lacks what is necessary. This applies equally to an Israelite and to a foreigner who lives in the town.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and he reminds them how to live justly. The verses before and after show God's care for the poor: returning the cloak by evening and paying the wage the same day. God hears the cry of the one who is treated unjustly.

For today: if you have someone who works for you, whether in your home or your business, pay them in full and on time, and treat them with respect.
exp.6:7:
This verse says that God did not bring Israel out of Egypt because of the people's merit, but out of love and out of faithfulness to his promise. The oath was a solemn promise made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The mighty hand speaks of God's power. The house of bondmen was slavery, and to redeem means to set someone free by paying a price or by a powerful act.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God chose them, even though they were few and had nothing special about them. He wants them to avoid pride and to respond with gratitude and obedience, because God is faithful to his covenant.

For today: we do not need to earn God's love through our achievements. If you have received his help or his forgiveness, remember it with humility and gratitude, and let that motivate you to live faithfully and to treat others with the same grace you received.
exp.18:10:
If someone hates his neighbor, lies in wait for him, rises up against him, strikes him so that he dies, and then flees to one of the cities of refuge, this case is different. "Hate" means to despise and wish harm; "lie in wait" means to watch in secret in order to attack; "strike him so that he dies" means to wound until death.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. The cities of refuge protected a person who killed without intending to. But here it is made clear that they did not protect a killer who acted out of hatred and planned the crime. In this way justice and innocent life were safeguarded.

For today: hatred kept in the heart can grow until it causes serious harm. Ask God to heal resentment before it becomes revenge, and seek reconciliation while you still can.
exp.9:1:
God tells Moses that he himself will write on new tables of stone the same words that were on the first tables, the ones Moses broke. Afterward Moses is to keep them inside the ark. "Brakest" means "broke." "Thou shalt put" means "you shall place."

Here Moses speaks to the people of Israel and reminds them of what happened after the sin of the golden calf. Moses had broken the first tables when he saw the people's rebellion. Even so, God decided to give them another chance and to renew his covenant with them. This shows his mercy.

For today: God does not give up on us when we fail. If we have gone wrong, we can come to him with sincerity, and he offers us forgiveness and a fresh start. His word remains the same, and we can keep it in our hearts.
exp.27:38:
It says that the people would plant vineyards and work hard in them, but would not drink the wine or gather the grapes, because the worm would destroy them. "Dress" means to tend and work the ground. "Gather" means to pick the harvest.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets out blessings if they obey God and curses if they turn away from him. This verse is part of a warning: disobedience would bring loss, frustration, and finally exile. What they worked for would not bear fruit.

For today: God invites us to trust him and not only in our own effort. We can work with diligence, but we should also ask ourselves whether we are placing our lives in his hands. His guidance gives meaning and fruit to what we do.
exp.16:10:
When a case was too difficult to decide, the Israelite was to accept the ruling given by the Levitical priests and the judge. The phrase "to the right hand, nor to the left" means neither to the right nor to the left; that is, not to turn aside from what they indicated. A "sentence" is the final decision of the case.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. In the verses just before this one, he explains what to do with disputes that the local judges could not settle. They were to go to the place that God would choose, where there was a central court, so that there would be order and justice throughout the nation.

For today: we can learn to respect authorities and wise counselors, without stubbornness or pride. When someone with wisdom and grounded in the Word of God corrects us, it is worth listening with humility.
exp.0:24:
This verse tells how the twelve men sent to explore the land took some of the fruit that grew there and carried it back to the people. Then the phrase "brought us word again" means that they reported to them, and all of them said the same thing: the land that God was giving them was good.

The one speaking is Moses, who reminds the people of Israel of what happened almost forty years earlier, near Kadesh-barnea. He reminds them that the spies confirmed the goodness of God's promise. However, the following context shows that, even with that good news, the people did not want to go up and did not trust God.

For today: sometimes God shows us clearly that his promises are good, and yet fear still holds us back. Let us remember what God has already done, and take the next step of obedience with confidence in his goodness.
exp.31:26:
He says that God would not punish Israel to the point of destroying them, because he takes into account what the enemies would say. Concern about how the adversary would react means worrying over how the enemy would respond. To be puffed up with pride means to be filled with arrogance. "Strong hand" means one's own strength or human power. The enemies would boast: "We did it, not the Lord."

God speaks in the Song of Moses, at the end of Deuteronomy. Israel has rebelled, and God announces severe discipline. But he holds back, because his name and his glory are at stake before the nations. Interpreters understand the idea of God fearing as a human way of speaking about God, not as real fear.

For today: God guards his honor and continues to work even when we fail. May his patience not lead us to take advantage, but to return to him and give him the glory, not to our own merit.
exp.10:4:
This verse recalls what God did for his people during the years in the wilderness, from the departure from Egypt until the moment they arrived at the plains of Moab. The word "until" here carries the sense of the time that passed up to that point, and the phrase "came into this place" refers to the same arrival. God cared for them, corrected them, and sustained them along that whole journey.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, just before they enter the promised land. They saw the works of God with their own eyes, and Moses brings them back to memory to encourage them to love the LORD and obey him. Remembering his faithfulness would give them firmness for what was coming.

For today: think about how God has sustained you in your own wildernesses. Write down three moments when he helped you and give him thanks. Remembering his faithfulness strengthens confidence for what lies ahead.
exp.17:4:
This verse says that God himself chose the tribe of Levi, out of all the tribes of Israel, to serve him. "Minister" means to serve, and "in the name of the Lord" means on behalf of God. That service would belong to the priest and also to his sons, from generation to generation.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He explains that the priests and Levites would not receive an inheritance of land like the other tribes, so the people were to support them with portions of the sacrifices and with the firstfruits, that is, the first of the harvest.

For today: God cares for those who dedicate their lives to serving him, and he invites us to be generous. We can gratefully support those who teach and serve in our church, giving joyfully from what God has given us.
exp.1:29:
