He says that Sihon, king of Heshbon, refused to let the Israelites pass through his land. The Bible explains that God had hardened his spirit and made his heart stubborn. "Hardened" means made stubborn, and "obstinate" means that he does not change his mind. "As this day" means "as it appears now."

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, and reminds them of what happened. Israel had asked for passage peacefully, offering to pay for food and water. Sihon rejected the offer and went out to fight. Scholars explain in several ways how God hardened his heart, but the text shows that Sihon made his own decision and that God was directing events toward his purpose.

For today: when someone shuts the door on your good intentions, do not become bitter. Do what is right with humility and trust that God governs history. And guard your own heart: do not harden it against the voice of God.
exp.4:8:
It says that we should not bow down to images or serve them, because Jehovah is a strong and jealous God. "Jealous" means that he does not share the love and loyalty of his people with others. "Visiting the iniquity" means that he takes account of sin and its consequences, which reach several generations of those who reject him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land, and repeats the Ten Commandments to them. God had rescued them from Egypt and wanted them to be faithful to him. The following verses show the contrast: his mercy reaches thousands of those who love him.

For today: examine what things hold first place in your heart, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Ask God to be first, and remember that your decisions also affect your family.
exp.10:29:
This verse describes where Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal are located: on the other side of the Jordan, toward the west, in the land of the Canaanites who live on the open plain, near Gilgal and the plains of Moreh. The plain here means open, level ground. Some scholars debate whether this Gilgal is the same one mentioned later in Joshua, so it is not certain which place is meant.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that when they cross the Jordan, they are to proclaim the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal. He gives them a specific location so they will remember that this decision will be real, not just an idea.

For today: obeying God is not something abstract. Think of one particular place or moment this week where you can choose his way, and decide ahead of time what you will do.
exp.25:12:
He says that the Israelite was to come before God and declare that he had already set apart from his house the holy portion of the tithe. He had given it to the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan and the widow, just as God had commanded.

It speaks of an Israelite who, in the third year, the year of the tithe, had shared his harvest with those in need. Before God he made a declaration of a clear conscience: he had obeyed and had not forgotten his commands. The Levites had no land of their own, and the other three groups were vulnerable.

For today: generosity is part of obedience to God, not an extra. We can ask ourselves honestly before Him whom I can help with what I have. And we can give with joy, without boasting, because everything comes from His hand.
exp.28:28:
It says that there are things God has not made known, and those belong only to Him. But what He has given us to know, His law and His word, is for us and for our children forever. The purpose is that we keep doing what He commands. "Hidden" refers to things that are concealed; "revealed" refers to what God has made known; "keep" means to obey.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in Moab, at the end of his life, as he renews the covenant before they enter the promised land. The verses before this one speak of judgment on those who turn away from God. Perhaps questions remained unanswered about that punishment, and Moses reminds them that not everything is explained, but what is essential has already been said.

Today we can live in peace even when we do not understand everything God does. Instead of being troubled by what we do not know, let us put into practice what we do know of His Word, and teach it to our children.
exp.27:57:
This verse is the beginning of a sentence that continues in the verses that follow. It says: "If thou wilt not observe to do" means "if you do not make the effort to keep" the whole written law. It also calls for fearing the name of God, that is, respecting it with deep reverence. The phrase about a God who is glorious and fearful speaks of a majestic God worthy of awe.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. After the blessings for obedience, he warns them of the consequences of abandoning the covenant. The images before this are very harsh, and they show how serious it would be to turn away from God.

For today: obedience to God grows out of a heart that respects and loves him. We can ask ourselves which teaching of the Bible we have stopped practicing, and ask God for help to take one concrete step of obedience today.
exp.32:8:
This verse says that the Levites put loyalty to God above their family ties. The phrase "I have not seen him" does not mean they rejected their family, but that they did not let kinship bend their obedience. That is why they keep your word and guard your covenant. "They have observed" means to carry out faithfully.

Moses is blessing the tribes of Israel before he dies. Here he speaks of Levi, the tribe of the priests. Many think it refers to the episode of the golden calf (Exodus 32:26-29), when the Levites sided with God, although the text does not name it and some interpret it more generally.

For today: loving our family is good, but when family pressure would draw us away from what God asks, we must choose to be faithful to Him, with respect and humility toward others.
exp.22:24:
It says that if you pass through another person's field of grain, you may pick ears of corn with your hand and eat the grain. But you may not use the sickle, which is the curved tool for cutting grain. The words "standing corn" mean the ripe grain still growing in the field, and "neighbour" means the person who lives next to you.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law protected the poor and hungry travellers, who could satisfy their hunger. It also protected the owner, because no one could carry off the harvest. Jesus mentions this practice in Matthew 12:1, when his disciples pick ears of corn on the Sabbath.

Today we can learn to combine generosity with respect. Helping someone in need is good, but without taking advantage of what belongs to others. We can be generous with what we have, and grateful and honest with what others share with us.
exp.7:6:
It says that God is leading his people into a good land, full of water: streams, springs, and fountains that rise up from the ground, both in the valleys and in the hills. Here "depths" refers to deep waters that come up out of the earth. "Lowlands" are low-lying, fertile ground. For a people coming out of the desert, this image spoke of life and abundance.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter Canaan, after forty years in the desert. He reminds them that God corrected them as a father corrects his child, and that the land is a gift from him. He asks them to obey and not to forget this when they have plenty.

For today: think about what God has given you and thank him in a concrete way. When things are going well, it is easy to forget; gratitude keeps us humble and attentive to him.
exp.27:60:
It says that if the people are disobedient, God will bring sicknesses and plagues even beyond those mentioned in the written law. The words "destroyed" and "descendants" in the source are rendered here by the verse's own wording: the verse ends with the phrase "until thou be destroyed," meaning brought to ruin or consumed. The phrase stresses that the consequences of turning away from God would be serious and without any set limit.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He presents to them the blessings of obedience and the curses of breaking the covenant. These warnings are part of an agreement between God and Israel, and they were meant to lead the people to take their faithfulness seriously.

For today: we should not read every illness as a punishment, since the Bible itself denies this in other passages, such as in Job and in John 9. But we can learn to take God's voice seriously and turn back to Him with humility, trusting in His mercy in Christ.
exp.15:9:
This verse commands that the feast of weeks be kept for the Lord. "Solemnity" means a sacred feast. "Voluntary sufficiency of your hand" means an offering given freely, according to what each person is able to give. The measure is how much God has blessed you.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the annual feasts, which began to be counted when the harvest started. This feast fell seven weeks later, and it is the one later known as Pentecost. It was a celebration of thanksgiving for the harvest, which everyone shared, including the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow.

For today: give with generosity and joy, not out of obligation, recognizing that what you have comes from God. And think about who near you needs you to share.
exp.10:18:
This verse commands parents to teach God's words to their children, speaking of them at all times: in the house, on the road, when lying down and when getting up. ó..." means "whether... or...." It describes a constant and natural kind of teaching, not just a special class.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that obeying God brings blessing and that forgetting him brings serious consequences. For this reason he asks them to keep his words in their hearts and pass them on to the next generation.

For today: make faith part of daily life. You can pray with your children in the morning, talk about a verse at mealtime, or speak about God while driving or walking together, letting the conversation flow simply.
exp.29:8:
It says that if the people return to God, He will make them prosper in everything: in their work, their children, their animals, and their crops. "Have plenty" means to have more than enough, and "will again rejoice" means that God will be glad once more to bless them, as He was with their ancestors. "For good" means that His purpose is good.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that, although they may fail and suffer the consequences, God will restore them if they repent and obey Him wholeheartedly. It is a promise given to Israel as a nation, within the covenant with God.

For today: God delights in blessing those who return to Him. If you have turned away, you can come back without fear, trusting in His goodness. His blessing is not always measured in money, but it is measured in His care and His presence.
exp.23:7:
It says that the people must be very careful when a sore of leprosy appears, that is, a serious skin disease. They were to obey with close attention what the Levite priests told them, because God had already commanded it.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of laws for living as a just and protected community. The priests served as guides in these cases, and the following verse mentions Miriam, who was affected by this disease. The word "leprosy" in the Bible may have included several skin diseases, not only the one we call that today.

For today: when we receive wise warning about our health or our lives, it is good to listen with humility and act in time, without thinking we know better.
exp.9:13:
This verse says that everything belongs to God: the heaven, the heaven of heavens (a way of saying the highest and most distant heavens), the earth, and everything in it. Nothing is outside his ownership.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what God asks: reverence, love, obedience, and service with all their heart. Then he states that God owns everything, and yet he chose to love their ancestors and them. This shows that their being chosen was a gift, not something they earned.

For today: if everything is God's, then what we have is a loan that we should take care of. Today you can thank God for something specific you have and use it to help someone, with a humble and grateful heart.
exp.2:13:
This verse tells that Jair, a descendant of Manasseh, conquered the whole region of Argob, all the way to the borders of the peoples of Geshur and Maacah. Afterward he gave that area his own name: Bashan-havoth-jair, which means something like "the villages of Jair." The phrase "unto this day" means that this name was still in use when Moses spoke.

Here Moses is speaking. He is recalling for the new generation, before they enter the promised land, how God gave them victories east of the Jordan and how that territory was divided among the tribes. Some scholars note that the phrase "unto this day" may have been clarified later by an editor; there is no single agreement on that.

For today: God uses ordinary people to carry out his promises. Ask yourself what task, however small it may seem, God has placed in your hands, and do it with courage and faithfulness, trusting him with the outcome.
exp.5:22:
This verse says that God brought his people out of Egypt with a purpose: to lead them into the land he had promised to their ancestors. The verse of the old wording is deleted here, since the verse your reader sees already reads "brought us out" and "give us," and the phrase "sware unto our fathers" is rendered in the verse itself. The word for a solemn promise made with firm commitment is also already shown in the verse, so no separate comment is needed. The "fathers" in this verse refer to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He teaches them how to answer when their children ask about the meaning of the laws. They are to tell the story of their deliverance: God not only rescued them from slavery, he also fulfilled what he had promised. In this way, obedience grows out of gratitude and not merely out of duty.

For today: when I explain my faith to my children or to others, I can share how God has been faithful to me. Remembering his promises that have been kept strengthens trust and encourages us to obey him with joy.
exp.31:25:
God says in the song of Moses that he had thought about wiping Israel off the earth. The phrase "I would scatter them into corners" means that God would have scattered them and made them disappear. The words "I would make the remembrance of them to cease from among men" mean that people would not even remember that they had existed.

Here God speaks in the Song of Moses. Israel had been unfaithful, worshiping other gods, and for that reason God announces harsh punishments. But the next verse shows that God holds back: he does not want the enemies to boast that they won by their own strength and fail to acknowledge the LORD.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but his patience is greater than our failures. If you have drifted away from him, do not harden your heart; return with humility, trusting that his mercy is still open.
exp.29:14:
Moses tells the people to look carefully: God sets two paths before them. One brings life and good; the other brings death and evil. This is not a hidden threat but a clear invitation to choose. The word "look" is like saying "pay close attention, this is serious."

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, just before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God's law is not far away or impossible, but is close, within their reach, in their mouth and in their heart. The verses that follow explain that life consists in loving God, walking with Him, and obeying Him.

For today: our daily decisions, even the small ones, lead us toward one path or the other. Today you can choose one concrete step of obedience and trust in God, knowing that His word is near you and that He helps you to follow it.
exp.15:21:
This verse forbids setting up a statue, that is, a pillar or sacred stone for worship. God says he hates this. The word "hates" means that he is deeply displeased by it. "LORD" is the name of the God of Israel.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions for worshiping God in a pure way. The neighboring peoples used pillars and images in their worship, and God did not want Israel to mix its worship with those customs. Many scholars think this protected the people from idolatry, although some details of how those pillars were used are debated.

For today: examine whether anything holds in your heart the place that belongs to God. Worship him as he has revealed himself, with simplicity and truth, and not with things you invent or copy from others.
exp.10:2:
This verse continues a list of things Moses wants the people to remember. The "signs" are the miracles that showed God's power, and the "works" are the actions God performed. All of this happened in Egypt, before Pharaoh and all his land.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they themselves saw how God acted, not only their children who did not live through it. He calls them to love God and obey Him, using as the reason what He has already done for them. The plagues of Egypt are part of that memory.

For today: when you doubt or feel afraid, remember what God has already done in your life and in His Word. Recalling His faithfulness in the past strengthens trust and the desire to obey Him today.
exp.25:1:
It says that once the people were living in the promised land, they were to set apart the firstfruits, that is, the first produce of the harvest. They would put it in a basket (a small basket) and take it to the place God chose "to place his name there," meaning the place of worship where God would be honored.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter Canaan. He teaches them how to thank God when they receive the land he promised to their ancestors. The firstfruits were a way of acknowledging that the harvest was a gift from God, not only the result of their own effort.

For today: before you spend or share what you receive, set something aside for God first, with gratitude. It can be money, time, or service. This helps you remember that everything you have comes from his hand.
exp.0:1:
This verse says that from Horeb (another name for Mount Sinai) to Kadesh-barnea there were eleven days' journey, that is, eleven days of travel. The route passed by Mount Seir, the region of Edom. A "journey" was what one could walk in a day.

Moses speaks to the people near the Jordan, at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He wants to remind them of their history before they enter the promised land. This detail about distance underlines something sad: a short trip took forty years, because the people doubted and disobeyed at Kadesh. Some scholars see here a note of gentle reproach; the text does not say this directly.

Today, our own paths sometimes stretch out because we lack trust in God. But He continues to guide with patience. Ask yourself: in what area do I need to obey today, without delaying any longer?
exp.5:19:
This verse looks ahead to a future moment: when a son asks his father what the commands the Lord our God gave them mean. The words "testimonies" are the reminders of what God has said and done, "statutes" are his instructions, and "judgments" are his just decisions. "In time to come" means "in the future."

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He asks them to obey God and also to teach their children. After the verse, the answer they are to give does not begin with rules but with the story: God brought them out of slavery in Egypt.

For today: if your children or people close to you ask why you follow God, do not answer only with rules. Tell them simply what God has done for you, and let your testimony explain your obedience.
exp.13:19:
It says that the people of Israel could eat any bird that God had declared "clean." This is the conclusion of a list of forbidden birds that appears just before it. "Clean" here does not refer to hygiene, but to what God allowed as food for his people.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, about to enter the promised land. He reminds them of the laws God gave them. The rules about food set them apart from other peoples, since the text says: "for you are a holy people unto the LORD your God." Scholars explain the reason for each forbidden animal in several ways, and not everything is clear.

For today: God calls us to live differently, and that begins in everyday life. Ask yourself in which daily decisions you can show that you belong to God, with gratitude and not with fear.
exp.31:36:
God asks, with irony, where the false gods are that his people trusted. He calls them "their rock in whom they trusted," that is, the place where they sought refuge and protection. To trust in something means to rely on it, to put yourself under its safety.

This is part of the Song of Moses, where God himself speaks. Israel had turned away from him to follow idols, and now it faces the consequences. God lets the people see that those gods cannot save anyone in the time of distress. But the passage also shows that God will have compassion on his servants when he sees their helplessness. Some see here a mockery by God, and others a painful call to return.

For today: ask yourself what you rely on when a crisis comes, such as money, work, or the approval of others. Entrust your confidence to God, for he alone is a firm rock.
exp.22:16:
This verse forbids prostitution connected with religion in Israel. A "whore" is a woman who sells her body. The word translated "sodomite" refers to a man who offered sexual services as part of pagan worship. Some scholars debate the details of this practice.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them laws to live as God's people, distinct from the Canaanite nations, whose cults sometimes included sexual acts. Furthermore, the context shows a God who protects the weak, such as the fugitive servant, and who desires pure worship.

Today we can learn that God cares for our dignity and that of others. Let us ask him for help to live with purity, not to use or exploit anyone, and to worship him with a whole heart.
exp.14:16:
It says that if a Hebrew servant had already completed six years and did not want to leave free because he loved his master and his household, the master was to take an awl (a pointed tool for piercing) and push it through his ear into the door. In this way he would remain a servant for life. The same applied to the female servant.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they were servants in Egypt and that God rescued them. For this reason the law commanded release in the seventh year and generous treatment of the servant. The act involving the ear was a public sign of a voluntary decision. Scholars do not fully agree on its exact meaning.

For today: remember how much you have received from God, and treat with generosity and respect those who depend on you, such as employees or family members. Let loyalty come from love, not from pressure.
exp.6:11:
If the people listen to God's laws and put them into practice, this verse says, God will keep with them the covenant and the mercy he promised to their ancestors. "Statutes" means God's rules or decrees. "Put them into practice" means that they obey them in truth. "Swore" means God made the promise with a solemn commitment.

Moses speaks to Israel, who are about to enter the promised land. He reminds them that God is faithful and calls them to respond with obedience. After this verse, Moses describes the blessings that will come. It is a covenant: God has already chosen them out of love, and now he invites them to live according to that relationship.

For today: God is faithful to his promises, and our obedience is a response of trust, not a way of buying his love. Today you can choose one concrete step of obedience to what you already know God asks of you.
exp.3:34:
This verse says that God showed Israel all his mighty works with a purpose: that they would know that the Lord is the only true God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what they lived through: the voice of God from the fire on the mountain and the deliverance from Egypt with signs and wonders. He wants their faith to rest on what God actually did, so that they would remain faithful to him and not turn aside to other gods.

For today: when you doubt or feel tempted to trust in other things, remember what God has done in your life and in his Word. Write down three moments when you saw his help, and give him thanks. Remembering strengthens confidence that he alone is worthy of all our faith.
exp.23:20:
It says that when the owner of the vineyard harvests the grapes, he must not go back over the vines to collect the clusters that were left behind. The words for "harvest the grapes" and "go back to gather what was left" are not explained here; the verse itself says that the clusters left behind are for the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of God's laws. The three groups mentioned had no land and no family protection, so they depended on the generosity of others. The verse that follows asks them to remember that they themselves were slaves in Egypt.

For today: think about what you have in excess, whether time, food, or money, and share it with someone in need. For example, you can set aside part of your income to help a widow, a migrant, or a child without parents in your community.
exp.20:2:
This verse says that when a dead body was found in the open country and no one knew who had killed the person, the leaders of the nearest city were to take a heifer, that is, a young cow. That heifer was not to have worked or pulled under the yoke, which is the wooden frame put on oxen for plowing. It was an animal that had never been put to use, set apart for this moment.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This ritual showed that innocent blood defiles the land and that the community is responsible for seeking justice, even when the guilty person is not known. The elders acted on behalf of everyone.

Today we can learn that injustice matters to all of us, even when we are not the direct guilty parties. We can ask God for wisdom to care for the vulnerable, speak the truth, and not look the other way.
exp.10:24:
No enemy will be able to stand against the people of Israel. God himself will put fear and dread of them over all the lands where they walk, just as he had promised.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan, near the end of his life. He reminds them that the victory would come from God, not from their own strength. But the next verse makes clear that the blessing depended on obeying his commands. The promise was tied to their faithfulness.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, do not rely only on your own strength. Seek God, obey him in what he has already shown you, and move forward with confidence, knowing that he goes before you.
exp.27:30:
It says that if the people turn away from God, they will lose what they have worked hardest for. Their ox will be slain before their eyes, and they will not even be able to eat it. Their donkey will be taken away by force, that is, seized from them, and it will never come back. Their sheep will pass into the hands of their enemies, and no one will rescue them. It is a picture of total helplessness: seeing the loss and being unable to do anything about it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. In this chapter he presents blessings for obeying the covenant and curses for disobeying it. These words are a serious warning, given in the hope that the people will choose faithfulness to God.

For today: do not place your security in what you have, since everything can be lost. Put your trust in God, be thankful for what He gives you, and live in a way that honors Him in everyday life.
exp.30:8:
He wrote down "this law," that is, the instructions God had given Israel, and handed it to the Levitical priests, who carried the ark of the covenant, and to the elders, the leaders of the people.

Moses is about to die, and Joshua will take command. Before he goes, Moses puts the law in writing and entrusts its care to both the spiritual and civil leaders. He then orders that it be read aloud every seven years, at the Feast of Tabernacles, so that all the people would hear it. Many scholars think "this law" refers to Deuteronomy or to a part of it, though not all agree.

For today: God's Word needs to be kept, read, and passed on. We can set aside a regular time to read the Bible as a family or in church, and not leave that to others on our behalf.
exp.1:8:
God tells Moses not to trouble the Moabites or go to war with them, because he will not give the Israelites any of their land. That land, called Ar, had already been given to the descendants of Lot. "Trouble" here means to provoke or harass, and "get into a fight" means not to start a conflict with them. An "inheritance" is land received as a family's portion.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel almost at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, and he reminds them of what God commanded him. Israel was passing near Moab, a people related to them through Lot, Abraham's nephew. God had already assigned lands to other peoples, and Israel was to respect those boundaries while they moved toward their own promise.

For today: God also cares for those who are not part of our own group. We do not have to take from others what God has given them. We can wait peacefully for what He has promised us, without envy or unnecessary quarrels.
exp.13:8:
This verse says that, of everything that lives in the water, the people of Israel could eat the animals that had fins and scales. That means fish like the ones we commonly know. The word "eat" here means "may eat," and "fins" are the parts a fish uses to swim.

Moses is speaking to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the laws God gave them so that they would live as a people set apart for Him. These rules about food were part of that covenant. The Bible does not explain every reason, and scholars offer different ideas: health, identity, or symbolism.

Today we are not under these dietary rules, since the New Testament teaches freedom in this matter. But we can still learn to ask ourselves whether our daily habits, even the simplest ones, show that we belong to God and obey Him with gratitude.
exp.1:11:
This verse says that in the region of Seir the Horites lived earlier, a people who were driven out by the descendants of Esau, also called the Edomites. They destroyed them, that is, they removed them from there, and settled in their place. The phrase about those who lived there is explained by the words "dwelt in their stead," and the word "succeeded" means that they took over the land. The parenthetical note compares this with what Israel did in the land that the Lord gave them.

The one speaking is Moses, reminding the people of their journey through the desert before entering Canaan. This comment about Edom, Moab, and other peoples shows that God also guided the history of other nations. Some scholars think this explanatory note may have been added later, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: God cares for his people and also works in history in ways we do not always understand. We can trust that his promises are fulfilled in his time, even when the path is long.
exp.11:0:
This verse opens a new section of laws. It says that what follows are "statutes and judgments," that is, rules and fair decisions that the people were to keep and put into practice. The phrase "put into practice" means to carry out, to do. This was to be done in the land God was giving them, throughout all the days of their lives there. "To possess" means to take it as an inheritance.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, who are about to enter Canaan after years in the wilderness. He reminds them that the land is a gift from God, the God of their ancestors. For this reason he asks them for faithfulness. What follows deals with removing the worship of other gods and worshiping the LORD as he directs.

For today: God's gifts are not meant for living by our own taste, but for obeying him with gratitude. Today you can choose one teaching from the Bible that you already know and put it into practice with steadiness, as a response of thanks for what God has given you.
exp.4:31:
The passage says that the people must take care to do everything God commanded them, without turning aside. "Ye shall observe" means "pay attention," and "to the right hand or to the left" means staying on the path without straying from it, like someone walking along a road and not stepping off it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, now close to the promised land. He reminds them of what happened at Mount Sinai, when the people were afraid of God's voice and asked that Moses hear it for them. Now Moses asks them to obey what God said, so that things will go well for them in the land they are about to receive.

For today: obeying God is a steady path, not an impulse of one day. You can choose one clear teaching from the Bible and put it into practice this week, even if it is difficult or unpopular, trusting that God cares for those who follow him.
exp.0:10:
Moses wishes that God, the God of Israel's ancestors, would make the people a thousand times more numerous than they already are, and that he would bless them just as he has promised. "Your fathers" refers to the ancestors, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life, as he reminds them of what they have lived through since Sinai. They were already as numerous as the stars, and that fulfilled God's promise. But Moses could not carry so many problems and disputes alone, so he asked them to choose wise men to help him lead. His wish for their blessing comes from a grateful heart, even in the middle of his weariness.

We can give thanks for God's blessings without hiding that sometimes they weigh on us. And if we are carrying everything alone, we can ask for help from wise and trustworthy people.
exp.31:30:
Moses says that the gods of the neighboring nations cannot be compared with the God of Israel, whom he calls "our Rock," meaning a firm and secure refuge. He also says that the enemies themselves can judge and see this. Some understand that they themselves acknowledge it; the Hebrew text can be read in several ways.

Moses sings this poem to the people before he dies. He warns them that, if they turn away from God, they will suffer defeats. They would not lose because their enemies were stronger, but because God had given them over on account of their unfaithfulness.

Today, when something promises you security apart from God, such as money, success, or the approval of others, compare it with Him. Ask yourself what you can truly depend on when problems come, and return to God as your refuge.
exp.15:5:
It says that the Passover was no longer to be celebrated in any town, but in the place that God would choose for his name to dwell there. The sacrifice was made in the evening, at the going down of the sun, that is, at dusk, remembering the hour when Israel came out of Egypt. The phrase about the place God would choose is not explained further here.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He repeats the law to them and teaches them to worship God together, not each person in their own way. Over time, that place came to be associated with Jerusalem, although this verse does not name it.

For today: God invites us to remember his deliverance deliberately, not out of habit. We can set aside a fixed time, alone or with the church, to thank him for the salvation he gave us in Christ, and to do so with an attentive and obedient heart.
exp.9:6:
This verse briefly recounts two stops of the people of Israel in the wilderness. They set out from Moserah toward Gudgodah, and from Gudgodah toward Jotbathah, which the Bible describes as a "land of rivers of waters", that is, a place with streams of water. "Journeyed" means that they set out on their way. It is not known with certainty where these places are today.

Moses speaks to the people and reminds them of their history. He reviews the journey they have made, the death of Aaron and the service of the Levites, so that they can see how God guided and sustained them. This verse sits within a parenthesis in his account.

For today: in the midst of long and weary roads, God also prepares places of rest and provision. You can remember with gratitude those "streams" He has given you and trust that He will guide you through the next stage.
exp.32:23:
Moses says that Asher will be blessed with many children, that his brothers will look on him with favor, and that he will dip his foot in oil. The words "á" and "dijo" are from old spelling. Dipping one's foot in oil is a picture of great abundance, as if the oil were so plentiful that one could step in it.

Moses is blessing the tribes of Israel shortly before he dies. Asher would receive a territory in the northwest, and many understand that it was fertile land with olive groves. This is a common interpretation, though the text does not explain it in detail.

For today: God's blessing is not only for oneself. Asher would be loved because his abundance reached others. We can ask God that whatever he gives us, whether time, money or affection, may make us pleasant and generous toward the people around us.
exp.6:17:
He says the people should not be afraid of the nations they are about to face. Instead of looking at their strength, they should remember well what the Lord their God did to Pharaoh and to all of Egypt. "Jehovah" is the name of God, and "remember well" means to bring to mind carefully and on purpose.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. They were thinking, "Those nations are more numerous than we are." Moses does not deny that they are many, but he reminds them of the plagues and the deliverance from Egypt. If God defeated the greatest power of that time, he could also fulfill his promise before these peoples.

When a problem seems bigger than your strength, do not start by looking only at the problem. Call to mind the times God helped you, sustained you, or brought you through. Remembering his faithfulness in the past strengthens your trust to face what lies ahead.
exp.21:26:
It says the man who attacked a young woman betrothed to be married in the field is the only guilty party. "Betrothed damsel" refers to a young woman who is already engaged to be married. "Cried" means she shouted out asking for help. "There was none to save her" means nobody was near enough to defend her. Since no one could come to her aid, the law considers her innocent.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, explaining laws for living justly. This law distinguishes between what happened in the town, where she could cry out and be heard, and what happened in the field, where she could not. In this way the victim is protected and only the attacker is condemned. Scholars point out that the text does not leave her under suspicion, since it declares her without fault.

For today: when someone suffers abuse, we must not blame them or doubt their pain. We can listen to them, believe them, defend them, and seek fair help for them.
exp.28:1:
Moses gathers all the people of Israel and reminds them of what they saw with their own eyes: the works of the Lord in Egypt against Pharaoh, his servants (his officials and attendants), and all his land.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, on the plains of Moab, before Israel enters the promised land. He is renewing the covenant with a new generation, one that was young when they left Egypt. He reminds them of their history so that they will obey God faithfully. The next verse shows that seeing miracles was not enough: a heart that understands is needed.

For today: take time to remember the times God has helped you, and thank him. Remembering what he has done strengthens trust and helps us obey him, and we can ask him for an attentive heart to understand it.
exp.3:5:
It says that Israel must keep God's laws, not just hear them. "Keep" means to obey them carefully, and "do them" means to put them into practice. Doing this would be their wisdom before the other peoples, who, on learning those laws, would say that Israel is a wise and great nation.

Moses speaks near the end of his life. He is on the plains of Moab and addresses the new generation of Israelites before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God gave them his commands and that obeying them would set them apart among the nations. The verses that follow show that what makes them great is having God near and having just laws.

For today: wisdom lies not only in knowing what God says, but in living it. Choose today a biblical teaching you already know, such as forgiving or being honest, and practice it in a concrete way. Your way of living can speak well of God.
exp.33:6:
This verse says that Moses was one hundred and twenty years old when he died. Despite his age, he could still see well and kept his strength. The phrase "his eye was not dim" means that he did not lose his sight, and "natural force" means his strength or vitality. This suggests that his death did not come from weakness or from extreme old age.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who closes the account of Moses. Tradition holds that Moses wrote most of the first five books of the Bible, but this ending was probably added by someone else, and there is no certainty about who that was. The text emphasizes that Moses died "according to the word of the Lord," and that Joshua then took over the leadership of Israel.

God can sustain a person until the end of their service. Today we can serve God wholeheartedly at every stage of life, without thinking that age takes away our worth. We can also trust that God cares for us and for those who will come after us.
exp.26:13:
This verse says that the Levites will speak out loud to all the men of Israel. The word "men" in the verse is the one used here, and "loud voice" means that everyone could hear them clearly. It is the introduction to the solemn words that follow.

Moses gives these instructions to the people before they enter the promised land. When they cross the Jordan, the tribes will stand facing Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, some for blessing and others for cursing. The Levites will read the warnings aloud, and the people will respond with "Amen," that is, "so be it." It was a ceremony to renew the covenant with God.

For today: God's Word was given to be heard and answered. When you read it or hear it, do not stay silent inside: respond with a sincere "Amen," deciding to obey what God shows you.
exp.18:2:
It says that Israel was to prepare the roads well leading to the cities of refuge. It also was to divide its land into three regions, so that in each one there would be a city nearby. The phrase about preparing the way means that you shall prepare the way. A slayer is the one who caused a death, and fleeing means escape.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions for when they are already living there. According to the verses that follow, these cities protected the one who killed without meaning to, so that an avenger would not kill him in the heat of anger. The law sought justice and mercy at the same time.

For today: God makes sure the way toward protection and forgiveness is clear. We can imitate him by removing obstacles so that others can find help, and by treating with compassion the one who made a mistake without bad intent.
exp.26:14:
It says that whoever makes an idol, whether carved from wood or stone or cast from molten metal, and sets it up in a hidden place, falls under a curse. God calls it an "abomination," something He utterly rejects. A carved figure is an image cut from wood or stone, a cast figure is one made of poured metal, and a craftsman is a skilled worker. At the end, all the people say "Amen," which means "so be it" or "we agree."

Moses gives these instructions before the people enter the promised land. The Levites would proclaim twelve curses before the gathered tribes between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim. This one concerns secret idolatry: even though no one saw it, God did. The people were renewing their covenant with Him.

Today we can ask ourselves what hidden things in our hearts occupy the place that belongs to God. Let us bring them into the light and surrender them to Him.
exp.25:14:
This verse is a prayer. The Israelite asks God to look down from his holy dwelling place, that is, from heaven, where He lives. He pleads that God would bless His people and the land He gave them, just as He promised them with an oath to their fathers. The phrase about the land flowing with milk and honey is a way of saying that the land was fertile and abundant.

A cruel-hearted person would not speak this way, but the speaker here is an Israelite who has brought the tithe of the third year before God. He has already declared that he gave it to the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow, and that he obeyed God's commands. Now, with a clear conscience, he asks for God's blessing. He does not demand a payment; he trusts in the promise God made.

For today: Obeying God and caring for those in need go hand in hand with praying with confidence. We can ask Him for His blessing, knowing that He keeps what He promises, and show our gratitude by sharing with those who have less.
exp.13:18:
It says that every "winged creeping thing," that is, flying insects that also walk on the ground, was unclean for the Israelites and was not to be eaten. "Unclean" means it was not fit to eat under the law. Other passages allow certain locusts, so some believe this verse refers to flying insects in general.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the rules about food, together with the list of unclean birds. The text says that God had set them apart as a holy people, and these rules helped them live differently from the neighboring nations.

For today: although Christians are not under these food rules, we can learn to live set apart for God. Ask yourself what daily habit, large or small, you can give to Him to show that you belong to Him.
exp.31:4:
Moses says that God has no part in the people's corruption. The fault is theirs, and because of their stain they no longer behave as his children. He calls them "a perverse and crooked generation," that is, people who turned away from the straight path. This verse is difficult in Hebrew, and translations express it in different ways, but the central idea is clear: the blame is not God's.

Moses sings this song shortly before he dies. He has just presented God as the perfect and righteous Rock. Now he contrasts him with Israel, which responded with unfaithfulness. He wants the people to remember who formed them and how he cared for them.

For today: when we fail, let us not blame God or our circumstances. Let us acknowledge our error with humility and return to the One who is faithful and upright.
exp.24:3:
It says that when the ox is treading out the grain, that is, stepping on the grain to separate it from the straw, it must not be fitted with a muzzle. A muzzle is a piece placed over the animal's mouth so that it cannot eat. In this way, the ox could eat some of the grain while it worked.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in his final addresses before they enter the promised land. The laws nearby deal with justice and dignified treatment: even the person being punished was to have his dignity protected, and the widow was given protection. This rule shows that this compassion extended to animals as well. Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 9:9 and 1 Timothy 5:18 to teach that the one who works deserves to be supported.

Today we can pay those who work for us with justice and generosity, and support with gratitude those who serve us in teaching the Word. The one who works deserves to benefit from his labor.
exp.8:11:
God tells Moses to go down quickly from the mountain, because the people he brought out of Egypt have ruined themselves. They turned aside very soon from the way God had commanded them, and they made themselves an image of melted metal. The word for "quickly" here is the same idea as the verse's "quickly," and the figure made of molten metal is the golden calf.

Here Moses reminds the people, years later, of what happened on Mount Sinai. While he was receiving the tablets of the covenant for forty days, the impatient people made an idol for themselves. Moses reminds them of this to show that their entry into the promised land was not due to their own goodness, but to God's mercy.

For today: how easily we turn aside when we feel that God is slow. We can ask him to keep us faithful while we wait, and not to look for shortcuts or for things that take the place of his rightful place in our hearts.
exp.1:28:
This verse is part of what Moses says he asked Sihon, king of Heshbon. He offers to pass through his land peacefully, buying food and water, just as the descendants of Esau in Seir and the Moabites in Ar had done for him.

Moses reminds the people what happened as they approached the promised land. Israel comes out of the wilderness and seeks a calm passage. There are different ways of understanding how Edom and Moab treated Israel, since other passages seem to say different things. Even so, here Moses presents his request as a gesture of peace. Sihon refuses it, and the text explains this as part of God's plan.

For today: seek peace and respectful dialogue first, even when you believe God is guiding you. Ask with humility, offer to pay what is fair, and leave the outcome in God's hands.
exp.24:7:
This verse describes what follows when a man refuses to marry his brother's widow. The elders of the city, who were the leaders and judges of the people, summon him and speak with him. If he stays firm and says, "I do not want to take her," the case moves to the next step. "Take her" means to marry her.

Moses gives this instruction to the people of Israel. It was the so-called law of levirate marriage: the brother was to give a son to the widow so that the name of the dead man would not disappear and the family would be protected. Before any consequence is applied, the elders talk with him. In this way there is room for conversation and not a hasty decision.

For today: before judging someone for failing to keep a commitment, let us speak with him face to face and listen to his reasons. And when it falls to us to care for someone vulnerable, let us do so with responsibility.
exp.26:24:
God condemns the person who accepts money or payment to kill someone who has done nothing wrong. The word "reward" here means a bribe or gift. "Cursed" means that person is under God's judgment and outside his blessing. And all the people respond "Amen," which means "so be it," accepting that this is just.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He orders a ceremony between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, where the Levites read curses and the people respond. Many of them deal with sins committed in secret. In this way, the people commit themselves to obey God's law and to protect life and justice.

For today: do not use your influence, your money, or your silence to harm an innocent person. Defend the truth and reject every bribe or unjust deal, even when no one sees you.
exp.0:3:
This verse says that Moses spoke to the people after God had given them victory over two powerful kings: Sihon, king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon, and Og, king of Bashan, who lived at Ashtaroth in Edrei. The word "slain" means that they were defeated in battle.

Moses speaks at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. Israel is east of the Jordan, about to enter the promised land. Before he says goodbye, he reminds them of what God did, so that they will trust Him and obey His law with a new generation.

For today: remembering the past victories God has given us strengthens faith in the face of the challenges ahead. We can write down the times God helped us and read them again when we feel afraid or doubtful about the future.
exp.27:13:
This verse calls for not turning aside from what God commanded, neither to the right hand nor to the left. The phrase about turning to the right or to the left means turning in any direction, and the other gods are the gods of other peoples. Serving them means worshiping them and obeying them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the blessings that would come if they kept the covenant with God. This verse closes that list of blessings, and right after it Moses warns of the consequences of disobedience. The central idea is exclusive faithfulness to God.

For today: ask yourself what things compete for first place in your heart, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Choose one concrete decision today in which you will put God first, and stay firm without turning aside.
exp.32:26:
This verse says that the eternal God, the one who has always existed, is a safe place where his people can hide and rest. Underneath you, there are strong arms that hold you up and never tire. God will also drive out the enemy, and the command to destroy them is understood as his order against those who opposed Israel in that conquest.

Moses speaks. He is close to death and blesses the tribes of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they will not advance alone: the same God who guided them through the wilderness will go with them and give them security.

For today: when you feel tired or threatened, do not depend only on your own strength. Stop for a moment, pray, and rest in God. He sustains you even when you feel you can no longer go on.
exp.10:23:
It says God promises Israel all the territory that the soles of their feet tread on. The boundaries are the desert to the south, Lebanon to the north, the river Euphrates to the east, and the uttermost sea, which is the Mediterranean Sea, to the west.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The promise depends on obeying God and loving Him faithfully. It is not an automatic guarantee but an invitation to trust and walk with Him. Scholars debate how this extension of borders was fulfilled over the course of Israel's history.

For today: God often gives us what He promises step by step, as we walk with Him. If you feel faced with something great, take the next step in obedience and trust, without expecting to see it all at once.
exp.4:12:
This verse says that God expects the people to work six days of the week. "All your work" refers to all the daily tasks and responsibilities. Work is not presented as a burden, but as a normal part of life, one that prepares the way for the day of rest.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He repeats the Ten Commandments to them. Here he explains the commandment about the day of rest, and shortly afterward he reminds them that Israel was enslaved in Egypt and that God rescued them.

For today: we can see our work as something worthy, and also set limits so that we can rest. This week, try to finish your pending tasks on time and set aside a time of rest, to be with God and with your family.
exp.8:26:
Moses asks God to remember Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, whom he calls "thy servants." He pleads that God not look upon the stubbornness of this people, nor to their wickedness, nor to their sin.

Moses speaks to the people and recalls how he interceded for them after they made the golden calf at Mount Sinai. He lay prostrate for forty days and forty nights. He does not defend the people by saying they deserve forgiveness; he appeals to the promises God made to the patriarchs and to his own reputation among the nations.

For today: when you fail, do not trust in your own merits, but in the faithfulness and promises of God. And, like Moses, pray also for others who go wrong, asking for mercy for them instead of condemning them.
exp.8:27:
He says that Moses asks God not to destroy Israel, so that the Egyptians and other peoples will not think badly of Him. They could say that the Lord was not able to bring His people into the promised land, or that He hated them and therefore brought them out to kill them in the wilderness. "Hated" means "hated"; "bring them in" means "to bring them into."

Moses speaks to the people and reminds them of his prayer after the sin of the golden calf. He had interceded for them on the mountain. He does not defend Israel's conduct, which was stubborn and rebellious, but appeals to God's reputation, to His promise to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and to His work of rescue.

For today: when we pray for others, or for ourselves, we can rely not on our merits but on the character and promises of God. Also, let us remember that our way of living as believers speaks of God to those who observe us.
exp.30:1:
Moses tells the Israelites that today he is one hundred and twenty years old and that he can no longer "go out and come in," meaning he no longer has the strength to lead the people as he once did. Moreover, God had told him he would not cross the Jordan River.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, on the plains of Moab, just before Israel enters the promised land. He encourages them by reminding them that God himself will go before them and that Joshua will be the new leader. Some think that "I can no more go out and come in" refers to his age; others, to his limit as a leader. The text joins both ideas.

For today: all of us reach stages in which we must let go of responsibilities. We can do so with peace, preparing others and trusting that God continues to guide his work, even when we are no longer at the front.
exp.8:5:
He says that God does not give Israel the promised land because they deserve it. "Righteousness" here means being good or upright before God. "Stiffnecked people" means stubborn and foolish, unwilling to be corrected, like an animal that will not bend its neck to receive the yoke.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He warns them not to become proud when God defeats the nations who live there. God gives them the land because of his faithfulness to the promise made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and because of the wickedness of those nations. Then Moses reminds them of their rebellions in the wilderness.

For today: everything good we receive from God is a gift, not a reward. When things go well for us, let us give thanks with humility instead of boasting.
exp.32:22:
Moses says that Naphtali is satisfied, that is, well content, with the favour of God, which means his grace and goodwill. He is full with the blessing of the Lord and will receive as his inheritance the west and the south. These words can also be understood as "the lake and the south," and it is not known with certainty which exact area they refer to.

Moses speaks shortly before he dies. He blesses each tribe of Israel before they enter the promised land. Naphtali was one of the tribes, and his blessing speaks of abundance and of an inheritance that comes from God.

For today: what we have comes from the goodness of God. Today you can give thanks for what he has given you and live content, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.27:14:
This verse says that if the people do not listen to the voice of God, nor make an effort to keep all his commandments and laws, all the curses listed below will come upon them and overtake them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: obeying him would bring blessing, and turning away from him would bring painful consequences. He says this so that they will choose the right path with seriousness.

For today: obedience to God is not a burden, but a way of caring for our lives. Today, as Christians, we trust that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law (Galatians 3:13). Even so, we can ask ourselves: in what area do I need to listen to God more carefully and obey him with love?
exp.12:17:
This verse closes a condition: God will show mercy and bless Israel when the people obey his voice, keep all his commandments, and do what is right in his sight. "Á" is an older form of "a," and "prescribo" means "I command."

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the Promised Land. The chapter deals with an Israelite city that had turned to idolatry, and the order to destroy it was very severe. Moses ends by reminding them that what matters most is total obedience to God, not isolated acts. It is a hard passage, and Christians read it carefully, within the particular history of Israel.

For today: obedience to God is not lived halfway or only when it is convenient. We can ask ourselves with humility: "Is there any area of my life where I am not doing what is right before God?" And we can ask him for help to change.
exp.23:21:
This verse reminds the people of Israel that they themselves were slaves in Egypt. That is why God commands them to leave some of the harvest for others. "Bondman" here means slave. To "gather what is left behind" means going back over the field to pick up what remained, and to "harvest the grapes" means gathering the fruit of the vineyard.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land, and passes on what God orders. The laws in this passage protect the most vulnerable: the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow, who had no land and no one to support them. God appeals to Israel's memory: whoever was oppressed and rescued must treat the needy with kindness.

Today we can remember how much grace we have received and share from what we have. Perhaps by setting aside a part of our income or our time to help someone in need, without expecting anything in return.
exp.4:7:
This verse says that the people of Israel were not to make any carved image or likeness of things in heaven, on the earth, or in the water, in order to worship them. A "graven image" is a carved figure, and the verse's list of three places, above, below, and in the waters, covers all of creation.

Moses speaks to the people, recalling the law that God gave on Mount Sinai. God had just freed them from Egypt, where they had seen many idols. The next verse makes clear that the problem was bowing down to those images and serving them, instead of the God who saved them.

Today we can ask what thing has taken God's place in our hearts: money, fame, work, or a person. Let us give God first place with gratitude, remembering all that he has done for us.
exp.15:14:
This verse commands the people to hold a seven-day feast to God in the place he would choose. The reason given is that God blessed them in their harvests and in all the work of their hands, so they were to be very joyful.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains how to celebrate the feast of booths after the harvest. This joy was to include everyone: the family, the servants, the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow. In this way no one was left out of the thankfulness.

For today: pause to thank God for what he has given you, and share that joy with someone who needs it. You can invite a person who is alone to a meal, or help someone with your time or your resources.
exp.1:0:
It says that the people of Israel turned around and set out into the desert, along the road that leads to the Red Sea (the "Bermejo Sea" of this old version), just as God had indicated to Moses. For many days they kept going around the mountain of Seir.

The one speaking is Moses, near the end of the people's time in the wilderness. He reminds them of their history before entering the promised land. He speaks of the years after the disobedience at Kadesh-barnea, when the earlier generation would not trust God. The following verse shows that the detour lasted until God pointed them in another direction.

For today: sometimes we go around in circles for a long time in the same place, without moving forward. It is good to stop, to listen to God, and to be ready to change direction when He shows us the way.
exp.27:36:
It says that the people of Israel, if they turn away from God, will become an object of horror, a case that others point to as a warning, and a subject of mockery or talk among all the nations where God takes them.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. After describing the blessings of obedience, he sets out the consequences of rejecting the covenant. This warning includes exile, and it was not an empty threat: it was meant to make Israel take its commitment to God seriously. Later texts of the Old Testament show that Israel did indeed live through something like this.

For today: our lives speak of what we believe. We can ask ourselves whether our decisions reflect faithfulness to God. When we go astray, He calls us to return with humility, and He always offers forgiveness to those who repent.
exp.26:19:
It says that God condemns the person who has sexual relations with his father's wife. The phrase "lie with" is an old expression for having intimate relations. To "uncover his father's skirt" means dishonoring him, treating as one's own what belongs to him within his marriage. All the people answer "Amen," which means "so be it," accepting this warning.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. Curses are pronounced in a ceremony where the people renew their covenant with God. This list deals with sins committed in secret, which the judges might not see. The verses nearby protect the weak and the purity of the family. Some think that "his father's wife" refers to a stepmother, not to one's own mother.

Today it reminds us to respect the boundaries of marriage and family. Even where no one sees us, we can take care of our relationships, honor our parents, and flee from what harms others.
exp.14:17:
It shall not seem hard unto you when you send him away free from you. He has served you for six years, and that was worth twice what a hired worker would earn, that is, a worker who is paid by the day. God promises to bless the one who obeys and lets him go with generosity.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law protected those who fell into debt and sold themselves as servants: after six years they were to go free (vv. 12-17). Many understand the double value as a reference to the great worth of his labor, though some interpret it in other ways.

Today, when you have to release a debt, let an employee go, or be generous with someone, do it with gratitude and not with bitterness. God sees your generosity and cares for you.
exp.6:6:
This verse says that God did not choose Israel because they were a great, strong, or numerous people. On the contrary, they were among the smallest. "Set his love upon" means that God placed his affection on them, and "chose" means that he selected them for himself.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they enter the promised land. He has commanded them to destroy the altars of the idols, and he wants them not to be filled with pride. He reminds them that their being chosen was not a reward for their merits. The following verse explains that it was for the sake of God's love and his promise to the patriarchs.

For today: God does not love us for what we accomplish, possess, or appear to be. If you feel small or inadequate, rest in the fact that his love does not depend on you. And if things are going well for you, live with humility and gratitude, not with pride.
exp.0:32:
It says that God himself went ahead of the people of Israel during their journey through the desert. He searched out the best place for them to camp. By night he guided them with a pillar of fire, and by day with a cloud.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the desert. He reminds them how God cared for them, even though they did not trust him and did not want to enter the promised land. Because of this, that generation lost the opportunity to enter.

For today: when the path is not clear, remember how God has cared for you before. That memory can help you trust him today, and take the next step even though you cannot yet see the whole way.
exp.31:49:
God tells Moses that he is going to die on the mountain he is about to climb, Mount Nebo. The phrase "be gathered to your people" is an old way of saying that he will die and join his ancestors. God reminds him how Aaron, his brother, died on Mount Hor. The word "unfaithful" in the older text means they failed in their duty, or were disloyal.

The Lord speaks on the same day that Moses finishes teaching the song to the people. Moses can see the promised land, but he will not enter it, because at Kadesh he did not honor God before Israel. Even so, God himself shows him how and where his journey will end, and does not leave him alone.

For today: our actions have consequences, and God is serious about obedience. But he is also faithful and close to us in our final days. We can live with humility, and trust that God cares for us until the last day.
exp.9:16:
This verse says that the Lord is the supreme God, above everything that people call god or lord. He is "great, mighty and terrible," that is, so awe-inspiring that he causes deep reverence. "Does not regard persons" means he shows no favoritism, and "does not take reward" means he cannot be bribed.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God chose them out of love, not because of merit, and he calls them to obey him wholeheartedly. Right away he shows what kind of God this is: he defends the orphan and the widow, and he loves the foreigner.

For today: if God shows no favoritism and cannot be bought with anything, neither should we treat some people better than others because of their money or position. This week, make an effort to treat with respect and kindness someone who usually goes unnoticed.
exp.17:20:
This verse raises an honest question from the people: "How will we know which message does not come from God?" In other words, how can they tell a true prophet from a false one? The name "Lord" is God's name, and "speaking in his name" means claiming that a message comes from Him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just warned them against the fortune-telling practices of other nations, and he promises that God will raise up prophets to guide them. But he also knows there will be false voices, so God gives them a sign by which to test them (v. 22).

Today, not everything said to come "from God" really does. We can examine each message calmly, comparing it with what the Bible teaches, and without fear of whoever speaks with great confidence.
exp.21:6:
This verse commands that the mother bird be let go, and that only the young be taken. "Let go" means to set her free, and the phrase "that it may be well with you" means that God promises blessing to the one who obeys. The verse's wording about "prolonging your days" speaks of a long life.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land, and reminds them of God's laws. This rule appears among other instructions about daily life, such as putting a railing on the roof to protect others. Together, they show care for life and respect for what God has created. Some think it also protected future provision, since the mother could keep laying eggs.

For today: practice compassion and restraint. When you use something God has created, do not take everything you can, but leave room for life to continue.
exp.31:35:
God says that he will do justice for his people, that is, he will judge them and also defend them. The phrase "repent himself" does not mean that God makes a mistake, but that he will change how he deals with them and will feel compassion. This happens when he sees that his people's strength is gone and that no one is left, neither free nor enslaved, to help them.

God speaks within the song that Moses taught Israel before he died. God warns that the people will suffer because of their unfaithfulness, but he also promises that he will not abandon them forever. His compassion comes when Israel no longer has anything to trust in.

For today: when you feel without strength and without a way out, do not despair. Recognize your limits, return to God with humility, and trust that his compassion sustains you.
exp.15:2:
It says that during the Passover, the people were not to eat bread with yeast, that is, with fermented dough. For seven days they would eat bread without yeast, called "the bread of affliction," because they left Egypt in haste, that is, quickly. God wanted them to remember that day all their lives.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He repeats the Passover instructions so they will not forget how God freed them from slavery. The flat bread reminded them of the suffering and the speed of that departure.

For today: remember the times God has helped you and brought you out of trouble. You can write them down or tell them with your family. Remembering his faithfulness strengthens gratitude and trust when hard times come.
exp.14:1:
This verse explains how the year of release worked. A person who had lent money to a fellow Israelite was to let that debt go and not demand it back again. To release a debt means to cancel it or let it go. A loan is what was given, and a neighbor is the person living nearby or a fellow countryman. The word "proclaimed" in this context means announced publicly: it was God himself who declared that time of forgiveness.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. The law aimed to protect the poor and to keep anyone from being in debt forever. Scholars debate whether the debt was fully canceled or only its collection was suspended for that year, but the spirit of the law is compassion between brothers.

Today we can ask ourselves whether there is someone who owes us something, whether money or an offense, and whom God invites us to let go. Forgiving generously reflects how God treats us.
exp.11:6:
This verse says that the people would eat in the place God chose, in his presence, and would rejoice together with their families over all the fruit of their labor. "Ye shall eat" and "ye shall rejoice" are older forms of "they will eat" and "they will rejoice." "The work of your hands" means what they produced with their effort. The blessing came from God.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that they must worship God in one chosen place, not wherever each person wanted, as they had done in the wilderness. There they would bring their offerings and celebrate with joy, like a thankful family feast.

For today: before you worry about what is still missing, pause with your family to thank God for what you have. A shared meal with gratitude can be a simple and joyful act of worship.
exp.13:24:
If the road to the place of worship is too long to carry the tithe (grain, wine, oil, and animals), the Israelite may sell it. The phrase "Then shalt thou turn it into money" means that the produce is turned into money. "Bind up the money in thine hand" means you should keep it safe, perhaps in a pouch, and carry it with you to the place the Lord your God chooses.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions so that, when they live far from the place of worship, they can still honor God. The purpose was that they would learn to fear him and to celebrate with joy in his presence, together with their families and the Levites.

For today: God cares that we worship him with sincerity and joy, and he does not place impossible obstacles in the way. Think of a practical way to give or serve with joy, even when your circumstances are difficult, and do it with a grateful heart.
exp.30:19:
It says that God will bring Israel into the land he promised to their ancestors, a land that "flows with milk and honey," meaning very fertile and abundant. There the people will eat until they are full and grow fat, that is, they will prosper. But God warns that then they will turn to other gods, serve them, offend him, and break his covenant.

God speaks to Moses shortly before Moses' death. God knows that the people, in comfort, will tend to forget him. For this reason he commands that a song be written, which the Israelites will learn and which will serve as a witness when troubles come. It is not a wish of God's, but an honest warning.

For today: prosperity can also be a test. When everything is going well, it is easy to stop praying and trusting God. Thank him today for what you have and look for a simple habit to remind you of it each day.
exp.27:8:
This verse says that God will establish Israel as his people set apart for himself, just as he promised with an oath. The verse's word "establish" means that he will make them firm and secure. "Holy" means set apart for God. This holds when the people keep his commandments and live according to his ways.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He presents the blessings of the covenant: if they obey, God will protect them, make them prosper, and the other nations will see that they belong to him. This promise rests on the oath God made to their fathers.

For today: obedience is not a burden but the path to living as God's people. Today you can choose one concrete step of obedience, such as forgiving, being honest, or setting aside time for prayer, trusting that God is faithful to his promises.
exp.4:27:
God heard what the people said to Moses and answered that all of it was good. "The Lord heard the voice of your words" means that God listened to them carefully. "They have well said all that they have spoken" means that what they asked for seemed right to him.

Moses reminds them of what happened at Horeb. After hearing God's voice from the fire, the people became afraid and asked Moses to be their go-between. They promised to listen and obey. God approved their reverence, but in the next verse he wished that this fear would become a truly faithful heart.

God listens to us and values our respect for him. But what he desires most is that our promises be seen in constant obedience. Today you can tell him honestly in prayer what you want to do, and then take one concrete step of obedience.
exp.5:13:
