This verse commands the people of Israel not to follow other gods, that is, the gods of the nations around them. "Going after" means to go behind someone, to follow them as a disciple. The phrase "of the gods of the people" refers to gods that belong to others, not to Israel. "Round about you" means the surrounding areas.

Moses speaks to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the LORD brought them out of Egypt, out of slavery. He warns them that, by living among peoples with other religions, they could forget God. For this reason he asks them for complete faithfulness, and tells them that God is jealous, that is, that he desires a love with no rivals.

Today, idols can be money, success, or the opinion of others. Ask yourself what you follow more than God, and offer it to him in prayer.
exp.25:10:
This verse says that the people were to rejoice in all the good things that God had given to them and to their household. It was not a solitary joy: the Levite and the foreigner who lived among them also took part. The phrase about God having given is rendered in plain modern English here, so the reader can follow the meaning directly from the verse as it stands.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains how to present the firstfruits, that is, the first part of the harvest, as an act of gratitude. The Levites had no land of their own, and foreigners were often vulnerable, so God includes them in the celebration.

For today: before enjoying your blessings, give thanks to God, and think about whom you can invite to share them. A meal, a helping hand, or time spent together can turn your gratitude into shared joy.
exp.28:6:
This verse recalls that, when the people reached the east side of the Jordan, they faced two kings: Sihon, king of Heshbon, and Og, king of Bashan. Both came out to fight against Israel, and the Israelites defeated them.

Moses speaks almost at the end of his life to a new generation about to enter the promised land. He reviews what they have lived through in the wilderness so that they see God cared for them and gave them victories. He wants them to renew their covenant with Him and obey Him.

For today: when you face a difficulty, remember the times God sustained you before. That grateful memory strengthens trust and encourages you to obey Him, without assuming that the victory depended only on your own strength.
exp.3:48:
This verse closes the list of places Israel had conquered east of the Jordan. It includes the whole eastern plain, down to the Dead Sea, and the slopes that run down from Mount Pisgah. The slopes are the sides of the hills where the water runs down.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He reminds them that God had already given them victory over two Amorite kings, Sihon and Og. This list of territories is meant to help them remember God's faithfulness and to obey the law he is about to give them.

For today: when you remember in detail what God has already done in your life, your trust grows. Write down the times he helped you, and let that encourage you to obey him and to trust him with what comes next.
exp.15:8:
It says the people were to count seven full weeks, beginning from the moment they first put the sickle to the ripe grain. The ripe fields ready for harvest are what the word refers to, and the sickle is the curved tool used for reaping. It was an orderly count between two harvests.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. After the Passover, which remembers the deliverance from Egypt, he explains the feast of Weeks, also called Pentecost in the New Testament. It was a festival of thanksgiving for the harvest, celebrated with joy, freewill offerings, and generosity toward the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow.

Today we can learn to count our blessings with intention. Before the season passes, take time to acknowledge what God has given you, and share something with someone in need, so that your gratitude becomes shared joy.
exp.14:22:
It says that when someone eats the meat of an animal with a defect (one that is not fit for the altar), they must not eat its blood. They must pour it out on the ground, the way water is poured out. "Only" here means "but with this condition." "You shall pour it out" means "you shall empty it out."

Moses speaks to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that animals with defects were not offered to God, but they could be eaten at home. Even so, blood remained something special, because in the law it represented life and was connected with the sacrifices (Leviticus 17:11).

For today: although we no longer live under those rules, we can learn to respect what God calls valuable, such as life. We can give God our best and treat even everyday things with reverence.
exp.21:9:
It says that the land should not be plowed by putting together, under the same yoke, an ox and a donkey. "Together" means "at the same time," and "plow" means breaking up the ground to sow it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and gives them instructions for their daily life. It sits in the middle of laws about mixing: seeds, cloth. Some believe it teaches separation and order; others, that it protects the animals, since the ox is stronger than the donkey and the donkey would suffer. The text does not explain the reason, so we cannot be certain of it.

For today: although we do not plow with animals, we can learn to make sure no one carries a burden they cannot bear. Let us think about our work, our families, or our church, and share the tasks with fairness and compassion.
exp.30:4:
God himself will hand the nations of Canaan over to Israel. After that, the people were to act toward them according to what God had already commanded. "Will give them over" means he will put them under their control. "According to" means "in agreement with." The victory comes from God, but the people must obey his instructions.

Moses speaks here as an old man, shortly before his death. He knows he will not cross the Jordan, so he encourages the people and Joshua, his successor. He reminds them of what God did to Sihon and Og so that they will trust that he will keep his promise. The orders about Canaan were tied to that specific time and place in Israel's history.

For today: when you face a great challenge, trust that God goes before you, but do not stand still. Do your part in obedience, following what he has already shown you in his Word.
exp.27:0:
It says that if the people listen carefully to God's voice, not only hearing it but putting it into practice by obeying all his commandments, God will place them in a high position, that is, of honor and blessing, above the other nations.

Moses speaks to Israel on the plains of Moab, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God and presents the blessings that would come from obedience. Later in the chapter he also warns of the consequences of disobedience.

For today: listening to God is not only knowing what he says, but deciding to do it. Today you can choose one simple command from the Bible, such as forgiving or being honest, and put it into practice faithfully, trusting that God cares for those who obey him.
exp.16:0:
It says that Israel was not to offer to God an ox or a sheep that had some defect or something bad about it, such as a deformity or an illness. The words "blemish" and "evilfavouredness" in the verse refer to physical defects of the animal. "Abomination" means something that God firmly rejects.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land, reminding them of God's law. The verse sits in the middle of instructions on how to live faithfully within the covenant. Right after this, he speaks about idolatry, so offering what is defective seems to show a divided or half-hearted heart toward God. Scholars connect it with that idea, although the text does not fully explain it.

For today: let us give God our best and not what we have left over. It can be our time, our money, or our attention, offered with sincerity and gratitude.
exp.30:27:
Moses asks for the elders of the tribes and the officers to be gathered together. He wants to speak some words to them so that they can hear them clearly. He also calls heaven and earth to witness against the people.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, shortly before Israel enters the promised land. He knows the people tend to rebel. That is why he has placed the law beside the ark and now asks for solemn witnesses. Afterward, he recites a song to them. Calling on heaven and earth was a firm way of putting a warning on record.

God speaks to us with clarity and with love, before we turn aside. We can take his Word seriously today, without waiting until we are in trouble. A good practice is to read the Bible every day and ask for help to obey it.
exp.4:4:
Moses says he stood between God and the people to pass on what God was saying. The people were afraid because of the fire on Mount Sinai and did not go up. Then Moses begins to repeat God's words.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what happened at Sinai, since they were children or had not yet been born. He says the covenant is for them too. This seems to contradict "face to face" in the previous verse; many understand it as God's real nearness, with Moses as the mediator.

Today we can approach God with reverence, but without a fear that keeps us away. His Word calls us to hear it personally, not only through what others tell us.
exp.32:3:
It says that Moses gave the people of Israel a law, and that this law is an inheritance for the whole community of Jacob, that is, the people of Israel. The word "inheritance" means something received and passed down to one's children. The "congregation" is the assembly or community of the people.

Moses speaks just before he dies, as he blesses the tribes of Israel. He has just recalled how God revealed himself at Sinai, where he gave his law. Here the people respond, and Moses implies that the law is not a distant burden but a treasure God gave them. Some understand that he speaks on behalf of the whole people.

For today: value the Word of God as an inheritance you have received, not as a mere obligation. Spend a few minutes each day reading it with gratitude, and think about how you can share it with your children, your family, or your friends.
exp.30:7:
This verse says that God himself goes before his people. He will be with Joshua, he will not fail him or leave him alone. That is why Joshua should not be afraid or feel weak.

Moses speaks in front of all Israel. He is old, he knows he will not cross the Jordan, and he is handing over leadership to Joshua. The people were about to enter the promised land and face strong enemies. Moses reminds them that the victory did not depend on them alone, but on God going with them, as he had promised their ancestors.

When you face a big change or a task that frightens you, remember that you are not alone. Pray, take the next step with humility, and trust that God goes before you. That does not remove the difficulties, but it gives you courage to keep going forward.
exp.4:29:
God tells Moses to go and say to the people: "Get you into your tents again." "Tents" are the tents where families lived in the desert. The old word "Get you" is an older way of saying "return," an order to go back to their homes.

God is speaking to Moses. The people had just heard his voice at Mount Sinai, and, frightened, they asked Moses to be the one to listen to God and then tell them what he said. God approved that request, but he wanted their hearts to always respect and obey him. While the people returned to their tents, Moses stayed with God to receive the commandments.

For today: Listening to God does not stay in one exciting moment; it is lived out in the routine of the home. After reading the Bible or praying, ask yourself: "What concrete change will I make today at home or at work?"
exp.28:23:
This verse shows a question that all the nations will ask when they see the land of Israel destroyed. They will wonder why the Lord did something so harsh, and what such a great anger means.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel just before they enter the promised land, while he renews the covenant with them. He warns them what the judgment would be like if they turned away from God. The answer comes in the following verses: the land would be left in that state because they abandoned the covenant and served other gods. In other words, the warning is meant to make them think about this before they reach that point.

For today: spiritual decisions leave marks that others can see. It is worth examining what we give first place to, and returning quickly to God with humility, because he is patient and seeks to restore us.
exp.3:27:
It says that if the people turn away from God, they will end up serving false gods, made by human hands, of wood and of stone. These are idols that do not see, do not hear, do not eat, and do not smell; in other words, they have no life and no power. The phrase "you will serve" is rendered as "you shall serve," and "there" refers to the lands where they will be scattered.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them that if they fall into idolatry, God will allow them to be scattered among the nations. But the verse that follows shows hope: from there they can seek the Lord with all their heart, and they will find him.

Today we may not carve idols of wood, but we can place our trust in things that cannot save us, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Ask yourself what has taken the place of God in your heart, and return to seeking him; he remains willing to hear you.
exp.12:12:
This passage describes a serious case: certain men, called "children of wickedness" (wicked people with no respect for God), went out from among the people and persuaded the inhabitants of their city to worship other gods. The word "instigated" means pushing or urging others to do something wrong.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains how to act if someone leads them to abandon the God who rescued them. The command to investigate the facts carefully follows right away. The severity of the sentence reflects that Israel was a nation under covenant with God, and idolatry was treated as betrayal of that covenant.

For today: let us be careful about whose spiritual influence we accept. Let us test every teaching against the Bible and not follow anyone who would turn us away from Christ, even if they speak with conviction or are popular.
exp.9:21:
This verse says that Israel's ancestors went down into Egypt as only seventy people. Now, by contrast, God has made them as numerous as the stars of the sky.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what God has done so that they will fear him, serve him, and remain close to him. The seventy refers to Jacob's family, according to Genesis 46. Moses uses this contrast to show God's faithfulness to his promise.

For today: when you feel small or think your beginnings were weak, remember that God can make grow what seems little. Make a list today of things God has done in your life, and thank him for them.
exp.28:19:
It says that if someone hears the warnings of the covenant and still reassures himself, thinking "nothing will happen to me, I can follow my own desires," the Lord will not forgive him. The phrase about the anger smoking means that his wrath will burn against him. The phrase about blotting out his name means erasing it, making it disappear. The word for jealousy describes the love of God that will not tolerate rivals.

Moses speaks to the people in Moab, when he renews the covenant before they enter the promised land. He warns them against idolatry and against a heart that turns away in secret. The problem here is not a fall caused by weakness, but the stubborn attitude of someone who despises the warning and believes he is safe.

For today: do not use God's grace as an excuse to keep doing what you know is wrong. If you feel your heart growing cold, return to God with humility and do it in time.
exp.27:46:
This verse says that the people did not serve God with joy or gladness of heart, even when they had abundance of everything. The comment about the wording is removed here because it explained a source-language word and an old spelling that do not appear in the verse your reader sees. The complaint is not that they did not serve, but that they did so without a grateful heart.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience. Here he explains the root of the problem: a heart that, in the middle of abundance, forgets to give thanks to God.

For today: even if you fulfill your religious duties, ask yourself whether you do them with gratitude. Today, before asking for something, set aside a few minutes to give thanks for what you already have. In this way your service to God comes from joy and not from habit.
exp.6:25:
This verse commands that nothing abominable be brought into the house, meaning something God rejects, such as idols. If someone did so, they would become set apart for destruction, a thing devoted to be destroyed. For this reason the people were to utterly detest and reject such things.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just told them to burn the images of the gods of Canaan and not to keep their gold or silver. God wanted to protect his people from idolatry, which could trap them and turn them away from him.

For today: ask yourself what things you have let into your home or your life that compete with God or pull you away from him. It may be something you see, hear, or keep. Ask God for wisdom and, with humility, set aside whatever makes you stumble.
exp.27:7:
It says that God will command his blessing upon the "storehouses," which were the places where grain and provisions were kept. It will also be upon everything the person does ("in all that thou settest thine hand unto," that is, in their work). And it promises to bless them in the land that God gives them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: if they obey him, they will live under his care. This promise was addressed to Israel as a nation and, according to the context, is tied to keeping God's commandments.

For today: we can work with confidence, remembering that everything we have comes from God. That confidence is shown in being honest, thankful, and generous. The Bible does not promise that everything will be easy, but it does invite us to place our work in God's hands.
exp.0:19:
Moses reminds the people that they had already arrived at the mountain of the Amorites, a region that God was handing over to them. The Amorites were one of the peoples living in Canaan. The name for God is "the Lord our God," and the phrase "doth give unto us" shows that the land was a gift from Him.

Moses speaks at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, just before Israel enters the promised land. He goes over their history to remind them how, at Kadesh Barnea, they came close to receiving the promise but doubted and sent spies instead of trusting.

Today we can learn that God often brings us to the doorway of what He promises. When He gives us a clear direction, it is wise to obey with confidence, rather than letting fear make us hesitate.
exp.28:26:
This verse says that God became very angry with the land of Israel and brought upon it all the curses that were written in the book of the law.

Moses is speaking to the people before they enter the promised land. He describes what the nations would say when they saw a ruined land: that the people had abandoned the covenant with God and served other gods. It is a warning so that they would not repeat that mistake. The verses that follow speak of exile as the consequence.

For today: God takes our faithfulness to him seriously. Examine whether anything has taken God's place in your heart, such as money, success, or comfort, and return to him with sincerity. His warning aims to protect us, and his grace always invites us to return.
exp.23:15:
This verse teaches that justice must be personal. A father was not to be put to death for the crime of his child, nor a child for the crime of his father. Each person answers for what they themselves did. The word "shall be put to death" here refers to the death penalty in Israel's courts.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the Promised Land, repeating God's law. This command stands among laws that protect the vulnerable: the poor day laborer, the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow. In this way, judges were not to punish innocent family members for another's guilt. Some scholars think it also corrects customs of other peoples of that time, but the text does not state this clearly.

For today: do not blame others for mistakes they did not commit. Do not use a family's past to judge a person. And when you are wrong, take responsibility with humility, trusting in God's mercy.
exp.23:12:
If a poor man gave you his pledge (an item, usually his cloak or coat, that he left as security for a loan), you must return it to him before the sun goes down. That way he can sleep warm. He will bless you, and God will count it as an act of righteousness on your part. Here "without fail" is what the word "in any case" conveys.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land, and explains how to live with justice. The law allowed lending, but it protected the poor so that their need would not be taken advantage of. The cloak was sometimes the only thing they had to cover themselves from the cold of the night.

Today, if you have power over someone because of a debt, a job, or a favor, do not take advantage of their need. Act with compassion and seek to treat them fairly and humanely, because God sees how we treat the weak.
exp.0:21:
The passage says that all the people came near to Moses with a proposal: to send men ahead to explore the land. They wanted someone to bring them a report about the route they would take up and the cities they would reach.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, recalling what happened at Horeb and Kadesh-barnea. God had already given them the land and told them not to fear. Even so, the people asked for scouts. Moses accepted the idea (v. 23), although Numbers 13 shows that God allowed it, and the report ended in fear and disobedience. Commentators differ on whether the request already showed a lack of trust.

Today, planning ahead and gathering information is wise, but it should not replace trust in God's promises. Before seeking more data, ask yourself whether God has already spoken and whether what you really seek is security to obey.
exp.15:7:
This verse commands eating unleavened bread for six days after the Passover. The seventh day would be a sacred gathering before the Lord, and no work was to be done on it. The term for unleavened bread refers to loaves made without yeast.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them how to celebrate the feast that commemorated their departure from Egypt. The bread without yeast reminded them of that hurried departure, and the rest of the seventh day taught them to pause and honor God.

Today we too can set apart a regular time to rest from work and remember what God has done for us. A weekly pause, without rush or pending tasks, can help us give thanks, pray, and renew our trust that God sustains us.
exp.30:23:
Moses finished writing the words of this law in a book, down to the last line. That means he did not leave the teaching only to be repeated by word of mouth; he put the whole of it in writing.

Moses is about to die, and the people are going to enter the promised land with Joshua as their new leader. For that reason he leaves the law in writing, so that it may serve as a guide and as a witness. Scholars debate exactly how much "this law" covers: the whole book of Deuteronomy or only part of it. The text does not fully specify this.

God speaks and wants his word to be preserved. Today we can value the Bible we have and set aside a fixed time each day for it. Reading it faithfully helps us remember what God says when hard times come.
exp.0:34:
This verse says that none of the men of that evil generation will see the good land that God promised with an oath to Israel's ancestors. "Evil generation" refers to those who rebelled. The phrase "had sworn to give" means "swore that he would give." "Fathers" here means the ancestors, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Moses speaks to the people as he recalls what happened near Kadesh-barnea. The Israelites were afraid, did not trust God, and grumbled, even though He had led them with fire and cloud. For this reason God swore that that generation would not enter the land. Only Caleb would be the exception, because he faithfully followed the Lord.

For today: unbelief has consequences, but faithfulness is also seen by God. When you are afraid, remember how He has guided you before and trust His promises, even when the path looks difficult.
exp.20:0:
This verse describes a specific case: someone finds a dead body lying in the field, in the land that God was giving to Israel, and no one knows who killed him. "Found" means discovered, and "struck" means killed or beaten to death.

Moses is giving these laws to the people before they enter Canaan. God wanted the land not to be stained by a death that went unanswered. For this reason, the verses that follow ask the leaders to measure the distance to the nearby cities, and the nearest one takes on a public responsibility. In this way, no life was treated as something unimportant.

For today: human life matters to God, even when no one claims it. We can be people who care about justice, help those who suffer, and do not look the other way when someone is harmed.
exp.30:15:
God tells Moses that he is soon going to die, and that "sleep with your fathers" is a gentle way of speaking about death. He also warns that the people, once they arrive in the promised land, will turn to whoring after other gods, that is, they will give themselves to idolatry the way a person betrays a spouse. In this way they will abandon God and break his covenant.

The Lord speaks in the tabernacle, where Moses and Joshua are waiting. Israel is about to enter Canaan, and God is preparing Joshua as the new leader. God knows the heart of the people and gives warning in advance. Afterward the consequences of that unfaithfulness are announced.

For today: let us not assume that we will remain faithful to God in comfort. When everything goes well, it is easy to neglect prayer and the Word. Let us tend our relationship with God each day, so that other things do not take his place.
exp.26:20:
This verse declares under a curse anyone who has sexual relations with an animal. The phrase that the old wording used for this act is not one your verse uses, so I will simply describe it. The people would answer together in agreement with the curse, meaning they affirmed it aloud and accepted it as true.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. A ceremony is commanded on Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, where the people would hear curses and accept them out loud. This sin also appears in other laws of Israel (Exodus 22:19; Leviticus 18:23). These are sins that often happened in secret, and God sees them.

For today: God calls us to live in purity even in what is hidden. We can ask him for help to guard what we look at, think, and do when no one sees us.
exp.3:25:
Moses tells the Israelites that he calls heaven and earth as witnesses against them, that is, as if they were judges who confirm what is being said. He warns that if they become corrupt, they will soon disappear from the land they are about to receive when they cross the Jordan.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He reminds them of the covenant with God and warns them against idolatry, because God is jealous, which means he demands complete faithfulness. The verses that follow explain that they would be scattered among the nations.

For today: let us not take for granted the good things God has given us. It is healthy to honestly examine what things occupy the place of God in our hearts, and to return to him with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.15:11:
This verse says that the people of Israel had to remember that they were once slaves in Egypt. For that reason they had to obey carefully the laws God gave them. The word "bondman" here means slave, and "statutes" are God's commands or rules.

Moses is speaking to the people before they enter the promised land. He has just explained the Feast of Weeks, a celebration in which everyone rejoiced together: family, servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows. Remembering their slavery helped them treat with kindness those who were in need, because they themselves had been rescued by God.

Today we can remember where God has brought us out from and how much grace we have received. That grateful memory moves us to obey him and to be generous, including toward those who have less or who feel alone.
exp.28:14:
God's covenant, the verse says, is not only for those who were present that day, but also for those who were not there. The word "but" here means "rather": the covenant includes everyone. The phrase "those who are not here with us" is understood as referring to Israel's future generations, although some also see a reference to those who were unable to attend.

Moses speaks to the people in Moab, at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He is renewing the covenant with God before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that this promise goes back to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and that it must be passed from generation to generation.

For today: faith is not inherited automatically, but it can be shared. Think of someone in your family, a son, a nephew, or a young friend, and this week tell them how God has been faithful to you.
exp.2:5:
Moses reminds the people how Israel defeated the cities of King Og of Bashan. The word "destroyed" means that they utterly destroyed them, as they had already done with Sihon, king of Heshbon. The text says that this included men, women, and children.

Moses speaks at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, before Israel enters the promised land. He reminds them of past victories so that they will trust God. This is a hard text. The Bible presents it as a judgment of God on the peoples of that time, and scholars debate how to understand the language of total destruction in these passages.

For today: when we remember how God helped us in the past, our confidence grows to face the challenges that lie ahead. And we should read these difficult texts with humility, never using them to justify violence today.
exp.25:13:
This verse is part of a declaration that the Israelite made before God. He says that he did not misuse the sacred tithe: he did not eat from it while in mourning, he did not take any of it while unclean according to the law, and he did not spend any of it on offerings for the dead. He concludes that he obeyed God in everything God commanded.

The speaker is an Israelite who, every three years, gave the tithe to the Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows. Then he declared this before God. It was not boasting, but an honest account. Scholars explain the practices with the dead that are mentioned in various ways, but the general sense is that what was set apart for God was not to be mixed with what was unclean or with funeral rites.

For today: what we dedicate to God and to those in need deserves care and sincerity. We can ask ourselves whether we give with integrity, and obey with a grateful heart, not for appearance.
exp.0:9:
Moses tells the people that God has greatly increased their numbers. Today they are so many that he compares them to the stars of the sky. "Has multiplied you" means that he made them grow in number. "Behold" is like saying "look" or "see here."

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God fulfilled what he promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob about a numerous descendance. Moses explains that governing a people so large was too heavy a burden for him alone, and for that reason leaders were later appointed to help him.

For today: when you look at what God has done in your life, take a moment to thank him for his promises fulfilled. And if responsibility feels heavy to you, do not carry it alone; ask for help and share it with others.
exp.1:22:
This verse tells that certain peoples called Avites lived in villages from Hazerim to Gaza. The Caphtorites, who came from Caphtor, destroyed them and settled in their land. "Destroyed" here means that they drove them out or wiped them out. Caphtor is often linked to the island of Crete, although not all scholars affirm this with certainty.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel as he recalls the journey through the desert. He explains that God had already given lands to other peoples, such as Esau, Moab, and Ammon. These examples prepare Israel to receive the land God had promised them, after the command to cross the Arnon.

For today: God governs history and cares for his people. You can trust that if He has guided others, He will also guide you, even when you cannot see the whole picture.
exp.29:10:
It says that what God commands is neither a secret nor something impossible to reach. The word "intimate" (meaning to command or declare with authority) and the word "hidden" (meaning concealed or hard to understand) are both explained here. The phrase "not far off" means it is within the reach of the people.

Moses speaks to Israel at the end of his life, shortly before they enter the promised land. He has just spoken to them about returning to the Lord with their whole heart, with the promise that God would bless them again. Here he makes clear that obeying is not a task beyond their reach, because God has already given them his word in writing.

Today we can approach the Bible without thinking it is only for experts. Read one passage each day, ask God to help you understand it, and put into practice one simple step you see there.
exp.2:23:
Here Moses addresses God with respect and admiration. He tells him that he has already allowed him to see the beginning of his greatness and of his "mighty hand," that is, his power. Then he asks whether there is any god, in heaven or on earth, who can do works and mighty acts like his.

Moses speaks near the end of his life, while Israel prepares to enter the promised land. He had just seen victories over the kings Sihon and Og. After praising God, he asks to enter that land, but God tells him no.

For today: before asking God for something, we can begin by remembering what he has already done. Sincere praise helps us to trust, even when his answer is not the one we expected.
exp.13:1:
This verse says that Israel is a people set apart for God, that is, dedicated to him. God himself chose them to be "peculiar," meaning special and unique, above all the nations "that are upon the earth."

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. Shortly before, he forbade them the mourning customs of other peoples, such as cutting the skin or shaving the forehead for a dead person. Their identity as children of God was to be seen in the way they lived and the way they grieved. Afterward come the laws about food.

For today: if you belong to God, your worth does not depend on what people think of you. Ask him to help you live with hope, even in pain, showing that you are his child.
exp.24:18:
It says that when God gives them rest from all their enemies and they are living in the land, they shall blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven. It ends with a warning: thou shalt not forget it. An inheritance is what is handed down, and to possess it means to take it as your own.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter Canaan. He reminds them that the Amalekites attacked from behind the weak and weary when they came out of Egypt, without fearing God. It is a command given at a very particular time and context, and throughout history it has been understood in various ways.

For today: do not repay evil with evil, but do not forget that God defends the weak. Care for those who are tired and lagging behind you, and trust that God will do justice in his own time.
exp.27:49:
It says the enemy people who would come would be cruel and harsh. "Fierce of countenance" means of hard look, without tenderness. They would have no regard for the old, which was a very serious matter in that culture, nor compassion for the child. In other words, they would show mercy to no one.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the Promised Land. He explains the blessings of obeying God and the consequences of abandoning him. This warning describes a foreign invasion as the result of breaking the covenant. Many relate it to later invasions, such as those of Assyria or Babylon, although the text gives no names.

For today: God speaks to us with clarity and with warnings because he loves us. It is worth listening in time, returning to him when we stray, and treating the elderly and children with respect and compassion, as that cruel people did not.
exp.27:15:
This verse says that if the people disobey, the curse will reach them everywhere: "in the city" (where people live and trade) and "in the field" (where people work and farm). The word "cursed" here means being under painful consequences, without the blessing of God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: if they obey, blessing will come; if they abandon it to follow other gods, the consequences will come. This verse is the reverse of verse 3, where blessing is promised in the city and in the field.

For today: our obedience to God is not only for the temple or Sundays, but for all of life, at home, at work, and in the street. Let us ask him to guide every space of our day, trusting in his grace.
exp.20:22:
It says that the body of a person condemned to death and hanged on a wooden beam was not to remain there overnight. It had to be buried that same day. The phrase "the one hanged is cursed of God" means that someone hanged was left exposed as a sign of judgment. "Defile" means to make dirty or to profane, and "inheritance" is the land received as an inheritance.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. These laws aimed to take justice seriously, but also to respect human dignity, even that of a guilty person. Scholars explain in various ways how the condemned person was hanged, but the command to bury him promptly is clear.

For today: Paul quotes this text in Galatians 3:13 to explain that Christ bore our curse. Today you can give thanks for him and treat all people with respect and compassion, even those who have failed seriously.
exp.23:10:
It says that the lender must stay outside, in the street, while the borrower goes into his house and brings out the item held as security. A "pledge" is an object left as a guarantee for a loan. The word "borrowed" means lent. The lender could not go in to fetch it on his own.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and reminds them of God's law. This rule protected the dignity and privacy of the one who owed money, especially the poor. The verse before mentions Miriam and what God did to her; scholars understand this as a reminder of how serious it is to obey God, though not all of them explain the connection in the same way.

For today: if someone owes you something, look after them and treat them with respect. Ask for what is fair, but never humiliate or intrude on the privacy of someone who is in a difficult situation.
exp.32:27:
It says that Israel, a descendant of Jacob, will live at rest and without fear, set apart from its enemies, in a land that yields grain and wine. Dew will also fall from the sky, which was an important source of moisture for the crops. "Will dwell in safety alone" means living secure, without depending on other peoples. "Fountain of Jacob" is understood as the offspring that springs from Jacob, though some interpret it in other ways.

Moses is speaking. He is blessing the tribes of Israel shortly before he dies. Just before this verse, he recalls that God is a refuge and that he drives out the enemy. For this reason, Israel's security does not come from its own strength, but from God's protection.

Today we can learn to rest in the fact that God cares for us. We can work hard, but without living ruled by fear, trusting that He is our refuge and provides what we need.
exp.7:15:
This verse says that God fed Israel with manna in the wilderness, a food that neither they nor their ancestors had known. The phrase "afflicting you and proving you" means that God allowed hard moments in order to test and shape their character.

Moses speaks to the people near the entrance to the promised land. He reminds them of the forty years in the wilderness so that, when they live in abundance, they will not fill up with pride or forget God. The verses that follow warn against thinking that wealth comes only from their own effort.

For today: when you go through a difficult season, remember that God may be caring for you and shaping you at the same time. And when things are going well, pause to thank him, because everything good comes from his hand.
exp.1:6:
This verse says that God has blessed the people in everything they did. He knows their walking through the great wilderness. For forty years he was with them, and they lacked nothing.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them of what they went through before passing through the land of Edom, the descendants of Esau. God told them not to fight with them and to buy food and water from them. Moses wants them to remember that God sustained them and that they do not need to take anything from anyone.

For today: when you go through long and difficult times, remember how God has sustained you up to this point. That helps you trust, live with gratitude, and treat others fairly, without greed or violence.
exp.31:37:
God speaks with sorrowful mockery about false gods. These are the ones who received the fat from the animals offered and the wine poured out in the offerings. Now God asks: if they are so powerful, why do they not rise up to help and protect those who worshiped them?

God speaks within the song of Moses, near the end of his life. Israel had turned away from God to follow idols. God announces that when his people are left without strength, they will see that those gods cannot save. In this way he wants to bring them back to himself, the only God.

For today: think about what you give your time, your money, and your trust to. If something cannot sustain you in a crisis, it does not deserve first place. Turn your heart back to God, who does listen and does help.
exp.19:1:
This verse says that, just before the battle begins, the priest was to come forward and speak to the people. The word "approach" in the verse is the key action here. It is not yet the message itself, but the indication of who would give it and when.

Moses is speaking to Israel before they enter the promised land. He has already told them not to be afraid, because God was with them, the same God who brought them out of Egypt. Now he explains that, on the battlefield, the priest would remind them of that truth. His task was to strengthen faith, not to direct military strategy.

For today: before facing a difficult moment, seek to hear the Word of God first. Pray, read the Bible, or ask someone of faith for encouragement. In this way your heart is steadied in God and not only in your own strength.
exp.27:17:
It says that if the people turn away from God, the blessings they would otherwise receive would become a curse. It speaks of their children ("the fruit of your body"), their harvests ("the fruit of your land"), and their animals: calves and lambs ("the increase of your cows" and "the flocks of your sheep"). In other words, family, food and work would be placed under misfortune.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: obeying him would bring blessing (Deuteronomy 28:1-14), and disobeying him would bring serious consequences. It is a warning meant to help them choose the path of faithfulness.

For today: do not see what you have, whether family, work or possessions, as secure in itself. Everything comes from God. Each day, put him first with gratitude and obedience, and trust him more than your achievements. Christians believe that Christ bore that curse for us (Galatians 3:13).
exp.26:16:
Deuteronomy 27:17 speaks of the one who moves his neighbour's landmark, that is, who shifts the stones or markers that set the boundary of a field in order to take a piece of his neighbour's land. The phrase "Cursed be he" means that such a person stands under God's disapproval and judgment. And all the people answer "Amen," which means "so be it," agreeing that this is just.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. Each family had received its inheritance, and the boundary markers protected that gift from God. This list of curses names sins that could be committed in secret, and so the people publicly commit themselves to reject them.

Today we can be honest in small matters: not taking advantage of someone's oversight, not altering measures, papers, or agreements to gain what is not ours. God sees what is hidden and cares for our neighbour.
exp.18:1:
God commands Israel that, once they are living in the promised land, they are to set apart three cities within their territory. "Set apart" here simply means setting them aside on purpose, marking them out from the rest.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. These cities, called cities of refuge, were there so that someone who killed another person without meaning to could flee there and save his life. In this way, a relative moved by revenge could not kill him unjustly. The verses that follow explain that the road to the cities had to be kept clear and that the case in view is that of someone with no earlier hostility toward the person he killed.

For today: God cares about justice and also about mercy. We can imitate him by being people who are not carried away by anger, who can tell a mistake from an evil intention, and who offer a safe place and forgiveness to someone who got it wrong without meaning to.
exp.25:16:
This verse says that the people of Israel declare today that the Lord is their God. The phrase "avouched" here means that they have acknowledged and proclaimed him as God, giving him first place. With this declaration they commit themselves to walk in his ways, keep his statutes, commandments, and judgments (that is, his laws), and listen to his voice. To "hearken unto his voice" implies obeying, not merely hearing.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they enter the promised land. He explains a ceremony: when presenting the firstfruits, each Israelite would remember God's faithfulness and renew their commitment to him. It is a response of gratitude within the covenant. The following verse shows that God, in turn, acknowledges them as his people.

For today: we can renew our commitment to God with gratitude, not out of simple obligation. A practical step is to begin the day by thanking him for something specific and asking his help to obey him in one particular decision.
exp.27:41:
It says that the locust, that is, the insect that comes in swarms and devours everything, will consume all the trees of your orchard and the crops of your field. The trees in the orchard are the fruit trees, and the produce of your land are the crops. All the farmer's work would be destroyed.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. In this chapter he presents blessings if they obey God and curses if they abandon him. This verse is part of the warnings: disobedience would bring losses, and the covenant with God was something very serious.

For today: our harvests, work and savings are not secure on their own. We can labor with diligence, but we must also trust in God, not in what we produce. Today, ask yourself: where am I placing my security?
exp.18:0:
When the Lord your God destroys the nations whose land the Lord your God is giving you, and you take their place and live in their cities and in their houses, they must do something. The word "destroys" is the same as the words "cut off" in the verse above, and "take their place" means receiving the land as an inheritance. Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter Canaan, in his farewell in the book of Deuteronomy. This verse introduces a command: to set apart three cities of refuge, where a person who had killed someone without intent could flee. In this way the life of the innocent was protected and unjust revenge was prevented.

For today: when God gives us something good, such as a home, a job, or an opportunity, he also calls us to use it with justice and mercy. We can ask ourselves how we might help someone who needs protection or a second chance.
exp.27:29:
It says that, as a punishment, the person would make important plans and others would enjoy the result. They would become engaged to be married, but another man would take his wife. They would build a house, but would not live in it. They would plant a vineyard, but would not gather its grapes.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them the blessings for obeying God and the curses for breaking the covenant. This verse is part of the curses: it describes the loss and frustration that would come if the people turned away from God and fell under the oppression of their enemies.

For today: do not place all your security in your plans, your work, or your achievements, because they can be lost. Seek God first and live with integrity, trusting that he gives the true foundation for your life and your family.
exp.21:8:
It says that an Israelite was not to sow other seeds in the middle of his vineyard. The source's quoted phrases are not to be carried over, so the verse of their meaning is rendered as: to be spoiled or set apart for another use, and the whole of what was sown together with the fruit of the vineyard.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and gives them laws to live as God's people. This command goes together with others about not mixing things, such as different kinds of animals or different kinds of cloth. Scholars do not fully agree on the reason: it may teach order, purity, and separation for God.

For today: seek not to divide your heart. Put God first, and take care that other priorities do not choke out the good that He wants to grow in you.
exp.14:11:
If a Hebrew brother, a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman, sold himself to another Israelite to serve him because he was in debt or in poverty, he was to serve only six years. In the seventh year, the master had to let him go free. "Let him go free" means "let him leave" or "send him away."

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and repeats God's law. Just before this, he asks for generosity toward the poor. This rule protected the most needy from endless slavery and reminded them that God had freed Israel from Egypt. Scholars discuss how it was applied in detail, but the intention of mercy is clear.

For today: if you have authority over someone, such as an employee, treat them with justice and dignity. Pay them well, do not take advantage of their need, and help them get ahead, remembering how much God has given you.
exp.13:15:
This verse is part of a list of birds that God declared unclean, meaning the Israelites were not to eat them. It mentions the little owl, the great owl, and the swan. Some of the ancient names are hard to identify: scholars are not sure which exact bird each one is, and translations vary.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the laws God gave them to live as a set-apart people, distinct from the neighboring nations. These food rules were part of that identity. The text does not explain the reason for each bird, so it is best not to invent reasons.

For today: although Christians are not under these food rules, the passage teaches us that God cares about every detail of daily life. We can ask ourselves whether what we eat, do, and say shows that we belong to Him.
exp.28:21:
This verse says that future generations, meaning the children of the Israelites and also foreigners who come from distant lands, will see the condition of the land and will ask what happened. The word "plagues" refers to blows or punishments, and "sicknesses" refers to the wounded and ruined land.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel as he renews the covenant with God before they enter the promised land. He warns them that abandoning God to serve other gods would bring serious consequences, and that this ruin would serve as a witness to other nations.

For today: our decisions affect those who come after us. It is worth guarding our faithfulness to God, because our lives can encourage or discourage our children and those who watch us.
exp.4:1:
This verse says that God, whom Moses calls "the Lord our God," made a covenant with his people at Horeb. Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai. A covenant is a solemn commitment between two parties: God binds himself to his people, and the people promise to respond to him.

Moses speaks to all Israel before they enter the promised land. Almost all the adults who were at Horeb had already died, so he addresses the new generation. He tells them that the covenant is not only a thing of the past: it is theirs too. That is why he calls them to hear, learn, and obey.

For today: do not live your faith only on what others have told you. Make it your own. Set aside a moment this week to read the Word and to answer God with a concrete decision of obedience.
exp.28:13:
It says that God is not making this covenant only with the people who were present that day. "Agreement" means "establish" or "make," and "oath" is a solemn promise. Moses makes clear that the commitment to God reaches more people than those who were listening at that moment.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel on the plains of Moab, at the end of forty years in the wilderness, before entering the promised land. He is renewing the covenant with a new generation. The next verse says it also includes those who are "not here with us today," which many understand as the children and future generations.

Our decisions of faith can affect others. If you follow God, your example, your prayers, and your teaching can leave a mark on your family and on those who come after you. Live today with them in mind.
exp.21:12:
This verse opens a law about a specific case: a man marries, has relations with his wife, and afterward stops loving her, that is, he comes to hate her. The phrase "went in unto her" is an older way of referring to the intimate side of marriage. The verse does not finish the thought; the law continues in the verses that follow.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, explaining laws for living as God's people. This law seeks to protect the woman from a false accusation made by a husband who no longer wanted her. Her honor and her life depended greatly on her good name.

For today: let us guard the truth in our words about others, especially when there is anger or lack of love. We must never damage someone's reputation with lies.
exp.11:19:
It says that when God enlarges Israel's territory, as he promised, and a person feels a desire to eat meat, that person may eat it freely, according to the longing of their heart. The phrase "enlarge your border" means "expand your boundaries"; since that phrase is not in the verse, the comment is dropped and only the meaning is kept. "Your soul" refers to oneself, to one's appetite and desire.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. Until then, the meat of animals for sacrifice was presented before God in a central place. Now, with a larger territory, many would live far from that place. That is why God permits eating meat at home, without it being an act of worship. Even so, the people are reminded to care for the Levites.

For today: God allows us to enjoy with gratitude what he gives, such as food. Let us enjoy without selfishness, remembering to share with those in need and to support those who serve.
exp.5:17:
This verse says that the people should do what is right and good in the sight of God. If they do so, it will go well with them, and they will be able to enter the good land and take it as their inheritance, just as God promised with an oath to their forefathers. The word "thou" in the verse is the old form of "you", and "possess" means you will receive it as your own.

Moses speaks to Israel, about to enter Canaan, after forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them that obeying God is not a meaningless burden, but the way to live in the blessing he promised. He mentions earlier Massah, where they doubted God for lack of water.

For today: before deciding something, ask yourself not only "What is good for me?" but "What pleases God?" Obeying him in small things, with trust, teaches us to rest in his faithfulness, even when we do not understand everything.
exp.21:25:
It says that nothing should be done to the young woman, because she is not guilty of a crime deserving death. The word "damsel" means a young woman, and "betrothed" means promised in marriage. The text compares her case to that of someone who attacks his neighbor and takes his life: she is the victim, not the one at fault.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, and their laws distinguish two cases. If it happened inside the city, it was assumed she could have called for help, and the text takes this as a sign of consent. If it happened in the field, where no one would hear her, she is protected as a victim. Some scholars see here a protection of the woman; others point out that the law reflects the customs of its time.

Today we learn not to blame someone who suffers an assault. If someone trusts you with an account of abuse, listen to them with respect, believe them, stand up for them, and help them seek protection and justice. God takes the side of the one who has been hurt.
exp.19:18:
It says that if Israel surrounds an enemy city and attacks it for many days, they must not cut down the trees that bear fruit. The phrase "lay siege" is what it means to surround a city in order to take it. The verse speaks of the trees in general, and the word "cut down" is what it means to chop them. The reason is that they will eat from those trees. The text adds that the tree is not a man who fights against them.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them rules for war. This law limits destruction and protects the food they will need later. Some understand that it also cares for the land, but the text mainly stresses the usefulness of the fruit.

For today: even in the middle of a conflict, do not destroy what you or others will need later. When you argue or are upset, take care of the good things God has given you, such as relationships, work and creation.
exp.7:13:
When you have plenty of food, good houses, and a lot of money, there is a danger: that your heart will become full of pride ("be lifted up") and you will forget God. He is the one who brought Israel out of Egypt, out of the house of bondage, that is, a place of slavery. Here the word "lest" introduces a warning: be careful that this does not happen.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the hard years in the wilderness, when God cared for them with water and manna. He fears that, once they prosper, they will think they achieved everything on their own.

For today: when things are going well for you, take a moment to thank God. Think of one specific blessing you have and give thanks for it in prayer, remembering that everything good comes from Him.
exp.21:3:
It says that if you see your brother's donkey or ox fallen down on the road, you must not pretend you did not see it or hide yourself from them. On the contrary, you must help him lift them up again. The word "donkey" here refers to the animal, and "brother" refers to another Israelite, your neighbor.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, explaining how to live as God's people. These animals were the livelihood of a family, so helping was a way of caring for their life. The previous verse asks you to return what has been lost; this one adds that it is not enough to avoid doing harm, you must also act. Some see here a principle that goes beyond animals.

Today, when you see someone in trouble, like a neighbor with a broken-down car or a coworker with too much work, do not look the other way. Offer your concrete help, even if it costs you time or effort.
exp.9:5:
The verse tells how the Israelites set out from a place called Beeroth Bene-jaakan and arrived at Moserah. There Aaron, the first high priest, died and was buried. His son Eleazar took his place as priest.

The speaker is Moses, who reminds the people of their history before they enter the promised land. This verse seems to be a short note within the account of the tablets and the ark. It shows that, although leaders die, the service of God continues. Some scholars note that the order of the account differs from that in Numbers 33, and they explain this in several ways.

For today: God does not depend on a single person to carry forward his work. Value those who teach you and serve, but trust that God cares for his people from generation to generation. You too can prepare yourself to serve.
exp.26:3:
It says that, after crossing the Jordan River, the people were to set up large stones on Mount Ebal and cover them with lime, a kind of white plaster. To "plaister" means to coat a surface with a layer of mixture. "When ye be gone over" means "when you have crossed over."

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before his death, when they are about to enter the promised land. He orders them to write God's law on those stones, as a visible reminder of their covenant. We do not know for certain whether the words were written on the plaster or in some other way; scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: God wants his Word to be in plain sight and not forgotten. You can choose a verse and place it where you will see it every day, and let it guide your decisions as you begin a new stage of your life.
exp.10:17:
It says that the people should keep God's words in the deepest part of their being, in the heart and in the soul. They should also keep them always in view: "bound" on the hand as a sign and set as "frontlets" between the eyes. A frontlet was something worn on the forehead. It is language of imagery: what I do and what I see should be guided by God's Word.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just warned them not to turn after other gods. He wants them to remember the LORD and his command. Later, some Jews took these words literally and used phylacteries. Others understand them as a figure of speech. Both readings exist.

Today we can choose one verse each week, memorize it, and go over it on the way to work or before going to sleep. In this way the Word guides our daily decisions and actions.
exp.9:19:
It says that Israel must have a deep, reverent respect for God ("fear"), obey and serve Him ("serve"), and remain faithfully joined to Him ("cleave" means "hold fast" or "draw close with firmness"), and use His name only to make true promises ("swear by his name").

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the God who loves the fatherless, the widow, and the stranger is the same God who deserves their full loyalty. He also reminds them of their history: they were few in Egypt, and God made them a multitude.

For today: serve God faithfully in everyday life, and let your word be trustworthy. When you promise something, keep it, remembering that God cares for the most vulnerable and expects you to do the same.
exp.22:1:
It says that a "bastard" could not enter the "congregation of the Lord," that is, the official assembly of the people of Israel, neither he nor his descendants down to the tenth generation. The Hebrew word (mamzer) is unclear: some believe it refers to a child born of a forbidden union, and others to someone of mixed origin or pagan worship. It is not known for certain.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. These rules, given to Israel under the covenant of the law, aimed to keep the people separate from the practices of the neighboring nations. The concern is participation in the assembly, not personal salvation.

Today, the New Testament shows that in Christ no one is left out because of their origin or their past (Galatians 3:26-28). We can welcome with compassion those who feel ashamed of their family history, reminding them that God calls them his children.
exp.7:7:
This verse describes the good land that God was going to give Israel. It names seven products: wheat, barley, vines (grapes), fig trees (figs), pomegranates (pomegranate fruit), olive trees (olives), and honey. The word that appears as "and" in the older wording is simply the ordinary "and" of the list, and the olives are the olive trees themselves. Many believe the "honey" could be bee honey or a sweet syrup made from dates or grapes; the text does not make this clear.

Moses speaks to the people at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, just before they enter Canaan. He reminds them that this abundance comes from God and that they must obey him. Later he warns them not to forget God when they are satisfied.

For today: look at what you have on your table as a gift from God, not only as the fruit of your own effort. Before you eat, give thanks from the heart, and let that gratitude lead you to obey him and to share with others.
exp.28:7:
This verse says that Israel took the land of the kings Sihon and Og, who had come out to fight against them, and gave it as an inheritance to three groups: the tribe of Reuben, the tribe of Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh. The phrase "we gave it" is the sense of the verb here, meaning the land was handed over to them. An inheritance is a portion of land received as a possession.

Moses is speaking, near the end of his life. He is reminding the people of what God did for them in the wilderness and in the recent victories. He recalls this so that they will renew their covenant with God on the plains of Moab, before entering the promised land. Those victories and that inheritance were evidence of God's faithfulness.

For today: remembering what God has already done in our lives strengthens trust and obedience. Recalling his past help helps us follow him with gratitude today.
exp.14:3:
The verse says that among Israel there should be no needy poor person forced to beg. The reason is that God promised to bless the people with abundance in the land He was giving them as an inheritance. The word "beggar" refers to someone reduced to asking others in order to live, and "inheritance" is the land received as a family's property.

Moses speaks to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He explains the year of release, when debts between brothers were forgiven, so that no one would remain trapped in poverty. The verse joins God's promise with obedience, as what follows shows. Later in the same chapter, the text acknowledges that there would always be poor people, so the ideal depended on the people's faithfulness.

Today we can ask ourselves how we use what God has given us. One concrete action is to help generously someone close to us who is in need, without humiliating them and without expecting anything in return.
exp.2:19:
This verse says that the tribes who had already received their land east of the Jordan (Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh) were to help their brothers conquer the land on the other side. Only when the Lord gave their brothers rest, that is, peace and security in their territory, could they return to their own possession, the land that had fallen to them as an inheritance.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life, recalling what he had commanded them earlier. He wanted no tribe to rest easily while the others were still fighting. It was a call to unity and loyalty between brothers.

For today: it is not enough to enjoy my own blessings. I can ask myself whom I can help, support, or walk alongside until they too find rest, whether in the family, the church, or the workplace.
exp.24:12:
It says we must not carry two different weights in our bag, one heavier and one lighter. In that time, merchants weighed metal or goods using stones as weights. The stone used to measure weight is what the verse calls a weight, so the word in the verse is the one to look at. Having two was a way of cheating: one for buying and another for selling.

Moses speaks to the Israelites before they enter the promised land, and reminds them of God's laws for living in justice. The verse before this one deals with another matter, and scholars explain it in several ways. Here the subject changes to honesty in business. God promises blessing to those who act with justice.

Today we can apply this by being honest with money: charging what is fair, paying on time, and not deceiving in prices, accounts, or work, even when no one is watching.
exp.28:20:
This verse says that God will set that person apart from all the tribes of Israel, to bring them harm. All the curses of the covenant written in the book of the law will fall on them. The phrase "the Lord shall separate him" means that he will be singled out for judgment, and "to evil" means that the outcome will be harmful to him.

Moses speaks to the people when he renews the covenant with God in Moab, before they enter the promised land. He warns anyone who hears the curses and thinks, "I will have peace, even if I do as I please." This is someone who despises the warning and follows his own heart, counting on a blessing he has never sought.

For today: do not take God's grace lightly or use his patience as an excuse to keep doing wrong. If you feel that God is speaking to you, respond with humility and repentance, not with a false sense of security. God welcomes those who return to him sincerely.
exp.24:15:
This verse says that God detests whoever does "this," that is, whoever uses false weights and measures, and everyone who commits injustice or fraud. Whatever is called an abomination is something God rejects strongly. Wrongdoing that harms another person is injustice toward them. The measure used for grain was an ephah.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that honesty in trade was part of living under the covenant with God. Then he mentions Amalek, who treated the weak without mercy; in this way injustice is set against the fear of God.

For today: be honest in your work and in your accounts. Do not cheat on prices, hours, change, or promises. Even if no one notices, God sees and values justice.
exp.13:2:
It says that God's people were not to eat anything "abominable," that is, something God regarded as unclean or repugnant for his people. It is a short phrase that opens the list of permitted and forbidden animals.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they are children of God, a holy people, set apart and special. For that reason, even the way they ate distinguished them from other nations. Some believe these rules had health reasons, others had to do with identity; the text emphasizes above all holiness and obedience.

Today, as Christians, we do not follow those dietary rules, but we do learn that belonging to God touches everyday life. We can ask ourselves which habits, words, or customs reflect that we belong to Him.
exp.20:15:
This verse says that when a father divided his inheritance among his sons, he could not give the rights of the firstborn to the son of the wife he loved most if the true firstborn had been born to the wife he loved less. The word "hated" in the verse means less loved or less preferred. "Firstborn right" is the right belonging to the eldest son.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law protected the weakest members of a family with several wives, something the Bible describes without presenting it as the ideal. The father's feelings were not to change what was just. The eldest son was owed a double portion.

For today: let us be fair even when our personal preferences lean us toward another side. In the family, at work, or in the church, let us give each person what is rightly theirs, without favoritism.
exp.31:28:
This expresses a sad wish: if only the people were wise and understood what is happening to them. "Latter end" is the end, that is, where their path leads and how it will finish.

This verse is part of the song that Moses taught Israel before they entered the promised land. God speaks through Moses. Many understand that it refers to Israel, which turned away from God and did not see that its defeats came from its unfaithfulness. Some apply it to the enemy nations, but the following verse supports the first reading more strongly.

Today we can take time to think about where our decisions are leading us. Ask God for wisdom to see the end of the road before you travel it, and return to Him with humility when you notice that you are straying.
exp.17:1:
This verse says that the Levites would not receive their own piece of land among the other tribes of Israel. The word "inheritance" in the verse means the portion of land given to each family as its share. Instead of land, the Levites' inheritance was the Lord himself, just as he had promised them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the tribe of Levi was set apart for service in worship. Because of this, they would not have fields of their own, but would live from the offerings and firstfruits that the people brought to the Lord. In this way the people cared for those who served in the sanctuary.

For today: God wants to be our greatest wealth and security, more than money or possessions. We can also support, with generosity, those who serve in our church.
exp.11:9:
It says that the people of Israel would cross the Jordan River and live in the land that God was giving them as an inheritance. There God would give them rest from the enemies surrounding them, and they would live peacefully and in safety. Here, "inherit" means to receive as one's own property a gift that comes from God.

Moses speaks to the people at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, shortly before he dies. He reminds them that they have not yet arrived at the promised land. For this reason he asks that, when they enter, they not each follow their own judgment, but worship God in the place he chooses, as the following text says.

For today: God promises rest, but he also asks for obedience. We can trust that he cares for our future and, in the meantime, live according to his Word and not according to what seems right to us at each moment.
exp.31:31:
They say that Israel's enemies have a vine that comes from Sodom and Gomorrah, cities famous for their wickedness. Their grapes are poisonous, that is, deadly, and their clusters are very bitter. It is an image: what those people produce with their lives looks like fruit, but it does harm.

The speaker is God, within the song that Moses taught Israel before he died. The verses before say that Israel would be defeated only if God allowed it. Interpreters debate whether "they" refers to the enemy nations or to Israel itself because of its unfaithfulness; the context favors the enemies. In either case, the message is that apart from God there is no good fruit.

For today: examine where what feeds you comes from, such as your habits, advice, and goals. If the root is far from God, the fruit will end up bitter. Seek to be rooted in Christ, who gives good fruit.
exp.1:19:
This verse says that the land of the Ammonites was also considered a land of giants. Long ago, giants lived there, and the Ammonites called them "Zamzummims." The phrase "was accounted" means that people regarded it that way. The word "giants" translates a Hebrew term (Rephaim), and it is not known for certain what they were like exactly.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them that God commanded them not to trouble the Ammonites, because that land had been given to the descendants of Lot. This detail shows that God had already allotted other lands before, even when it meant removing powerful peoples.

For today: God governs history and keeps His promises in His time. We do not need to take what He has already given to others, nor envy it. We can trust what He has promised us and respect the limits He sets.
exp.6:5:
It calls Israel a "holy" people, that is, set apart for God, who belongs to him. God chose them to be his "special" people, that is, his own treasure, out of all the peoples on the earth. "Upon the face of the earth" means the surface of the earth. "Chosen" speaks of a choice made by God himself.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He warns them not to mix with the nations living there or adopt their gods. That is why they must destroy their altars. He reminds them that their identity comes from God. The verses that follow make clear that they were not chosen for being great, but because of God's love and his promise to the patriarchs.

Today we can remember that our worth does not depend on our achievements, but on the love of God. That love invites us to live set apart for him, with faithfulness and gratitude, and to remove from our lives whatever competes with him.
exp.23:14:
This verse says that a poor worker should be paid his wages the same day, before the sun goes down. A "day's wage" is the payment for one day of work, and the verse's word "hire" fits that meaning. "Sustains his life" means that with this money he feeds himself and supports his family. If he is not paid, he may cry out to God against his employer, and that would be sin for the one who kept back the payment.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of God's law. This command protects the poor day laborer, whether he is an Israelite or a foreigner.
