In that time many people lived from day to day and had no savings. God shows that he hears the cry of the weak.

For today: if you employ someone, whether in your business or in your home, pay them in full and on time. Do not use delays to gain an advantage. Paying justly is one way of honoring God.
exp.24:1:
It says that if a guilty person deserves to be punished with lashes, the judge must order that he be laid down on the ground and beaten in his presence. The punishment must match his offense ("according to his fault") and be counted ("by a certain number"). The guilty one is the "wicked man," "laid down" means stretched out on the ground, and "shall cause him to be beaten" means the judge will have him beaten.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of laws for life in community. This rule limits the punishment: the judge watches to make sure it is fair, measured, and does not turn into revenge. The next verse sets a maximum of forty lashes, so that the person is not humiliated.

For today: when we have to correct someone, whether a child, a student, or an employee, let us do it with justice and with limits, without overdoing it or humiliating them. Correction seeks the good of the person; it is not meant to vent anger.
exp.3:3:
This verse says that the Israelites who stayed united with God were still alive that day. The phrase "ye that did cleave" means that they drew close to Him and held fast to Him, with loyalty and trust. The phrase contrasts with those who turned away from God and died.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what happened at Baal-peor, where many followed a false god and were destroyed (Numbers 25). He wants them to learn from that experience and to obey God's word without taking away from it or adding to it.

For today: faithfulness to God is not only a duty but a path of life. Today you can draw close to Him through simple decisions, such as praying each day, reading his word, and turning away from whatever pulls you away from Him.
exp.31:5:
Moses asks the Israelites: "Is this how you repay the Lord, you foolish and unwise people?" He reminds them that God is their Father, the one who bought them, made them, and established them as a nation. "Foolish" here means senseless, without wisdom; "possessed" means that he made them his own; "established" means set up firmly or made secure.

Moses is near the end of his life, and he teaches this song to Israel. Earlier he described God as a faithful and just Rock, and his people as crooked. Now he confronts them with sorrow: God cared for them, and they responded with ingratitude and disobedience.

For today: before we complain, let us remember what God has done for us. Today, thank God for one specific blessing, and respond with obedience in something you have neglected.
exp.23:19:
It says that when someone shakes or beats the branches of their olive trees to gather the olives, they must not go back over the branches to pick the ones left behind. Those leftover olives were for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow. The phrase "you shall go over the boughs" is simply about checking again, branch by branch, on a second pass.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they were slaves in Egypt and that God rescued them. For that reason he commands them to treat with kindness those who had no land and no protection. He asks the same with the wheat and the grapes.

For today: you do not have to squeeze every gain down to the last penny. You can leave a margin of generosity, such as sharing part of your time, food, or money with someone in need, remembering how much God has given you.
exp.0:4:
This verse says that Moses was on the east side of the Jordan River, in the land of Moab, and that there he set out to explain the law to Israel. The phrase "resolved" means he began to do it with determination. "To declare" here means to explain clearly, not merely to repeat.

The narrator introduces the beginning of Moses' speeches. Forty years have passed since the exodus from Egypt, and the people are about to enter the promised land. Moses knows he will not cross over with them, so he uses this time to remind them of what God commanded them and of what they have lived through, so that the new generation may understand it.

For today: it is not enough to hear the Word of God; we should understand it and explain it patiently, especially to those who come after us.
exp.8:14:
Moses tells how he came down from Mount Sinai, which was burning with fire, carrying in his hands the two tables of the covenant, that is, the stones on which the Ten Commandments were written.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of their history so that they do not forget their failure. While he was receiving God's law, the people were already making a golden calf. That is why God calls them stiff-necked, that is, stubborn and rebellious.

For today: God gives us his word with great seriousness and love, and we fail with ease. Remembering our mistakes with humility leads us to ask for forgiveness and to obey again, trusting in God's mercy.
exp.10:9:
This verse compares the promised land with Egypt. It says that Canaan is not like Egypt, where the people sowed their seed and watered it "with your foot." That phrase probably refers to moving some kind of irrigation system with the foot, although some scholars think it could mean opening the water channels between the furrows with the foot.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that in Egypt everything depended on human effort to bring water to the crops. In Canaan, by contrast, they would depend on the rain from heaven, that is, on God's provision. For this reason he asks them to obey his commandments with confidence.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we live relying only on our own effort. Work is good, but we can do it with gratitude and prayer, remembering that everything we need ultimately comes from the hand of God.
exp.33:4:
This verse says that Moses, whom the Bible calls the servant of the Lord, died in the land of Moab. The phrase "according to the word of the Lord" means that everything happened in line with God's word, that is, as He had said or allowed. The expression can also be understood as "at the mouth of the Lord," and some interpret it as meaning that God Himself guided that moment.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, not Moses. God had just shown him the promised land from the mountain, but told him he would not enter it. This verse closes the life of a man who led Israel for forty years in the desert.

For today: our life has an end, and perhaps we will not see fulfilled everything we long for. Even so, being faithful to God until the last day is worth more than any achievement. We can trust that He fulfills His plan.
exp.32:19:
Moses says that God is blessed, the one who enlarged the territory of Gad. Gad is compared to a lion that lives at rest and tears its prey apart. The phrase about tearing the arm and the crown of the head means that Gad will overcome his enemies, from the arm all the way to the head.

Moses is blessing the tribes of Israel shortly before he dies. Gad received land east of the Jordan, and he agreed to cross over armed with the other tribes to help them conquer Canaan. The verses that follow remind us of this. Some understand "the one who enlarged Gad" as God himself, and that is the most common reading.

For today: God gives us room and strength, but not so that we can stay comfortable. We can use what God has given us to help others in their struggles, as Gad did with his brothers.
exp.8:7:
In Horeb (another name for Sinai), the people of Israel made God angry with their disobedience. "Provoked to wrath" means they caused him to become angry, and "to have destroyed you" shows that their sin was so serious they deserved to be destroyed. The verse uses the word "ye," which is the older way of saying "you."

Moses speaks to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He wants them not to think of themselves as better than other peoples. He reminds them that God gives them the land because of his goodness and his promise, not because they earned it. Next he recounts what happened at Horeb, when the people sinned while he was receiving the tablets of the law.

For today: when you receive blessings, do not think you deserve them because you are good. Remember your own failures and thank God for his patience and his mercy.
exp.17:17:
God promises that he will raise up a prophet from among the people of Israel, one of their own brothers, like Moses. He will put God's words in his mouth, and that prophet will faithfully speak everything God commands him.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that at Horeb (Mount Sinai) they were afraid of God's voice and of the fire, and they asked for a mediator. God accepted their request. The verses that follow show that the true prophet was to be obeyed and the false prophet rejected. Many Christians also see here a sign pointing to Jesus, as the New Testament does in Acts 3:22; Jews have understood it in other ways.

For today: listen to God's Word with humility, and always compare it with the Bible before accepting what any voice says in God's name.
exp.8:0:
Moses tells the people that today they are about to cross the Jordan River to take possession of the promised land. There lived nations more numerous and stronger than Israel, with enormous cities and walls, fortified like strongholds. The phrase "reaching up to heaven" is an exaggeration to say that their walls seemed extremely tall.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, in his addresses before Israel enters Canaan. He reminds them of the reality without hiding the danger. The verses that follow explain that the victory will not depend on their own strength, but on God himself going ahead of them.

For today: there is no need to deny the size of our challenges. We can recognize them honestly and, at the same time, trust that God goes before us. His presence weighs more than our fears.
exp.29:3:
It says that even if the people of Israel were scattered to the farthest place imaginable, to the edge of the heavens, the far end of the horizon, the limit of the known world, God himself will seek them out and bring them back. The verse's language of gathering and fetching shows God as one who will personally go to rescue them.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He warns them that disobedience would bring exile, but he promises that if they turn back to God wholeheartedly, he will have mercy on them and restore them. It is a promise conditioned on repentance and rooted in God's faithfulness.

For today: if you feel far from God because of your mistakes or because of your circumstances, there is no distance he cannot cross. Return to him sincerely, trusting that he will receive you with mercy.
exp.5:4:
It says God deserves complete love. The command to love is an order, but it grows out of a relationship. "Heart" was the center of thoughts and decisions; "soul" is life itself, the whole person; "might" means strength or resources (some translations say "strength"). Spelling and wording from older editions are not discussed here.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God is one and calls them to obey him. This verse is part of what is called the Shema, which Jews still recite today. Afterward, Moses asks that they teach this to their children every day.

For today: loving God is not only a feeling. You can choose a daily moment, such as when you wake up, to give thanks to him, read a passage of the Bible, and ask him how to live that day with honesty and love toward others.
exp.4:24:
This verse says the people were afraid they would die. They had seen the mountain burning and heard the voice of God, and they thought that hearing it again would destroy them. "We shall hear the voice again" means "if we hear the voice of the Lord any more." The phrase "will consume us" means "then we shall die."

Moses is recalling what happened at Mount Sinai. The leaders of the tribes and the elders came to him, amazed that God had spoken to them and they were still alive. Even so, they felt that his presence was too overwhelming, and they asked Moses to speak with God on their behalf.

For today: God is holy and deserves reverence, but his nearness is not meant to frighten us without hope. Today we can draw near to Him with respect and confidence, listening to His word with a humble heart willing to obey.
exp.15:1:
It says the people were to offer the Passover sacrifice to the Lord with animals from their flock, whether sheep or cattle. They were to do this only in the place God would choose, a place where God would be worshiped and remembered in a special way. The phrase about making his name dwell there means that place where God would be worshiped and remembered in a special way.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the Passover celebrates the night God brought them out of Egypt. By asking them to worship in one single place, he wanted the feast to be carried out with order and unity. Scholars often understand that this place was later Jerusalem, although it is not named here.

For today: let us not take for granted what God has done for us. We can set aside specific times to remember his deliverance and give him thanks, and to do it together with other believers, not only in private.
exp.4:23:
This verse says that the people of Israel acknowledge that God showed them his glory and his greatness on the mountain. They heard his voice out of the midst of the fire, and they were amazed that God speaks with human beings and that they remain alive.

Moses is speaking to the new generation, before they enter the promised land, and reminds them of what happened at Mount Sinai (Horeb). He quotes what the leaders and elders said to him after hearing the Ten Commandments. They felt great fear, and asked Moses to listen to God and then pass on his words to them.

For today: God speaks, and his Word deserves respect and attention. We can approach the Bible with humility and gratitude, remembering that listening to God is a privilege, and that he speaks to us to give us life, not to destroy us.
exp.3:35:
This verse says that God caused his people to hear his voice from heaven, with a purpose: to teach them. He also showed them his great fire upon the earth, and they heard his words coming out of the midst of that fire. The phrase "made to hear" means that God himself spoke in such a way that they heard him.

Moses speaks to Israel, toward the end of their time in the wilderness, before entering the promised land. He reminds them of what happened at Mount Horeb (Sinai), when God gave the commandments. Moses wants them not to forget that the LORD is the only God and that he spoke to them clearly and really.

For today: God continues to speak to teach us and guide us, today above all through his Word. We can read it with respect and attention, without taking it for granted, and put it into practice, because God speaks to us so that we may know him and live according to his will.
exp.31:7:
It says that God, the Most High, was the one who divided the land among the nations when the peoples separated. "To give inheritance to the nations" means giving each nation its territory, and "bounds" are the borders. It says these borders were set "according to the number of the children of Israel." That phrase is understood in several ways: some think God had Israel in mind from the beginning; others, following ancient manuscripts, read "according to the number of the sons of God," which is interpreted in various ways.

Moses speaks in his final song, before he dies. He wants the people to remember their history and not repay God with ingratitude. He asks them to ask their fathers and elders.

For today: God governs history, even what seems confused among the nations. Today you can rest in the knowledge that your life is not left to chance. Remember how God has cared for you, and give thanks.
exp.24:14:
This verse commands the use of accurate weights and measures when buying and selling. "Perfect" and "just" mean complete and honest, without deceit. The ephah was a measure for dry goods, such as barley or flour. God promises that whoever lives with this honesty will have long days in the land He gives.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter Canaan. He reminds them of laws for living justly in community. The verses before this one forbid having double weights, one for buying and another for selling, which harmed the poor above all. The verses that follow say that God detests fraud.

For today: be honest with your money and your work. Charge what is fair, pay what you owe, keep what you promise, and do not take advantage of someone who trusts you. Integrity in small things honors God and builds trust around you.
exp.7:16:
This verse warns against a dangerous thought: saying in your heart that you yourself, by your own strength and effort, have become rich. "The power and the might of mine hand" means one's own ability and labor. The phrase "say in thine heart" speaks of what is thought in the inmost self, even if it is never said out loud.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God cared for them in the wilderness: He gave them water and manna. He warns that when they have houses, livestock, and abundance, they might forget the One who gave them everything and feel self-sufficient.

For today: working hard is good, but it is wise to pause and thank God for health, opportunities, and what we have. A simple practice is to pray giving thanks before each meal or when receiving a paycheck, and to share something with someone who is in need.
exp.3:28:
It says that even if the people end up far from their land because they turned away from God, they can still seek him and find him. The condition is to seek him "with all your heart and with all your soul," that is, with sincerity and complete devotion. The sentence explaining the old wording is removed, since its quoted words do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

Moses is speaking to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He warns them that idolatry would bring discipline and scattering among the nations. But in the middle of the warning, he shows them hope: God is merciful and does not forget his covenant with their fathers.

For today: if you feel far from God because of mistakes or neglect, do not wait to get yourself in order first. Return to him honestly, pray, read his Word, and seek him with a sincere desire. He promises to let himself be found.
exp.1:18:
It says that Israel was going to draw near to the land of the Ammonites, and that they must not provoke them or get into conflict with them. God gives the reason: he would not give the Israelites that land as a possession, because he had already given it to the descendants of Lot. The word "possession" in the verse above is the one used here; it means property that is received as an inheritance. "Get into conflict with them" means do not attack them or harass them.

Here Moses speaks, reminding the people of what the LORD told him during the journey through the desert, near the end of the forty years. The Ammonites were descendants of Lot, Abraham's nephew. God had given lands to other peoples, and Israel was to respect those boundaries while moving toward the promised land.

God rules over all nations and carries out his purposes with each of them. We do not need to fight over what God has already given to others, nor envy their blessings. We can live in peace, respect what belongs to others, and trust that God will care for what is ours.
exp.1:12:
He says that God, through Moses, commanded the people to set out and cross the brook Zered, and that they did so. "Rise up" means "get up," and a "brook" is a small stream of water, which here marks a boundary on the road.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, and reminds them of their history. Crossing Zered marked the end of thirty-eight years of waiting, from Kadesh-barnea, a time in which the generation that did not believe died out. The verses that follow explain this. The exact details of the location of the brook are debated among scholars.

When God says "go forward," it is wise to obey without delay. Perhaps you have spent a long season of waiting or correction. God knows when it ends, and his call to move ahead comes at its appointed time. Respond in faith and take the step.
exp.11:14:
This verse says that the Israelite could slaughter animals and eat meat in his own town, according to his desire and according to what God had given him. Both the person who was ritually unclean and the person who was clean could eat it, just as one eats the meat of the roe deer or the deer, animals that were hunted. The word "unclean" refers to ritual impurity, not to a moral failing.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He explains that sacrifices were to be offered only in the place God would choose, and here he makes clear that eating ordinary meat did not require going to that place. In this way the sacred is distinguished from the everyday.

For today: God allows us to enjoy everyday things, such as food, with gratitude, and to recognize them as his blessing. Before eating, we can give thanks from the heart, without turning it into an empty routine.
exp.9:20:
He himself is the reason for his people's praise. He does not merely receive praise; he is the cause of it. The verse also states that he is "your God," the one who did things that were great and awe-inspiring, that is, astonishing, the kind that produce a reverent fear. Israel saw them with their own eyes, such as the departure from Egypt.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what God did so that they would remain faithful to him. Shortly before, he asked them to love the foreigner, because they had been foreigners in Egypt. Then he notes that seventy people went down to Egypt and are now countless like the stars.

For today: when it is hard to give thanks, make a list of concrete things God has done in your life. Remembering them will help you praise him with more sincerity and treat with kindness those who feel like strangers or alone.
exp.27:50:
It says that the foreign enemy will eat up the harvests and the livestock of the people until they are left ruined. The new juice of the grape and the young of the cattle are things the verse is listing among what would be taken from them. Everything that sustained the life of the people would be taken away from them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings if they obey God and serious warnings if they turn away from him. This warning describes a cruel invasion. Many believe it was fulfilled in the falls of Israel and Judah, although some also connect it to other moments in history.

Today we can remember that the goods of this life are not a secure foundation. Harvests, work and savings can disappear. It is good to thank God for what we have, to manage it with humility, and to place our trust in him, not in our fortifications.
exp.27:28:
In it, it says that, as punishment, the person will walk around groping at midday, just like a blind person in the dark. Nothing they set out to do will go well. They will live oppressed and stripped of their possessions every day, and no one will come to rescue them. "Grope" means to feel with the hands to find the way, and "prosper" means to go well for someone.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them the blessings for obeying God and the curses for abandoning his covenant. This verse is part of the consequences of disobedience. It was a warning so that the people would recognize how much they needed God.

For today: when we live without asking for God's guidance, we can feel lost even in the midst of what seems clear. Take a moment each day to pray and ask him for direction before you decide.
exp.16:12:
This verse says that when the punishment was carried out on someone who acted with arrogance against the decision of the priest or the judge, all the people would hear of it, would be filled with fear, and would no longer act presumptuously. "Shall hear" means they would find out about it; "fear" speaks of serious respect; "do no more presumptuously" means they would stop acting with pride or rebelliousness.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions for resolving difficult cases at a central court. The sentence was severe because it dealt with deliberate rebellion, not a simple mistake. This was a time and a legal system particular to Israel.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we accept correction and authority with humility. When someone advises us with wisdom, it is good to listen before defending ourselves with pride.
exp.11:15:
It says that the people could eat meat in their own towns, but they were not to eat the blood of the animal. Instead, they had to pour it out on the earth, like water poured out on the ground. "Only" means "except that," and "pour out" means to let a liquid fall to the ground.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that the sacrifices were to be made in one place chosen by God, but that meat for everyday use could be eaten in any town. The blood was treated with respect because it represented life, and life belongs to God (Leviticus 17:11).

For today: We can learn to treat life as a gift from God, with gratitude and respect. Before eating, thanking God for food is a simple way to recognize that everything we have comes from Him.
exp.14:13:
This verse commands that when a Hebrew servant is set free, his master must not send him away empty-handed. The phrase "furnish him liberally" means giving to him generously, like someone filling a full supply. The "floor" is the place where grain was threshed, and the "winepress" is where grapes were trodden to make wine. In other words, the master was to give him from his flock, from his harvest of grain, and from his wine, according to what God had blessed him with.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. In that time, a person could sell himself as a servant because of debt or poverty. After six years he was to go free. The law wanted him not to fall back into poverty, and it reminds Israel that they too had been servants in Egypt and that God redeemed them.

For today: if God has blessed us, we can give generously to someone who is coming out of a difficult situation, for example by helping someone who has lost a job or is starting over. Giving with gratitude reflects the kindness God showed us.
exp.3:36:
It says that God loved Israel's ancestors, that is, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Because of that love he chose their descendants and brought them out of Egypt with his great power. The phrase "brought thee out in his sight" means that God himself brought them out, being present with them.

Moses speaks to the people at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what God did so that they will not forget who their God is. Their deliverance was not because of their own merit, but because of God's love and his faithfulness to his promises.

For today: when you doubt your worth, remember that God loved you first. Your life does not rest on your achievements, but on his faithful love. Respond with gratitude and obedience, trusting that he keeps what he promises.
exp.30:20:
God says that when many evils and troubles come upon the people for having turned away from Him, the song that Moses will teach them will speak against them as a witness. That song will not be forgotten, because their descendants will keep repeating it.

"Imagination" here means what is in their mind and heart, their inclinations. God already knows them, even before they enter the promised land.

God speaks with Moses shortly before Moses dies. God knows that Israel, while living in abundance, could forget Him and follow other gods. For this reason He commands that a song easy to remember be put in writing, so that it would serve as a warning and also as a call to return.

For today: let us not wait for troubles to remember God. Let us learn His Word or a faithful song by heart, so that in good days it guards our heart and in difficult days it guides us back to Him.
exp.0:44:
This verse says that the people returned after their defeat and wept before God, but God did not answer them or pay attention to them. "You returned" means they came back to the camp. "Did not give ear to you" means he did not respond to their plea.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, now close to the promised land, and reminds them of what happened forty years earlier. God had told them not to go up to fight, but they, in pride, disobeyed and were defeated by the Amorites. Afterward they wept, but without any real change of heart. Moses speaks to them so they will not repeat that mistake.

For today: weeping or lamenting does not replace obedience. When we fail, God looks for a humble heart that listens and corrects itself in time, not just tears after the consequences. Today you can ask yourself in what area you need to obey God without waiting to regret it afterward.
exp.22:11:
It says that inside the camp of Israel's army there had to be a set-apart place, outside the camp, where people would go out to relieve themselves. It was not done just anywhere, but in a designated spot.

Moses is speaking to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He gives them rules for when they go out to war. God was present in the middle of the camp, so it had to be kept clean and orderly. Besides, these rules helped protect everyone's health, although the text stresses above all holiness.

For today: God cares about the everyday, not only about what is "spiritual." We can honor him with order, cleanliness, and respect for others in the home, at work, and in church, remembering that he is close to us.
exp.4:17:
It says we should not commit adultery, that is, have sexual relations with someone who is not our husband or wife, or with someone who is married to another person. The word "adultery" here means being unfaithful in marriage.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He repeats the Ten Commandments that God gave on Mount Sinai. This commandment protects marriage and trust within the family, and it comes between the command to honor one's parents and the command not to murder.

For today: take care of your faithfulness through concrete actions. If you are married, be honest with your partner and set healthy limits on your friendships, your conversations, and what you look at. If you are not, respect other people's marriages. Faithfulness is built in the small decisions of each day.
exp.31:39:
Here God speaks as if he were making a solemn oath. In ancient times, lifting the hand toward heaven was a way of swearing. "I lift up my hand" means that God commits himself with complete seriousness. And he says, "I live for ever," that is, that he is eternal and that his word cannot fail.

The one speaking is God, in the Song of Moses, near the end of Moses' life. God reminds Israel that its idols could not help them. Only the Lord has power over life and death, and he promises to act with justice against his enemies.

For today: when everything around you changes or falls apart, rest in the fact that God is eternal and faithful. You can trust him more than anything that passes away, because his word remains.
exp.27:64:
This verse says that among the nations where the people would be scattered, they would find no peace and no place of rest. "The sole of your foot" refers to the sole of the foot, meaning they would have nowhere to settle. God would give them a trembling heart (filled with fear), failing eyes (tired eyes that grow dim from long waiting or weeping), and sorrow of mind (a downcast spirit).

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings if they obey and curses if they abandon the covenant with God. This passage describes the consequences of persistent disobedience: exile and anguish far from their land.

For today: a life far from God can fill us with restlessness, even when we have everything. We can return to Him with sincerity and rest in His forgiveness, for Jesus invites: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."
exp.31:38:
God says: "Look carefully: I am the only God, and no other god is with me." He has power over life and death, and also over pain and healing. No one can take anyone out of his hand. The words "see" and "look" are the same command, and "deliver" means to rescue.

These words are part of the Song of Moses, at the end of his life. God himself speaks and rebukes Israel, who had turned away from him to follow idols. Earlier he mocks those false gods: where are they now to help? The passage shows that only the Lord has true power. Some understand that the wounding and the healing include God's discipline, which seeks to restore.

Today, when things do not turn out the way you hope, do not place your security in money, success, or people. Rest in God, who governs your life and sustains your future. Bring to him in prayer today whatever worries you.
exp.30:2:
This verse says that God himself will go ahead of Israel. He will destroy the nations that live in the promised land, and the people will take possession of it as their inheritance. The word "possess" means that they will receive the land as a gift, not by their own strength. "Nations" refers to the peoples who live there. Joshua will also go before them, as the Lord had already said.

Moses is speaking, and he is one hundred and twenty years old. God has told him that he will not cross the Jordan. So he says goodbye to the people and assures them that they will not be left alone. God will continue to guide them, and Joshua will be the new leader who will bring them into the land.

For today: leaders and people change, but God remains. If you face a difficult change or a new season, remember that God goes ahead of you. Walk in obedience and trust, without depending only on your own strength.
exp.0:2:
This verse says that, when forty years had passed since the exit from Egypt, on the first day of the eleventh month, Moses spoke to the people of Israel. He told them everything that God had commanded him to tell them.

The book records the last words of Moses. The people are east of the Jordan, about to enter the promised land. The earlier generation had died in the wilderness, so Moses reminds them of what God did and commanded. The text stresses that he spoke faithfully, without adding ideas of his own.

For today: God has spoken clearly, and it is good for us to remember and repeat his Word faithfully. This week, choose a passage of the Bible, read it calmly, and share it with someone in your family, just as it is, with humility and affection.
exp.23:6:
It says that if someone kidnaps a person from the people of Israel and treats them as merchandise, whether by using them as a slave or selling them, that person must die. "Stealing a person" means that the thief robbed or kidnapped a human being. "Dealing in them" means that he traded them. And "putting evil away from among you" means that the people were to remove that wickedness from their community.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and he repeats God's laws to them. The commands nearby protect the most vulnerable: the newly married wife and the poor man who gives something necessary for living as a pledge. Here the freedom of people is protected, since they are worth too much to be treated as things.

For today: God values the freedom and dignity of every person. We can reject every form of exploitation or human trafficking, and support those who help the victims.
exp.5:20:
This verse says that when a son asks why God's laws exist, the father should answer by telling the story of deliverance. "Bondmen" means slaves. "Mighty hand" speaks of God's power. "Lord" is the name of God in the covenant with Israel. "Thou shalt say" is a command: "you shall say to him."

Moses speaks to the Israelite parents before they enter the promised land. He wants faith to be passed on from generation to generation. The answer does not begin with rules, but with what God did: he rescued them when they were slaves. Obedience is born from that rescue.

For today: when your children or anyone else asks about your faith, do not begin with a list of rules. Simply tell how God has helped you and rescued you. Your personal testimony can open a heart.
exp.22:8:
It says that when Israel's army went out to war against its enemies, they had to keep themselves away from every wrong thing. The phrase "goeth forth" means going out to battle, and "keep thee" means take care of yourself, or stay away from. The expression "every wicked thing" covers everything that was unclean or improper.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The verses that follow show that this "wicked thing" included ritual uncleanness in the camp, because God was present in the midst of his people. For Israel, war was not only a matter of strength, but also of living clean before God.

Today, when we face a difficult struggle, whether at work, in the family, or in health, we can ask ourselves which habits or attitudes we should leave behind. Taking care of our conduct and our heart helps us face problems with a clear conscience and trust in God.
exp.32:14:
It says that the land of Joseph will be blessed also with the best of the ancient mountains and of the everlasting hills. The "precious things" of the ancient mountains and everlasting hills are the good and valuable gifts God gives. The mountains and hills are called ancient and everlasting because they have existed for a very long time, and that conveys the idea of a firm and lasting blessing.

Moses speaks just before he dies. He blesses each tribe of Israel, and here he addresses Joseph, that is, the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh. He promises them a fertile land, with water, fruit and good pasture. Some think the images of the mountains refer to the abundance of the land they would receive.

For today: learn to see the good things in your life, such as provision, nature and family, as gifts from God. Give thanks for them and share them generously.
exp.10:31:
It says the people must take great care to carry out, that is, to truly practice, all the laws God gives them. The "statutes" are God's commands, and the "judgments" are his rules of justice. "To do" means putting into practice what one hears.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they cross the Jordan River to enter the promised land. He reminds them that God is giving them that land, and that living in it means obeying what God has taught them. Moses wants them not only to know the law, but to live it.

For today: it is not enough to hear or know the Bible. Choose one teaching you already know, such as forgiveness, honesty or helping someone, and practice it today with one concrete action.
exp.26:11:
It says that, after crossing the Jordan, six tribes would stand on Mount Gerizim to pronounce a blessing over the people: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph (which includes Ephraim and Manasseh), and Benjamin.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before his death, when Israel is about to enter the promised land. He wants them, upon arriving, to renew their covenant with God in a public ceremony. The other six tribes would stand on Mount Ebal, facing them. Blessing and curse were meant to remind them that obeying or disobeying God brings real consequences.

For today: obedience to God is not a private matter, but something lived out and remembered in community. You could gather with other believers to read the Bible, encourage one another, and remember that God keeps his promises to those who trust in him.
exp.27:34:
It says that God would strike the one who disobeyed him with a painful, malignant sore or ulcer in the knees and legs, one that could not be cured. It would spread from the sole of the foot up to the top of the head.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them the blessings for keeping the covenant and the consequences for rejecting it. These curses are serious warnings, growing harsher as they go, which culminate in oppression and exile among foreign nations. Some scholars think the illness is literal, and others think it describes total suffering.

For today: do not read this text to frighten yourself or to judge someone who is suffering, for illness is not always punishment. Rather, take it as an invitation to take God's voice seriously and to return to him with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.11:7:
It says that when the people entered the promised land, they were no longer to worship God each one in their own way, as they had done in the wilderness. "Each one doing what seems right" means "every man whatsoever is right in his own eyes." God was asking for order in worship.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they cross the Jordan. In the wilderness, life was temporary, without a land of their own. Once they settled, God would show them a chosen place to bring their offerings and to rejoice before Him. Some scholars also see here a warning against the practices of the neighboring peoples.

For today: it is not enough that something seems right to us when we worship God. We can ask what pleases Him according to His Word, and seek a sincere, orderly, and joyful worship, together with other believers.
exp.31:47:
This verse says that God spoke to Moses that very same day, right after Moses finished teaching the people. The words "the Lord spake" mean that the Lord himself gave him a message. "That selfsame day" points to the day when Moses sang and repeated the law to Israel.

The speaker here is the narrator, who presents God's words to Moses. Moses had just urged the people to keep the law as their life. Now God tells him that he must go up to Mount Nebo, look out over the promised land, and die there. So his long task as leader comes to an end, though he will not enter Canaan.

For today: God keeps speaking to his people through his Word, and sometimes he reminds us that our time of serving has an end. We can live each day faithfully, teaching the truth to others and trusting that God cares for what comes next.
exp.22:15:
This verse says that a servant who runs away from his master and arrives among Israel may stay and live among them. He may choose the town and the place where he feels it is best for him.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them laws to live as a holy people, because God is present among them. Many understand this to refer to a slave who escapes from a foreign land, although the text gives no further details. Either way, it shows God's care for the vulnerable.

For today: let us be a safe refuge for anyone fleeing oppression or abuse. We can welcome, listen to, and help those who suffer, without taking advantage of their need.
exp.1:21:
He says that God had already done something similar for the descendants of Esau, who lived in Seir. Before them, the Horites lived there, a people whom God drove out from before them. The Edomites replaced them and stayed in that land "to this day," that is, up to the time this was written. The phrase "to this day" means that they remained there until the present time, and the verse above says "even unto this day," which conveys the same idea.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them that God had already given lands to other nations, such as Edom, Moab, and Ammon. In this way Israel understood that God rules over the nations and could also give them the promised land.

For today: if God cares for the nations and carries out his plans, he can also guide your life. Trust him when the way seems uncertain, and remember how he has helped you before.
exp.0:6:
God tells the people of Israel to rise up, leave Mount Horeb, and set out toward the promised land. He names the regions they will pass through: the mount of the Amorites, the plains, the hills, the valleys, the south, the seashore, the land of the Canaanites, Lebanon, and as far as the great river Euphrates.

Moses speaks to the people in Moab, near the Jordan, almost at the end of his life. He reminds them of what God commanded them forty years earlier. They had stayed a long time at Horeb, and it was now time to move forward and receive the promise made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

For today: God blesses us at every stage, but he does not want us to remain stuck when he calls us to move forward. We must trust his promise and take the next step in faith, even when it means leaving what is comfortable.
exp.27:11:
It says that God will open the heavens like a good and full storehouse, to send rain on the land of Israel at the right time, and to bless all the work of their hands. Because of this, they will have more than enough and will be able to lend to many nations without needing to borrow.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: the blessings come within a promise made to that nation, and they depend on obeying Him and not following other gods. For a people of farmers, rain was life.

For today: although this promise was given to Israel and does not guarantee wealth to every believer, it does teach us that everything we have comes from God. Work with effort, be thankful for what you receive, and live generously, trusting that God cares for you.
exp.12:4:
It says that the prophet or dreamer who tries to turn the people away from the LORD must be put to death. The reason is that he spoke of rebellion against the God who brought them out of Egypt, and the verse calls Egypt "the house of bondage," that is, a place of slavery. He wanted to draw them off the way God had commanded them to walk. With that, the text says, the evil is put away from the midst of the people.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. God allowed a false prophet to appear, even with signs, to test whether the people truly loved him. This was a law for the nation of Israel under the covenant of that time, where idolatry was treated as treason against their King.

Today we do not apply this penalty, but we do apply the principle: let us examine every teaching in the light of what God has already revealed. If anyone, however impressive he may seem, draws us away from Christ and the Bible, we should not follow him.
exp.13:28:
This verse says that the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow who lived in the towns of Israel could come and eat until they were satisfied. "Inheritance" means land received as a family possession, and "towns" are the villages or cities. God promises to bless those who act this way in everything they do.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The Levites served in worship and did not receive land of their own, so they depended on the generosity of the people. Every third year, the tithe was stored in the towns to help them and the most vulnerable, who had no one to support them.

For today: God cares for those in need, and our generosity is a way of obeying him. You could set aside a fixed part of your income to help a person or a work that serves the most vulnerable in your community.
exp.27:26:
God would strike Israel with diseases like the "plague of Egypt," sicknesses similar to those the Egyptians suffered. Hemorrhoids are painful swellings, and the scab is a skin infection. Being unable to be healed means there would be no human remedy.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He sets out blessings for keeping the covenant and curses for abandoning it. These warnings were meant to lead them to take their faithfulness to God seriously.

For today: we should not see every illness as punishment, since the Bible does not teach that. But we can take God's voice seriously, live with humility, and turn to Him when we feel there is no way out.
exp.5:8:
He says God wanted his people to write his words on the doorposts of the house and on the gates, that is, on the frames of the doors and on the entrances of the city or the courtyard. In this way, every time someone went in or out, they would see God's commandments.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just reminded them to love God with all their heart and to teach his words to their children. Then he warns them that, when they receive houses and harvests they did not work for, they must not forget who gave them to them. Some Jews carry out this command literally with the mezuzah; others understand it as a way of living with God present.

For today: place in a visible spot in your home a verse that reminds you to trust God, and read it aloud with your family when you leave or come home.
exp.2:10:
This verse says that Og, king of Bashan, was the last of the giants called Rephaim. His bed was made of iron and measured nine cubits long and four cubits wide. A cubit is the distance from the elbow to the tip of the finger, about 45 centimeters, so the bed measured nearly four meters by almost two. "Rabbath" was the main city of the Ammonites. Some think "iron" could refer to basalt, a dark, hard stone, but this is not known for certain.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the victories God gave them over powerful kings. The bed served as a visible proof that Og had existed and had been defeated.

For today: when you face something that seems like a giant, remember that God has already overcome things far greater. Trust in Him and move forward in faith.
exp.3:32:
Moses asks whether any people has ever heard the voice of God speaking out of the midst of the fire, as Israel did, and lived. The sentence that explains the old wording is removed, since its quoted words do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

Moses speaks to the people in his final addresses, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what they experienced at Mount Horeb (Sinai), when God gave the Ten Commandments. He wants them to value that privilege and not forget God or fall into idolatry.

For today: God has made himself known, and that is a gift, not something ordinary. We can take a moment each day to thank him that he speaks to us, above all through his Word, and to listen to him with attention and respect, without taking it for granted.
exp.9:11:
This verse sums up what God asks of his people: that they honor him with reverence (the sense of "fear" here), that they live according to his ways, that they love him, and that they serve him with their whole being. "Heart" and "soul" speak of the whole person: thoughts, desires, and will.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just reminded them that God forgave them, despite their sin with the golden calf, and that he continues to lead them. After so much mercy, Moses explains how they should respond: with a whole life of love and obedience.

For today: faith is not only keeping rules, but responding with warmth to a God who has already shown us his goodness. Today you can give God the first moment of your day, thank him for his mercy, and ask him to help you obey him with joy.
exp.12:2:
It says that if someone presents himself as a prophet or a dreamer, and even performs a sign that comes true, but invites people to follow other gods, they should not be listened to. The phrase about not giving ear is explained by its meaning: not listening to or obeying. Where the verse speaks of God proving his people, it means that God examines the heart of his people. "Other gods" are the gods of other peoples.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the Promised Land. He warns them that a miracle is not enough to prove that a message comes from God. What matters is whether that message agrees with what God had already said and whether it leads people to love him alone.

Today we can measure any spiritual message, however impressive it may seem, by the Word of God. If something draws us away from Jesus and from the truth of the Scriptures, it is best not to follow it, even if it comes with signs or sounds very convincing.
exp.27:45:
This verse says that the curses mentioned earlier will be upon Israel as a sign and a wonder, that is, something that draws attention and serves as a warning to everyone. The word "seed" means descendants, so the effect would reach their children and grandchildren as well, upon them forever, that is, for a long time.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: if they obey, there will be blessing; if they turn away from Him, there will be serious consequences. What is especially emphasized is the lack of gratitude and joy in serving Him, even while having abundance.

For today: let us not take God's blessings for granted. We can begin the day by thanking Him sincerely and obeying Him with joy, not out of obligation, knowing that our decisions also affect our family.
exp.31:17:
It says that the people of Israel forgot God. It calls him "the Rock," an image of someone firm, secure, and faithful. It also says that God is the one who "formed" them, meaning the one who gave them life and shaped them into a people. Here "formed" means the one who brought them into being. To forget is not only to fail to remember, but to live as if God did not matter.

Moses is speaking. Before he dies, he teaches them a song to warn them. He reminds them that God cared for them, but they turned away after other gods. That is why, in the verses that follow, God grieves and becomes angry, and shows the consequences of their unfaithfulness.

For today: it is easy to forget God when everything is going well. You can set aside a few minutes each day to thank him for something specific he has given you, and so keep your heart steady in him.
exp.4:16:
It says that we must not take the life of another person. It is the sixth of the Ten Commandments. The Hebrew word used refers above all to murder, that is, taking a life unjustly. Scholars discuss how it applies to cases such as war or the death penalty, since the Law itself treats these separately.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, just before they enter the promised land. He repeats to them the Ten Commandments that God gave on Mount Sinai. God had freed them from slavery in Egypt, and now he teaches them to live as a free people who respect life, because every person is precious to God.

For today: care for the life of others also with your words and attitudes. Jesus taught that hatred and contempt also cause harm (Matthew 5:21-22). Today you can choose to forgive someone or speak to them with respect.
exp.10:1:
Moses tells the people to understand clearly what he is about to remind them of. He is not speaking to their children, who have not yet seen or experienced how God corrects and disciplines. The adults did live through it: God's greatness, his mighty hand, and his outstretched arm, which are expressions for his power to rescue and to act.

Moses speaks at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, shortly before Israel enters the promised land. He addresses the generation that left Egypt and saw the miracles with their own eyes. He asks them to love God and obey, relying on what they themselves witnessed.

For today: remember and tell what God has done in your life. Your experience with him can strengthen your obedience and help your children or younger people come to know him.
exp.6:19:
It says that God himself will send "hornets" against the peoples of Canaan, until even the survivors and those who hide to escape are gone. The word "destroyed" here is the one in the verse above, meaning that they die or are wiped out. Scholars are not sure whether the hornets are real insects or a picture of the terror and confusion that God would send upon them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. They feared nations that seemed larger and stronger. Moses reminds them how God delivered them from Egypt, so that they will trust that He will also fulfill His promise now.

For today: when you feel afraid in the face of a problem that seems enormous, remember the times God helped you in the past. That remembrance strengthens trust and encourages you to take the next step, knowing that God goes with you.
exp.1:1:
This verse says that God spoke to Moses. "Jehovah" is the name of the Lord in this older translation. It is a short phrase that serves as a bridge: the people had been going around in circles, and now God is going to give them new direction.

Moses is speaking to Israel and recalling their history. They had circled the mountain of Seir for many days without making much progress. Then God steps in and tells them that it is enough and that they should turn toward the north. The verses that follow show that God guides them with care, even in how they treat their neighbors.

For today: sometimes we go around in a situation without moving forward. Stop to pray and listen to God through his Word. He can show you when it is time to change course.
exp.3:7:
Moses asks what great nation has laws and decrees as just as the ones God gave Israel. The words "statutes" and "judgments" in the verse refer to commands and rules, and to fair and right decisions. The question answers itself: no other nation had anything like it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of forty years in the wilderness, before they enter the promised land. He asks them to keep the law so that the other peoples will see their wisdom. Earlier he said that God is near to them whenever they call on him. Then he asks them not to forget what they experienced at Horeb and to teach it to their children.

For today: God's Word is a treasure, not a burden. We can read it with gratitude, put it into practice at home and at work, and share it with our children through our example and in simple words.
exp.3:41:
Deuteronomy 4:42 says that Moses set apart three cities east of the Jordan so that a person who had killed another by accident could flee there. By fleeing to one of those cities, that person saved his life.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel just before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that obeying God brings good to their families. These cities of refuge protected the accused from revenge by the relatives of the victim while what had happened was being clarified. In this way justice was not confused with violence.

For today: God cares for both justice and mercy. We can learn not to judge in haste, to distinguish between a mistake and an act of wickedness, and to offer protection and a second chance to someone who erred without evil intent.
exp.11:31:
This verse says that the people must be very careful to obey everything God commands. They must not add their own rules or practices to his commands, nor remove parts that they find unappealing. "Be careful to observe" means the same as "take care to do"; adding means putting something extra in, and removing means taking something out.

Moses is speaking to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He has just warned them not to copy the way the peoples of Canaan worshiped their gods, since those practices included things God detests, such as burning their children. God wants to be worshiped as he himself has directed, not as people happen to think of.

For today: when you read the Bible, try to receive it as it is, without bending it to your tastes or to the culture of the moment. Ask yourself honestly: "Am I adding something God did not ask for, or ignoring something he did say?" Then ask God for help to obey him with humility.
exp.5:23:
He says that God commanded us to keep all his laws and to live them with respect and reverence toward him. Here "fear" does not mean being afraid, but honoring him and taking him seriously. "Statutes" are the rules God gave. The goal is twofold: that things go well for us always, and that he preserves our lives, as is already evident in the present.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He asks them to explain to their children why they obey: God rescued them from Egypt with great signs and promised them a land. Obedience springs from remembering what God has already done, not from mere obligation.

For today: before thinking about rules, remember how God has cared for you. From that gratitude, choose one concrete act of obedience today, and tell someone else why you are doing it.
exp.8:1:
It says that Israel is going to face a people great and tall, descendants of the children of the Anakims, such as the Anakites. The Israelites had already heard of them and were repeating a saying: "Who can stand before the children of Anak?" The phrase about the children of Anak refers to people of great height and a reputation for strength.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they cross the Jordan, near the end of his life. He wants them to remember the fear they felt when the spies returned forty years ago. He reminds them that the victory will not depend on their strength, but on God, who will go before them.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, do not deny it, but do not let fear speak louder than God's promises. Do what is yours to do with confidence in Him, and if God gives you the victory, thank Him with humility instead of boasting.
exp.13:17:
This verse continues a list of birds that the Israelites were not to eat. It mentions the stork, the heron, the hoopoe, and the bat. "After her kind" means "of each kind." The exact identities of several of the Hebrew birds are uncertain, and ancient and modern translations do not always agree. Today it is known that the bat is not a bird, but the Hebrew list groups together the animals that fly.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the dietary laws God gave them. These rules set them apart as a holy people, consecrated to God. The Bible does not explain the reason for each animal, so it is not appropriate to invent reasons.

For today: God wants his people to live with attention to him, even in everyday matters. We can ask ourselves which daily habits show that we belong to God, and offer them to him with gratitude and obedience.
exp.27:58:
It says that if the people disobey, God will send very severe punishments on them and on their children. "Plagues" are blows or calamities; "seed" means descendants; "lasting" means they cannot be easily removed; and "harmful and long-lasting" describes serious and prolonged sicknesses.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: obeying it would bring blessing, and rejecting it would bring painful consequences. It is a serious warning, given so that the people would take God and his law seriously. Some understand these words as directed mainly to Israel under that covenant.

For today: God calls us to take his voice seriously, not out of empty fear, but because our decisions affect others, especially our family. Today you can choose one concrete act of obedience and do it with confidence in his grace.
exp.31:44:
This verse says that Moses finished speaking aloud the whole song that God had given him, and that he did it in front of all the people of Israel. To "recite" means to say something out loud, either from memory or by reading it. "Finished" means that he came to the end.

Moses is speaking near the end of his life, shortly before Israel enters the promised land. This song was a reminder of God's faithfulness and a warning against disobedience. Joshua was with him, since he would soon take his place as leader. Afterward, Moses asks the people to take these words seriously.

For today: hearing God's Word just once is not enough. Moses repeated it in full and asked that it be taught to the children. We can choose a fixed time each week to read the Bible as a family or with someone close to us, and talk about what we are learning.
exp.26:21:
It says God regards as cursed anyone who has sexual relations with his half-sister, whether on the father's side or the mother's side. The phrase "lie with" is an old expression for having intimate relations. And all the people respond with "Amen," which means "so be it," to show that they agree.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He orders a ceremony at Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, where the Levites would proclaim curses and the people would say "Amen." This list includes sexual sins and sins committed in secret, to protect the holiness of the family and so that the people would live in covenant with God.

Today it reminds us that God cares for the family and for healthy boundaries within it. We can ask him to help us live with purity, respect, and responsibility, even when no one sees us.
exp.8:15:
Moses says that he came down from the mountain and saw that the people had sinned. They had made a calf of cast metal, that is, a figure of a young bull made from melted metal. They turned aside quickly from the way that the Lord had commanded them.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, reminding them what happened at Sinai. He repeats this story before they enter the promised land, so that they do not think God gives them the land because they are good. Rather, they need to remember their need for God's grace and mercy.

Today we can learn that it is easy to turn aside quickly when we stop putting God at the center. It is wise to ask ourselves what things have taken his place in our hearts. And if we fail, we can return to him with humility, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.10:7:
It says that Israel must obey all the commandments that Moses gives them that day. The purpose is that they be strong and firm, so they can enter the promised land and take possession of it. The words for "prescribe" and "command" are rendered here as giving instructions, and the word for "you cross over" refers to crossing the Jordan River.

Moses speaks to the people at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, just before they enter Canaan. He reminds them of what they saw with their own eyes: God's discipline, as in the case of Dathan and Abiram, and his great works. He wants their memory to produce obedience.

For today: the strength to face new challenges does not come only from our own courage, but from remembering what God has done and walking in what He teaches us. Today you can write down one occasion when God helped you and choose one concrete step of obedience.
exp.1:15:
This verse says that all the men of war from that generation of Israel had now died. The phrase "were consumed and dead" means that they died off, one by one, until none of them were left. This closes a long period of waiting in the wilderness.

Moses speaks to the new people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that their parents did not believe at Kadesh-barnea, and for that reason God swore that they would not enter. Thirty-eight years passed on the journey until that generation came to an end. Only after that did God give Moses a new direction to move forward.

For today: God keeps what He says, both His warnings and His promises. If you feel that you are in a time of waiting, trust that God is at work even there. Learn from the unbelief of the past, obey Him, and be ready to take the next step when He shows the way.
exp.6:1:
When the Lord your God hands those nations over to you and you defeat them, you must destroy them completely. You were not to make any covenant with them or show them mercy. The term "anatema," or total destruction, was the word used for things set apart to God.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they enter the promised land. He warns them that those nations were numerous and strong, and that the greater danger was not the war itself but the influence of their gods and customs. The verses that follow make this clear: they were not to intermarry with these peoples, so that they would not turn away from God. This command is difficult, and it has been interpreted in various ways; many see it as a unique charge given for that particular moment.

Today we are not commanded to fight anyone, but we are called to guard our faithfulness to God. We can examine which influences, habits, or relationships pull us away from Him, and be firm in turning away from them.
exp.5:7:
God's words are meant to accompany the people in everything they do. The phrase about binding them "as a sign upon your hand" speaks of their actions, and the phrase about being "between your eyes" speaks of what a person sees and thinks. In the older wording, a band or ornament placed on the forehead was described with a word that is no longer common.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the command to love God with all their heart. Some Jews have taken this verse literally and use phylacteries, small boxes containing Bible passages. Others understand it as a figurative expression. Both readings exist.

Today we can let God's Word guide what we do and what we look at. For example, before starting the day, read a verse and ask God to direct your decisions, your work, and the way you treat others.
exp.10:16:
It says that if the people turn away from God to serve other gods, the anger of the Lord will burn against them. He would shut up the heavens, so there would be no rain, the land would not yield its crops, and they would quickly perish from the good land that God was giving them. The verse of the word "quickly" and the word for intense anger is removed, since those words do not appear in the verse.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the rain and the harvests depend on God, not on the gods of Canaan. The verse is a serious warning, part of the covenant: obeying brings blessing, and turning away brings consequences.

For today: let us not give anything the place of God, such as money, success, or comfort. Each day, thank God for what you receive and ask Him for a faithful heart that does not forget Him.
exp.1:7:
This verse says that Israel went on its way without fighting the descendants of Esau, whom it calls "brothers." They passed through the plain road that leads to Elath and Ezion-geber, places near the Red Sea. Then they turned and took the road of the wilderness of Moab. "We passed by" means "we went past without stopping or attacking."

Moses speaks, reminding the people, almost at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. God had commanded them to respect the land of Edom, because it was the inheritance of the children of Esau, relatives of Israel. Moses reminds them that God took care of them and that nothing was lacking to them.

For today: God asks us to respect the boundaries and dignity of others, even when we have the strength to impose ourselves. We can trust that he provides, and so live without envy, without quarrels, and with honest dealing toward others.
exp.4:19:
This commandment says that we must not lie about another person, especially in order to harm them. To "bear false witness" means to declare something that is not true, as a lying witness would do. The "neighbour" is anyone close to us, the person who lives beside us.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, who are about to enter the promised land. He reminds them of the Ten Commandments that God gave at Mount Horeb (Sinai). This new generation needed to hear the law again in order to live in justice and trust with one another. In legal cases, a lie could ruin the life of an innocent person.

For today: before repeating a rumour or posting something about someone, ask yourself whether it is true and whether you would say it to their face. Caring for the truth protects the good name of others.
exp.20:21:
It says that if a person commits a crime so serious that it deserves death, and after the execution the body is hung on a pole or a tree, that body must be treated with care. The quoted phrase in the source, "Hubiere pecado de sentencia de muerte," means that the person committed a crime punishable by the death penalty. The next verse makes clear that the body was not to be left hanging overnight.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land, going over God's laws. These rules governed the justice of that people. It is believed that the hanging happened after death, although some understand it in a different way. The emphasis is on respecting human dignity and keeping the land clean.

For today: even someone who has failed gravely deserves to be treated with dignity. This invites us to reject mockery and cruelty, and to seek justice with humility and respect.
exp.6:10:
This verse says that the people must take care to obey everything God commands them. The word "keep" means to carry out with attention. "Commandments" are God's general orders, "statutes" are his fixed rules, and "judgments" are his just decisions. "This day" stresses that obedience is lived in the present.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God is faithful and that his covenant is real. That is why obedience is not a cold burden, but the response of a people who have already known God's faithfulness. Afterward, Moses speaks of blessings that accompany that path.

For today: do not wait until you feel ready to obey God. Choose one concrete step today, such as forgiving someone, being honest at work, or setting aside time for prayer. Do it trusting that God is faithful and good to you.
exp.13:6:
It says that the Israelites were not to eat animals that chew the cud but do not have a divided hoof. As examples it mentions the camel, the hare, and the coney. It calls these animals "unclean," that is, not fit to eat according to the law. Instead of a word that appears in the verse, here it is in plain terms: they are forbidden as food under the law. "Nevertheless" means "but," and "chew the cud" means that they bring up their food to chew it again. Some translators doubt which exact animal the "coney" of the Hebrew text is, since it could be another small animal that lives among the rocks.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the laws God gave them so that they would live as a people set apart, distinct from the neighboring nations. The text does not explain all the reasons for these rules, and scholars offer several explanations.

For today: God cares for every aspect of the life of his people, even everyday matters such as food. We can ask ourselves whether we are willing to obey him in small things too, showing that we belong to him.
exp.21:23:
This verse speaks of a young woman who was promised in marriage and who has relations with another man inside the city. Both would be brought out to the gate of the city, where judgment was given, and stoned. "Cried out" means that she asked for help by shouting. "Humbled" means that he dishonored or abused her. The law assumes that, in the city, she would have cried out if she were being forced.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. These civil laws protected marriage and the community. A promised woman was already considered committed as a wife. The verses that follow protect the young woman attacked in the field, where no one could hear her.

Today we do not apply those civil penalties. But we do learn to respect commitments, to care for purity, and to defend those who suffer abuse. Jesus also showed mercy toward sinners without making light of sin.
exp.0:40:
Here Moses recalls how the people reacted to God's punishment. They admit, "We have sinned against the Lord," and decide to go up and fight, saying they will obey what God commanded them earlier. Each man put on his weapons of war and got ready, that is, prepared himself, to go up into the hill.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in the wilderness, almost at the end of the forty years. He reminds them that because they did not trust God, they did not enter the promised land. Now, too late, they want to obey the earlier command, but God had told them not to go up. Their repentance sounded good, but it did not follow God's word for the present moment.

For today: true repentance includes listening to what God is asking of us now, not merely doing something religious with good intentions. Before acting, ask God and examine his Word with humility.
exp.3:0:
Moses asks the people of Israel to listen carefully to the laws and commands he teaches them. The words "statutes and judgments" refer to the fair rules and decisions that God gave. Here, "do" means to carry out or put into practice. The purpose is that they obey, live, enter the promised land, and possess it.

Moses speaks at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. A new generation is about to enter Canaan, and he reminds them that life in that land will depend on following God's word. Shortly after, he mentions what happened at Baal-peor, as a warning of what happens when people turn away from Him.

For today: hearing God's Word is not enough; it must be practiced. You might choose a Bible teaching you already know and decide this week how to live it out in one concrete step, such as forgiving, being honest, or helping someone.
exp.7:19:
It says that if the people of Israel forget God, they will meet the same fate as the nations that God is going to destroy when they enter the land. The phrase about hearing and obeying the voice of God means having listened and obeyed. The word meaning "perish" means they will be destroyed or disappear as a people in that land.

Moses speaks to the Israelites at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, just before entering the promised land. He warns them that abundance can make them believe they achieved everything on their own. He reminds them that God is the one who gives the ability to prosper and that his covenant requires faithfulness. It is a serious warning, given with love, so that they do not repeat the mistakes of other peoples.

When things go well for us, it is easy to stop giving thanks and to stop listening to God. Today we can set aside a moment each day to thank him for what we have and to ask him how to obey him with it.
exp.0:14:
Moses reminds the people that he chose the chief men of each tribe, wise and experienced men, and set them over the people as leaders.
