He organized them into groups of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. "Captains of tens" means those in charge of small groups, and "officers" were those who oversaw each tribe.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, in the wilderness, before Israel enters the promised land. He goes over what they have lived through. He could not carry all the people's problems alone, so the people agreed to this idea. Afterward he commanded the judges to judge with justice, without showing favoritism. Scholars debate whether this arrangement was exactly the same as in Exodus 18, but the account shows the same principle.

For today: no one should carry the whole burden alone. If you lead a family, church, or workplace, share responsibilities with wise and trustworthy people, and always seek to act with justice.
exp.27:40:
It says that parents will have sons and daughters, but they will not be able to enjoy them or keep them, because they will be taken away as prisoners to another land. "Shalt beget" means "shall have as children." "Captivity" means being carried off as a prisoner and living far from home.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. In this chapter he sets out blessings if they obey God and curses if they turn away from him. This verse belongs to the curses: labors and joys that are lost. The nearby verses speak of vineyards, olive trees, and ruined harvests. Later, the history of Israel shows exiles, although how each passage relates to each event is understood in different ways.

For today: value your family as a gift from God, pray for them, and give them your time now. Put God first in your home, because what is dearest also needs his care.
exp.7:10:
It says we must be careful not to forget God, and that this forgetting shows up when we stop obeying what He commands.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He describes a land that is good and plentiful. But he warns them that when they have food, houses, livestock and riches, it will be easy to forget God and to believe they achieved everything on their own.

For today: when things are going well is when we most need to remember God. You can thank Him each day for what you have and ask yourself whether your comfort is pulling you away from Him or leading you to obey Him with greater gratitude.
exp.9:15:
This verse says that the people must remove whatever blocks their heart, just as the skin was removed in circumcision. The foreskin is that skin, and here it is an image of inner hardness. The word "stiffnecked," which appears in the verse, means being stubborn and refusing to obey. God asks for an open and teachable heart.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God, the owner of the whole universe, chose them out of love and not because of merit. Furthermore, God is just, does not accept bribes, and cares for the orphan, the widow, and the foreigner. For this reason he asks them for an obedience that springs from the heart and not only from the outward sign.

Today we can ask ourselves in what area we have become stubborn before God. With humility, let us ask him to soften that point, and let us obey with love, especially by treating well those who need it most.
exp.32:9:
It says that the Levites would have two tasks: teaching and worship. They would teach Jacob's judgments (the decisions and commands of God) and the law to all the people. They would also offer the incense and the whole burnt offering (the offering burned completely) on God's altar.

Moses speaks just before he dies and blesses each tribe of Israel. Here he blesses Levi, the tribe set apart for service in the sanctuary. The verses before it recall their faithfulness to God in difficult moments. Some think it refers to the episode of the golden calf, although the text does not say so clearly.

For today: faith needs both the teaching of the Word and sincere worship. This week, set aside time to read the Bible and another time to pray and praise God, and share with someone what you have learned.
exp.4:20:
It says we should not covet what belongs to another person: not his wife, not his house, not his land, not his workers, not his animals, nor anything else that belongs to him. The verse's own words "covet" and "desire" mean wanting something that belongs to someone else with a strong longing. The "manservant" and "maidservant" were the hired workers or servants of a household. "Neighbour" means the person who lives nearby, someone close to us.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel, reminding them of the Ten Commandments that God gave them on the mountain, before they entered the promised land. This commandment is different from the others, because it looks not only at what is done, but at what is in the heart, from which theft, lying and other wrongs come.

Today we can practice it with gratitude: when you feel envy for what someone else has, thank God for something specific he has already given you, and ask him for a contented heart.
exp.14:2:
It says that a loan made to a foreigner could be collected, but the debt of a fellow Israelite was to be forgiven.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. Every seven years a release was given to debtors, to care for the poor and to keep anyone from being trapped in debt. Scholars discuss whether the debt was canceled completely or only suspended for that year. The foreigner, probably a passing merchant, was not under that same arrangement.

For today: if someone close to you owes you and cannot pay, ask God for a generous heart. Consider forgiving the debt or giving them more time, protecting their dignity and without humiliating them.
exp.28:18:
This verse speaks of someone who hears the warnings of the covenant with God but takes them lightly. He blesses himself in his heart, reassuring himself and saying, "I shall have peace, though I walk in the imagination of mine heart." The phrase "to add drunkenness to thirst" is a hard saying; many understand it to mean that sin drags along more sin, or that what is good and what is evil are both destroyed.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in Moab, when they renew the covenant before entering the promised land. He warns them against idolatry and against a heart that turns away in secret, like a root that sends up poison and wormwood, a bitter plant.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are deceiving ourselves with thoughts like "God will understand, it's no big deal." A false peace does not heal. Let us rather listen to God with humility and return to Him in time.
exp.2:21:
This verse says that there is no need to be afraid of the enemies, because God himself is the one who fights on behalf of his people. The phrase "do not fear them" simply means "do not be afraid of them." The word "ye" is an old form of "you."

The speaker is Moses, reminding the people of Israel what he had told Joshua. They had already seen how God defeated two kings east of the Jordan. Moses wanted Joshua to trust that God would do the same with the kingdoms they would face when Israel entered the promised land.

For today: when you face a problem that seems bigger than you, remember what God has already done in your life and in his Word. Do what is yours to do with responsibility, but rest in the fact that you are not alone. God is faithful and can work in the middle of what frightens you.
exp.30:9:
Moses gives the people a command: every seven years, in the year of release (the year when debts were forgiven), during the Feast of Booths (or Tabernacles, when they camped in shelters of branches to remember the wilderness), the law was to be read aloud.

Moses is about to die, and Joshua will take command. He has just handed the written law to the priests and the elders. Now he makes sure that Israel hears it regularly, so that the new generations, including children and foreigners, will know it and honor God.

For today: God wants his Word to be heard with constancy, not just once. We can set aside a fixed time each week to read the Bible as a family or with others, and so remember his promises and obey them.
exp.2:9:
This verse lists the territories Israel conquered east of the Jordan: the cities of the plain, all the region of Gilead, and all of Bashan, as far as Salchah and Edrei. All of this was part of the kingdom of Og, king of Bashan. The Amorites were a people who lived in that area.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life, recalling what God did along the way. He reviews the victories over the kings Sihon and Og to encourage the new generation to trust God before entering the promised land. Those lands were then divided among Reuben, Gad, and part of Manasseh.

For today: remembering what God has already done in our lives strengthens faith for the challenges ahead. Write down a few occasions when God helped you, and thank him for them.
exp.5:21:
This verse says that God showed great and painful signs and wonders in Egypt, and that the people saw them with their own eyes. These wonders fell upon Pharaoh and all his household and his people. The word "harmful" here means damaging or painful, because they were hard blows against Egypt. "Gave" is the same as "shewed," and "signs" are events that show the power of God.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He teaches them how to explain to their children why they obey the law of God. The answer is to tell the story: they were slaves, and God rescued them.

For today: when you teach the faith to your children, or to others, do not limit yourself to giving rules. Tell also what God has done in your life and in his people. Obedience is better born from grateful remembrance.
exp.9:10:
God told Moses to get up and lead the people forward, so that Israel would enter the land and take it as their own. "Go ahead of them" means to go at the front. "Swore" means promised with an oath. "Their fathers" refers to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the ancestors of Israel.

Moses speaks to the people and reminds them of what happened after the sin of the golden calf. He interceded on the mountain, and God did not destroy them. Now God renews the command to move forward. This shows his mercy and his faithfulness to the promise. Moses will soon explain what God expects of them: to fear him, love him, and obey him.

For today: when God gives us a new opportunity after we have failed, let us not stay trapped in guilt. Let us respond with gratitude, trust, and obedience, and take the next step he shows us.
exp.8:17:
Moses tells how he threw himself down before God, as he had done before, for forty days and forty nights. He neither ate nor drank. "Falling down" here means bowing low to the ground in humble prayer. He did this because of the sin of the people, who did evil and provoked God's anger.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the episode of the golden calf, so that they will not think they deserve the land for being good. What he recounts here is that he interceded for them when they deserved punishment.

Today we can imitate Moses by praying for others, even for those who have failed. Instead of only criticizing the mistakes of family, friends, or our community, we can ask God for mercy for them and for ourselves.
exp.2:15:
This verse says that Moses gave the tribes of Reuben and Gad a territory east of the Jordan River. Their land ran from part of Gilead to the Arnon stream, with the middle of the stream serving as the boundary. On the other side it reached to the Jabbok stream, which was the border with the Ammonites. The word "dí," which appears in the verse, means "I gave," and the word "término" refers to a boundary or limit.

Here Moses is speaking near the end of his life. He is reminding the people how the conquered land was divided before they entered Canaan. He reminds them that God kept his promise and that each tribe received a place with clear boundaries.

For today: God cares for us with order and generosity. We can learn to recognize what He has given us, live thankfully within our limits, and not envy what others have received.
exp.8:22:
God told Israel, from Kadesh-barnea, to go up and take the land he had already given them. But they rebelled against that command: they did not trust God, and they did not listen to his voice. The quoted phrases in the source comment are not something your reader will see, so they are left out here; the rest of the verse follows.

Moses speaks to the people, now close to the promised land, years after those events. He reminds them that they do not deserve the land because they are good, but because of God's faithfulness. Kadesh-barnea was the place where, out of fear, they refused to enter (Numbers 13–14). Moses lists their failures to strip away any pride they might have.

Today we can ask ourselves: is there something God has clearly told us in his Word that we have not obeyed out of fear? We can confess it with humility and take a step of trust in him today.
exp.25:9:
It says that the Israelite presents the firstfruits to God, that is, the first portion of his harvest, and acknowledges that the Lord gave him the land. The phrase "behold" in the verse above is the word that means "look," and the verse's wording "set it before" points to a gesture of worship and humility. Here the text moves from the prayer to the command to leave the offering and worship.

Moses is speaking, instructing the people before they enter the promised land. He teaches them a prayer to say when they offer the firstfruits. Before this verse, the person recalls the deliverance from Egypt. In this way the offering is not a mere formality, but gratitude for what God has done. Afterward comes the shared joy with the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow.

Today we can give God the first and not what is left over, remembering that everything comes from Him. Giving with gratitude also moves us to share with those in need.
exp.25:8:
This verse says that God brought his people into the promised land and gave it to them. The verse here points to the words "brought" and "given," which are the verse's wording in the King James version: "hath brought us" and "hath given us." The phrase about the land is a way of saying it was a fertile land, good for living and with plenty of food. In the King James wording, that is the phrase "a land that floweth with milk and honey."

The speaker is an Israelite who arrives at the sanctuary with the firstfruits, that is, the first products of his harvest. He was to recite this short confession of faith before the priest. By remembering the oppression in Egypt, the people's cry, and God's deliverance, he acknowledged that the harvest was a gift and not merely the fruit of his own effort.

For today: before thinking about what we lack, we can stop to remember how God has helped us in the past. Giving thanks sincerely, and sharing some of what we have, helps us live with a grateful and generous heart.
exp.32:10:
It says that Moses asks God to bless the work of the tribe of Levi and to accept with favor what their hands do. He also asks that God strike down their enemies, those who hate them, so that they never rise again. "Smite through the loins" is an old expression that means striking the strength of the adversary, that is, taking away his power.

Moses is saying farewell to Israel and blesses each tribe. Here he speaks of Levi, the ones appointed to teach the law and offer the sacrifices. In the verse before, their faithfulness to God is praised, even above family ties. This prayer asks for protection for their service.

For today: pray for those who serve God in your church, such as pastors, teachers, and volunteers. Ask God to bless their labor and to sustain them against opposition. And offer your own work to the Lord, trusting that he receives it with favor.
exp.29:0:
This verse begins a promise. Moses says that the people of Israel will experience the blessings and the curses that God has set before them. If they end up far from their land, scattered among other nations, they will take these things to heart, meaning they will reflect honestly and remember God.

Moses speaks to the people in his final addresses, before they enter the promised land. He had already warned them that obedience would bring blessing and disobedience would bring consequences. Here he shows them that, even after failure, there is hope of restoration, as the next verse continues.

For today: when you make a mistake or feel far from God, do not stay in guilt or distraction. Stop, reflect with honesty, and return to Him, because God still welcomes whoever comes back.
exp.27:55:
This verse describes a woman who lived with such luxury and delicacy that she had never set her bare feet on the ground. The phrase "her eye shall be evil" refers to a selfish and hard gaze: she will not want to share anything, neither with her husband nor with her children. The husband she held close with affection is the one she embraced with tenderness.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them of the consequences of abandoning the covenant with God. One of them would be a siege so terrible that hunger would lead to dreadful acts. It is a warning, not a promise of what God desires for them.

For today: disobedience to God and hardness of heart come at a very great cost. Today we can choose to trust God and care for those near us, sharing what we have instead of clinging to what is ours.
exp.26:25:
It says that whoever does not uphold or put into practice the words of this law falls under a curse. The word translated "confirmeth" here means to affirm and stand behind something with one's own life; the word "cursed" means that such a person falls under God's disapproval and its consequences. All the people respond "Amen," which means "so be it," accepting the commitment.

Moses speaks to Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He orders a ceremony in which the Levites proclaim twelve curses, and the people respond to each one. This is the last and sums up all of them: it is not enough to know the law, it must be obeyed. Paul quotes this verse in Galatians 3:10 to show that no one keeps the law perfectly, and that is why we need Christ.

For today: do not be content with just listening to the Bible; choose one teaching and put it into practice this week. And when you fail, remember that Christ bore that curse for us.
exp.33:7:
It says that the people of Israel mourned the death of Moses for thirty days, on the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan. The word for "wept" means to cry out in grief, and "days of weeping and mourning" refers to the time of grieving. When those thirty days were over, the period of sorrow was considered complete.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who tells of the end of Moses' life. He had led the people for forty years in the wilderness. Now Israel is about to enter the promised land, and the account shows that they first paused to honor their leader. Then Joshua takes command, as the following verses say.

For today: grief is healthy and needs time. God does not ask us to hide our pain, but to live through it with honesty and hope. Then, like Israel, we can move forward with confidence that God is still guiding us.
exp.8:9:
This verse says that God gave Moses two tablets of stone. They were written "with the finger of God," a way of saying that the work came directly from Him. On them were all the words that God had spoken to the people from the mountain, out of the midst of the fire, in the day of the assembly. "Gave" is the word for "delivered" in this verse, and "assembly" refers to the time when the people gathered before the mountain.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them how they rebelled at Horeb, that is, Sinai. While he was receiving the law on the mountain, they were about to make a golden calf. Moses wants them to see that God was faithful, even though they failed.

God gave us His Word with clarity and care. Today we can read it not as a burden, but as a sign of His nearness, and respond with humble and grateful obedience.
exp.20:19:
This verse records what the parents were to say before the elders: that their son is "stubborn" (set in his ways, unwilling to yield) and "rebellious," that he does not heed their voice, and that he is a "glutton and a drunkard," meaning he gives himself over to excess without control.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law brought the case before the elders at the city gate, and it did not leave the parents to decide alone. It concerns persistent rebellion, even after being corrected. Scholars debate how often it was applied; later Jewish tradition set such strict conditions that it was almost never carried out.

For today: obedience and self-control matter. If you are a son or daughter, receive correction with humility. If you are a parent, correct with patience and love, seeking wise help when you need it.
exp.28:15:
Moses reminds the Israelites of something they lived through themselves: they dwelt in Egypt and then passed through the territories of other peoples on the way. When he says "ye know," he asks them to draw on their own memory. The word "nations" here refers to foreign peoples.

Moses speaks to the people on the plains of Moab, before they enter the promised land. He is renewing the covenant with God. He reminds them of what they have seen, because in the verses that follow he warns them about the idols of those peoples and the danger that someone might turn away from God.

For today: remembering what we have lived through and what God has done helps us stand firm. If we live alongside customs that draw us away from God, it is wise to examine our hearts honestly and remain faithful to him.
exp.14:0:
Verse 1 says that every seven years the people of Israel were to make a release, that is, to forgive or cancel debts. The word "release" means letting someone go free from what they owe.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land and repeats the law God had given them. This year of release protected the poor so that a debt would not bind them for life. It applied to fellow Israelites; a foreigner could be charged interest. Scholars debate whether the debt was canceled completely or whether only the collection of it was suspended during that year. The text says that the proclamation is made in the name of the LORD, that is, announced on behalf of God.

Today we can practice the same generosity: if someone in need cannot repay you, consider forgiving the debt or giving them more time, remembering that God has treated us with great mercy.
exp.6:16:
It says that the people of Israel, looking at the nations of Canaan, might secretly think: "They are more numerous than we are; how are we going to drive them out?" The word "dispossess" means to tear out by the roots, to remove completely from a place. "Nations" here means peoples or nations.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they enter the promised land. He knows the fear they will feel before enemies who are stronger in number. So he names that fear honestly and immediately invites them to remember how God rescued them from Egypt with power.

Today, when a problem seems bigger than your strength, do not hide it in your heart. Bring it to God with sincerity and recall the times He helped you before. Remembering His past faithfulness strengthens confidence to face what lies ahead.
exp.4:26:
Here the people ask Moses to come near to God, listen to everything He says, and then tell it to them. They promise: "we will hear it, and do it," that is, we will listen and obey. The phrase rendered here as "Go thou near" in the verse above is the same request, so no further explanation is needed.

Moses is reminding the people of what happened at Mount Sinai (Horeb). The Israelites had heard God's voice in the midst of the fire and were very afraid. That is why they asked Moses to be their go-between. God approved what they said, though He wished that their hearts would truly be marked by reverence and constant obedience.

For today: promising to obey is easy; the hard part is keeping that promise every day. Before making a decision, you might read a passage of the Bible and ask God for a heart willing to put into practice what you are learning.
exp.21:5:
If someone comes across a bird's nest along the way, in a tree or on the ground, with young birds or eggs and the mother sitting on them, they must not take the mother together with her young. According to the next verse, the person could let the mother go and take the young birds.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and explains how to live according to God's law. This rule appears among commands about helping one's neighbor and protecting life. It shows that God also cares for animals, and that what creation provides should be used without abuse. The text promises well-being and a long life to those who obey; some see in it a call to compassion and to thinking about the future.

For today: make use of what God gives you with respect and moderation, without abusing it or destroying its source. Take care of what sustains you, whether it is your work, nature, or your relationships.
exp.2:1:
It says that God spoke to Moses when Og, king of Bashan, came out to fight against Israel. God told him not to be afraid, because he had already placed the king, his people, and his land into his hand. He reminded him that he would do to Og what he had done to Sihon, the king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon. "Said unto me" means "told me," and "delivered" means that God was already giving them the victory.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life, in the book of Deuteronomy. He reviews what they experienced in the wilderness so that they will trust God before entering the promised land. By recalling the victory over Sihon, he encourages Israel to believe that God will remain faithful. This story also shows how God acted during that time and place with his people.

For today: when you face a great fear, remember how God has helped you before. That memory strengthens your confidence to take the next step.
exp.28:25:
This verse describes what the people did: they went after the gods of other nations, served them, and bowed down before them. They were gods they did not know, and they had never given the people anything. "Foreign" means strange, belonging to other peoples. "Bowed down" means they prostrated themselves to worship them.

Moses speaks to Israel at the end of his life, when he renews the covenant with God before they enter the promised land. He warns them what would happen if they abandon it. The neighboring nations would see the land ruined and ask why. The answer would be this: they left the covenant with the God who brought them out of Egypt.

For today: ask yourself what things are taking the place of God in your heart, such as money, fame, or fear. None of them has given you what God has already given you. Give thanks to Him again and trust in Him.
exp.31:46:
It says that God's law is not an empty or worthless thing. It is the very life of the people. Obeying it would help them live many years in the land they were going to enter by crossing the Jordan. The word "vain" here means empty or of no importance, and the phrase "prolong your days" means to live a long time.

Moses is speaking at the end of his last address to Israel. He is about to die and will not enter the promised land. He wants the people to take God's words seriously and to teach them to their children. Afterward, God tells him that he will go up Mount Nebo to see the land from a distance.

For today: let us not treat the Word of God as a decoration or a boring duty. Set aside a moment each day to read it, ask God to guide you, and look for one specific thing to put into practice. In this way it becomes a path of life, not just information.
exp.27:31:
It says that the sons and daughters of the people will be handed over to another nation. Their parents will see it with their own eyes, and their strength will drain away from longing for them, looking and waiting all day long. "Fail" here means they will grow weak or be worn down by sorrow. "There shall be no might in thine hand" means they will be unable to do anything to prevent it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He is explaining the blessings of obeying God and the curses of abandoning him. This verse is part of a warning: if they break the covenant, they will lose what they love most, even their family and their freedom.

For today: value your family and tend your relationship with God while you still have time. Invest in your children through prayer, presence, and a good example, and trust that God is merciful when a person returns to him.
exp.5:14:
It says that the Lord, the jealous God, lives among his people. For that reason it warns that his anger should not be kindled against them, because he could destroy them from the earth. The phrase about the face of the earth refers to the surface of the earth. "Jealous" here means that God wants to be the only one his people love and worship, as in a covenant of faithfulness.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them not to follow the gods of the neighboring nations. Their closeness to God is a blessing, but also a serious responsibility, because God takes his covenant with them seriously.

For today: examine what things compete with God for first place in your heart, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Today, bring one of them before God in prayer and decide to give God his rightful place.
exp.31:48:
God tells Moses to go up to Mount Nebo, in the Abarim range, in the land of Moab, facing the city of Jericho. From there he will be able to look out over the land of Canaan, which God gives to the people of Israel as an inheritance. An inheritance is something received as a gift, not earned by one's own merit.

The Lord speaks on the same day that Moses finished teaching his song to the people. After forty years in the wilderness, Israel is about to cross the Jordan. God allows Moses to see the land, but not to enter it, because at Kadesh he did not honor God before the people, as the following verses explain.

For today: God keeps his promises even when we do not see the full result. We can serve him faithfully, trust that his work continues, and learn to take seriously the call to honor him at all times.
exp.20:12:
She was to take off the clothes she wore when she was captured, and live in the Israelite's house. There she would have one full month to mourn her father and mother. After that month, the man could marry her.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law regulated war in a very harsh world, where captive women were highly exposed to abuse. It required waiting, acknowledging her grief, and giving her a protected status. Interpreters debate how much this limited the customs of its time, but the text shows an intention to curb abuse.

For today: do not act on impulse toward someone who has less power than you. Give them time, respect, and space for their grief. God cares about the vulnerable, and we too should do the same.
exp.27:39:
It says the people will have olive trees throughout all their land, but they will not be able to use the oil to anoint themselves, because the olives will fall before their time. "Territory" means land or region. "Anoint" means to rub oil on oneself, something common for caring for the body and for celebrating. Having the trees and not enjoying the fruit.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the Promised Land. He presents blessings if they obey God and curses if they turn away from him. This verse is among the consequences of disobedience: labor without fruit, as happens with the sowing and the vineyard that surround it.

Today it reminds us that having things does not guarantee enjoying them. We can examine whether we live thankful to God and in obedience to him, trusting that the true blessing comes from his hand, not only from our effort.
exp.26:8:
Moses and the Levitical priests speak together to all the people. They ask them to pay close attention and listen carefully. They tell them that "this day" Israel has become the people of the LORD. The verse of "Take heed" is to pay careful attention, and the phrase "become the people" means that they are now confirmed as God's people.

Moses is taking leave and preparing the new generation to enter the promised land. Earlier, they had been commanded to write the law on stones and to celebrate with peace offerings. Here they pause to remind them who they are. The call to obey will come afterward. Some think that "this day" renews the covenant made at Sinai; the text does not explain this in more detail.

For today: before thinking about what God commands us, let us remember to whom we belong. Our obedience comes from a relationship with God, not from fear. Today you can stop, listen carefully to his Word, and respond with gratitude.
exp.31:1:
He says that Moses' teaching will fall gently, like the rain and dew that refresh the field. "Doctrine" means teaching; "speech" is his word or discourse; "tender herb" is young grass; "distil" is to fall drop by drop; "small rain" is a fine rain.

Moses speaks almost at the end of his life, in the song he gives to Israel before they enter the promised land. He calls the heavens and the earth as witnesses. He wants the people to remember who God is and not turn away from Him, since the song also warns about their future unfaithfulness.

For today: receive the Word of God like gentle rain, without hurry. Set aside a few quiet minutes to read a passage, and let it slowly nourish your heart and bear fruit over time.
exp.25:17:
This verse says that God chose Israel that day to be his special people, just as he had promised. That choosing had a purpose: that the people would obey all his commandments.

Moses speaks to the people at the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant: Israel declares that the Lord is their God, and God declares that Israel is his people. It is like a mutual commitment, and obedience was the response to his love and his care.

For today: God values us and calls us his own, and that gives us identity and security. We can respond with sincere obedience, not out of fear, but out of gratitude. Today you can choose one concrete action that honors God.
exp.17:11:
This verse says that God regards as detestable anyone who practices the things mentioned before: sacrificing children in the fire, divining, interpreting omens, casting lots, using charms, calling up spirits, or consulting the dead. "Abomination" means something repugnant to God. "Drove them out from before you" means that God drove out the nations of Canaan because of these practices.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them not to imitate the peoples they are going to displace. God wants a people who trust in him and not in hidden powers. The text says that these nations were driven out in part because of these practices.

Today, when you are afraid or uncertain about the future, instead of looking for horoscopes or hidden spiritual advice, bring your worry to God in prayer and seek guidance in his Word and from wise people of faith.
exp.30:26:
Moses tells the people that he knows well their rebellion and their "stiff neck," an expression that describes someone stubborn, who will not bend the neck or obey. He reminds them that even while he was still alive and present with them, they were already rebelling against God. So how much more would they do so when he was dead?

Moses speaks at the end of his life, about to say farewell to Israel. He has just asked that the book of the law be kept beside the ark, as a witness. He knows the history of the people in the wilderness and speaks to them frankly, not out of contempt, but to warn them and to make them take the law seriously.

For today: it is not enough to depend on leaders or on good spiritual moments. Ask God for a humble heart willing to obey him, reading his Word honestly, even when no one is watching you.
exp.11:1:
It says that the people of Israel were to completely destroy all the places where the nations of Canaan worshiped their gods: on the high mountains, on the hills, and under every green tree.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they enter the promised land. He gives them the rules for living there. He wants them to worship only the LORD and not to mix in with the practices of the neighboring peoples. High places and leafy trees were common sites of pagan worship.

For today: this is not about destroying other people's things, but about examining our own hearts. We can ask ourselves what habits, influences, or "places" pull us away from God, and decide with courage to remove them from our lives so that we give Him first place.
exp.3:24:
It says that when the people have lived a long time in the land, with children and grandchildren, and have settled in, there is a risk that they will corrupt themselves. "Beget children" means having children; "remained long in the land" means living there for a long time. "Graven image" refers to idols made by hand. "Provoke him to anger" means stirring up his displeasure through that kind of conduct.

Moses speaks to Israel before they cross the Jordan. He warns them that God is faithful to his covenant, but also that he is a consuming fire and jealous, meaning he does not share the exclusive love of his people. After several generations, the danger would be forgetting what God has done.

For today: comfort and the passing of time can cool our faith. It is wise to remember often what God has done and not to put anything, whether money or success, in his place.
exp.3:33:
This verse asks whether any god has ever tried to take a nation out from the midst of another nation, as the Lord did with Israel in Egypt. The verse of the source's word "probado," "tried or tested," is not needed in the reader's English, since the verse already gives "assayed" and the reader can see that word directly. Signs are actions that show his power; wonders are events that cause great awe; the "mighty hand and stretched out arm" speaks of God's power in action.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, now close to the promised land. He reminds them of what God alone did: he freed them from Egypt and spoke to them out of the fire. He wants them, with that memory, to recognize him as the only God and to obey him with gratitude.

For today: when you doubt or feel forgotten, remember what God has already done in your life and in his history with his people. Write down three things in which you have seen his help, and thank him for them.
exp.25:11:
It says that when an Israelite had finished setting aside the tithe of his harvest in the third year, called "the year of tithing," he was to give it to the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow. To "tithe" means to give the tenth part. "Gates" refers to the towns or cities. They would eat within their towns until they were satisfied.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The Levites received no inheritance of land, and strangers, orphans, and widows often lacked provision. This tithe every three years ensured their food. Then the Israelite declared before God that he had obeyed.

For today: God joins generosity with care for the vulnerable. We can set aside a fixed part of what we earn to help, with a name and a face, a person in need near us, and do it with gratitude, not out of obligation.
exp.13:3:
This verse opens the list of animals that the people of Israel were allowed to eat. It names three domestic animals that were common in their daily life: the ox (the bull or cattle), the sheep, and the goat. These were animals they raised in their fields and also offered in sacrifice.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God chose them as a holy people, set apart for him. For that reason, even what they ate was meant to show that they belonged to God. Scholars explain the reasons for these laws in various ways, and the Bible does not give all the details.

For today: God is interested in our whole life, even the everyday. We can ask ourselves whether our daily decisions, such as what we do and what we consume, reflect that we belong to him and give thanks to him.
exp.27:27:
This verse says that God would strike the people with "madness," meaning a loss of sound judgment; with "blindness," which can be physical blindness or a lack of clarity in seeing the way ahead; and with "astonishment of heart," a phrase that speaks of dread, confusion, or a heart paralyzed by fear.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings if they keep the covenant and curses if they abandon it. These words are a serious warning, not a desire for punishment, so that Israel will faithfully choose God.

For today: turning away from God brings confusion and inner fear. We can seek his guidance every day, ask him for wisdom and peace, and trust that Christ offers us forgiveness and a renewed heart.
exp.2:25:
Here Moses tells how God was angry with him "for your sakes", that is, because of the people, and for that reason did not allow him to enter the promised land. The phrase "let it suffice thee" means "enough is enough, that is enough". God tells him not to keep pressing that matter.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, near the Jordan, at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them that he begged God to be allowed to cross over. According to Numbers 20, Moses acted in disobedience at Meribah. Here he also connects this with the people. Even so, God lets him see the land from the top of Pisgah and charges him to encourage Joshua.

For today: sometimes God says "no" to a sincere request. We can pray with confidence, accept his answer with humility, and keep serving where he places us, preparing others for what is to come.
exp.17:5:
It says that if a Levite lives as a stranger in any town of Israel, and desires with all his heart to go to the place of worship that God chooses, he may do so. "Living as a stranger" means he lived there as an outsider, without an inheritance of his own. "With all the desire of his soul" means with sincere and deep longing.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The Levites did not receive territory, so they lived scattered among the tribes and depended on the offerings. Here, anyone who longs to serve God is protected: he must not be kept from doing so. The verses that follow say he would serve and receive a share equal to the other Levites.

For today: God values the sincere desire to serve him. If someone longs for that service, let us give them room and support, and if that longing is in you, do not put it out.
exp.31:32:
Deuteronomy 32:33 says that the "wine" of God's enemies, meaning what they produce and what fills them, is like the poison of snakes. The words the verse uses for such creatures are large or venomous serpents and vipers, and the poison is the venom of asps. The picture is of something that looks appealing but kills.

This is part of the Song of Moses, which Moses teaches to Israel before he dies. God himself, through Moses, warns that nations without God, and also a people who turn away from him, bear bitter and destructive fruit. Interpreters debate whether "they" refers only to hostile nations or also to an unfaithful Israel. The context that follows speaks of God's justice and judgment.

Today we can ask what "wine" we are drinking: ideas, habits, or pleasures that seem good but harm the soul. It is wise to examine the fruit and return to the Rock, who is God.
exp.14:4:
It says that the abundant blessing promised in the verses before depends on a condition: faithfully listening to the voice of God and putting all his commandments into practice.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains the law of the year of release, when debts between Israelite brothers were forgiven. The goal was that there would be no poor among them. This verse makes clear that the blessing and the mutual care go hand in hand with obedience to God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our obedience includes how we treat those who are in need. Listening to God is not only believing or feeling, but acting with generosity. This week, think of someone in need near you and help them in a concrete way.
exp.26:4:
This verse says that the people were to build an altar to God on Mount Ebal, using stones just as they were found, without carving them. The word "iron" refers to metal tools, such as chisels or picks; the verse says "any iron tool," so the term here means the same thing. The phrase "and there shalt thou build an altar unto the Lord thy God" means "there you shall build an altar for the Lord."

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they cross the Jordan into the promised land. He gives them instructions to renew their covenant with God as soon as they arrive. The altar would be a place of offerings and gratitude. As to why iron was not to be used, the text does not fully explain it; many think the aim was simplicity, and that the altar should not be the product of human ingenuity.

For today: draw near to God with simplicity and sincerity. You do not need to impress him with ornaments or human effort; he looks for a grateful and obedient heart.
exp.33:1:
This verse continues the list of what God showed Moses from the mountain. It names the territory of Naphtali, the lands of Ephraim and Manasseh, and all the land of Judah. "The utmost sea" is the Mediterranean Sea, the western boundary of the land. In this way, Moses sees the promised land from north to west.

The narrator tells of Moses' final moments. God himself shows him the land from Mount Nebo, before his death. Israel is about to enter Canaan, but Moses will not enter, as God had told him. The book is traditionally attributed to Moses, although this final chapter is told by another voice; scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: God keeps his promises, even though we do not always see them fulfilled in our lifetime. We can trust Him and work in faith, knowing that others will receive what God began with us.
exp.3:9:
This verse recalls the day the people stood before God at Horeb, another name for Mount Sinai. The Lord said to Moses, "Gather me the people together," so that they could hear his words. The purpose was twofold: that they would learn to fear God, that is, to respect and honor him with reverence, all the days of their lives, and that they would teach those words to their children.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, before they enter the promised land. Many of them were children or had not yet been born at Horeb. He reminds them of that encounter so that they do not forget what God said and what God did.

For today: faith is passed on from one generation to another. Set aside regular time, even if brief, to read the Bible with your children, nephews, nieces, or younger people, and tell them how God has worked in your life.
exp.6:21:
It says that God would drive the peoples of Canaan out of the land gradually, "little and little," and not all at once. The verse uses "put out" to mean drive out. "Consume" means to destroy completely. The reason is that if the land were suddenly left empty, the wild beasts would multiply and become a danger to Israel.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God would fight for them and asks them not to be afraid. The slow pace had a practical purpose: caring for Israel while it took possession of the territory. Scholars understand in different ways how this was fulfilled, but the text emphasizes that God guides the pace.

Today we can learn to trust God when things move slowly. If you do not see quick changes, it may be that God is caring for you and preparing you to sustain what He will give you.
exp.27:54:
It says that during an enemy siege the hunger will be so terrible that a man will eat his own children, and he will not want to share that flesh with anyone, because nothing else will be left to him.

The word "siege" (the verse's "siege" in the King James wording) means the enemy surrounding the city. "Distress" is extreme anguish.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings for obeying God and curses for abandoning him. This scene is a very harsh warning about the consequences of rejecting their covenant. Later, the Bible records similar famines during sieges (2 Kings 6:28-29; Lamentations 4:10).

For today: let us take seriously our faithfulness to God, because turning away from Him brings deep harm. But let us also remember that He warns us out of love, and always invites us to return to Him.
exp.22:0:
This verse says that a man whose genitals were damaged by a blow or a cut, or who was deliberately castrated, could not be admitted into the "congregation of the Lord," that is, the official assembly of the people of Israel. The phrase "wounded in the stones" refers to someone whose testicles were crushed or injured.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, reviewing the laws of the covenant. Many believe this rule was meant to keep Israel separate from pagan practices, where mutilation was associated with the worship of gods. The text does not give all the reasons, so there are different interpretations.

For today: Isaiah 56:3-5 promises a place and a name in God's house to the eunuchs who remain faithful to him. In Christ, no one is left outside because of their body or their history; we can welcome everyone with kindness.
exp.31:43:
This verse says that Moses went and recited the whole song before the people, and that Joshua, son of Nun, was with him. The phrase "in the ears of the people" means that the people heard it directly. In this Bible, "Joshua" is the same leader who would later guide Israel.

The narrator of the book describes how Moses, near the end of his life, gives Israel a song that God had given him. This song recalls God's faithfulness and warns about the consequences of forgetting him. Joshua appears at his side because he would soon take up leadership. Afterward, Moses asks the people to keep these words and teach them to their children.

For today: God's truths are passed on when someone speaks them aloud and others listen carefully. Look for a moment this week to share with your family or friends a promise or teaching from the Bible that has strengthened you.
exp.18:20:
This verse says that the judge must not feel pity or show favoritism when passing sentence. "Your eye shall not pity" means "you shall not have compassion." The phrase "eye for eye" establishes that the punishment must match the harm caused, no more and no less.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. The passage deals with the false witness who accuses an innocent person. If the judges discovered this, the punishment was the one the accused would have suffered. It was a rule for the courts, not a license for personal revenge. Its purpose was to restrain evil and protect justice in the community.

Today we can learn that justice requires truth and honesty. Before speaking badly of someone, let us consider the harm that a false word can cause. Jesus, moreover, calls us not to take revenge and to respond with mercy in our personal relationships (Matthew 5:38-39).
exp.25:7:
He says that God brought Israel out of Egypt with a "strong hand" and an "outstretched arm," that is, with visible power. The "great terror" refers to events that caused fear and amazement, such as the plagues. The "signs and wonders" were extraordinary acts that showed God was acting on behalf of his people.

Here the Israelite speaks as he comes to the sanctuary to present the firstfruits, the first produce of his harvest. Moses teaches him to recite the story of salvation: the oppression, the cry for help, and how God heard. In this way the offering is not merely a formality but a grateful response to what God has done.

For today: remember the times God helped you in difficult moments. Before asking for something new, thank him with concrete words and with a generous offering, acknowledging that what you have comes from his hand.
exp.33:8:
It says that Joshua, son of Nun, was full of the spirit of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands on him. For this reason the people of Israel obeyed him and did what God had commanded Moses.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who recounts what happened after Moses' death. Tradition attributes the book to Moses, but this ending is usually understood as added by another hand; scholars explain this in different ways. The people were in mourning and about to enter the promised land, so they needed a new leader. Laying on of hands was a gesture of blessing and of handing over authority (see Numbers 27:18-23).

Today we can learn that God takes care of his people through times of transition and change. If he calls you to serve, ask him for wisdom and do not rely only on your own strength. And if someone else receives a responsibility, support them with respect and prayer.
exp.17:2:
This verse says that when someone from the people offered an ox or a sheep, they were to give the priest three parts of the animal: the shoulder (the foreleg), the two cheeks (the jaws), and the maw (the animal's fourth stomach). That was the portion due to the priest by right.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The Levites would not receive land like the other tribes, so God sustained them through the offerings of the people. Their inheritance was to serve the LORD. Scholars explain the details of these parts in different ways, but the central idea is clear: a fair provision for those who served.

Today we can support with generosity and gratitude those who dedicate their lives to teaching and caring for others spiritually, and also remember that God himself is our greatest inheritance.
exp.4:0:
Moses gathers all the people of Israel and asks them to listen carefully. He is going to repeat God's laws and commands to them. "Statutes and judgments" are the commands and fair decisions that God gave. "Putting them into practice" means doing them, not just hearing them. The call is to learn them, keep them, and obey them.

Moses speaks at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, before Israel enters the promised land. Many of the listeners had been young or children when God spoke at Horeb (Mount Sinai). That is why Moses reminds them of the law and shows them that the covenant is theirs too, today.

For today: it is not enough to hear God's Word in church or read it at home. We can choose one teaching from the Bible this week, review it, and ask God for help to live it out in one concrete action.
exp.28:16:
Moses reminds the Israelites of what they saw in Egypt and along the way. There they encountered the "abominations," that is, things detestable to God, along with idols made of wood, stone, silver, and gold. The phrase "which were among them" speaks of peoples who kept those gods as their own.

Moses speaks to the people on the plains of Moab, when he renews the covenant with God, and he also includes future generations. He reminds them of what they saw in order to warn them: what is seen up close can attract. Right after this, he asks them to take care that no one turns away from God and becomes a bitter root that contaminates everyone.

Today's idols are not always statues; they can be money, success, or anything that takes the place of God. Ask yourself honestly which things attract you more than He does, and ask Him for help so that they do not take root in your heart.
exp.13:14:
It says that the people of Israel were not to eat certain birds: the owl, the screech owl, the cuckoo, and the hawk, along with all the birds like each of these, "after their kind." The exact names of these birds are hard to pin down. Scholars do not always agree on which animal each Hebrew word refers to, and that is why translations vary.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He repeats the laws that God gave them so they could live as his people. The list of clean and unclean animals set them apart from other nations. Many think these were birds of prey or birds that were active at night, but not everyone explains it the same way.

For today: God cares about the details of the daily life of his people. We can ask ourselves whether we also give him the ordinary things, such as what we eat, see, and do, so that we live in a way that shows we belong to him.
exp.11:11:
This verse commands the whole people to rejoice before God at the place of worship. It includes the fathers, the sons, the male servants and the female servants. It also includes the Levite who lives within their gates. The word "gates" here refers to the towns and cities where they live, and an inheritance is a portion of land given as a family's share. The Levites received no land, so they depended on the generosity of the people.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that, once they settle there, they must bring their offerings to the place God chooses, and not to just any place. Worship was to be orderly, but it was also meant to be joyful and shared with everyone.

For today: when we worship or give thanks to God, we should not do it alone. Let us invite the family, the workers, and those who do not have much, so that they too may rejoice with us.
exp.21:7:
This verse commands that when a new house is built, a low wall or railing (a parapet) be placed around the flat roof, the terrace of the house. The reason is to prevent someone from falling and dying, and so that the house does not carry guilt for a death that could have been prevented.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. In those times houses usually had flat roofs, and people used them to rest, work, and gather. The laws near this one deal with caring for life and with order in everyday living. This law shows that God values life and expects responsibility.

For today: think of a risk you could prevent in your home, your work, or your church, such as a loose stair, damaged electrical wiring, or a place without protection for children. Fix it in time. Caring for the safety of others is also a way of loving your neighbor.
exp.24:8:
The text says that if a man refuses to marry his brother's widow, she will come before the elders of the town. She will take off his sandal from his foot, spit in his face, and declare that this is what is done to the man who will not build up his brother's house.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel and explains the law of levirate marriage. If a brother died without children, the other brother was to marry the widow so that the name and inheritance of the deceased would not be lost. If the brother-in-law refused, this public act shamed him and protected the widow. Scholars understand the gesture as a sign of giving up a family right or duty.

Today we do not practice this rite, but we learn that God cares for the vulnerable, such as widows. We can ask ourselves whom we should care for and not abandon: taking on our family and community obligations with responsibility and compassion.
exp.0:39:
Here the text says God tells the people of Israel to turn around and set out toward the wilderness, by the way that leads to the Red Sea.

Moses speaks to the people and reminds them of what God told them years earlier. Because they did not trust Him, that generation did not enter the promised land. After hearing this, they said they would go up to fight, but God warned them not to, because He would not go with them. Their repentance came too late, and they wanted to obey in their own way.

For today: obeying God means doing it in His timing and in His direction, not only when it suits us. If we have gone wrong, let us ask forgiveness and listen humbly to what He shows us now, instead of making plans on our own.
exp.31:29:
This verse asks how it is possible for one enemy to chase away a thousand Israelites, and two to put ten thousand to flight. The answer is that their Rock, that is, God, had handed them over and given them up to the enemy. The word "sold" here means left in the hands of the enemy. The word "end" refers to what awaits them afterward.

Moses speaks in his song near the end of his life, before Israel enters the promised land. He warns that if they turn away from God and follow their own foolishness, their defeats will not be bad luck but the consequence of having lost his protection. Some think that "their Rock" here refers to the God of Israel, and the contrast with "their rock" in verse 31 speaks of the gods of the nations.

For today: when you face failures or struggles, examine your heart with humility and ask whether you have turned away from God. He corrects those he loves, and he is always ready to restore whoever returns to him.
exp.3:15:
This verse warns the people not to ruin themselves by making a carved image of any figure, whether of a man or of a woman. "Lest ye corrupt yourselves" means "so that you do not bring destruction upon yourselves." An "image" is a statue or likeness of someone. A "male" is a man, and a "female" is a woman.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that when God spoke at Mount Horeb, they heard his voice from the midst of the fire, but they saw no form. For this reason they must not invent an image to represent God.

Today we might ask whether we are reducing God to what is comfortable or familiar to us. A practical application is to know him through what he said about himself in the Bible, and not through our own ideas, customs, or mental images. In this way we worship him as he really is.
exp.28:17:
This verse is a warning. Moses says that there might be among the people a man, a woman, a family, or a tribe whose heart turns away today from the Lord our God, to go and serve the gods of other nations. He compares that sin to a root that produces poison and wormwood, a plant with a very bitter taste.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in Moab, when he renews the covenant with God before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the idols they saw in Egypt and along the way. He wants no one to believe that they can be unfaithful in secret and still remain at peace.

For today: a small turning away of the heart, if we let it grow, can make a whole community bitter. It is wise to examine honestly which things compete with God in our hearts and to ask him for help in time, before they take root.
exp.17:8:
It says that when the people of Israel enter the land God is giving them, they must not learn to imitate the detestable practices of the nations who lived there. "Abominations" are customs that God hates. "Shalt learn to do" means copying or adopting those customs.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they enter Canaan. He has just spoken about the Levites, who served God and lived from the offerings. Now he warns against magic, divination and contact with the dead, and reminds them that God himself would guide them, especially through his prophets.

Today we can ask ourselves where we look for direction and security. It is easy to copy the customs around us without thinking. This verse invites us to trust God, to seek his Word and to pray, instead of turning to horoscopes, spiritualists or superstitions.
exp.20:13:
If a man of Israel no longer takes pleasure in the captive woman he married, he must let her go free. He may not sell her or profit from her. "Trade with her" means doing business with her or treating her as merchandise; "humbled her" refers to taking her as his wife in a way that leaves her without rights.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law regulates a situation of war in ancient times and sets limits on what a man could do. The woman was not property; she had the right to mourn, and if she was rejected, the right to her freedom. Some see here a protection for her; others stress how harsh the context was.

For today: God cares for those who have less power. We should treat vulnerable people with dignity and never take advantage of them.
exp.24:0:
This verse describes a legal situation: two people have a dispute and bring it before the judges. The judges must declare innocent the one who is in the right and guilty the one who acted wrongly. A "dispute" here means a disagreement or a legal case. Something "unjust" means unfair or wicked. To "acquit" means to declare someone free of blame.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions for living with order and justice. This verse opens a law about punishments, which continues in the verses that follow: even the guilty person was to be treated with limits and with respect for their dignity.

For today: when there is a conflict, let us seek the truth honestly, without favoritism. And if someone turns out to be guilty, let us correct them without humiliating or exaggerating, remembering that they are still a person of value.
exp.0:37:
Deuteronomy 1:38 says that Joshua, son of Nun, who now stands before Moses, will be the one who enters the promised land. Moses receives the command to encourage him, that is, to give him courage and strength, because Joshua will be the one who gives the land to Israel as an inheritance. "Inherit" here means to give the land as a possession.

Moses speaks to the people, recalling what happened when Israel did not trust God and refused to enter the land. Because of that failure, that generation would not enter, except Caleb. Moses also tells how God said to him that he too would not enter. Then God points to Joshua as the next leader.

For today: God continues to care for his work even when leaders change. We can encourage those who serve, with a kind word or a prayer, instead of criticizing them.
exp.31:8:
This verse says that the people of Israel are the portion that belongs to God. The word "portion" means what falls to God as his own. "Measuring line" refers to the cord used to measure out a piece of land, and "inheritance" is property received as a family's heritage. In other words, Jacob, that is Israel, is the land that God measured out and chose for himself.

Moses speaks in a song meant to teach the people before his death. He wants them to remember how God cared for them from the beginning, so that they would not turn away from him. The verses that follow show that care: God found them in the wilderness and guarded them as the apple of his eye.

For today: if God considers us his own, our worth does not depend on what we accomplish. When you feel alone or unimportant, remember that God cares for you with love and sustains you as the eagle carries its young.
exp.9:12:
Moses tells the people to keep the commandments and laws of God, which he is giving them that day. Here "statutes" means rules or instructions, and the phrase "for thy good" means that it may go well with you. Obedience is not presented as a burden, but as a path to well-being.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God is not asking them for something impossible: he asks for reverence, love, and sincere service. He says this in the context of God's grace, who chose them even though the whole world belongs to him.

For today: remember that God's instructions come from his love and his desire to care for you. Choose one teaching from the Bible that you know you should practice today, and obey it with gratitude, not out of fear, trusting that God seeks your good.
exp.3:17:
This verse continues a list of things Israel was not to make as an image for worship. Here it names two more: animals that crawl on the ground, such as reptiles and insects, and fish that live in the waters. The phrase "under the earth" refers to the waters, seas and rivers.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that at Horeb they heard the voice of God but saw no form. For this reason he warns them not to corrupt themselves by making idols, as other peoples did.

For today: God cannot be contained in anything we make. Examine whether something created, such as money, success or a person, has taken the place that belongs only to God, and return to worshiping Him.
exp.0:35:
God makes an exception: Caleb, son of Jephunneh, will indeed see the promised land. God will give him the land he has walked on, and also to his children. The reason is that Caleb wholly followed the Lord, that is, he followed God completely, with faithfulness and without turning back.

Moses speaks to the people and recalls what happened at Kadesh-barnea. The spies explored Canaan, and the people were filled with fear and did not trust God. For that reason that generation died in the wilderness. Caleb, together with Joshua, had encouraged the people to trust God.

For today: faithfulness to God does not go unnoticed by Him. When everyone around you gives in to fear or doubt, you can keep trusting and obeying, not being perfect, but with a wholehearted heart. God knows how to honor that constancy, even though sometimes it may take a while to be seen.
exp.16:17:
This verse says that when the king of Israel begins to rule, he must copy God's law by his own hand into a book. The copy was to be made from the original kept by the Levitical priests, who were in charge of guarding the law.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions in case they someday ask for a king. Earlier he had warned against accumulating horses, wives, and riches, things that could make a ruler proud or unfaithful. Copying the law was a way of reminding the king that he too was under God's authority.

For today: whoever has some authority, at home, at work, or in the church, needs to let God's Word correct him first. You could copy out one Bible passage by hand each week and meditate on it slowly.
exp.4:6:
This is the first commandment. "Other gods" are foreign gods, different from the true God. "Before me" can be understood as "in my presence" or "above me." In either case, God asks to be the only one we worship and serve.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, who are about to enter the promised land. He reminds them of what God said at Mount Sinai. Before giving the command, God presents himself as the one who freed them from slavery in Egypt. His demand arises from what he has already done for them, and from a covenant relationship with them.

Today we can ask ourselves what holds first place in our hearts: money, success, a person, or our comfort. This week, put God first with a daily moment of prayer, and bring him your decisions and worries.
exp.12:10:
The passage says the punishment was to be public, so that the whole people would hear, feel fear, and never again commit a wickedness like that. Old words: the verse's first archaic word, which here means "turn back," is rendered as "turn back," and the small preposition is simply "to." The phrase about "evil thing" refers to trying to lead others into worshiping false gods.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God brought them out of Egypt, and that their faithfulness to Him was the foundation of their life as a nation. This law deals with the extreme case of someone who drew others into idolatry. Many scholars see here a protection for the identity of the covenant people. We should read it in its historical context, not as a model for today.

Today we can take seriously whatever pulls us away from God, and lovingly care for those around us so that no one falls into what harms their faith. We can remember who has saved us and stand firm in Him.
exp.30:12:
This verse says that the children of Israel, those who did not yet know God's law, were to hear it and learn to revere and honor the Lord. They were to do this all the days they lived in the land they were about to enter, crossing the Jordan. "Fear" here means holding the Lord in reverence and taking him seriously, not living in terror. The word "know" in the verse is the key to understanding what the children lacked, and the phrase "as long as ye live" points to the whole span of life in that land.

Moses is speaking to the people shortly before his death. He had already written the law and commanded that it be read aloud in public every seven years, at the Feast of Tabernacles. He wanted the new generation, which had not lived through everything in the wilderness, not to forget God in the new land.

For today: faith is not inherited on its own; it has to be taught. We can set aside regular time to read the Bible with our children or with younger people, and talk about it simply.
exp.22:19:
It says that a foreigner could be charged interest on a loan, but an Israelite brother could not. The reason given is that God would bless their work in the land they were about to possess.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He gives them laws for living as God's community. Lending to a poor brother was a way of helping him, not of profiting from his need. With the foreigner, who often borrowed or traded for business, the rule was different. Some understand this as a difference in economic situation, not in the worth of the people.

For today: when someone in your family or your church is in a difficult spot, help them with generosity and without taking advantage of their need.
exp.3:12:
He tells us that God himself made his covenant known to them, that is, his solemn commitment to the people. He commanded them to keep it, and that covenant is summed up in the ten commandments, the Ten Commandments. God wrote them on two tables of stone. The word "declared" means that he made it plainly known, and "perform" means to put it into practice, not just to hear it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, now close to the promised land. He reminds them of the day when God spoke from the mountain amid fire and darkness. They heard his voice, but they saw no form at all. Moses stresses this so that they will obey God and not make images to worship.

For today: God spoke to us clearly, and his Word is not only to be admired, but to be lived. Today you can choose a teaching of the Bible that you already know and put it into practice in your home or at work.
exp.22:3:
This verse gives the reason why the Ammonites and Moabites were not allowed to enter the congregation of the LORD. It says that they did not come out to meet Israel with bread and water when they came out of Egypt, and that Moab hired Balaam, the son of Beor, from Pethor in Mesopotamia, to curse the people. "Hired" means paid for, in exchange for payment.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, now close to the promised land, and reminds them of laws for living as God's people. The texts say that it was Moab who hired Balaam (Numbers 22). Scholars discuss how this restriction was applied, and later Ruth, a Moabite woman, was accepted and became an ancestor of David.

For today: hospitality matters to God, and hostility toward others has consequences. We can generously help someone who is on the way, without doing harm or taking advantage of anyone.
exp.31:13:
This passage describes the abundance with which God fed his people: cow's butter, sheep's milk, tender meat from lambs, rams from the region of Bashan (known for its good livestock), male goats, and the finest wheat. The phrase "the fat of kidneys of wheat" is a poetic way of saying the finest wheat. "Blood of the grape" is the juice of the grape, that is, pure wine.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, in a song addressed to Israel. He recalls how the LORD guided and sustained his people without the help of other gods. But the song also sets up a warning: the verses that follow say that, once they had grown fat, Israel forgot God.

For today: when God gives us blessings, it is easy to trust in them and not in him. Today you can thank him for something specific you have and ask him to keep you grateful and humble.
exp.30:18:
God tells Moses and Joshua to write down a song and teach it to Israel, to put it on their lips. The verse's wording "write ye this song for you" rendered as "write for yourselves" is an older way of saying the same thing. This song will serve as a witness from God against the people, that is, as a reminder of what He had already warned them about.

God speaks near the end of Moses' life. He knows that once the people enter the promised land and live in abundance, they will forget Him and follow other gods. The song (chapter 32) would stay in their memory and remind them that they had been warned in time.

For today: keep God's Word in your memory, perhaps through songs or verses you have learned. In times of comfort or of distress, those truths can bring you back to God.
exp.31:24:
The verse says that judgment will come from every side: outside, the sword will bring death and destruction; inside, in the rooms of the houses, there will be terror. No one will be spared: not the young man, nor the young woman, nor the infant still nursing, nor the old man with gray hairs.

It is part of the Song of Moses, near the end of his life. God himself speaks and warns what would happen if Israel, after receiving so many blessings, turned away from him to follow other gods. These are harsh words, but they were meant to call the people to return and trust in God. Interpreters see here a serious warning, not any delight of God in suffering.

For today: do not take lightly the care of God. If you notice that you are drifting away from him, return soon, with humility and trust in his mercy.
exp.30:29:
This verse says that Moses spoke before the whole people of Israel and recited the song completely, from beginning to end. The phrase about speaking into their hearing means that he spoke so that they would hear it. "Congregation" refers to the gathering of the people, and "song" is a chant or poem.

Moses is near the end of his life. God had told him that the people would turn away from Him after his death. For this reason, Moses gathered the elders and officers to leave them this song as a witness. His purpose was that, when troubles came, they would remember the warning and return to God. The song appears in chapter 32.

For today: we often forget easily what God has taught us. We can keep his word in our memory, perhaps through a verse or a song, so that it stays with us when we are weak or tempted to drift away.
exp.7:12:
This verse describes a time of prosperity: the herds grow, the silver and the gold increase, and everything the person has becomes more. The cattle and the sheep were the main form of wealth in that era. The word for "multiplied" simply means that they grow in number.
