Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them that abundance can bring a danger: thinking they are self-sufficient and forgetting God, who brought them out of Egypt and cared for them in the wilderness. The verses that follow make this clear.

For today: when things are going well, it is easy to stop praying and stop giving thanks. We can take a moment each week to thank God for what we have and ask him how to use it to help others.
exp.8:24:
Moses reminds the people that he fell down before God for forty days and forty nights. "Fell down" means bowing down to the ground in humble prayer. He did this because God had said he would destroy Israel for their sin. "Fell down" is the same as "I fell down."

Moses speaks to the new generation, now close to the promised land. He reminds them that Israel was rebellious from Kadesh-barnea, where they did not believe God. Many understand that here he repeats what happened after the golden calf, and that he tells it so they will not think of themselves as righteous on their own. His prayer that follows appeals to God's mercy and to his promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Today we can learn to pray persistently for others, even when they fail. Intercede for someone you love, without accusing them, trusting in God's mercy.
exp.14:14:
This verse asks the people of Israel to remember their past. They were servants, that is, slaves in Egypt, and God redeemed them, setting them free by paying the price of their liberty. That is why God gives them this command: to treat with kindness the one who leaves servitude.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He repeats the law about Hebrew servants, who were to be set free in the seventh year. When they sent them away, they were to give them generous provision. The reason for the command is memory: Israel knew from experience what it was to live without freedom and to receive the mercy of God.

For today: when you remember how much grace you have received from God, let that make you generous. Think of someone who needs help and share something concrete with them, expecting nothing in return.
exp.4:32:
This verse says that the people are to walk, that is, to live, following everything God commanded them. The promise is that in this way they will have life, things will go well for them, and they will live many years in the land they are about to receive. The verse's "walk" means to live, and a long life means a life that is lasting and secure.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, close to entering the promised land. He has just reminded them of the Ten Commandments and of how the people were afraid at the voice of God on the mountain. Now he asks them to obey without turning aside to the right or to the left. Their obedience would be a response to the God who had rescued them.

For today: God invites us to trust that his ways are good. Today you can choose one concrete step of obedience, such as forgiving, being honest, or setting aside time for his Word, and do it trusting that he cares for your life.
exp.18:7:
It says that if the Lord your God enlarges your territory, just as he solemnly promised your ancestors, and gives you all the land he pledged to give them, then something more will happen (this is completed in the next verse). "Enlarge" means to extend, and "boundary" refers to the territory or its borders. "Swore" indicates a solemn promise.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He had already commanded that three cities of refuge be set apart, where someone who killed another person without intending to could flee. Here he looks ahead: if the land grows, three more cities will be added, so that innocent blood is not shed. It is not certain when or how this was fulfilled in history, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: God cares for justice and mercy even when his people prosper. If we receive more blessings or responsibilities, we should also use them to protect and give opportunity to the vulnerable.
exp.1:23:
God tells the people to get up, set out and cross the Arnon stream. He assures them that he has already handed Sihon, king of Heshbon, an Amorite, and his land over into their hand. The phrase "contend with him in battle" means to enter into combat with him, and "begin to possess it" means to start occupying that land.

Moses recalls what God commanded when the years in the wilderness were coming to an end. Israel was near the promised land. It was an order for that specific moment in their history. According to the text that follows, Moses first sent messengers with words of peace to Sihon.

God often gives us promises, but he also asks us to take the step. Trusting him means moving forward in obedience and seeking peace first, without using this passage to justify violence today.
exp.10:26:
This verse says that the blessing comes to the people if they listen to and obey the commands of God. The words quoted from the source are not in the verse you read, so I have left them out. In the Bible, the idea of listening includes paying attention and acting on what is heard, not just hearing it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He sets two paths before them: blessing or curse. He reminds them that God brought them out and cared for them, and he wants them to respond with trust and obedience. Afterward the ceremony on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal will take place.

Today we can remember that listening to God is more than knowing what the Bible says. It is deciding to put it into practice, even in small things. You might choose one clear command of God today and obey it with confidence in his goodness.
exp.2:12:
Moses says that he gave to the half tribe of Manasseh the rest of Gilead and all of Bashan, which had been the kingdom of King Og. He also mentions the region of Argob, within Bashan. That area was known as "the land of giants," since the Rephaim, a people of great stature, had lived there.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, near the end of the forty years in the desert. He reminds them how God gave them victory over Og and Sihon, and how the lands east of the Jordan were divided among Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh. He wants them to remember God's faithfulness before entering Canaan.

For today: God keeps what He promises, even when the obstacles seem enormous. Remembering how He helped us in the past strengthens our confidence to face the "giants" of today, such as fear or debt, and encourages us to give thanks.
exp.0:22:
Moses says that the people's proposal seemed good to him, so he chose twelve men, one from each tribe. "The saying" means "what they said" or "the proposal." "Men" refers to men, that is, adult males. Their task was to explore the promised land.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel almost forty years later, near the promised land, and recalls what happened at Kadesh-barnea. God had already told them to go up and not be afraid, but the people asked to send spies ahead. Moses agreed to the plan. Later, most of them gave a report that caused fear. Here we see the beginning of that story.

For today: planning and seeking information is not wrong, but it should not replace trust in what God has already said. Before deciding, ask yourself whether you are looking for facts so you can obey better, or for excuses to doubt.
exp.25:2:
This verse says that the Israelite was to present himself before the priest who was serving at that time. There he would make a declaration. The phrase "I profess this day" means that he publicly declares and admits that God has kept his promise. The word "sware" means that God made the promise with a solemn commitment. "Our fathers" refers to the ancestors, such as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He explains how to offer the firstfruits, that is, the first fruits of the harvest, carried in a basket to the place that God would choose. By saying these words, each person remembered that the land was a gift from God and not merely the fruit of their own effort.

Today we can pause to acknowledge out loud what God has done for us. Before asking for more, give thanks in your own words for a promise he has already fulfilled in your life.
exp.14:21:
This verse says that the firstborn animal that had some defect was not offered on the altar, but was eaten at home, within the towns of the people. Everyone could eat it, both the ceremonially unclean person and the clean one, just as one eats the meat of a roebuck or a hart, game animals that were not offered in sacrifice. The "gates" mentioned in the verse refer to the town gates, the places where the people lived and gathered within their settlements.

Moses speaks to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that what is given to God must be the best, without defects. But the animal with a defect was not wasted: it served as food and was shared. Then follows the prohibition against eating blood.

For today: let us give God the best of our time, affection and resources, not the leftovers. And let us generously share what we have, without wasting or excluding anyone.
exp.0:42:
Moses reminds the Israelites what happened when he warned them not to attack. He tells them that they did not listen to God, that they rebelled against his command, and that, full of pride, they went up into the hill anyway.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. Earlier, out of fear, they had refused to enter the promised land. Then, feeling guilty, they wanted to fight on their own, but God had already said not to do so because he would not go with them. They were defeated by the Amorites.

Today: obeying God is not just doing something good, but doing it when and how he asks. Before making a decision, ask God and listen to his Word with humility, without letting yourself be carried away by pride or haste.
exp.31:51:
God tells Moses that he will be able to see the promised land from afar, but he will not enter it. "You shall see the land before you" means that he will look at it face to face. The land is the one God gives to the children of Israel.

God speaks on Moses' last day, shortly before his death on Mount Nebo. The previous verse gives the reason: at Kadesh, by the waters of Meribah, Moses and Aaron did not honor God as holy before the people. Scholars understand in different ways exactly what the failing was, but the text calls it a lack of trust and of honoring God.

For today: God is merciful, but actions have consequences, even for his most faithful servants. We can humbly accept what God permits, and trust that his plan continues, even when we do not live to see everything fulfilled.
exp.1:24:
This verse says that God, from that day, would begin to make the peoples of the whole earth feel dread and terror before Israel. They would hear about Israel's reputation, tremble, and be in anguish because of Israel's presence. The words "before you" in the wording of the verse point to being in Israel's presence. The phrase "This day will I begin" shows that this was a process only just started.

The one speaking is God, addressing Israel through Moses. After nearly forty years in the wilderness, the people were about to enter the promised land. God encourages them to face Sihon, the Amorite king. It is interesting that Moses, even so, first offers him words of peace (v. 26).

For today: when you face a great challenge, remember that God goes before you and prepares the way. Trust in Him, take your steps with courage, and seek peace before conflict.
exp.26:7:
It says that, upon crossing the Jordan, the people were to write all the words of the law on stones, and to do so "very plainly," that is, in a way that is clearly legible and easy to understand. Earlier, verse 2 speaks of covering those stones with lime.

Moses speaks, together with the elders of Israel, to a new generation that was about to enter the promised land. The stones would be a public reminder of the covenant with God, placed beside the altar where they would offer sacrifices and rejoice before Him. It is not known with precision how the text was carved or written, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: God wants His Word to be understood, not kept hidden. Make a habit of reading the Bible attentively and explaining it simply to your family, so that others can understand it too.
exp.11:28:
It says that when God has removed from the way the nations who live in the promised land, the people of Israel will take possession of it and live there. The verse of the word that meant ruined or laid waste is not needed here, since that word does not appear in the verse. For the idea of receiving the land as an inheritance, it means they would receive it as a gift and not by their own strength. Living there means dwelling in the land.

Moses is speaking near the end of his life. He is preparing Israel before they enter Canaan. He reminds them that God will act on their behalf, but that they must obey him. The verse is the opening of a warning: do not copy the religious practices of the peoples who will be displaced.

For today: when God gives us a new stage, such as a job, a home, or a community, it is easy to imitate the customs around us without thinking. Before adopting something, ask yourself whether it pleases God, and thank him for what you receive as his gift.
exp.13:27:
This verse says that every three years the Israelite was to set aside the whole tithe of what he produced that year and store it in his own town. "Tithe" is the tenth part of the harvest or of earnings. "Produce" means the fruits of the land and of labor.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. In the other years, the tithe was brought to the place of worship. But every third year it stayed at home to help the Levites, who had no land, and also foreigners, orphans, and widows.

For today: God joins worship with compassion. You might set aside in an orderly way a portion of your income to help someone in need near you, such as a widow, an immigrant, or a family in difficulty, and do so with joy.
exp.15:6:
Moses says that the Passover lamb must be roasted and eaten in the place that God chooses, not in just any town. To "roast" is to cook over fire, and the phrase about returning to your home means going back to your house. Some understand that the "morning" is the one after the night of Passover, and others that it is at the end of the feast. The text does not fully make this clear.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the Passover celebrates the departure from Egypt. By asking for one single place to worship, he teaches them that the feast belongs to the whole people and that God is the one who sets how they are to draw near to Him.

For today: God calls us to gather to remember his work, but also to return home. May your time with him, alone and with other believers, renew you so that you live your routine with gratitude.
exp.27:9:
This verse says that all the nations of the earth will notice that the people of Israel belong to God. The phrase "the name of the Lord is called upon you" means that God acknowledges them as his own, like someone who puts his family name on his household. "They shall be afraid of you" here speaks of respect and admiration, not of terror.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains the blessings that would come if they obeyed God and walked in his ways. That visible blessing would serve as a testimony before the other peoples. The verse is tied to that condition of obedience.

For today: those of us who follow Christ bear his name, and people are watching us. Today you can live with honesty, kindness and faithfulness at your work and at home, so that others see that God is at work in your life, without showing off or seeking applause.
exp.27:6:
It says that God will cause the enemies who attack Israel to be completely defeated. The phrase about the enemies being broken up is explained as meaning they will be beaten and thrown into disorder. They come against the people by one road, well organized, but they flee by seven, that is, in total confusion. "Seven" here expresses something complete.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them the blessings of the covenant if they obey God. This promise was given to Israel as a nation, within that covenant, and it is not an automatic guarantee of victory in every conflict.

Today we can learn that God cares for his people and that obedience is the way to live trusting in him. In the face of life's fears and opposition, we can pray, keep doing what is right, and rest in the knowledge that God is our refuge.
exp.26:0:
This verse says that Moses, together with the elders of Israel, gave a command to the people. He asked them to keep all the commandments that he was giving them that day. In this verse, "commanded" is the word for giving a firm order. It is interesting that here Moses does not speak alone, but is accompanied by the leaders of the people.

Moses is speaking almost at the end of his life, close to the entrance to the promised land. The people are preparing to cross the Jordan, and Moses reminds them that their life there must be guided by the law of God. The elders accompany him as witnesses and support, showing that this was a commitment of the whole community.

For today: obeying God is not only something personal; it is also strengthened in community. Seek out people of faith who encourage you to live out the Word with constancy, and encourage them too.
exp.1:4:
He says the Israelites were not to stir up or fight against the descendants of Esau. God would not give them so much as a foot's breadth of that land, because he had already given it to Esau as an inheritance. "Seir" is the mountainous region where the Edomites lived.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness and reminds them of what God commanded them. The Edomites were their kinsmen because they descended from Esau, the brother of Jacob. God had a plan for Israel, but he also respected what he had given to others.

For today: you do not need to take from others what is theirs in order to receive what God has for you. Trust his provision, respect the boundaries of others, and avoid envy and unnecessary conflict.
exp.3:42:
This verse names the three cities that Moses set apart east of the Jordan. Bezer was in the wilderness, in the plain country, and belonged to the tribe of Reuben. Ramoth, in Gilead, belonged to the tribe of Gad. Golan, in Bashan, belonged to the half-tribe of Manasseh. These were cities of refuge. "Unintentionally" means without meaning to, by accident.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of God's law. These cities protected anyone who caused a death without intent, so that an angry avenger would not kill them and justice could be carried out calmly. In this way both life and justice were cared for.

For today: God cares about justice and also about mercy. We can imitate him by not judging in haste, by listening before we condemn, and by offering a safe place to someone who has made a mistake and needs help to get back on their feet.
exp.26:1:
It says that when the Israelites crossed the Jordan River and entered the land God was giving them, they were to set up large stones and cover them with lime. "Plaister" means to cover or coat a surface. "Pass over" means to cross. The lime formed a smooth, white layer, useful for writing on it.

Moses speaks, together with the elders of Israel, shortly before he dies. The people were about to enter Canaan, and Moses wanted them always to have the words of God's law in view. The verses that follow say that on those stones they would write the law, and that they would set them up on Mount Ebal. Scholars do not fully agree on how the writing was done, but the purpose is clear.

For today: God wants his Word to be clearly visible in our lives. We can choose a verse and put it where we see it every day, as a sign that we want to obey him.
exp.9:8:
This verse says that the tribe of Levi did not receive a territory of its own like the other tribes of Israel. The word "inheritance" in the verse refers to the land or possession that is left to one's children. Instead of land, the Levites received God himself as their portion, just as he had promised them.

Moses speaks to the people and reviews their history after the sin of the golden calf. He explains that God set the Levites apart to care for the ark, to serve before him, and to bless in his name. Their lives would depend on serving God and not on owning fields. Some scholars see in this passage a brief note within the account of the journey.

For today: even though most of us are not priests, we can learn to find our main security in God and not only in money, a house, or a job. When material things are lacking or change, he remains our portion.
exp.19:2:
This verse says that, before the battle, the priest speaks to the people and asks them for four things: that their hearts not be softened (that they not lose courage), that they not be afraid, that they not be alarmed (that they not panic), and that they not be discouraged (that they not lose their strength) in the face of the enemy. The word translated here as "approach" means "gather together to fight."

These words are part of the instructions Moses gives Israel before they enter the promised land. Before fighting, the priest would remind the people that God, who brought them out of Egypt, was going with them. The enemy might be more numerous and have horses and chariots, but Israel's confidence had to rest in God, not in their own strength.

For today: when you face a situation that frightens you, remember what God has already done for you and ask him to give you calm. You do not depend only on your own strength, and his presence helps you keep going with courage.
exp.0:36:
Moses says that God was also angry with him because of the people. He told him that he too would not enter the promised land.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, near the land, when he recalls the rebellion at Kadesh-barnea, where the people refused to trust God. Other passages, such as Numbers 20, connect Moses' prohibition with what happened at Meribah, when he struck the rock. Here he emphasizes how the people's attitude affected him too. Interpreters explain this in different ways.

For today: our decisions and attitudes influence others, especially in family, church, and work. Let us ask God for faith and humility to obey him, and if we experience painful consequences, let us trust that his plan goes forward.
exp.14:19:
It says that the firstborn male of the cattle and of the sheep, already set apart for God, was to be eaten each year in the presence of the Lord. The whole household ate it, in the place God would choose to worship him. The sentence about the old word and the old phrase is removed, since those words do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them how to live grateful to God. Just before, he speaks of freeing servants generously, and here he commands them to give God the first and to celebrate it together as a community. Many understand that it was a feast of thankfulness, not only a duty.

For today: set aside time to thank God as a family or with your church. You can share a meal, remember God's blessings from the year, and give him the first and the best, not what is left over.
exp.21:19:
This verse continues a legal case. A husband accuses his newly married wife of not having been a virgin. The case is being discussed here: what would happen if the accusation were true and no proof of virginity were found.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, reminding them of the laws that would govern their lives in the promised land. This law was meant to restrain false accusations, since it punished the man who slandered without cause. It also reflected how seriously Israel regarded the marriage covenant and purity. The penalty was harsh, typical of that time and culture. Some scholars debate how it was applied and what kinds of evidence were accepted.

Today we learn that accusing someone requires truth and responsibility. Before speaking ill of another person, let us think about the harm our words can cause. Let us guard our words and always seek justice with mercy.
exp.15:19:
This verse says that the people must pursue justice with earnestness. Repeating "justice, justice" emphasizes that it is something very important. "Follow" means to pursue, to go after it with effort. "That thou mayest live" means "so that you may live." "Inherit" means to receive as an inheritance the land that God was giving.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just commanded that they appoint honest judges in every city, without favoritism or bribes. Then he warns against imitating the worship practices of the neighboring peoples. In this way he joins justice with loyalty to God.

For today: practice justice in small things, such as your work, your family, or your business. Do not lie to come out ahead, do not favor anyone out of sympathy, and treat everyone with the same honesty.
exp.8:6:
This verse asks the people to remember and not forget something important: they angered God in the wilderness. From the day they left Egypt until they arrived at this place, they were rebellious against Him. "Provoke to wrath" means to make someone angry, and the old spelling of the word is "provoke" itself, which appears in the verse as "provokedst."

Moses speaks almost at the end of his life, before Israel enters the promised land. He has just told them that God gives them that land not because they are good, but because of the wickedness of the nations living there and because of the promise made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Now he reminds them of their record in order to strip away any pride.

For today: when God blesses us, remembering our failures keeps us humble. We can thank Him for His grace instead of thinking we deserve what we have.
exp.4:14:
This verse reminds the people that they were slaves in Egypt and that God brought them out of there with great power. The phrase about a strong hand and an outstretched arm describes the strength of God in rescuing them. That is why God commanded them to keep the Sabbath, the day of rest.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, before they enter the promised land. He repeats the Ten Commandments to them. Here the reason for rest is liberation: no one was to work without stopping, neither servants, nor foreigners, nor animals. Whoever had been a slave was to remember what it means to be unable to rest.

For today: God freed us from burdens and does not want us to live exhausted. Set aside time to rest and to thank him. If you are a boss or have people under your care, look after their rest too.
exp.18:12:
It says that when someone deliberately kills another person and takes refuge in a city of refuge, the judges must not feel pity for him. The phrase about pity is explained as meaning that no compassion should be allowed to bend justice. In this way Israel is cleared of the guilt of blood that was shed unjustly, and things will go well for them.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The cities of refuge protected the one who killed by accident, but not the murderer who had planned the crime. God wanted to protect life and keep injustice from defiling the nation.

For today: compassion is good, but it must not be used to excuse wrongdoing. When you face a decision that affects others, seek to be just and honest, caring for the life and dignity of people, even when that costs you.
exp.3:10:
It says that the people of Israel came near and stood at the foot of Mount Horeb (Sinai). The mountain was burning with fire that rose up to the midst of heaven, that is, very high. It was surrounded by darkness, cloud, and thick darkness: a dense cloud and a very dark sky. The phrase about coming near is simply the verb for "came near."

Moses speaks to the new generation, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the day God gave his law. He wants them not to forget what their parents lived through, so that they will fear God and teach it to their children.

For today: do not let your experiences with God grow cold. Write down what He has done in your life and tell it to your children, or to someone close to you, so that your faith and theirs stay strong.
exp.23:17:
It says that the people must remember that they were once slaves in Egypt and that God himself set them free. For this reason God commands them to act with justice and compassion. Here "bondman" means a slave, and the phrase "redeemed thee" means that he brought them out of that slavery at a great cost.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He repeats God's law to them. Just before this, he asked them not to pervert justice for the stranger, the fatherless, or the widow, who were people without protection. Their own history of suffering was meant to make them sensitive toward the weak.

For today: when God has shown you mercy, use it as a reason to treat others well. Think of someone vulnerable near you, such as a migrant, an orphan, or a widow, and help them with something concrete this week.
exp.1:25:
Moses tells that he sent messengers to Sihon, king of Heshbon, from the wilderness of Kedemoth, a place east of the river Arnon. The messengers carried words of peace, that is, a friendly message and not a threat. The verse ends with "saying," and the message continues in the next verse.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, before they enter the promised land, and reminds them of what happened. God had said that Sihon would be delivered into their hand, yet Moses first offered a peaceful passage anyway. Some readers see mercy here; others see an opportunity that made clear Sihon's responsibility when he rejected it.

For today: when facing a conflict, try first to speak with respect and seek peace. You can trust God and, at the same time, choose words that build up rather than wound.
exp.0:38:
It says that the little children of Israel, the ones the people had said would become plunder in war, and who still could not tell good from evil, would be the ones who entered the promised land. God would give it to them, and they would receive it as an inheritance. The word "little ones" refers to young children, and the phrase "should be a prey" means "as spoils of war."

Moses speaks to the people in the desert, near the end of his life, and recalls what happened at Kadesh-barnea. The adults did not trust God and were afraid to enter Canaan, so that generation did not go in. Even so, God kept his promise through the next generation. Moses also mentions that he himself would not enter.

For today: God can carry out his plans even when we fail. When fear or doubt holds us back, we can return to trusting him, knowing that he cares even for those we worry about most, such as our children.
exp.7:11:
This verse is part of a warning that begins in verse 11.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, after forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them that the abundance they will receive is a gift from God. His concern is that comfort will lead them to forget the one who gave it to them.

For today: when things are going well, it is easy to stop praying and giving thanks. A good habit is to thank God each day for what you have, food, shelter and work, and to remember that all of it comes from his generous hand.
exp.0:15:
Moses reminds the judges of Israel what he commanded them. He asked them to listen carefully to cases between brothers and to judge fairly, whether the dispute was between two Israelites or involved a foreigner. The word "hear" in this verse means to listen attentively, and the foreigner is the stranger who lived among them.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, before entering the promised land. He reminds them that, when they saw how heavy the burden of governing was, they appointed wise leaders to help him. Here he repeats the first instruction he gave those judges: impartial justice, even for someone who was not one of the people.

For today: before you give an opinion or make a decision about a conflict, listen patiently to all sides. Treat with the same justice the people you know and those you do not, without favoritism, because God is concerned with justice.
exp.15:20:
It says that the Israelite was not to plant a grove or cluster of trees of any kind beside the altar that was built to worship the Lord. In the Reina-Valera 1909, the word "grove" translates the Hebrew word "asherah," which can refer to a tree or wooden pole tied to the worship of a Canaanite goddess. Scholars debate its exact form.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He warns them not to mix the worship of the Lord with the religious practices of the neighboring peoples. That is why the next verse also forbids statues, which God detests.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are mixing our faith with customs or ideas that do not honor God. Worshiping him with simplicity and truth is better than decorating our faith with things foreign to his Word.
exp.19:17:
This verse gives the reason for the command given just before it: Israel was to destroy the Canaanite cities completely so that those peoples would not teach them their "abominations," that is, their religious practices that were detestable to God. The phrase "so that they do not teach you" is the same as "so that they do not teach you" in the sense of "so that they would not teach you." The danger was to copy the worship of their gods and in this way sin against the LORD.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land, giving them instructions for war. This command refers only to those specific nations, and the text presents it as tied to their idolatry. It is a difficult passage, and scholars understand it in various ways. All agree that the emphasis is on protecting Israel's faithfulness to God.

Today we do not use violence, but we can take seriously the influences that pull us away from God. It is worth asking ourselves which things, friendships, or habits draw us into sin, and setting wise limits to protect our faith.
exp.21:24:
It says that if a man finds in the field a young woman who is engaged to be married, and he takes her by force and lies with her, only the man must die. "Young woman" is a girl who is young, "engaged" means promised in marriage, and "take by force" means to seize her against her will.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in his instructions before they enter the promised land. In the field, far from other people, no one could come to help the young woman. For this reason the law presumes that she cried out and was a victim, and it declares her free of guilt. All the guilt falls on the attacker, and the text compares this crime to a murder.

For today: God takes the side of the person who has been attacked and does not blame her. We can imitate him by believing those who suffer abuse, caring for them carefully, and insisting that the one responsible answer for his actions.
exp.9:9:
Moses recalls that he went up the mountain again, Sinai (also called Horeb), and stayed there forty days and forty nights, just as he had the first time. God listened to him once more and chose not to destroy the people.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel, who are now close to entering the promised land. He reminds them of what happened after the sin of the golden calf: he interceded for them, and God showed mercy. The verses that follow mention the Levites, and then God commands the people to move forward. The purpose is to show that God forgave them by grace, not because they earned it.

For today: God listens to those who pray for others. Pray with confidence for someone who has failed, and remember that you too live by God's mercy, not by your own merits.
exp.24:5:
It says that the firstborn son the widow has with her dead husband's brother will carry the name of the one who died. So the name of the dead man will not be "put out," that is, blotted out, from Israel.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. This law of marriage to a brother-in-law protected a widow with no children, who was left very vulnerable, and it cared for the family's inheritance and memory. The verses that follow show that the brother-in-law could refuse, though that brought public shame. Scholars debate how it was applied in detail.

For today: God cares for those who are left alone and unprotected. We can ask ourselves who is near us, such as a widow, an orphan, or a relative in need, and help them with concrete commitment, not only with kind words.
exp.7:3:
What it says: Moses reminds the people that for forty years in the wilderness their clothing did not wear out until it was worn, and their feet did not swell from so much walking.

Context: Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He asks them to remember how God cared for them in their trials, with hunger and with manna. Some understand the clothing as a miraculous provision; others take it as a way of saying that God sustained them. The text does not explain how it happened.

For today: Before you worry about what lies ahead, make a list of the times God has sustained you. Remembering His care in the past helps you trust Him and obey Him with gratitude.
exp.23:2:
This verse describes a second case within the same situation. The second husband comes to hate the woman, gives her a certificate of divorce, puts it into her hand, and sends her out of his house. Or else, that second husband dies. "Hate" here means to stop loving or to reject. The "certificate of divorce" is the document of divorce.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law does not command divorce; it regulates a practice that already existed, in order to set limits and give the woman legal protection. The verses that follow forbid the first husband to marry her again. Jesus later explained that God did not intend divorce from the beginning (Matthew 19:8).

For today: let us take marriage seriously and not lightly. Let us care for our spouse with respect, and if there are wounds or separations, let us seek the grace and wisdom of God.
exp.2:7:
This verse sums up the conquest of the lands east of the Jordan River. It says that Israel took the territory of the two Amorite kings, from the Arnon stream in the south to Mount Hermon in the north. The phrase "on this side Jordan" means the eastern side, where Moses was speaking.

Moses addresses the people near the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the recent victories over Sihon and Og, to strengthen their confidence that God keeps what he promises. Some readers feel uneasy about the violence in these accounts; the Bible presents them as part of a particular moment in Israel's history, not as a model for today.

For today: remember the times God has sustained you. Recalling his past faithfulness helps you face the challenges ahead with confidence.
exp.0:11:
Moses asks how he can carry by himself all the troubles that the people brought. The first word in the verse is "cumbrance," which means the trouble and weight of looking after so many people. "Burden" means the responsibilities. "Strife" means the disputes and conflicts between people.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land, and he recalls what happened in the wilderness. God had multiplied them like the stars, just as he had promised their ancestors. But a people so large brought many conflicts. That is why Moses proposed choosing wise, understanding, and experienced men from each tribe to help him lead and judge.

No one was made to carry everything alone. If you feel exhausted by your responsibilities, ask for help and share the burden with trusted people. Doing so is not weakness; it is wisdom.
exp.9:7:
This verse says that God chose the tribe of Levi for three tasks: to carry the ark of the covenant, to stand before Him to serve Him, and to bless the people in His name. "Separated" means that He chose them and set them apart for a special purpose. "Unto this day" means that this task was still in effect when Moses was speaking.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land, and reviews their history. The parentheses around it recall journeys and the death of Aaron. It is then explained that the Levites did not receive territory, because their inheritance was God Himself. Many scholars see this passage as a reminder within Moses' account.

For today: God calls each person to serve Him with what they have. Ask Him how you can serve others this week, trusting that He is your greatest wealth.
exp.5:16:
This verse calls the people to obey carefully everything God commanded. The words "keep" mean to carry out and to protect. The "commandments" are his orders, the "testimonies" are what God declared about himself and his covenant, and the "statutes" are his rules for daily life.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God is present among them and that they must not test him, as they did at Massah, when they doubted that he would take care of them. Obedience is presented as a response of trust in a faithful God.

For today: let us not treat the Word of God as optional. We can choose a specific teaching from the Bible and put it into practice this week, for example forgiving, telling the truth, or helping someone. Obeying is not a way to earn God's love, but a way of living that trusts in him.
exp.5:18:
It says that if the people obey God, He himself will drive out all their enemies from before them. The phrase "to cast out" means to drive out or push back. And "as the Lord hath spoken" reminds us that this is a promise God had already made before.

Moses speaks to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that obeying the commandments is tied to possessing that land. Notice that the victory is presented as the work of God, not only of the people's own strength. The conquest of Canaan is a subject that many scholars debate, and it is best read within its historical context and the whole biblical account.

For today: when we face struggles, we can trust that God keeps what He says, and respond with simple, daily obedience, without relying only on our own strength.
exp.26:22:
This verse says that whoever has sexual relations with his mother-in-law falls under a curse. The phrase "lieth with" is an old way of saying to have intimate relations. All the people respond "Amen," which means "so be it," and by doing so they accept that this conduct is serious before God.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives instructions for a ceremony on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, where the Levites would read curses and the people would say "Amen." These are warnings about sins, many of them committed in secret, and about protecting the family. This list of forbidden relationships appears near other similar laws, such as those in Leviticus 18 and 20.

Today, this verse invites us to care for holiness in the family. We can set clear boundaries, flee from temptation, and respect our relatives, so that our home is a safe and trustworthy place.
exp.2:27:
God tells Moses to give orders to Joshua, to encourage him, and to strengthen him. Joshua will be the one who crosses the Jordan at the head of the people, and the one who will make them receive as their inheritance the land that Moses will only be able to look at from a distance. The word "charge" here means to entrust or commission him, and "encourage" means to give him strength.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel, almost at the end of his life. He tells them that he asked God to enter the promised land, but God said no. Even so, God does not leave him with sadness without purpose: he gives him one last task, to prepare the one who will continue leading the people.

For today: even though we may not achieve everything we desire, we can keep serving. Encouraging and preparing others, in the family, the church, or the workplace, is a valuable way to take part in what God wants to do.
exp.12:5:
This verse speaks of someone very close to you, such as a brother, a son, your wife, or a dear friend ("as your own soul," that is, someone you hold very dear), who invites you in secret to worship other gods. The word "entice" means to urge or push someone to do something.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He had already warned against false prophets, and now he shows that the temptation can also come from the people we love most. God wanted to protect the people He had rescued from Egypt.

For today: do not underestimate an influence that pulls you away from God just because it comes from someone you love. Love that person, but stay firm in your faith, and seek God in prayer and in His Word.
exp.1:17:
God tells Moses that the people of Israel will pass today through the territory of Moab, until they reach a city called Ar. The word "boundary" in the source means border or limit, and the old spelling of "to" is simply the ordinary word "to" in modern English.

Moses is reminding the people of their journey through the desert. About thirty-eight years have passed, and the fighting men of that generation, who did not trust God, have already died. Now a new generation is moving toward the promised land. God shows them the way to go, and in the verses that follow, he asks them to respect Moab and Ammon, since God had given those lands to the descendants of Lot.

For today: God guides step by step and also sets limits. We can trust his direction and learn to respect what does not belong to us, without envy or abuse.
exp.31:14:
This verse says that Israel, called here "Jeshurun" (a affectionate name meaning something like "the upright one"), grew fat and strong, and rebelled like an animal that kicks. Words in the verse such as "waxed fat" and "covered with fatness" describe prospering and being well fed. Dios los bendijo, but they left him and despised their Rock, their secure refuge.

Moses speaks in a song that teaches the people before he dies. He recalls how God cared for them abundantly in the promised land. He warns them that when everything is going well, they could forget God and seek other gods, as the following verses show.

For today: when we are in times of comfort, it is easy to stop praying and stop depending on God. Let us pause to thank him for what we have and remember that everything comes from his hand.
exp.3:47:
This verse marks the boundaries of the land that Israel conquered east of the Jordan. It ran from Aroer, on the edge of the Arnon stream (to the south), up to Mount Sion, which here is another name for Mount Hermon (to the north). This is not the Sion of Jerusalem. The word "bank" means the edge of the water, and the "stream" here refers to a channel or torrent.

The one speaking is Moses. He is on the plains of Moab, about to die, and he reminds the people how God gave them victory over the kings Sihon and Og. He gives them the exact boundaries so that they will remember that this land was a real gift, not a legend.

Today, remembering in detail what God has done for you strengthens your trust. Write down a few specific times when he helped you, and use them to thank him and to face what lies ahead with faith.
exp.26:23:
God condemns the one who strikes another person in secret, that is, in hiding, where no one sees. The word "cursed" means under the judgment of God, cut off from his blessing. The word "neighbour" refers to any person nearby, such as a neighbour or a fellow countryman. The word "smiteth" means to strike or hit, and under the law of Moses it can include an attack that ends in death. All the people answer "Amen," which means "so be it," accepting this warning.

Moses and the elders speak to Israel before they enter the promised land. The Levites would pronounce these curses, and the people accepted them as part of their covenant with God. Many of these sins were committed in secret, which is why the list stresses that God sees what human judges cannot see.

For today: take care how you treat others when no one is watching. God sees hidden harm, whether a blow, a slander, or a betrayal. Live with integrity in private too.
exp.3:11:
God spoke to the Israelites from the midst of the fire on Mount Horeb (another name for Sinai). They clearly heard his voice and his words, but they saw no form or shape at all. The phrase "except" in the verse is the same as "apart from" or "other than" what they heard.

Moses speaks to the people almost forty years later, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of that day so that they will not forget what God said. Later he warns them not to make idols, because they never saw God in any form. What they received was his word, not an image.

For today: God makes himself known above all through his word. Instead of seeking spectacular experiences or images that picture God, we can set aside time to read the Bible and listen to him carefully, trusting what he has said.
exp.1:26:
It says that Israel wants to cross the land of King Sihon, but only along the main road. "I will go along by the high way" means they will not turn aside. "I will neither turn unto the right hand nor to the left" means they will not go to the right or to the left, that is, they will not touch fields, houses or other property.

Moses is speaking, reminding the people what he asked of Sihon, king of Heshbon. He made the request with words of peace, before any fighting. He promised to buy food and water, and only asked for passage to the land God was giving them. The text shows that they first sought a peaceful agreement.

For today: when you face a conflict, try first to speak with respect and clarity. Say what you need, promise to act honestly and keep your word. Even if the other person does not accept, you will have acted with integrity and peace.
exp.5:9:
This verse announces that God is going to bring his people into the land he promised, under oath, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. There they will find large, good cities that they did not build. The phrase "brought in" means taken inside, and "swore" means that God bound himself solemnly to his promise.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter Canaan. He has just taught them to love God with their whole heart and to teach his words to their children. Now he warns them that they will receive blessings they did not earn with their own effort, and that this gift can lead them to forget God.

For today: when you have plenty, remember that much of what you have is a gift. Today, thank God for something you received without having earned it, and think about how you can share it.
exp.3:4:
Moses reminds the Israelites that he taught them the statutes and the commandments just as God ordered him. The "statutes and judgments" are the rules and the just decisions that God gave to his people. The phrase "to possess it" in the verse means to take it as an inheritance. The goal is that they live this way in the promised land.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan, and he will not go in with them. He has just reminded them of the punishment for following Baal-peor and of the life of those who stayed faithful to God. He warns them that obedience is not optional: it is what will set them apart before the other nations.

For today: faith does not stop at knowing what God says, but lives it out where we are. Choose one teaching from the Bible that you already know and practice it this week in your home, your work, or your community.
exp.33:3:
God tells Moses that this is the land he promised with an oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Moses sees it with his own eyes, but God makes clear to him that he will not enter it.

The Lord speaks, and Moses is on the mountain, looking out over the whole land: from Naphtali to Judah, the south, and the valley of Jericho. After leading the people for forty years, Moses cannot enter. Deuteronomy 32:51 connects this with his failure at Meribah, although the text here only stresses that the promise passes on to the next generation. Shortly afterward he dies.

God keeps his promises, even though we do not always see them fulfilled in our own time. You can serve faithfully and leave to others what you will not live to see. Trust that God finishes what he began, and accept with humility your part in his plan.
exp.16:19:
This verse says that the king was to read God's law every day so that his heart would not be filled with pride over his fellow countrymen. It also says he was not to turn aside from the commandments, neither to the right hand nor to the left. If he obeyed, he and his children would reign for a long time in the midst of Israel.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions in case they someday ask for a king. That king would not be an absolute ruler, but someone under the authority of God's word, just like his brothers. Many scholars see here a check against the abuse of power.

For today: if you have any responsibility, whether in your home, your work, or your church, set aside a moment each day to read the Bible with humility. Ask God to remind you that you serve others and are not above them.
exp.17:18:
This verse says that God will hold accountable anyone who does not listen to the words that the prophet speaks on his behalf. The word "require" in the King James wording means to call someone to account or to hold them responsible. In other words, God himself will deal with the one who rejects his message.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel, and he recalls what God told him at Horeb. The people had been afraid to hear God's voice directly, so God promised to raise up prophets who would speak for him. Christians often see here a reference to Jesus as well, although the text has first of all a meaning for the prophets of Israel.

For today: when we hear God's Word, we should not take it lightly. We can open the Bible with humility and ask ourselves what God is asking us to obey today.
exp.8:12:
This verse says that God spoke to Moses and told him that he had seen his people, Israel, and that they were "stiffnecked." The neck is the back of the head or the throat area. An animal with a stiff neck will not let its owner guide it. It is a way of saying that the people were stubborn and rebellious.

Here Moses speaks, reminding the people of what happened at Mount Sinai. While he was receiving the tablets of the covenant, Israel made a cast calf. God tells Moses what he sees and says that the people had turned aside very quickly from the way he had commanded them.

For today: stubbornness closes our ears to God. We can ask him for a heart willing to listen and to correct itself. When someone corrects us with love, it is better to bow the head than to stiffen the neck.
exp.27:25:
It says that, if the people turn away from God, their dead bodies will be left lying out and become food for birds and wild animals. The phrase "thy carcase" is rendered here as "your dead body," and "fray" in the sense of scaring away is simply rewritten as "no one will be there to drive them off or to give burial."

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings for obeying the covenant and curses for breaking it. In the ancient world, being left without burial was a great dishonor. This image shows how serious it is to abandon God: defeat, shame, and abandonment.

For today: God speaks to us with seriousness because he loves us and wants us to live well. This week, prayerfully consider whether there is something you have been ignoring that God is asking of you, and take one concrete step of obedience, trusting in his mercy.
exp.32:11:
He says that Benjamin, whom God calls "the beloved of the Lord," will live at rest and in safety beside God. The Lord will cover or protect him all day long, and he will dwell as one carried with care, close to God.

Moses speaks just before he dies, blessing each tribe of Israel. He blesses Benjamin with the image of a cared-for child. Some think the phrase about dwelling between his shoulders points to Benjamin's land, where Jerusalem and the temple later stood, but this is not certain; others see it only as a picture of God's care.

For today: if you belong to God, you can rest in his care. When you feel fear or pressure today, pause for a moment and pray, remembering that God sustains and protects you.
exp.27:4:
This verse says that God will bless what the people use to store and prepare their daily food. The basket in which the fruits of the harvest were carried is what it refers to. The word translated "store" is an old one, and some render it as a trough or kneading bowl, the container in which bread was mixed. So the verse speaks of never lacking food.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that if they listen to and obey God, their daily life, in the field and in the home, will be under divine care. This is part of a covenant, and not a general promise for everyone in every age.

For today: we can thank God for our daily bread and trust that He cares for everyday life. We can also live generously, sharing what we have with those who are in need.
exp.31:9:
This verse says that God found his people in a desert, an empty, dry and dangerous place. He did not leave them there: he surrounded them with his care, taught them and protected them. "Waste" means land without cultivation or inhabitants, and "the apple of his eye" is the pupil, something very delicate that is guarded with every ounce of strength.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in the song he leaves them before he dies. He reminds them that God chose them as his inheritance and led them out of Egypt through the desert. Many understand the "desert" as that journey; others also see an image of Israel's fragile beginnings as a nation.

For today: when you find yourself in a desert, remember that God does not see you as a burden. He cares for you with tenderness, teaches you along the way and protects you. Respond with gratitude and trust.
exp.13:4:
This verse continues a list of wild animals that the people of Israel were allowed to eat: the deer, the roe deer, the buffalo, the wild goat, and others like them. The word "unicorn" is an old translation; scholars are not sure which animal is meant, and many think it refers to a kind of wild ox or antelope. The phrase "wild goat" means something like a goat of the mountains.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God called them to be a set-apart people, and so he gives them clear instructions about what they could eat. For them, even food was a way of obeying and remembering their identity.

For today: God is interested in the details of our everyday lives. We can ask ourselves whether what we do, eat, or decide each day reflects gratitude and obedience to God, not out of fear, but out of love.
exp.3:37:
This verse says that God brought Israel out of Egypt to drive out before them nations greater and mightier than they were. Then he would bring them into the land of those nations and give it to them as an inheritance, that is, as a possession that is received as a gift and passed down to the children.

The phrase "as it is this day" means "as it is seen on this day," since the promise was already about to be fulfilled.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God spoke to them from the fire, loved their ancestors, and rescued them with great power. He wants them to respond with obedience and faithfulness.

For today: what we have is not due to our own strength, but to the grace of God. This invites us to live with gratitude and trust, and to obey him with humility, knowing that he cares for us.
exp.22:21:
This verse says that no one is obligated to make vows to God. If you decide not to make a promise, you do not commit sin. "But if thou shalt forbear to vow" means "if you choose not to do it," and "vow" refers to making a solemn promise to God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the law about vows: they were voluntary, but once made, they had to be fulfilled promptly. God takes seriously the words spoken in his presence. That is why this verse gives freedom: not making a vow is no fault, but making a vow and not keeping it is.

Today we can think before we say "I promise you" or "I promise God." It is better to speak little and follow through than to promise much out of emotion and fail afterward. Be sincere and careful with your word.
exp.2:3:
This verse tells that Israel took all the cities of the kingdom of Og, king of Bashan. There were sixty cities in the region of Argob, and not one of them was left untaken.

Here Moses speaks, reminding the people of their history before entering the promised land. He reviews the victories that God gave them so that they would trust in Him. These conquests were part of Israel's war at that time, and the text presents them as the work of God. They are hard passages, which many scholars read within their ancient historical context.

For today: remembering how God helped you in the past strengthens your faith in the face of new challenges. Write down those occasions and thank Him for them, so that you can face the future with greater confidence.
exp.12:9:
It says that anyone who tries to lead the people of God away, even through deceit or signs, must be stoned to death. The reason is clear: that person tried to turn them away from the Lord, the God who brought them out of Egypt, out of the house of bondage, that is, out of slavery. To "try" means to attempt, and to "turn back" means to return.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. Israel was a nation under a covenant with God, and idolatry was seen as treason against that covenant and as a danger to the whole community. This law was for that time and that structure of government; Christians do not apply it as a civil rule today.

For today: take faithfulness to God seriously, and guard your heart against voices that would pull you away from Him. Remember what God has done for you, and seek Christ with firmness, always responding in truth and love, never with violence.
exp.8:18:
Moses says he was afraid of God's very strong anger against the people, since they deserved to be destroyed because of their sin. But God listened to him once more.

Words like "fury" and "wrath" are words for a very intense anger, and "because of" means "for the cause of."

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, reminding them of what happened at Mount Sinai when they made the golden calf. He pleaded on their behalf during forty days of fasting. He tells them this so that they will not think they deserve the land because they are good, but so that they will recognize God's mercy.

For today: praying for others, even for those who have failed us, is an act of love. God listens to those who come to Him with humility. We can ask for forgiveness and mercy for our family, our church, and our community, trusting that He hears.
exp.25:15:
This verse says that God commands you today to keep his statutes and ordinances, that is, his laws and rules for living. "Putting them into practice" means carrying them out, not just knowing them. And it asks you to do this "with all your heart and with all your soul," that is, with sincerity and total devotion.

Here Moses speaks to the people of Israel, close to entering the promised land. He has just explained the ceremony of the first fruits and the tithe, where the Israelite declared that he had obeyed. Now he closes that section with a call to obey sincerely. What follows shows that this is a covenant relationship: God and his people belong to each other.

For today: choose a teaching from the Bible that you already know and practice it this week with sincerity, not just to fulfill an obligation, but out of love for God.
exp.22:5:
God tells Israel not to seek the peace or the prosperity of the Ammonites and the Moabites. The word "seek" here means to look out for, or to work toward. "Prosperity" is the word for good, which means their wellbeing and success. The point is not to make alliances with them or to help them grow strong, and this applies forever.

Moses is speaking to the people before they enter the promised land. He explains that these nations did not give them bread or water on the road, and that they hired Balaam to curse them. God turned that curse into a blessing. This is a rule for politics and for the nation, not a command of personal hatred. The verses that follow ask them not to despise the Edomite or the Egyptian.

For today: learn to be hospitable toward someone in need. And do not use this text to justify resentment; Jesus asks us to love our enemies and to pray for them.
exp.1:20:
This verse says that the ancient inhabitants of the land of Ammon were a great, numerous people of tall stature, similar to the Anakim. But the Lord destroyed them before the Ammonites, and these took their place and settled there.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of their journey through the wilderness, reminding them of what happened. God had commanded them not to attack Ammon, because that land had been given to the descendants of Lot. Moses shows them that God had already done something similar with other peoples, even against giants.

For today: God cares for others as well as for us, and he distributes according to his will. We can trust that no giant stops him, and learn to respect what God has given to others, without envy or abuse.
exp.18:11:
It says that if someone deliberately kills another person out of hatred and flees to a city of refuge, he will not go free from guilt. The leaders of his hometown, called "elders," will send for him, take him from that place, and hand him over to the "avenger of blood," the family member responsible for seeking justice for that blood. So the guilty person will pay with his life. The phrase "then they shall deliver him" is simply the verse's own wording, meaning the elders will hand him over.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. The cities of refuge protected someone who killed without meaning to, but they were not to shelter a murderer. The purpose was to protect the land from the guilt of innocent blood.

For today: God takes human life and justice seriously. We can seek forgiveness sincerely, but we must not hide the wrong we do, and we should defend the innocent.
exp.16:13:
This verse speaks of a future time. When Israel has already come into the promised land, taken it, and is living peacefully in it, the people might ask for a king, "like all the nations" around them. The words "when thou art come" and "possess it" are older forms that mean "when you enter" and "when you take possession."

Moses speaks to the people before they cross the Jordan, repeating God's law. Just before this, he speaks of obeying priests and judges. Here God does not forbid having a king, but He sets out rules so that the king is someone chosen by Him, a brother among the people, and one who does not trust in human power. The phrase "like all the nations" shows the danger of copying others.

For today: before deciding something important, ask yourself whether you want it only because everyone else does. Seek God's guidance and do not imitate others without thinking.
exp.28:0:
This verse introduces a new moment: God commands Moses to make a covenant with the people of Israel in the land of Moab. This covenant is in addition to the one God had already made at Horeb, which is another name for Mount Sinai. The word "beside" in the verse means that this covenant comes alongside the earlier one, and the word "make" means that Moses was to set up or agree on this commitment with them.

Moses speaks at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. The generation that came out of Egypt was almost gone, and the Israelites were about to enter the promised land. That is why the covenant is renewed, so that the new generation would take it on as their own. Some understand this covenant as a renewal of the one at Horeb, and others as a complement to it; the Bible does not fully make this clear.

For today: it is not enough to inherit the faith of others. Each person can renew their commitment to God, remembering what He has done and deciding to follow Him sincerely.
exp.11:30:
It says that Israel must not worship the Lord by imitating the customs of the peoples of Canaan. Those nations did things that God hates when they served their gods; they even burned their sons and daughters in the fire. The verse of the old spellings and the word "hates" is left out here, since those words do not appear in the verse your reader sees; "hates" in the verse above means that God rejects such things with strong disapproval.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He warns them that, when God gives them that land, they should not be curious about how those nations worshiped. God wants to be worshiped as He Himself has directed, not according to human ideas or the religious fashions of other peoples.

For today: before adopting a spiritual practice, ask yourself whether it comes from God's Word or only from a popular custom. A sincere heart also needs a faithful guide, and God gives us that guide in Scripture.
exp.31:27:
This verse says that the people of Israel had made foolish and aimless decisions. The phrase "a nation void of counsel" means that their plans were of no use and led to failure. The phrase "neither is there any understanding in them" means that they lacked the wisdom to see what was happening around them.

The one speaking is Moses, in the song he teaches the people shortly before his death. There he expresses how God feels: Israel had turned away from Him and therefore suffered defeats. Some scholars think this verse refers to Israel and others think it refers to the enemy nations; the following context favors Israel more.

For today: before deciding, ask God for wisdom and listen to His Word. Also pay attention to what is happening around you, because God often speaks to us through consequences, and learning to see them keeps us from following paths that lead nowhere.
exp.27:23:
What it says: Instead of rain, God would send dust and ash upon the land of Israel, like sandstorms falling from the sky. This would be a sign of total drought. The phrase "until you are destroyed" means until the people are wiped out or left in ruins.

Context: Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them the covenant with God: blessings if they obey and curses if they abandon it. A heaven that is bronze and an earth that is iron describe a drought without hope. These were serious warnings, given so that the people would choose the good path.

For today: God speaks to us clearly because He wants us to live well. Today we can take His voice seriously, return to Him when we stray, and trust in His mercy, which in Christ is offered to all who repent.
exp.25:18:
It says that God promises to set Israel high above all the nations he has made, so that it receives praise, a good name, and honor. Also, Israel must be a holy people, that is, set apart for God, just as he has said. The word "praise" is what is meant by the old word for praise, and "good name" is the meaning of the word for good name.

Moses speaks to the people at the end of his teaching, when they are about to enter the promised land. They have just been reminded of how God rescued them, and now the passage speaks of a covenant relationship: they choose God and God chooses them. That "height" does not speak of pride, but of being a witness to God before the nations, and it depends on obeying him.

For today: if we say we belong to God, let us live with humility and obedience, so that our honest and kind conduct shows others what he is like.
exp.16:4:
If a person in Israel, man or woman, had worshiped other gods and the matter was clearly proven, the verse commands that they be brought to the gates (the entrance of the city, where judgment was given) and stoned. Stoning was the form of public execution used at that time. The word "strangers" means outsiders, people from other nations.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. Israel lived in covenant with God, and idolatry was seen as betrayal of that covenant, a serious unfaithfulness. Notice that the law required careful investigation and demanded at least two witnesses, to prevent unjust condemnations. This law was for Israel as a nation under that ancient covenant.

For today: God deserves first place in our hearts. Today it is not about punishing anyone, but about examining what things occupy the place of God in our lives, and seeking the truth with justice before judging others.
exp.2:6:
It says that the people of Israel kept all the livestock and the goods they found in the cities they had defeated. "Spoil" refers to the valuable things taken when winning a war.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life. He reminds them of the victories over Sihon and Og, kings east of the Jordan, before they enter the promised land. He presents those conquests as the work of God, and his purpose is to encourage them to trust Him. The text also mentions the total destruction of those cities, which is very harsh. Scholars interpret it in different ways, and it is best read within its specific historical moment.

For today: remember with gratitude how God has sustained you in the past. That strengthens your trust for the challenges ahead, and it helps you receive what you have as a gift, not as your own merit.
exp.1:31:
This verse tells how King Sihon came out with all his army to meet Israel and fight at a place called Jahaz (Jahaza). The phrase "came out against us" means that he came out to oppose us. It was not a meeting of peace but a battle.

The one speaking is Moses, who reminds the new generation of Israel of their history before entering the promised land. Israel had asked for peaceful passage, but Sihon refused. The text says that God hardened his spirit, and this has been understood in several ways: as a judgment on a king already opposed to God, or as the biblical way of saying that God governs even human decisions. The verses that follow include a total destruction, something difficult that we must read with humility.

For today: Moses recalled what had been experienced in order to strengthen trust in God. Remembering how God has helped you before can give you courage to face the challenges of today.
exp.3:18:
Moses warns that when you look up at the sky and see the sun, the moon, and the stars, you must not be drawn in or bow down to worship them. The words "lift up thine eyes" and "driven" in the verse are the key points here: the warning is against being pulled toward those heavenly bodies and turned to their worship. The final clause can be understood in several ways: that God gave those heavenly bodies to all the nations to give them light, or that God allowed other nations to look upon them with reverence. Scholars do not fully agree.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that at Sinai they saw no form of God, so they must not make images or worship creation. He wants them to remain faithful to the God who brought them out of Egypt.

Today we can admire the beauty of creation without making it the most important thing. Give thanks to God for what you see, and worship only the Creator.
exp.27:24:
It says that if the people turn away from God, he will allow their enemies to defeat them. They would go out to fight together, "one way," but would flee in disorder, "seven ways," that is, in every direction. "You will be tossed among all the kingdoms" means they would be shaken, scattered, and mistreated among the nations. "Delivered up wounded" means letting them be defeated.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings for obeying the covenant and curses for disobeying it. This verse is part of the warnings, and it aims to make Israel take its commitment to God seriously.

For today: obedience to God is not a burden but a path of protection. When you notice that you are drifting away from him, do not harden your heart; return soon, confess, and ask for his help. God is patient and seeks to restore.
exp.21:27:
It says that if a man finds a young woman who is a virgin and not engaged, takes hold of her, lies with her, and they are discovered, what follows in verse 29 applies. The verse notes that the word for "young woman" means a young girl, and that the phrase "lies with her" means they had sexual relations. Another word here means a woman who is engaged to be married. The text on sexual violence is hard to read, and scholars debate how to understand each detail of this law.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land and repeats God's laws to them. In that society, a young woman who was dishonored in this way risked being left without support or a future. The law aimed to make the man answer for what he had done and to hold him responsible.

For today: God cares for those who have been hurt and expects justice. We can protect the vulnerable, listen to someone who has suffered abuse, and help them find support and justice.
exp.12:14:
It says that if a city in Israel was proven guilty of collective idolatry, it had to be destroyed completely: its inhabitants, its goods, and also its animals. "Without fail" means with no exception and no pardon. "With the edge of the sword" means putting people to death with the sword.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. Israel was a nation with a covenant with God, and idolatry was seen as betrayal of that covenant. Before any action was taken, the matter had to be carefully investigated and confirmed to be true. This is an ancient law for that Israel, and Christians do not apply it as a rule for today.

For today: this passage shows how seriously God takes exclusive faithfulness to Him. Today the response is not violence, but examining our hearts and removing from them whatever takes the place of God, always seeking the truth before we judge.
exp.22:13:
This verse says that God walks in the middle of Israel's camp to protect them and to give them victory over their enemies. For this reason the camp had to be holy, meaning set apart and clean. That way God would not see anything unclean in them and would not turn away from them.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He is giving instructions for when they go out to war.
