The verse before this one commands them to dig a hole outside the camp to cover their waste. It was a rule of order and of respect for God's presence; it also clearly helped health, although the text emphasizes the spiritual reason.

For today: God wants to dwell in the middle of his people and in our daily life. Ask yourself what small or hidden mess you should clean up, such as a habit, an attitude or a debt, so that you can live with more reverence and closeness to God.
exp.24:11:
If a wife, wanting to defend her husband in a fight, grabs the other man in an improper way, by his private parts, her hand is to be cut off. The phrase "thine eye shall not pity her" means that the judge was not to show compassion. "Shame" refers to the private parts.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This is one of the civil laws that regulated community life. It protected dignity and the ability to have children, something very valued in that culture. It is one of the few biblical laws with this kind of corporal punishment, and scholars debate whether it was applied literally or whether it was replaced by a fine, as some later Jewish traditions did.

For today: even when we want to defend someone we love, we cannot do so by violating another person's dignity or body. A good end does not justify means that cause harm.
exp.8:2:
This verse says that Israel must know for certain that God himself will go over ahead of them. He is called "a consuming fire," an image of his power and of his holiness set against evil. "Bring them down" means that he will cause them to fall or leave them without strength. The promise is that God will win, and that the people will take part by driving those nations out.

Moses speaks to them just before they cross the Jordan. The people were afraid of fortified cities and of people who were very tall and strong. Moses reminds them that the victory will not depend on their strength, but on God. Right away he warns them not to think of themselves as better than others.

Today we may face problems that seem too big. This verse invites us to trust that God goes with us, to obey him and to act, and to give him the glory with humility.
exp.15:10:
It says that at the Feast of Weeks the people were to rejoice before God, in the place where He would set His name. And not only the head of the household: also his sons, his servants, the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow. Here a "servant" means a worker of the house, and the Levite was a man from the tribe set apart for the service of worship, who had no land of his own.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This feast came after the wheat harvest, and each person gave a freewill offering according to what God had given him. The following verse reminds them that they were slaves in Egypt, so they were to treat those in need well.

For today: when God blesses you, do not celebrate alone. Invite to your table someone who is lonely or in need, and share generously.
exp.28:12:
This verse says that God wants to make Israel his people and to be their God, just as he had said and as he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. To "establish" you means to make you firm and secure. The phrase "as he hath sworn" speaks of a solemn promise.

Moses is speaking to the people on the plains of Moab, before they enter the promised land. He asks them to renew their covenant with God. Everyone was there: children, women, foreigners, and workers. No one was left out of this invitation, and Moses reminds them that everything rests on God's faithfulness to his ancient promises.

For today: our relationship with God does not rest on our own strength, but on his faithfulness. Today you can respond to him with confidence and obedience, remembering that he keeps what he promises. Take a moment to thank him for this.
exp.24:9:
This verse says that the man who refused to fulfill his duty to his widowed sister-in-law would receive a public nickname in Israel: "the house of him that hath his shoe loosed." "Loosed shoe" means someone whose sandal had been pulled off. It was a mark of shame, a reminder that he had refused to act on behalf of his brother's family.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, near the time they were to enter the promised land. This law of levirate marriage required that, if a man died without children, his brother should marry the widow so that the dead man's name would not be lost and she would be protected. If the brother refused, there was a public act before the elders. Scholars agree that the removed shoe pointed to giving up a right to an inheritance, although the details are interpreted in several ways.

Today we can learn that family responsibilities are not avoided in silence. God cares for the vulnerable, and he calls us not to abandon those who depend on us, but to serve them faithfully and honestly.
exp.16:16:
What it says: God sets limits on the future king of Israel. He must not have many wives, because that could turn his heart away from God. Nor should he pile up huge amounts of silver and gold. "Turn away" means to drift from the right path. "Greatly multiply" means to gather in great quantity.

Context: Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land, reminding them of God's instructions for a future king. Together with the prohibition against multiplying horses, these rules keep the king from trusting in power, pleasure, or wealth. He is then commanded to copy the law and read it every day. Many see here a foreshadowing of the failings of King Solomon, though the text itself only gives the warning.

For today: When you have power, money, or influence, set simple limits for yourself and read God's Word faithfully. In this way your heart will remain loyal and will not depend on what you accumulate.
exp.30:22:
God gives Joshua, son of Nun, a charge: "Be strong and of good courage." He tells him that Joshua will bring the Israelites into the land that God promised them with an oath. And he adds: "I will be with you."

Moses is about to die, and Joshua will be the new leader. Before that, God warns that the people will turn away from Him, and for this reason Moses writes a song to serve as a witness. In the text, the one speaking here seems to be God himself, because he says "I sware" and "I will be with thee." Some read these as the words of Moses, but the preceding context favors God.

When God gives you something difficult to do, your courage does not come from how strong you are, but from the fact that He goes with you. Take the next step by trusting in his promise.
exp.4:25:
This verse is a question that expresses amazement and fear. "All flesh" means every human being, frail and mortal. The people are asking who could hear the voice of the living God, who spoke from the fire, and still remain alive. In other words, they feel small before the holiness of God.

Moses is reminding the people of what happened at Mount Horeb (Sinai). After hearing the Ten Commandments, the Israelites became afraid and asked that Moses speak with God on their behalf. God approved of that attitude of respect, as the following verses say.

For today: draw near to God with reverence and humility, without losing your confidence. Christians believe that through Jesus we can approach Him with confidence, but without forgetting that He is holy. Today, before you pray or read the Bible, acknowledge who God is and listen to Him with an attentive heart.
exp.18:17:
It says that the judges must investigate the case thoroughly. If they discover that the witness lied and falsely accused his fellow Israelite, that witness will be considered a false witness. "They shall make careful inquiry" means they will ask questions and examine the matter with care. "It turns out" or "it becomes plain" is how the word translated as "behold" in the verse should be understood, meaning the truth clearly comes to light.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He is explaining how justice was meant to work. An accused person could not be condemned on the strength of a single word, and the case was brought before God, the priests, and the judges. In this way the innocent were protected and the sin of lying was taken seriously.

For today: before repeating an accusation, ask questions, verify the facts, and do not let yourself be carried along by rumors. And if you are asked to give an opinion or testify about someone, say only what you truly know, because your words can either harm or protect another person.
exp.28:4:
It says that during the forty years in the wilderness, the people's clothing and sandals did not wear out. The word "wax old" that the verse uses means to become worn down or old through use. "Shoe" here refers to footwear in general, such as sandals. God cared for them in a remarkable way.

Moses is speaking to the new generation of Israel, close to entering the promised land. He reminds them of what God did so that they might renew their covenant with Him. Here Moses says "I have led you," speaking on God's behalf. Many of them were children or young people during those years, yet they had seen the signs and still found it hard to grasp their meaning.

For today: Remember how God has sustained you in difficult times, even if you did not notice it at the moment. Write down three specific ways God has cared for you in your life and give thanks for them, trusting that He will remain faithful in what lies ahead.
exp.12:7:
If someone close to you secretly invites you to worship other gods, you must not agree or listen to them. Nor should you feel pity for them, and you must not shield them or hide what they have done. "Consent" here means to agree.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. God had made a covenant with them, and loyalty to Him was the foundation of the nation. This law, part of the framework of ancient Israel, treats idolatry as serious betrayal, even among family members. The verses that follow mention a death penalty, which belonged to that society and that covenant.

For today: do not place any bond, not even the dearest one, above your faithfulness to God. When someone invites you to turn away from Him, be firm and kind, without giving in or keeping your faith silent out of pressure or affection.
exp.5:10:
This verse describes what God would give Israel in the promised land: houses full of good things that they did not fill, wells of water that they did not dig, and vineyards and olive groves that they did not plant. The words "filled" and "eat until satisfied" are explained by the verse itself, which says "when thou shalt have eaten and be full." The sentence is left open and is completed in the next verse.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He reminds them that everything they will receive will be a gift from God, not the fruit of their own effort. For that reason he warns them that, when they live in abundance, they must not forget the One who gave it to them.

For today: when you have food, shelter, work, or peace, pause to give thanks. Much of what we enjoy we receive from others and from God. A grateful heart helps us not to forget this in good times.
exp.13:21:
This verse commands Israel to set apart the tenth part of everything that their sowing produced each year. "Without fail" means it was not optional but something they had to do without exception. The tithe means giving ten percent. The "seed" refers to the grain that was sown, and what the field yielded is the harvest.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they are a holy people to God. According to the verses that follow, this tithe was eaten before God in the place he would choose, so that they would learn to revere him and to depend on him each day.

For today: before you spend what you receive, recognize that everything comes from God. Set aside a portion first for him and for helping others. Do it with gratitude, not out of obligation, and in this way you will learn to trust his provision.
exp.8:10:
This verse says that when the forty days and forty nights that Moses spent on the mountain came to an end, God gave him the two tables of stone. They are called "the tables of the covenant" because they contained the words of the agreement between God and his people.

Here Moses speaks, almost at the end of his life, recalling the people's history. He tells them this so that they will not think of themselves as righteous on their own. While God was giving him the law, the people were already turning away from Him with a cast idol calf.

For today: God speaks to us with clarity and invites us into a relationship of faithfulness. We can set aside time to listen to His Word calmly, and remember that His grace sustains us when we fail.
exp.27:62:
This verse says that God, just as He rejoiced to do you good and to multiply you, will also delight in ruining and destroying you if you turn your back on Him. Here "delight" does not speak of cruelty; it means that God acts with complete resolve, whether to bless or to judge. Being "plucked" means being pulled up by the roots, that is, driven out of the land you were about to possess.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them the blessings for obeying the covenant and the curses for disobeying it. His aim is that they take their commitment to God seriously. Some scholars see here very strong language meant to warn clearly; others see it as a foreshadowing of the later exile.

For today: God takes our relationship with Him seriously. Ask yourself in what area you need to obey Him again, and do it today, trusting in His mercy.
exp.18:14:
This verse says that one person alone is not enough to accuse someone of a crime or a sin, whatever it may be. For a matter to be proven, the testimony of two or three witnesses was required. The phrase about the matter being settled means that the case was made firm. Where the verse mentions a word meaning what someone declares, that refers to what a person states.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them laws so that justice is even-handed and no one is condemned on the word of a single accuser, who could be mistaken or lying. What follows deals precisely with the false witness.

For today: before believing or repeating an accusation against someone, do not rely on just one version. Ask, verify, and listen calmly. In this way you care for the truth and protect the good name of others.
exp.17:10:
This verse follows a list of forbidden practices. "Caster of spells" refers to someone who casts charms or incantations. The one described as "consulting a spirit of divination" is someone who seeks answers from a spirit of divination, a medium. The "wizard" is someone who practices magic or claims knowledge of hidden things. The "necromancer" is someone who tries to speak with the dead to obtain answers.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them not to imitate the customs of the neighboring nations, who sought guidance from hidden things. God wanted His people to trust Him and to listen to the prophets He would send, as the following verses show.

Today we can ask ourselves where we look for direction when we are afraid or doubtful. Instead of turning to horoscopes, fortune-tellers, or attempts to contact the dead, we can pray, read the Bible, and seek counsel from wise believers, trusting that God guides those who seek Him.
exp.11:27:
It says that God wants his people to keep and listen carefully to everything he commands. The reason is so that things may go well for them and for their children forever. "Á" is the old form of "a," which needs no comment for this reader, so that sentence is deleted.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just given them instructions about worshiping God in the place he chooses, with offerings and sacrifices. He reminds them that obedience is not a meaningless burden but a path of blessing for them and for the generations that follow. Then he warns them against imitating the pagan nations.

Today we can ask ourselves not only what seems good to us, but what pleases God. Obeying him in our everyday lives also leaves a good mark on our children and on those who come after us.
exp.19:4:
Before a battle, this verse says, the officers would ask the people who had built a new house and had not yet dedicated it, meaning had not yet begun to live in it. That person was allowed to return home, because he might die in the war and another man would enjoy the house he had built.

This comes from Moses' instructions to Israel before they entered the promised land. First the priest encouraged the people to trust that God would go with them. Then the officers gave these exemptions. Many understand that they showed God's care for ordinary human life and that Israel did not depend only on the strength of its soldiers.

For today: God cares for our real needs and does not ask us to set aside what he himself has given us. We can serve him with courage, but also with wisdom, recognizing our limits and caring for our home and our family.
exp.20:9:
This verse begins a law about war. It says that when Israel goes out to fight against its enemies, and God gives them the victory, and they take prisoners, they must follow certain rules.

Moses speaks to the people in Deuteronomy, shortly before they enter the promised land. He reviews God's law for their life there. This verse opens a rule that protects a captive woman, since it limits what a soldier could do with her. It was a law given in an ancient and harsh world, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: even when we have power over others, God calls us to act with respect, limits, and justice, never with abuse.
exp.29:12:
It says God's law is not on the other side of the sea, as if it were something far away and impossible to reach. No one needs to ask: "Who will cross the sea to bring it to us and explain it to us, so that we can obey it?" Here "represent" means to make known or explain clearly, and "so that" means "in order that."

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God has already given them his commandment and that they can understand it. He takes away the excuse that obeying is too hard or beyond their reach. Right after this, he calls them to choose between life and death.

Today we can stop making excuses like "I don't know enough" or "that is for more spiritual people." God has spoken clearly in his Word. You can start by reading one passage each day and putting into practice one simple thing you understand.
exp.19:0:
It says that when Israel goes out to fight against its enemies and sees horses, chariots, and an army larger than its own, it should not be afraid. The reason is that the LORD is with them, the same God who brought them out of Egypt.

Moses speaks to the people in his final addresses, shortly before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions for war. Horses and chariots were the most feared military force of that time. Moses reminds them that their confidence is not in weapons, but in what God has already done in rescuing them from Egypt.

For today: when you face a problem that seems bigger than you, remember how God has helped you before. Make a list of those occasions and use it to pray with confidence.
exp.19:9:
Deuteronomy 20:10 says that before attacking a city, Israel was to offer it peace. The verse's quoted words and their meanings have been rewritten for the verse your reader sees: "comest nigh" means "come near," "fight against it" means attack it, and "proclaim" means announce or formally offer. First, an offer of a way out without war was made.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan, giving rules for war. The following verses explain that if the city accepted, it came under tribute and service; if not, a siege followed. These instructions are for distant cities. For the nations of Canaan, the text gives harsher rules (vv. 15-18). Some scholars debate how to understand that difference.

For today: before entering a conflict, seek dialogue and reconciliation first. Offering peace first, with humility and clarity, can prevent wounds that later take a great deal of effort to heal.
exp.27:12:
God says he will make his people the head and not the tail, meaning a place of honor and not of humiliation. "Thou shalt be above only" and not "beneath" speaks of standing in a favored position. All of this depends on one condition: obeying the commandments of the Lord, keeping them and carrying them out. The word "ordeno" means "command."

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, just before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: if they obey, blessings will come; if they turn away to serve other gods, curses will come. These promises were given to Israel as a nation under that covenant, not as an automatic guarantee of wealth for every believer.

Today we can learn that obeying God is the wise path, even though it does not always bring visible success. This week, choose a teaching from the Bible that you have neglected and put one concrete step into practice to fulfill it, trusting that God cares for you.
exp.18:18:
It says that if a witness lied in order to harm his brother, the judges must apply to him the same punishment he wanted to fall on the other. The phrase about doing to him what he had planned for his brother means that the punishment is returned to the liar, and the phrase about putting the evil away from among you means cleansing the people of that wickedness.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law protected the innocent in legal cases. A false witness could destroy a life, so he had to face the consequence of his lie. The judges had to investigate carefully, and the punishment would also serve so that others would fear lying.

For today: the truth matters. A lie, a rumor, or a false accusation can deeply hurt another person. Let us try to speak with honesty, not repeat what we have not verified, and defend the one who is wrongly accused.
exp.0:31:
This verse says that, even though the people had seen so many signs of God's care, they still did not trust Him. The word "believe" here means more than accepting that God exists: it means relying on Him and obeying Him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them of what happened at Kadesh-barnea, when they were afraid to enter the promised land. Moses shows them that God had carried them as a father carries his child, and still they doubted. That is why God was angry.

For today: when you are afraid, remember how God has cared for you before. Write down those moments and use them to trust Him today, even when the path looks hard.
exp.31:6:
It says that the people should remember the past and reflect on what God has done across the generations. To do this, they should ask their father and the elders, who will tell them that story. The sentence explaining the quoted word about telling is removed, since it refers to wording not found in the verse above.

Moses speaks to Israel at the end of his life, in a song. Earlier he rebuked the people for their unfaithfulness and for forgetting that God is their Father, who made them and cared for them. Now he invites them to turn their attention to the history of God's faithfulness, which continues in the verses that follow.

For today: ask the older members of your family or your church how they saw God at work in their lives. Listening to them strengthens faith and helps us not to forget his faithfulness.
exp.10:12:
This verse begins a conditional promise. The old wording you may meet elsewhere, which some read as "if you obey," simply means "if you obey" in plain modern terms, and the verse as you see it says "if ye shall hearken diligently unto my commandments." God asks for careful obedience to his commandments, for love toward him, and for service with all your heart and all your soul, meaning the whole person, holding nothing back.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. That land depended on rain, not on great rivers like Egypt. Moses reminds them that God cares for that land, and that its blessing is tied to a life of faithfulness to him.

For today: God is not looking only for people to keep rules, but for a love that shows itself in obedience. Today you can choose one concrete area of your life, such as your work or how you treat your family, and give it to God sincerely, trusting that he cares for you.

sum.1: After years of wandering in the desert, God tells Israel not to attack Edom, Moab, or Ammon, because he has given those lands to their relatives, and to buy the food they need as they pass through. When the rebellious generation had died off, God gave them victory over King Sihon, whom they destroyed.
sum.18: God commands that three cities of refuge be set apart, where a person who has killed someone unintentionally can flee to be protected from the avenger of blood. But a murderer who acted out of hatred must be handed over and put to death. The chapter also orders people not to move their neighbors' boundary markers, and it requires at least two or three witnesses before a charge can be upheld. A false witness is to receive the same punishment he had intended for the person he accused.
sum.21: Moses gave Israel laws for living with care and justice: helping one's neighbor with lost animals and lost belongings, protecting life by putting a railing on the roof, and respecting creation. He also set rules about marriage and sexual purity, defending a woman who had been falsely accused and punishing adultery and abuse.
sum.2: Moses recalls how God gave Israel victory over Og, king of Bashan, and how the land east of the Jordan was divided among the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh. He asks them to help their brothers conquer the rest, and he encourages Joshua to trust that God fights for them. Moses begs to enter the land, but God tells him that he will only see it from the top of Mount Pisgah.
sum.31: Moses sings a song in which he praises God as the faithful and just Rock. He recalls how God cared for Israel, and how Israel forgot Him and turned to other gods. God announces punishment, but also that He will judge His enemies and have compassion on His people. At the end, Moses urges the people to obey the law, and God tells him that he will see the promised land but will not enter it.
sum.9: Moses recounts that God gave him new tablets of the law, which were kept in the ark, and that God listened and did not destroy the people. He then explains that God asks for reverence, love, obedience, and service with all one's heart. God is great and just, and He loves the orphan, the widow, and the foreigner, and for that reason His people must love them too.
sum.24: God teaches Israel to be just and humane. Punishments have a limit (no more than forty lashes), the name of a deceased man's family is to be cared for, and false weights are forbidden. The passage also commands Israel to remember what Amalek did when he attacked the weak, and that his memory is to be blotted out once Israel has rest.
sum.20: Deuteronomy 21 gives laws so that Israel can live justly: a purification ritual when a dead body is found and no guilty person is known, and protections for the captive woman, for the firstborn son of the less-loved wife, and for the body of someone who has been executed. It also commands that a rebellious and stubborn son be punished.
sum.15: Moses reminds the people that they must celebrate three festivals each year before God: Passover, Weeks, and Booths, with joy and with offerings according to how God has blessed them, and including servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows. He also commands that fair judges be appointed who do not accept bribes, and he forbids setting up sacred trees or statues beside the altar.
sum.28: Moses gathers all of Israel in Moab to renew the covenant with God. He reminds them of what God has done for them and warns that if anyone turns away from the LORD to serve other gods, judgment will fall on that person and on the land. He concludes by saying that the secret things belong to God, but the things revealed are for us to obey.
sum.22: God gives laws to keep his people set apart and clean: who was allowed to enter the assembly, how to take care of the camp during war, and not to return a slave who has run away. It also teaches not to charge interest to a fellow Israelite, to keep the promises made to God, and to be fair to one's neighbor.
sum.16: God asks that sacrifices offered to him be without defect, and he commands that idolatry be punished only after a careful investigation and on the testimony of at least two or three witnesses. Difficult cases are brought to the Levitical priests and the judge, and their ruling must be obeyed. In addition, the future king must be chosen by God, must be an Israelite, must not accumulate horses, wives, or wealth, and must read the law every day so that he remains humble.
sum.5: Moses tells Israel to listen: the LORD is the only God, and they must love him with all their heart, soul, and strength. His words are to be taught to their children every day and kept constantly in mind. When they enter the promised land, they must not forget God or follow other gods, but remember how he delivered them from Egypt.
sum.13: Moses reminds Israel that they are children of God and a holy people, so they must live differently from others, including rules about which animals they may eat and which they may not. He also commands them to give a tithe so they can eat it with joy before God, and every three years to share it with the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow.
sum.17: God takes care of the Levites, who have no land of their own because the LORD is their inheritance, and the people give them offerings for their support. God forbids divination, sorcery, and consulting the dead, and promises to raise up a prophet like Moses, whom the people must listen to. A false prophet, whose words do not come true, should not cause fear.
sum.12: Moses warns Israel not to follow anyone who invites them to worship other gods, whether it is a prophet who performs signs, a close family member, or an entire city. God tests them to see whether they love him with all their heart. For this reason he commands them to follow him alone and to remove this evil with severity.
sum.14: Deuteronomy 15 commands that debts between fellow Israelites be canceled every seven years. It instructs people to give generously to the poor without hesitating because of the approaching year of release. It also says that a Hebrew servant is to be set free in the seventh year and sent off with provisions, with the reminder that Israel was redeemed from Egypt. In addition, it orders that firstborn animals without defect be set apart for God, and that the blood must not be eaten.
sum.23: The chapter gives laws about divorce, the care of newlyweds, and respect for loans, for the poor, and for the worker. It commands that wages be paid on the same day, and that each person answers for their own sin. It also calls for justice for the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow, reminding the people that Israel was enslaved in Egypt.
sum.29: Moses says that even if the people are scattered because of their disobedience, if they turn back to God with all their heart, God will have compassion, gather them together, and bring them back to their land. His word is not far away but near, in the mouth and in the heart. For this reason Moses sets before the people life and death, and asks them to choose life by loving God.
sum.7: Moses asks the people to remember how God cared for them and tested them in the wilderness for forty years, teaching them to depend on his word and not on bread alone. Soon they will enter a good and fertile land. He warns them not to forget God or become proud of their wealth, because forgetting him would bring ruin.
sum.19: God tells Israel not to be afraid in battle, because He goes with His people and fights for them. Rules for war are also given: first offer peace, let certain men return home, and take care of the fruit trees. It also commands that the peoples of Canaan be completely destroyed, something that many scholars explain in different ways.
sum.10: Moses urges Israel to love God and obey Him, reminding them of what He did in Egypt, at the sea, and in the wilderness. The promised land depends on rain and God's care, so there is blessing if they obey and curse if they follow other gods. They must teach these words to their children and choose the path of blessing.
sum.3: Moses asks Israel to obey God's law without adding anything to it or taking anything away from it, and not to make idols, because at Horeb they heard only his voice and saw no form at all. He warns them of punishment if they turn away, but promises that God, who is merciful, will receive them back if they seek him with all their heart. Three cities of refuge are also set apart.
sum.27: Moses tells Israel that if they obey God, they will be blessed in every area of life: in their homes, their fields, their harvests, and against their enemies. But if they turn away from God, terrible curses will come, such as disease, famine, defeat, and exile. The central teaching is that serving God with joy and obedience brings life, and abandoning him brings ruin.
sum.0: Moses reminds the people how God told them to leave Horeb and head toward the promised land, and how he appointed leaders to help him guide them. At Kadesh, the people were afraid and refused to obey, so that generation did not enter the land. The lesson is to trust God and obey him.
sum.32: Before he dies, Moses blesses the tribes of Israel, recalling how God came with his law and became their king. To each tribe he asks for protection, strength, teaching, or abundance, according to its place. He ends by saying that there is no one like the God of Israel, his eternal refuge, who gives victory to his people.
sum.30: Moses, now 120 years old, encourages Israel and Joshua not to be afraid, because God will go with them into the promised land. He puts the law in writing so it can be read every seven years, and God warns him that the people will turn away, so he is commanded to teach them a song to serve as a witness.
sum.11: Moses commands that the places of worship and altars of the nations living in Canaan be destroyed, and that God be worshiped only at the place he chooses. There, people are to bring their offerings and rejoice together with their families, not forgetting the Levite. He allows them to eat meat at home, but not the blood. He warns them not to imitate the gods of those nations or to add to or take away from the law.
sum.4: Moses gathers Israel and reminds them that God made a covenant with them at Horeb. He repeats the Ten Commandments to them, which speak of loving only God, keeping the Sabbath day of rest, honoring parents, and respecting one's neighbor. The people, filled with fear, ask that Moses be the one who listens to God, and God commands them to obey so that things will go well for them.
sum.6: Moses tells Israel that, when they enter the promised land, they must not make treaties or intermarry with the nations living there, and that they must destroy their altars and idols so they will not turn away from God. God chose them not because they were great, but out of love and faithfulness to his promise, and he asks them to trust in him and obey him.
sum.8: Moses tells Israel that God himself will go ahead of them to defeat strong nations, but they must not think they are receiving the land because they are righteous. He reminds them of their rebellion, such as the golden calf at Horeb, and of how he prayed that God would not destroy them. Everything shows that the land is a gift from God and a result of his promise.
sum.25: When Israel enters the promised land, they must bring the firstfruits to the sanctuary and remember with gratitude how God delivered them from Egypt. They must also share the tithe of the third year with the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow. God calls his people to obey him wholeheartedly and to be his holy people.
sum.26: Moses and the elders gave Israel this command: when you cross the Jordan, set up large stones with the law written on them, and build an altar on Mount Ebal, and worship with joy before God. Six tribes would stand on Mount Gerizim to pronounce blessings, and six on Mount Ebal to pronounce curses. The Levites would read twelve curses against idolatry, injustice, and secret sin, and the people would respond, "Amen."
sum.33: Moses climbs Mount Nebo, and God shows him the promised land, but he will not be allowed to enter it. There he dies at the age of 120, with his eyesight still good and his strength intact, and God buries him in a place no one knows. Israel mourns him for thirty days, and Joshua, who is full of wisdom, takes his place.
